Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 10, verses 1–2 (part 1 of 2):

Surah Yunus
One hundred and nine verses
Makkan
In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

(p-120) ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. These are the verses of the Wise Book.﴾ ﴿Is it a cause of wonder for the people that We revealed to a man from among them: "Warn the people, and give good tidings to those who believe that they have a firm standing (qadam sidq) with their Lord"? The disbelievers said: "This is indeed a clear sorcerer."﴾ ﴿Indeed your Lord is Allah, who created the heavens and the earth in six days, then established Himself upon the Throne, arranging the affair. There is no intercessor except after His permission. That is Allah, your Lord, so worship Him. Will you not remember?﴾ [Yunus: 3] ﴿To Him is your return, all of you. The promise of Allah is true. He originates creation, then repeats it, that He may reward those who believe and do righteous deeds with justice. As for those who disbelieve, they will have a drink of scalding water and a painful punishment because they used to disbelieve.﴾ [Yunus: 4] ﴿It is He who made the sun a radiance and the moon a light, and determined for it stations, that you may know the number of years and the reckoning. Allah did not create that except with truth. He details the signs for a people who know.﴾ [Yunus: 5] ﴿Indeed, in the alternation of night and day, and in what Allah has created in the heavens and the earth, are signs for a people who are mindful of Allah.﴾ [Yunus: 6] ﴿Indeed, those who do not expect to meet Us, and are content with the life of this world and at peace with it, and those who are heedless of Our signs—﴾ [Yunus: 7] ﴿those, their abode is the Fire because of what they used to earn.﴾ [Yunus: 8] ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, their Lord will guide them by their faith. Rivers will flow beneath them in Gardens of Bliss.﴾ [Yunus: 9] ﴿Their call therein will be: "Glory be to You, O Allah." Their greeting therein will be "Peace," and the close of their call will be: "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds."﴾ [Yunus: 10] ﴿If Allah were to hasten evil for the people as they seek to hasten good, their term would surely have been decreed for them. But We leave those who do not expect to meet Us to wander blindly in their rebellion.﴾ [Yunus: 11] ﴿When harm touches man, he calls upon Us, lying on his side, or sitting, or standing. But when We remove his harm from him, he passes on as if he had never called upon Us to remove a harm that touched him. Thus is made attractive to the extravagant what they used to do.﴾ [Yunus: 12] ﴿And We destroyed generations before you when they did wrong, and their messengers came to them with clear proofs, but they were not going to believe. Thus We recompense the criminal people.﴾ [Yunus: 13] ﴿Then We made you successors in the earth after them, that We may see how you will act.﴾ [Yunus: 14] ﴿And when Our clear verses are recited to them, those who do not expect to meet Us say: "Bring a Qur'an other than this, or change it." Say: "It is not for me to change it on my own accord. I follow only what is revealed to me. Indeed, I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a tremendous day."﴾ [Yunus: 15] ﴿Say: "If Allah had willed, I would not have recited it to you, nor would He have made it known to you. I lived among you a lifetime before it. Will you not reason?"﴾ [Yunus: 16] ﴿Who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against Allah or denies His signs? Indeed, the criminals will not succeed.﴾ [Yunus: 17] ﴿They worship, besides Allah, what neither harms them nor benefits them, and they say: "These are our intercessors with Allah." Say: "Do you inform Allah of what He does not know in the heavens or on the earth?" Glory be to Him, and exalted is He above what they associate with Him.﴾ [Yunus: 18] ﴿Mankind was but one community, then they differed. Had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord, the matter between them would have been decided concerning that over which they differ.﴾ [Yunus: 19] ﴿They say: "Why has a sign not been sent down to him from his Lord?" Say: "The unseen belongs only to Allah, so wait; indeed, I am with you among those who wait."﴾ [Yunus: 20] ﴿And when We let the people taste mercy after adversity has touched them, behold, they have a scheme against Our signs. Say: "Allah is swifter in planning." Indeed, Our messengers record what you plot.﴾ [Yunus: 21] ﴿It is He who enables you to travel on land and sea, until when you are in ships and they sail with them by a favorable wind, and they rejoice in it, a violent wind comes upon them, and waves come to them from every place, and they think they are encompassed. They call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion: "If You deliver us from this, we will surely be among the grateful."﴾ [Yunus: 22] ﴿But when He delivers them, behold, they commit tyranny on the earth without right. O mankind, your tyranny is only against yourselves. It is the enjoyment of the life of this world. Then to Us is your return, and We will inform you of what you used to do.﴾ [Yunus: 23]

Al-qadam (precedence): Al-Layth and Abu al-Haytham said: al-qadam is precedence (al-sabiqa). Dhu al-Rummah said:
"You are a man from the household of the Dhu'aba clan, for whom there is a known precedence and glories."
Abu 'Ubayda and al-Kisa'i said: every precedent in good or evil is a qadam. Al-Akhfash said: it is precedence in sincerity, as in the words of Hassan:
"For us is the high precedence toward you, and behind us follow those who came first in obedience to Allah."
Ahmad ibn Yahya said: it is everything good that you have sent forward. Ibn al-Anbari said: it is a deed that is sent forward, in which there is no delay or slowness.

Al-murur (passing): It is passing beyond a thing and crossing over it. You say: "I passed by Zayd (marartu bi Zayd)," meaning I went beyond him. Al-mirrah is strength, and from it comes ﴿possessor of strength﴾ [al-Najm: 6]. Marra al-habl means he strengthened the rope. From it is the hadith: "Charity is not lawful for the wealthy, nor for one who has sound strength." Al-'asif is the severe one; it is said: "the wind blew violently (asafat al-rih)." A poet said:
"Until, when a violently shaking wind blew, in which there was a cloud-column, and thunder whose voice is a roar."
And a wind "a'safa" (blew hard). A poet said:
"Every violent, foolish storm-wind swooped upon it, having no reason in its mind."
Abu Tammam said:
"Indeed, when the winds blow violently, they snap the stalks of Najd and do not regard the thorny shrubs."

Al-mawj (waves): It is what rises from the water when the wind blows. It is called mawj because of its agitation.

* *

﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. These are the verses of the Wise Book.﴾ ﴿Is it a cause of wonder for the people that We revealed to a man from among them: "Warn the people, and give good tidings to those who believe that they have a firm standing with their Lord"? The disbelievers said: "This is indeed a clear sorcerer."﴾ (p-121) This surah is Makkan except for three verses, which were revealed in Madina, beginning with ﴿If you are in doubt﴾ [Yunus: 94] to the end. This is what Ibn 'Abbas said. Al-Kalbi said: except His saying ﴿Among them are those who believe in it, and among them are those who do not believe in it﴾ [Yunus: 40], for it was revealed concerning the Jews in Madina. Some said: about its first part, approximately forty verses were revealed in Makka, and the rest was revealed in Madina. Al-Hasan, 'Ata' and Jabir said: it is entirely Makkan. Its occasion of revelation: the people of Makka said: "Allah did not find a messenger except the orphan of Abu Talib," so it was revealed. Ibn Jurayj said: Quraysh were amazed that a man from among them should be sent, so it was revealed. It was also said: when he informed them about resurrection, the return, and the rising from graves, they were astonished.

Its connection to what precedes it: When He revealed ﴿And when a surah is sent down﴾ [al-Tawba: 124] and mentioned the denial of the hypocrites, then said ﴿There has certainly come to you a messenger﴾ [al-Tawba: 128], meaning Muhammad (ﷺ), He followed that with mention of the Book that was sent down and the Prophet who was sent, and that the way of the misguided, their followers, and their polytheists is one in denying the divine books and the one who brought them. Since the mention of the Qur'an preceded the mention of the Messenger at the end of the surah, it likewise came at the beginning of this surah, so the mention of the Book preceded the mention of the Messenger. The commentators' statements on the opening of this surah, which begins with letters of the alphabet, have preceded. Here they mentioned sayings from the commentators, among them: "I am Allah, the All-Seeing"; among them: "I am Allah, the Most Gracious"; among them: that it is composed of these and of "Ha-Mim" and the nun of al-Rahman. So the Ra is part of the letters of al-Rahman, separated. Among them also: "I am the Lord," and other things. The apparent meaning is that "tilka" (those) remains in its proper usage, because the thing referred to is distant. Mujahid and Qatada said: by "tilka" He refers to the earlier books, the Torah, the Gospel and the Psalms, so the verses are the stories described in those books. Al-Zajjaj said: it refers to the verses of the Qur'an that have been mentioned. It was also said: it refers to the preserved Book that is written and kept with Allah, from which every book was copied, as He said: ﴿Rather, it is a glorious Qur'an, in a preserved tablet﴾ [al-Buruj: 21–22], and He said: ﴿And indeed it is in the Mother of the Book﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 4]. It was also said: it refers to the Ra and its companions among the letters of the alphabet, meaning: those letters with which the surahs begin, though their words are close, their meanings are far to reach (p-122). They are "the verses of the Book," meaning the Book is recited by them and its words return to them. This is what Ibn al-Anbari mentioned. It was also said: "tilka" is used with the meaning of "hadhihi" (this), and the thing referred to is present and near. This is what Ibn 'Abbas said, and Abu 'Ubayda chose it. It was said: the verses of the Qur'an. It was said: the verses of the surahs mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿And when a surah is sent down﴾ [al-Tawba: 124]. It was said: the thing referred to is the Ra, for it contains the treasures of the Qur'an, and the sciences by which Allah has singled Himself out. It was said: it refers to what the surah includes of verses. "Al-kitab" here means the surah.

Al-hakim (the Wise): It means the Judge, or the one possessing wisdom because it includes it and is connected to it, or the "muhkam" (firmly established), or the one judged by, or the one made a judge. These are sayings. The hamza in ("akana") is interrogative in the sense of denial, because wonder arises from revelation to a human among them with warning and good tidings. That is: there is no wonder in that. It is Allah's custom with the earlier nations: He sent down books to their messengers with glad tidings and warnings through those whom He chose from among them. The subject of (kana) is ﴿an awhayna﴾ (that We revealed), and (ajaban) is the predicate. As for (lil-nas), it was said: it is in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (hal) for (ajaban), because if it had come after, it would have been an adjective, and since it preceded, it became a hal. It was also said: it is related to (ajaban), and it is not a verbal noun but has the meaning of "astonishing," and a verbal noun in the sense of an object may have its complement placed before it, like the active participle in the sense of an object. It was also said: it is an explanation, meaning: "I mean, for the people." It was also said: it is related to (kana), even if it is defective; this does not hold unless it is taken to indicate an event, for if it is purely indicating time, it is not valid for it to be related. 'Abd Allah read: (ajabun). It was said: (ajabun) is the subject of (kana) and ﴿an awhayna﴾ is the predicate, so it is like the saying:
"Its mixture will be honey and water."
This is considered an anomaly. This is the interpretation of al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya. It was also said: (kana) is complete, and (ajabun) is its agent, and the meaning is: wonder arose among the people because We revealed. This interpretation is good. The meaning of ﴿lil-nas ajaban﴾ is that they made it for themselves an object of amazement, which they marvel at, and they set it up as a banner toward which they direct their mockery and denial. Ru'ba read ﴿ila rajulin﴾ with the jim vowelless. This is a Tamimi dialect in which they vowel-reduce a form, like: sab'un and 'adhdun for sabu'un and 'adhudun. Since warning is general, its object, which is "the people," is general. Good tidings are specific, so its object is specific, which is "those who believe." As for ("an andhir"), "an" is either explanatory or the light form of the heavy "anna," originally meaning that the matter is "we said: warn the people," as al-Zamakhshari said both of them. It is also possible that it is the "an" that is a verbal particle with a binary form, not the light form of the heavy, because it is connected to the perfect, the imperfect and the imperative, and here it is connected to the imperative, and with it a verbal noun is formed, whose estimate is: "by the warning of the people." This aspect is better than the explanatory, because the Kufans do not accept that "an" can be explanatory, nor the light form of the heavy, since that would require deleting its subject and implying its predicate, which is the saying; thus deletion of both subject and predicate would be combined. Also, grounding is better than claiming deletion through lightening.

﴿And give good tidings to those who believe that they have﴾, that is, that they have. The preposition was deleted. As for ﴿qadam sidq﴾ (a firm standing of truth): Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, al-Rabi' ibn Anas and Ibn Zayd said: it is the righteous deeds of worship. Al-Hasan and Qatada said: it is the intercession of Muhammad (ﷺ). Zayd ibn Aslam and others said: it is the affliction with Muhammad (ﷺ). Ibn 'Abbas and others said: it is the happiness that precedes them in the Preserved Tablet. Muqatil said: a precedence of good with Allah that they sent forward. To this meaning Wadday al-Yaman alluded in his saying:
"What is wrong with you, Wadday, constantly in love-poetry? Do you not fear the nearness of your term?"
"Pray to the Lord of the Throne and take a qadam that will save you on the day of stumbling and slipping."

Qatadah also said: "a sound predecessor" (salaf sidq). ʿAṭāʾ said: "a true station" (maqam sidq). Yamān said: "a true faith" (iman sidq). Al-Hasan also said: "a righteous child whom they sent ahead." It was also said: it is God's advancing of this community in resurrection and in their entry into Paradise, as He said: "We are the last, but the first on the Day of Resurrection." It was also said: it is precedence of nobility (taqaddum sharaf), and from it is the verse of al-ʿAjjaj:

*"He humbled the sons of al-ʿAwwam from the family of al-Hakam,
and they left the kingship to a king of ancient precedence (dhi qadam)."*

Al-Zajjaj said: a lofty rank (darajah ʿaliyah). And it is reported from him: an elevated position (manzilah rafiʿah). From it is the verse of Dhu al-Rummah:

*"To you is a precedence (qadam) that people do not deny,
which with noble ancestry has overflowed upon the sea."*

Al-Zamakhshari said: "a station of sidq with their Lord" means priority, merit, and an elevated position. Since striving and forerunning are done by the foot (qadam), the noble endeavour and the precedence were called a qadam, just as a blessing is called a yad (hand), because it is given by the hand, and a bawʿ (span/reach), because its possessor stretches out with it. So it is said of a man, "He has a qadam in goodness." Its being idafa (annexed) to sidq indicates an increase in excellence and that it is among the great precedences. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: sidq in this verse means righteousness (salah), as you say, "a man of sidq." It is reported from al-Awzaʿi that he read (qidam) with a kasrah on the qaf, as a naming by the verbal noun (tasmiyah bi-l-masdar).

﴿Said the disbelievers﴾: Al-Tabari held that the speech contains an omission indicated by the apparent context, its implied sense being: "When he warned and gave good tidings, the disbelievers said such and such." Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: "Said the disbelievers" may be an explanation of His saying, "Is it a marvel for people that We revealed to a man among them...," meaning: the disbelievers said concerning it such and such.

Al-Jumhur, al-ʿArabiyyan and Nafiʿ read *la-siḥrun* ("this is indeed magic"), referring to the revelation. The rest of the Seven, Ibn Masʿud, Abu Razin, Masruq, Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, Ibn Wththab, Talhah, al-Aʿmash, Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn Kathir, and ʿIsa ibn ʿAmr, with a variant reported from two of them, read *la-sahirun* ("indeed a magician"), referring to the Messenger ﷺ. In the codex of Ubayy: ﴿This is nothing but magic﴾ [al-Qasas: 36]. Al-Aʿmash also read: *ma hadha illa sahirun* ("this is nothing but a magician"). Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: their saying about the warning and good tidings that it is magic arises only because he separated their word and came between a person and his close relative, so it resembled what the magician does, and they assumed it belonged to that category. Al-Zamakhshari said: this is evidence of their inability and their admission of it, even though they were lying in calling it magic. Since their claim concerning what cannot possibly be magic is manifestly corrupt, their statement required no answer, because they knew his upbringing among them in Makkah and his association with them, and that he had no lack of knowledge. Moreover, the revelation he brought contained what no divine scripture contained: the stories of the earlier peoples, the reporting of unseen matters, and the inclusion of the interests of this world and the Hereafter, together with an eloquence and excellence that defeated them; besides other meanings that it comprised, all of which decides the corruption of their statement. Their saying that is the habit of the unbelievers with their prophets when they brought them miracles, as Pharaoh and his people said about Musa, peace be upon him: ﴿Indeed, this is a knowing magician﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 109], ﴿They said: two magics supporting each other﴾ [al-Qasas: 48]; and the people of ʿIsa, peace be upon him: ﴿This is nothing but manifest magic﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 110]. The claim of magic is only by way of obstinacy and denial.

﴿Indeed your Lord is Allah, who created the heavens and the earth in six days, then established Himself upon the Throne﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 54]. The explanation of this sentence has already been given in Surah al-Aʿraf. Both come after the mention of the Qur'an and the reminder of the Return. In al-Aʿraf: ﴿And We have certainly brought them a Book which We have detailed﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 52], and His saying: ﴿On the Day its interpretation comes﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 53]; and here: ﴿These are the verses of the Book﴾, and the mention of warning and good tidings, whose fruit appears only in the Return. The connection of this to what precedes is that whoever is able to create this great upper and lower creation, and He is your Lord who watches over your interests, it is not strange that He should send to His creation one who warns against opposing Him and gives good tidings for obeying Him, since their creation is not in vain, but according to what His wisdom requires and what His will has decreed. For the Mighty Creator is able to do what is lesser by way of greater precedence.

It was also said: when he informed them about resurrection, the return, and the rising from graves, they were astonished.

Its connection to what precedes it: When He revealed ﴿And when a surah is sent down﴾ [al-Tawba: 124] and mentioned the denial of the hypocrites, then said ﴿There has certainly come to you a messenger﴾ [al-Tawba: 128], meaning Muhammad (ﷺ), He followed that with mention of the Book that was sent down and the Prophet who was sent, and that the way of the misguided, their followers, and their polytheists is one in denying the divine books and the one who brought them. Since the mention of the Qur'an preceded the mention of the Messenger at the end of the surah, it likewise came at the beginning of this surah, so the mention of the Book preceded the mention of the Messenger. The commentators' statements on the opening of this surah, which begins with letters of the alphabet, have preceded. Here they mentioned sayings from the commentators, among them: "I am Allah, the All-Seeing"; among them: "I am Allah, the Most Gracious"; among them: that it is composed of these and of "Ha-Mim" and the nun of al-Rahman. So the Ra is part of the letters of al-Rahman, separated. Among them also: "I am the Lord," and other things. The apparent meaning is that "tilka" (those) remains in its proper usage, because the thing referred to is distant. Mujahid and Qatada said: by "tilka" He refers to the earlier books, the Torah, the Gospel and the Psalms, so the verses are the stories described in those books. Al-Zajjaj said: it refers to the verses of the Qur'an that have been mentioned. It was also said: it refers to the preserved Book that is written and kept with Allah, from which every book was copied, as He said: ﴿Rather, it is a glorious Qur'an, in a preserved tablet﴾ [al-Buruj: 21–22], and He said: ﴿And indeed it is in the Mother of the Book﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 4]. It was also said: it refers to the Ra and its companions among the letters of the alphabet, meaning: those letters with which the surahs begin, though their words are close, their meanings are far to reach (p-122). They are "the verses of the Book," meaning the Book is recited by them and its words return to them. This is what Ibn al-Anbari mentioned. It was also said: "tilka" is used with the meaning of "hadhihi" (this), and the thing referred to is present and near. This is what Ibn 'Abbas said, and Abu 'Ubayda chose it. It was said: the verses of the Qur'an. It was said: the verses of the surahs mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿And when a surah is sent down﴾ [al-Tawba: 124]. It was said: the thing referred to is the Ra, for it contains the treasures of the Qur'an, and the sciences by which Allah has singled Himself out. It was said: it refers to what the surah includes of verses. "Al-kitab" here means the surah.

Al-hakim (the Wise): It means the Judge, or the one possessing wisdom because it includes it and is connected to it, or the "muhkam" (firmly established), or the one judged by, or the one made a judge. These are sayings. The hamza in ("akana") is interrogative in the sense of denial, because wonder arises from revelation to a human among them with warning and good tidings. That is: there is no wonder in that. It is Allah's custom with the earlier nations: He sent down books to their messengers with glad tidings and warnings through those whom He chose from among them. The subject of (kana) is ﴿an awhayna﴾ (that We revealed), and (ajaban) is the predicate. As for (lil-nas), it was said: it is in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (hal) for (ajaban), because if it had come after, it would have been an adjective, and since it preceded, it became a hal. It was also said: it is related to (ajaban), and it is not a verbal noun but has the meaning of "astonishing," and a verbal noun in the sense of an object may have its complement placed before it, like the active participle in the sense of an object. It was also said: it is an explanation, meaning: "I mean, for the people." It was also said: it is related to (kana), even if it is defective; this does not hold unless it is taken to indicate an event, for if it is purely indicating time, it is not valid for it to be related. 'Abd Allah read: (ajabun). It was said: (ajabun) is the subject of (kana) and ﴿an awhayna﴾ is the predicate, so it is like the saying:
"Its mixture will be honey and water."
This is considered an anomaly. This is the interpretation of al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya. It was also said: (kana) is complete, and (ajabun) is its agent, and the meaning is: wonder arose among the people because We revealed. This interpretation is good. The meaning of ﴿lil-nas ajaban﴾ is that they made it for themselves an object of amazement, which they marvel at, and they set it up as a banner toward which they direct their mockery and denial. Ru'ba read ﴿ila rajulin﴾ with the jim vowelless. This is a Tamimi dialect in which they vowel-reduce a form, like: sab'un and 'adhdun for sabu'un and 'adhudun. Since warning is general, its object, which is "the people," is general. Good tidings are specific, so its object is specific, which is "those who believe." As for ("an andhir"), "an" is either explanatory or the light form of the heavy "anna," originally meaning that the matter is "we said: warn the people," as al-Zamakhshari said both of them. It is also possible that it is the "an" that is a verbal particle with a binary form, not the light form of the heavy, because it is connected to the perfect, the imperfect and the imperative, and here it is connected to the imperative, and with it a verbal noun is formed, whose estimate is: "by the warning of the people." This aspect is better than the explanatory, because the Kufans do not accept that "an" can be explanatory, nor the light form of the heavy, since that would require deleting its subject and implying its predicate, which is the saying; thus deletion of both subject and predicate would be combined. Also, grounding is better than claiming deletion through lightening.

﴿And give good tidings to those who believe that they have﴾, that is, that they have. The preposition was deleted. As for ﴿qadam sidq﴾ (a firm standing of truth): Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, al-Rabi' ibn Anas and Ibn Zayd said: it is the righteous deeds of worship. Al-Hasan and Qatada said: it is the intercession of Muhammad (ﷺ). Zayd ibn Aslam and others said: it is the affliction with Muhammad (ﷺ). Ibn 'Abbas and others said: it is the happiness that precedes them in the Preserved Tablet. Muqatil said: a precedence of good with Allah that they sent forward. To this meaning Wadday al-Yaman alluded in his saying:
"What is wrong with you, Wadday, constantly in love-poetry? Do you not fear the nearness of your term?"
"Pray to the Lord of the Throne and take a qadam that will save you on the day of stumbling and slipping."

Qatadah also said: "a sound predecessor" (salaf sidq). ʿAṭāʾ said: "a true station" (maqam sidq). Yamān said: "a true faith" (iman sidq). Al-Hasan also said: "a righteous child whom they sent ahead." It was also said: it is God's advancing of this community in resurrection and in their entry into Paradise, as He said: "We are the last, but the first on the Day of Resurrection." It was also said: it is precedence of nobility (taqaddum sharaf), and from it is the verse of al-ʿAjjaj:

*"He humbled the sons of al-ʿAwwam from the family of al-Hakam,
and they left the kingship to a king of ancient precedence (dhi qadam)."*

Al-Zajjaj said: a lofty rank (darajah ʿaliyah). And it is reported from him: an elevated position (manzilah rafiʿah). From it is the verse of Dhu al-Rummah:

*"To you is a precedence (qadam) that people do not deny,
which with noble ancestry has overflowed upon the sea."*

Al-Zamakhshari said: "a station of sidq with their Lord" means priority, merit, and an elevated position. Since striving and forerunning are done by the foot (qadam), the noble endeavour and the precedence were called a qadam, just as a blessing is called a yad (hand), because it is given by the hand, and a bawʿ (span/reach), because its possessor stretches out with it. So it is said of a man, "He has a qadam in goodness." Its being idafa (annexed) to sidq indicates an increase in excellence and that it is among the great precedences. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: sidq in this verse means righteousness (salah), as you say, "a man of sidq." It is reported from al-Awzaʿi that he read (qidam) with a kasrah on the qaf, as a naming by the verbal noun (tasmiyah bi-l-masdar).

﴿Said the disbelievers﴾: Al-Tabari held that the speech contains an omission indicated by the apparent context, its implied sense being: "When he warned and gave good tidings, the disbelievers said such and such." Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: "Said the disbelievers" may be an explanation of His saying, "Is it a marvel for people that We revealed to a man among them...," meaning: the disbelievers said concerning it such and such.

Al-Jumhur, al-ʿArabiyyan and Nafiʿ read *la-siḥrun* ("this is indeed magic"), referring to the revelation. The rest of the Seven, Ibn Masʿud, Abu Razin, Masruq, Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, Ibn Wththab, Talhah, al-Aʿmash, Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn Kathir, and ʿIsa ibn ʿAmr, with a variant reported from two of them, read *la-sahirun* ("indeed a magician"), referring to the Messenger ﷺ. In the codex of Ubayy: ﴿This is nothing but magic﴾ [al-Qasas: 36]. Al-Aʿmash also read: *ma hadha illa sahirun* ("this is nothing but a magician"). Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: their saying about the warning and good tidings that it is magic arises only because he separated their word and came between a person and his close relative, so it resembled what the magician does, and they assumed it belonged to that category. Al-Zamakhshari said: this is evidence of their inability and their admission of it, even though they were lying in calling it magic. Since their claim concerning what cannot possibly be magic is manifestly corrupt, their statement required no answer, because they knew his upbringing among them in Makkah and his association with them, and that he had no lack of knowledge. Moreover, the revelation he brought contained what no divine scripture contained: the stories of the earlier peoples, the reporting of unseen matters, and the inclusion of the interests of this world and the Hereafter, together with an eloquence and excellence that defeated them; besides other meanings that it comprised, all of which decides the corruption of their statement. Their saying that is the habit of the unbelievers with their prophets when they brought them miracles, as Pharaoh and his people said about Musa, peace be upon him: ﴿Indeed, this is a knowing magician﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 109], ﴿They said: two magics supporting each other﴾ [al-Qasas: 48]; and the people of ʿIsa, peace be upon him: ﴿This is nothing but manifest magic﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 110]. The claim of magic is only by way of obstinacy and denial.

﴿Indeed your Lord is Allah, who created the heavens and the earth in six days, then established Himself upon the Throne﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 54]. The explanation of this sentence has already been given in Surah al-Aʿraf. Both come after the mention of the Qur'an and the reminder of the Return. In al-Aʿraf: ﴿And We have certainly brought them a Book which We have detailed﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 52], and His saying: ﴿On the Day its interpretation comes﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 53]; and here: ﴿These are the verses of the Book﴾, and the mention of warning and good tidings, whose fruit appears only in the Return. The connection of this to what precedes is that whoever is able to create this great upper and lower creation, and He is your Lord who watches over your interests, it is not strange that He should send to His creation one who warns against opposing Him and gives good tidings for obeying Him, since their creation is not in vain, but according to what His wisdom requires and what His will has decreed. For the Mighty Creator is able to do what is lesser by way of greater precedence.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 10, verse 3:

﴿Surely your Lord is God, who created the heavens and the earth in six days, then established Himself upon the Throne, governing the affair. There is no intercessor except after His permission.﴾ Mujahid said: that is, He decrees it alone. And tadbir (governance, the arranging of affairs) is the placing of matters in their proper ranks and the consideration of their outcomes and final consequences. As for al-amr (the affair), it has been said that it is all creation, both its upper and lower parts. It has also been said that He sends down the command through angels: Jibril for revelation, Mika'il for rain, 'Izra'il for taking souls, and Israfil for the Trumpet. This sentence is an explanation of the greatness of His station and His dominion. Having mentioned creation (ijad), He mentioned what occurs within it of affairs, and that He alone is the One who does it, in both creation and governance, none sharing with Him in that, and that no one dares to intercede with Him except by His permission, since He, exalted is He, knows best the place of wisdom and rightness. In this is evidence of the greatness of His might and His majesty, as He said: ﴿On the Day when the Spirit and the angels stand in ranks﴾ [al-Naba': 38], to the end of the verse. Since the address is general, and the disbelievers used to say of their idols, "These are our intercessors with God," God rejected that from them, and the mention of intercession that takes place on the Day of Resurrection fits after the mention of the beginning, so as to join the two extremes: the beginning (al-ibtida') and the end (al-intiha').

Abu Muslim al-Isfahani said: "Shafi'" here is from the shaf' (even number) which is the opposite of the witr (odd number). So the meaning of the verse is that He brought the world into existence alone, with no partner to help Him, and nothing came into being in existence except after He said to it: "Be." Abu al-Baqa' said: ﴿yudabbiru al-amr﴾ may be a new (independent) sentence, or a second predicate, or a circumstantial clause (hal).

﴿That is God, your Lord, so worship Him﴾: that is, the One characterized by creation, governance and majesty, is your Lord, who looks after your welfare, so He is the one deserving of worship, since none is fit to be worshipped except Him, exalted is He. So do not associate with Him any of His creation.

﴿Will you not then take heed?﴾: an exhortation to reflect and contemplate the signs that point to His lordship and to making worship purely for Him.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 10, verse 4–5:

﴿To Him is your return, all of you. The promise of Allah is true. Indeed, He originates creation and then repeats it, so that He may reward those who believed and did righteous deeds with justice. But those who disbelieved will have a drink of scalding water and a painful punishment because they used to disbelieve.﴾ He mentioned that which calls for reminder, namely that the return of all of them is to Him, and he emphasized this report by saying that it is the promise of Allah, about whose truth there is no doubt. Then he resumed the report, and in it is the sense of causation: the origination of creation and its repetition, and that the requirement of wisdom in this is the recompense of the responsible people for their deeds. ﴿وعْدَ اللَّهِ﴾ (wa'da Allah, "the promise of Allah") and (ḥaqqan, "truly") are in the accusative because they are two infinitive nouns (maṣdar) emphasizing the content of the sentence. The estimate is: Allah promised a promise. When the governing verb was omitted, he made the infinitive a genitive construction with the agent, as in His words: ﴿ṣibghata Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 138] and ﴿ṣun'a Allah﴾ [al-Naml: 88]. The estimate is: in (ḥaqqan), that is truly so, true. It was also said that (ḥaqqan) is in the accusative by (wa'd), with the estimate: in whatever promise of Allah is in truth. ʿAlī ibn Sulaymān said: the estimate is: a time of truth. And he recited:

*Is it true, servants of Allah, that I am not going out, nor entering, except that a watcher is over me?*

ʿAbd Allah, Abu Jaʿfar, al-Aʿmash and Sahl ibn Shuʿayb read (annahu yabda'u, "that He originates") with a fatḥah on the hamzah. al-Zamakhshari said: it is in the accusative by the verb, i.e., Allah promised the beginning of creation and then its repetition, and the meaning is the repetition of creation after its beginning. "Allah promised" is in the form of the verb. It is permissible that it be in the nominative by what put (ḥaqqan) in the accusative, i.e., the beginning of creation is true as truth, like his words:

*Is it true, servants of Allah, that I am not coming, nor going, except that a watcher is over me?*

End. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: its position is accusative by the estimate "Is it true that He..." Al-Farrāʾ said: its position is nominative by the estimate "Indeed it is true that He..." Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: in my view it is permissible that "annahu" be a substitute (badal) for His words ﴿وعْدَ اللَّهِ﴾. Abu al-Fath said: if you wish, estimate: "because He originates; whoever has this power is free from breaking the promise." And if you wish, estimate: "Allah promised, truly, that He originates," and the infinitive which is ﴿وعْدَ اللَّهِ﴾ does not govern it, because it has described that with its completion and cut off its governing. Ibn Abi ʿAbla read (ḥaqqun) with a nominative, so this is a beginning (mubtada'), and its predicate is "annahu." End. That (ḥaqqun) is the predicate of a subject and "annahu" is the subject is the preferred construction in grammar, as you say: "It is correct that you are going out," because the noun of "inna" is definite, while what precedes it in such an example is indefinite.

The apparent meaning is that the beginning of creation is the first origination, and its repetition is the resurrection from the graves. (Li-yajziya, "so that He may reward") is related to (yuʿīduhu, "repeats it"), i.e., so that the recompense may fall upon the deeds. It was said: the beginning is from dust, then He repeats it into dust, then He repeats it into resurrection. It was said: the beginning is its formation from water, then He repeats it from state to state. It was said: He originates it from nothingness, then returns it to it, then brings it into existence. It was said: He originates it among the company of the wretched, then at death returns it to the company of the friends, and the reverse. Ṭalḥah read (yubdi'u) from (abda'a) in the quadriliteral form, and (badā) and (abdā') have the same meaning. (Bi-l-qisṭi, "with justice") means with equity, and it is related to His words (li-yajziya). I.e., so that He may reward the believers with justice and fairness in their recompense, giving each his recompense and reward according to the degree of their superiority in deeds, so He is equitable and just among them, since they are not all equal in measures of reward. On this, "with justice" is from Him, exalted is He. al-Zamakhshari said: or He gives them their due by what they did justly, and were equitable, and did not wrong when they believed and did righteous deeds, because shirk is wrong; Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, shirk is a great injustice﴾ [Luqman: 13]. Sinners are wrongers of themselves. This is more fitting to the contrast with His words: ﴿because they used to disbelieve﴾. End. So he made justice an act of those who believed, in the manner of the Muʿtazilah. The apparent meaning is that (wa-alladhina kafaru, "and those who disbelieved") is a subject, and it may be that it is conjoined to His words (alladhina amanu), so the recompense with justice would include both groups. Since the discourse with the disbelievers is the opening of the surah with them, He mentioned some kinds of their punishment, saying: ﴿For them is a drink of scalding water and a painful punishment because they used to disbelieve﴾. The explanation of this was given earlier in Surat al-Anʿam.

﴿He it is who made the sun a radiance and the moon a light, and determined for it stations that you may know the number of years and the reckoning. Allah did not create that except in truth. He details the signs for a people who know﴾: When He mentioned the proofs of His lordship from the bringing into existence of this upper and lower world, He mentioned what He deposited in the upper world of these two bright luminous substances. So He made the sun a radiance, i.e., possessing radiance or radiant, or the very radiance for emphasis. (Ja'ala, "made") may be in the sense of ṣayyara ("made into"), so that ḍiyā'an is a second object. It may be in the sense of khalaqa ("created"), so that it is a circumstantial state (ḥāl). (Wa-l-qamara nūran, "and the moon a light") i.e., possessing light, or illuminated, or the very light for emphasis, or both are infinitive nouns. It was said: ḍiyā'an may be a plural, like ḥawḍ and ḥiyāḍ, but this is remote. Since the sun is greater in mass, it was specified with radiance, because that is what has brilliance and shining, and it is greater than light. The people of the science of astronomy said: the sun's size is one hundred and sixty-four times the earth, and the moon is not like that, so the greater was specified with the greater. The difference between ḍiyā' and nūr was already mentioned in His words: ﴿When it lit up what was around it, Allah took away their light﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17]. His words: ﴿Allah is the light of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Nur: 35] indicate that nūr is greater and more eloquent in brightness, otherwise why would He turn to the lesser, which is nūr? Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: the word nūr is more decisive and more eloquent, because He compared His guidance and the subtlety that reaches a people who are guided, and others who go astray with Him, to the light which is always present in the night and during darkness. If He had compared it to ḍiyā', it would have been necessary that it never misguide anyone, since guidance would be like the sun, with which no darkness remains. So the meaning of the verse is that He placed His guidance in disbelief like light in darkness, so one people is guided and another people goes astray. Had He made it like radiance, it would have been necessary that no one go astray, and radiance on this account remains more eloquent in shining, as this verse requires.

Qanbal read (ḍiyā'an) here, and in al-Anbiya' and al-Qasas, with a hamzah before the alif in place of the yā'. It was construed as metathesis: its lām was made an ʿayn, so it became a hamzah. The wāw which was an ʿayn, after an extra alif, at the end became a hamzah. This was considered weak, since the analogy is to avoid the meeting of two hamzahs by easing one of them; how is it imagined that there is a transposition leading to their meeting when they were not so originally? The apparent meaning is that the pronoun returns to the moon, i.e., its course stations, or He determined it as having stations, or He determined for it stations, so the verb was omitted and connected, and it is accusative according to these estimates as an adverbial or circumstantial or object, as in His words: ﴿And the moon, We determined for it stations﴾ [Ya-Sin: 39]. The pronoun returned to it alone, because it is the one regarded in knowing the number of years and the reckoning among the Arabs. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: it is possible that He intends both together, insofar as both are used in knowing the number of years and the reckoning, but mention of one of them was sufficient, as He said: ﴿Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 62], and as the poet said:

*He threw at me a matter from which I and my father were innocent, and for the sake of the well he threw me.*

The stations (manāzil) are the mansions of the moon, and the Arabs used to attribute the seasonal rains (anwā') to them. They are twenty-eight stations: al-Sharatān, al-Buṭayn, al-Thurayyā, al-Dabarān, al-Haq'ah, al-Han'ah, al-Dhirāʿ, al-Nathrah, al-Ṭarf, al-Jabhah, al-Darbah, al-Ṣarfah, al-ʿAwwāʾ, al-Simāk, al-Ghafr, al-Zibānān, al-Iklīl, al-Qalb, al-Shawlah, al-Naʿāʾim, al-Baldah, Saʿd al-Dhābiḥ, Saʿd Balʿ, Saʿd al-Suʿūd, Saʿd al-Akhbiyah, al-Farʿ al-Muʾakhkhar, and al-Rishāʾ, which is the fish. The lām is related to His words: (wa-qaddarahu manāzila, "and determined for it stations"). al-Aṣmaʿī said: Abu ʿAmr was asked about al-ḥisāb, whether it is with its accusative or its genitive, and he said: "Who knows what the number of the reckoning is?" End. He means that the genitive would imply that the reckoning's number is known, whereas the reckoning cannot have its ultimate number known, and the reckoning is the reckoning of times of months, days and nights, of what is benefited in livelihood, leases and other matters in which one is compelled to know dates. It was said: He sufficed with mention of the number of years in place of the number of months, and He alluded to the reckoning by the transactions, and the reference by that is to His creation. That is referred to with one, and may also be referred to a plural. (Bi-l-ḥaqq, "in truth") means bound up with truth, which is the far-reaching wisdom, and He did not create it in vain, as came in His words: ﴿Our Lord, You did not create this in vain﴾ [Al ʿImran: 191], ﴿We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in play. We did not create them except in truth﴾ [al-Dukhan: 38]. Ibn Jarir said: the truth here is Allah the Exalted, and the meaning is: Allah did not create that except by Allah alone, with no partner with Him. End. What he said is an awkward construction, since it would become like "I hit ʿAmr only with Zayd." It was said: the bāʾ means lām, i.e., for the truth, which is the display of His craftsmanship, the explanation of His power, and an indication of His oneness. Ibn Muṣarrif read (wa-l-ḥisāb) with a fatḥah on the ḥāʾ, and Abu Tawbah related it from the Arabs. Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr and Ḥafṣ read (yufaṣṣilu) with yā' following the form of the word Allah, and the rest of the seven with nūn by way of the shift of person (iltifāt) and the report with the nūn of majesty. Those who know are specified with the detailing of the signs for them, because they are the ones who benefit from the detailing of the signs, and reflect upon them in inference and sound reasoning. The signs (āyāt) are the indicators (ʿalāmāt), or the verses of the Qur'an.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 10, verse 4–5:

﴿To Him is your return, all of you. The promise of Allah is true. Indeed, He originates creation and then repeats it, so that He may reward those who believed and did righteous deeds with justice. But those who disbelieved will have a drink of scalding water and a painful punishment because they used to disbelieve.﴾ He mentioned that which calls for reminder, namely that the return of all of them is to Him, and he emphasized this report by saying that it is the promise of Allah, about whose truth there is no doubt. Then he resumed the report, and in it is the sense of causation: the origination of creation and its repetition, and that the requirement of wisdom in this is the recompense of the responsible people for their deeds. ﴿وعْدَ اللَّهِ﴾ (wa'da Allah, "the promise of Allah") and (ḥaqqan, "truly") are in the accusative because they are two infinitive nouns (maṣdar) emphasizing the content of the sentence. The estimate is: Allah promised a promise. When the governing verb was omitted, he made the infinitive a genitive construction with the agent, as in His words: ﴿ṣibghata Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 138] and ﴿ṣun'a Allah﴾ [al-Naml: 88]. The estimate is: in (ḥaqqan), that is truly so, true. It was also said that (ḥaqqan) is in the accusative by (wa'd), with the estimate: in whatever promise of Allah is in truth. ʿAlī ibn Sulaymān said: the estimate is: a time of truth. And he recited:

*Is it true, servants of Allah, that I am not going out, nor entering, except that a watcher is over me?*

ʿAbd Allah, Abu Jaʿfar, al-Aʿmash and Sahl ibn Shuʿayb read (annahu yabda'u, "that He originates") with a fatḥah on the hamzah. al-Zamakhshari said: it is in the accusative by the verb, i.e., Allah promised the beginning of creation and then its repetition, and the meaning is the repetition of creation after its beginning. "Allah promised" is in the form of the verb. It is permissible that it be in the nominative by what put (ḥaqqan) in the accusative, i.e., the beginning of creation is true as truth, like his words:

*Is it true, servants of Allah, that I am not coming, nor going, except that a watcher is over me?*

End. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: its position is accusative by the estimate "Is it true that He..." Al-Farrāʾ said: its position is nominative by the estimate "Indeed it is true that He..." Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: in my view it is permissible that "annahu" be a substitute (badal) for His words ﴿وعْدَ اللَّهِ﴾. Abu al-Fath said: if you wish, estimate: "because He originates; whoever has this power is free from breaking the promise." And if you wish, estimate: "Allah promised, truly, that He originates," and the infinitive which is ﴿وعْدَ اللَّهِ﴾ does not govern it, because it has described that with its completion and cut off its governing. Ibn Abi ʿAbla read (ḥaqqun) with a nominative, so this is a beginning (mubtada'), and its predicate is "annahu." End. That (ḥaqqun) is the predicate of a subject and "annahu" is the subject is the preferred construction in grammar, as you say: "It is correct that you are going out," because the noun of "inna" is definite, while what precedes it in such an example is indefinite.

The apparent meaning is that the beginning of creation is the first origination, and its repetition is the resurrection from the graves. (Li-yajziya, "so that He may reward") is related to (yuʿīduhu, "repeats it"), i.e., so that the recompense may fall upon the deeds. It was said: the beginning is from dust, then He repeats it into dust, then He repeats it into resurrection. It was said: the beginning is its formation from water, then He repeats it from state to state. It was said: He originates it from nothingness, then returns it to it, then brings it into existence. It was said: He originates it among the company of the wretched, then at death returns it to the company of the friends, and the reverse. Ṭalḥah read (yubdi'u) from (abda'a) in the quadriliteral form, and (badā) and (abdā') have the same meaning. (Bi-l-qisṭi, "with justice") means with equity, and it is related to His words (li-yajziya). I.e., so that He may reward the believers with justice and fairness in their recompense, giving each his recompense and reward according to the degree of their superiority in deeds, so He is equitable and just among them, since they are not all equal in measures of reward. On this, "with justice" is from Him, exalted is He. al-Zamakhshari said: or He gives them their due by what they did justly, and were equitable, and did not wrong when they believed and did righteous deeds, because shirk is wrong; Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, shirk is a great injustice﴾ [Luqman: 13]. Sinners are wrongers of themselves. This is more fitting to the contrast with His words: ﴿because they used to disbelieve﴾. End. So he made justice an act of those who believed, in the manner of the Muʿtazilah. The apparent meaning is that (wa-alladhina kafaru, "and those who disbelieved") is a subject, and it may be that it is conjoined to His words (alladhina amanu), so the recompense with justice would include both groups. Since the discourse with the disbelievers is the opening of the surah with them, He mentioned some kinds of their punishment, saying: ﴿For them is a drink of scalding water and a painful punishment because they used to disbelieve﴾. The explanation of this was given earlier in Surat al-Anʿam.

﴿He it is who made the sun a radiance and the moon a light, and determined for it stations that you may know the number of years and the reckoning. Allah did not create that except in truth. He details the signs for a people who know﴾: When He mentioned the proofs of His lordship from the bringing into existence of this upper and lower world, He mentioned what He deposited in the upper world of these two bright luminous substances. So He made the sun a radiance, i.e., possessing radiance or radiant, or the very radiance for emphasis. (Ja'ala, "made") may be in the sense of ṣayyara ("made into"), so that ḍiyā'an is a second object. It may be in the sense of khalaqa ("created"), so that it is a circumstantial state (ḥāl). (Wa-l-qamara nūran, "and the moon a light") i.e., possessing light, or illuminated, or the very light for emphasis, or both are infinitive nouns. It was said: ḍiyā'an may be a plural, like ḥawḍ and ḥiyāḍ, but this is remote. Since the sun is greater in mass, it was specified with radiance, because that is what has brilliance and shining, and it is greater than light. The people of the science of astronomy said: the sun's size is one hundred and sixty-four times the earth, and the moon is not like that, so the greater was specified with the greater. The difference between ḍiyā' and nūr was already mentioned in His words: ﴿When it lit up what was around it, Allah took away their light﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17]. His words: ﴿Allah is the light of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Nur: 35] indicate that nūr is greater and more eloquent in brightness, otherwise why would He turn to the lesser, which is nūr? Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: the word nūr is more decisive and more eloquent, because He compared His guidance and the subtlety that reaches a people who are guided, and others who go astray with Him, to the light which is always present in the night and during darkness. If He had compared it to ḍiyā', it would have been necessary that it never misguide anyone, since guidance would be like the sun, with which no darkness remains. So the meaning of the verse is that He placed His guidance in disbelief like light in darkness, so one people is guided and another people goes astray. Had He made it like radiance, it would have been necessary that no one go astray, and radiance on this account remains more eloquent in shining, as this verse requires.

Qanbal read (ḍiyā'an) here, and in al-Anbiya' and al-Qasas, with a hamzah before the alif in place of the yā'. It was construed as metathesis: its lām was made an ʿayn, so it became a hamzah. The wāw which was an ʿayn, after an extra alif, at the end became a hamzah. This was considered weak, since the analogy is to avoid the meeting of two hamzahs by easing one of them; how is it imagined that there is a transposition leading to their meeting when they were not so originally? The apparent meaning is that the pronoun returns to the moon, i.e., its course stations, or He determined it as having stations, or He determined for it stations, so the verb was omitted and connected, and it is accusative according to these estimates as an adverbial or circumstantial or object, as in His words: ﴿And the moon, We determined for it stations﴾ [Ya-Sin: 39]. The pronoun returned to it alone, because it is the one regarded in knowing the number of years and the reckoning among the Arabs. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: it is possible that He intends both together, insofar as both are used in knowing the number of years and the reckoning, but mention of one of them was sufficient, as He said: ﴿Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 62], and as the poet said:

*He threw at me a matter from which I and my father were innocent, and for the sake of the well he threw me.*

The stations (manāzil) are the mansions of the moon, and the Arabs used to attribute the seasonal rains (anwā') to them. They are twenty-eight stations: al-Sharatān, al-Buṭayn, al-Thurayyā, al-Dabarān, al-Haq'ah, al-Han'ah, al-Dhirāʿ, al-Nathrah, al-Ṭarf, al-Jabhah, al-Darbah, al-Ṣarfah, al-ʿAwwāʾ, al-Simāk, al-Ghafr, al-Zibānān, al-Iklīl, al-Qalb, al-Shawlah, al-Naʿāʾim, al-Baldah, Saʿd al-Dhābiḥ, Saʿd Balʿ, Saʿd al-Suʿūd, Saʿd al-Akhbiyah, al-Farʿ al-Muʾakhkhar, and al-Rishāʾ, which is the fish. The lām is related to His words: (wa-qaddarahu manāzila, "and determined for it stations"). al-Aṣmaʿī said: Abu ʿAmr was asked about al-ḥisāb, whether it is with its accusative or its genitive, and he said: "Who knows what the number of the reckoning is?" End. He means that the genitive would imply that the reckoning's number is known, whereas the reckoning cannot have its ultimate number known, and the reckoning is the reckoning of times of months, days and nights, of what is benefited in livelihood, leases and other matters in which one is compelled to know dates. It was said: He sufficed with mention of the number of years in place of the number of months, and He alluded to the reckoning by the transactions, and the reference by that is to His creation. That is referred to with one, and may also be referred to a plural. (Bi-l-ḥaqq, "in truth") means bound up with truth, which is the far-reaching wisdom, and He did not create it in vain, as came in His words: ﴿Our Lord, You did not create this in vain﴾ [Al ʿImran: 191], ﴿We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in play. We did not create them except in truth﴾ [al-Dukhan: 38]. Ibn Jarir said: the truth here is Allah the Exalted, and the meaning is: Allah did not create that except by Allah alone, with no partner with Him. End. What he said is an awkward construction, since it would become like "I hit ʿAmr only with Zayd." It was said: the bāʾ means lām, i.e., for the truth, which is the display of His craftsmanship, the explanation of His power, and an indication of His oneness. Ibn Muṣarrif read (wa-l-ḥisāb) with a fatḥah on the ḥāʾ, and Abu Tawbah related it from the Arabs. Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr and Ḥafṣ read (yufaṣṣilu) with yā' following the form of the word Allah, and the rest of the seven with nūn by way of the shift of person (iltifāt) and the report with the nūn of majesty. Those who know are specified with the detailing of the signs for them, because they are the ones who benefit from the detailing of the signs, and reflect upon them in inference and sound reasoning. The signs (āyāt) are the indicators (ʿalāmāt), or the verses of the Qur'an.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 10, verse 6–8:

﴿Indeed, in the alternation of the night and the day, and in what Allah has created in the heavens and the earth, there are signs for a people who fear Allah.﴾ Al-ikhtilaf (alternation) is the succession of the night and the day, and one of them coming after the other. What Allah has created in the heavens includes the luminous bodies in them, the angels who dwell therein, and other things that Allah, exalted is He, knows; and [what He has created in] the earth includes inanimate matter, minerals, plants and animals. He singled out the God-conscious (al-muttaqun) because they are the ones who fear the consequences, so their fear moves them to reflect and to consider.

﴿Indeed, those who do not hope for meeting Us, and are content with the life of this world and are at rest in it, and those who are heedless of Our signs﴾ ﴿—those, their abode is the Fire, because of what they used to earn.﴾ The apparent meaning of raja' (hope) here is expectation and longing, i.e., they do not expect the meeting with Our reward and Our punishment. It has been said that its meaning is "they do not fear." Ibn Zayd said: this verse concerns the disbelievers, and the meaning is that one who denies the Resurrection does not hope for mercy in the Hereafter, nor does he think well that he will meet Allah. In the speech there is an ellipsis, i.e., "and they were content with the life of this world instead of the Hereafter," as in His saying: ﴿Are you content with the life of this world instead of the Hereafter?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 38]. The meaning is that the final aim of their purpose and the utmost of their hopes is confined to what they attain in this world. "And are at rest in it" means they settled into it, were satisfied with it, and rejected whatever is other than it. The apparent meaning is that His saying "and those who" is a category of disbelievers distinct from the first category, and this repetition with the relative pronoun indicates difference; it is coordinated with the subject of "inna" (indeed), and "those" refers to the two categories of disbelievers: the one who is absorbed in this world and expansive in it, looking at the signs, yet the hope of meeting Allah has no weight with him, but he is content with the life of this world because of his denial of the Resurrection and the recompense; and the one who lacks expansiveness and is heedless of the signs of Allah that point to guidance. It is also possible that it is a coordination of attributes, so that ﴿and those who are heedless of Our signs﴾ are the same as those who do not hope for the meeting with Allah. The apparent meaning is that ﴿and are at rest in it﴾ is coordinated with the relative clause, and it is possible that it is a waw of circumstance, i.e., "while they have been at rest in it." As for "the signs," it has been said: the signs of the Qur'an. And it has been said: the indicators that point to the Oneness and the power [of Allah]. Ibn Zayd said: what We have sent down of lawful and unlawful, and obligations, limits and legal rulings. And His saying "because of what they used to earn" indicates that the earlier deeds are the cause of the punishment, and in this is a refutation of the Jabriyyah (determinists), and an explicit statement that punishment is tied to acquisition (kasb). Its coming in the present tense (mudari') is evidence that they continued to persist in this in their past time and their future.

That is, He increases them in their guidance because of their earlier faith and their steadfastness. As for those who believe, their [faith] increases them, or He guides them to the path of Paradise by the light of their faith, as He said: ﴿Their light runs before them and on their right hands﴾ [al-Hadid: 12]. Mujahid said: "Their faith will be a light by which they walk."

In a hadith: "When a person rises from his grave, a man of beautiful face and pleasant fragrance will appear to him and say, 'Who are you?' He will reply, 'I am your righteous deed.' Then it will lead him to Paradise." The opposite applies to the disbeliever.

Ibn al-Anbari said: "Their faith guides them to the special qualities of knowledge and to favours through which their hearts are gladdened and doubts and confusions are removed from them, like His saying: ﴿And those who are guided, He increases them in guidance﴾ [Muhammad: 17]. These increases and benefits may be attained in this world before death, and they may be attained after death."

Al-Qaffal said: "If we take the verse in this sense, the meaning is: their Lord guides them by their faith, and the rivers flow beneath them, except that the waw (conjunction) has been omitted." It was also said: its meaning is "their advance toward the reward," from the Arab saying: "The foot guides the leg" (al-qadam tahdi al-saq). Al-Hasan said: "He has mercy on them." Al-Kalbi said: "He calls them."

The apparent view is that (tajri, "flows") is a resumptive new clause (mustaʾnafan, i.e., not grammatically dependent on what precedes), so He has informed of them two great matters: one is God's guidance of them, which is in this world, and the other is the flowing of the rivers, which is in the Hereafter. Just as the verse included two matters concerning the disbelievers: one is their attribute of having no hope of meeting God and what is joined to it, and the second is their abode and dwelling place, which is the Fire. Thus it constitutes a division of the two groups in meaning.

Al-Qaffal's view has already been mentioned: that (tajri) is conjoined with a particle that has been omitted, and that it may be a circumstantial clause (hal). The meaning of (min tahtihim) is "from beneath their dwellings." It was also said: "from in front of them." The "beneath" here is not a distance, but refers to a direction relative to the person. From this usage: ﴿Your Lord has placed a stream beneath you﴾ [Maryam: 24], and He said: ﴿And these rivers flow beneath me﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 51].

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you say: this verse indicates that the faith by which the servant deserves guidance, success and light on the Day of Resurrection is qualified faith, which is faith accompanied by righteous deeds, and faith not accompanied by righteous deeds has no success or light for its possessor." I say: The matter is as you say. Do you not see how He placed the relative clause (silah) including both faith and righteous deed together? It is as if He said: 'Those who combine faith and righteous deeds,' then said: (bi-imanihim), that is, by their faith to which this righteous deed is joined. This is clear and evident, with no doubt in it." End of quote. This is in the manner of the Mu'tazila (al-i'tizal, the rationalist school).

They permitted ﴿in the Gardens of Bliss﴾ to be connected to (tajri), or to be a circumstantial clause of (al-anhar, the rivers), or to be a predicate following the predicate of inna. The meaning of (daʿwahum) is their supplication and their calling, because (Allahumma) is a call to God. The meaning is: "O God, we glorify You," like the words of the one reciting the qunut (the supplication of standing prayer): "O God, You alone we worship, and to You we pray and prostrate." It was also said: their worship is like His saying: ﴿And I will withdraw from you and from what you call upon besides God﴾ [Maryam: 48]. There is no obligation in Paradise, so this is in the manner of joy and delight, and worship is applied to it metaphorically. Abu Muslim said: "Their action and their affirmation." Al-Qadi said: "Their way of sanctifying God and praising Him."

(Wa-tahiyyatuhum) means: what each of them greets the other with. It is a verbal noun (masdar) added to the plural, not in the sense of an operative governing object, but like His saying: ﴿And We were witnesses to their judgment﴾ [al-Anbiya: 78]. It was also said: it is added to the object, and the agent is God Most High or the angels, meaning: God's greeting to them, or the angels' greeting to them.

﴿And the last of their supplication﴾, that is, the conclusion of their calling and their remembrance. Al-Zajjaj said: "God Most High informs that they begin by glorifying Him and exalting Him, and conclude with thanking Him and praising Him." Ibn Kaysan said: "They open with monotheism and close with praise." It is related from al-Hasan al-Basri, attributing it to the Messenger (ﷺ), that the people of Paradise are inspired with praise and glorification.

The (an) here is the light form of the heavy (anna), its noun is an implicit pronoun of the matter (damir al-shan), which must be omitted, and the clause after it is the predicate of (an), and (an) with its clause is the predicate of the phrase (wa-akhiru). Ikrima, Mujahid, Qatada, Ibn Yamar, Bilal ibn Abi Burda, Abu Mijlaz, Abu Haywa, Ibn Muhaysin and Ya'qub read (an al-hamdu) with the heavy form and the accusative (al-hamda). Ibn Jinni said: "It indicates that the reading of the majority, with the light form and nominative (al-hamdu), is that (an) is the light form, as in the words of al-A'sha:

"Among youths like Indian swords, they know that every man who goes barefoot and sandal-shod is doomed."

He means: that he is doomed. When it is made light, it does not govern anything other than an omitted pronoun of the matter. Al-Mubarrad permitted its operation as it is when heavy. Sahib al-Nazm claimed that (an) here is superfluous, and (al-hamdu lillah) is the predicate of ﴿and the last of their supplication﴾, but this contradicts the explicit statement of Sibawayh and the grammarians, and this is not one of the positions where it is added.

Al-Qaffal's view has already been mentioned: that (tajri) is conjoined with a particle that has been omitted, and that it may be a circumstantial clause (hal).
