From this usage: ﴿Your Lord has placed a stream beneath you﴾ [Maryam: 24], and He said: ﴿And these rivers flow beneath me﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 51].

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you say: this verse indicates that the faith by which the servant deserves guidance, success and light on the Day of Resurrection is qualified faith, which is faith accompanied by righteous deeds, and faith not accompanied by righteous deeds has no success or light for its possessor." I say: The matter is as you say. Do you not see how He placed the relative clause (silah) including both faith and righteous deed together? It is as if He said: 'Those who combine faith and righteous deeds,' then said: (bi-imanihim), that is, by their faith to which this righteous deed is joined. This is clear and evident, with no doubt in it." End of quote. This is in the manner of the Mu'tazila (al-i'tizal, the rationalist school).

They permitted ﴿in the Gardens of Bliss﴾ to be connected to (tajri), or to be a circumstantial clause of (al-anhar, the rivers), or to be a predicate following the predicate of inna. The meaning of (daʿwahum) is their supplication and their calling, because (Allahumma) is a call to God. The meaning is: "O God, we glorify You," like the words of the one reciting the qunut (the supplication of standing prayer): "O God, You alone we worship, and to You we pray and prostrate." It was also said: their worship is like His saying: ﴿And I will withdraw from you and from what you call upon besides God﴾ [Maryam: 48]. There is no obligation in Paradise, so this is in the manner of joy and delight, and worship is applied to it metaphorically. Abu Muslim said: "Their action and their affirmation." Al-Qadi said: "Their way of sanctifying God and praising Him."

(Wa-tahiyyatuhum) means: what each of them greets the other with. It is a verbal noun (masdar) added to the plural, not in the sense of an operative governing object, but like His saying: ﴿And We were witnesses to their judgment﴾ [al-Anbiya: 78]. It was also said: it is added to the object, and the agent is God Most High or the angels, meaning: God's greeting to them, or the angels' greeting to them.

﴿And the last of their supplication﴾, that is, the conclusion of their calling and their remembrance. Al-Zajjaj said: "God Most High informs that they begin by glorifying Him and exalting Him, and conclude with thanking Him and praising Him." Ibn Kaysan said: "They open with monotheism and close with praise." It is related from al-Hasan al-Basri, attributing it to the Messenger (ﷺ), that the people of Paradise are inspired with praise and glorification.

The (an) here is the light form of the heavy (anna), its noun is an implicit pronoun of the matter (damir al-shan), which must be omitted, and the clause after it is the predicate of (an), and (an) with its clause is the predicate of the phrase (wa-akhiru). Ikrima, Mujahid, Qatada, Ibn Yamar, Bilal ibn Abi Burda, Abu Mijlaz, Abu Haywa, Ibn Muhaysin and Ya'qub read (an al-hamdu) with the heavy form and the accusative (al-hamda). Ibn Jinni said: "It indicates that the reading of the majority, with the light form and nominative (al-hamdu), is that (an) is the light form, as in the words of al-A'sha:

"Among youths like Indian swords, they know that every man who goes barefoot and sandal-shod is doomed."

He means: that he is doomed. When it is made light, it does not govern anything other than an omitted pronoun of the matter. Al-Mubarrad permitted its operation as it is when heavy. Sahib al-Nazm claimed that (an) here is superfluous, and (al-hamdu lillah) is the predicate of ﴿and the last of their supplication﴾, but this contradicts the explicit statement of Sibawayh and the grammarians, and this is not one of the positions where it is added.

﴿And if God were to hasten evil for people as they seek to hasten good, their term would surely have been decreed for them. So We leave those who do not expect to meet Us in their transgression, wandering blindly.﴾ Mujahid said: It was revealed concerning a man who supplicates against himself, his wealth, his child, or the like. God informs that if He were to answer people's supplications against themselves with the harm they wish for, just as He answers them with the good they wish for, He would destroy them. Then, after this statement, He omitted a clause that the apparent wording implies, whose estimated form is: "So He does not do that, but We leave those who do not expect [to meet Us]." He thus cut short the speech and reached this meaning through His words ﴿So We leave those who do not expect﴾. Reflect on this estimation and you will find it sound. This was said by Ibn Atiyya.

It was also said that it was revealed concerning their words ﴿Bring us what you promise us﴾ [al-A'raf: 70] and what goes in the same direction. Al-Zamakhshari said: The intended people are the people of Mecca. Their words ﴿then rain down upon us stones﴾ [al-Anfal: 32] mean: if We hastened for them the evil they called for, just as We hasten the good for them, they would have been made to die and be destroyed.

He said: If you ask, how is ﴿So We leave those who do not expect to meet Us﴾ connected to this, and what is its meaning? I say: His words ﴿And if God were to hasten﴾ contain the meaning of negating hastening, as if He had said: We do not hasten evil for them, nor do We decree their term for them, so We leave them in their transgression, or We give them respite, and We keep bestowing blessing upon them despite their transgression, as an establishment of proof against them.

The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that when He mentioned people's astonishment at God's revelation to a man among them, and that what was revealed to him included warning and good tidings, and they used to mock this and did not believe in the arrival of what he warned them of, they said ﴿then rain down upon us stones﴾ [al-Anfal: 32], and He said, reporting about them: ﴿and they ask you to hasten the punishment﴾ [al-Hajj: 47], and they said ﴿then bring us what you promise us﴾ [al-A'raf: 70]. Then He digressed from that to His oneness, mentioning His bringing the world into existence, then to the division of people into believers and disbelievers, and mentioned the abodes of the two groups. Then He returned to the point that this threatened matter, whose occurrence they sought hastily, would, if it occurred, destroy them. There would then be no hope in their destruction of the faith of some of them, or of bringing a believer out of their loins. Rather, His wisdom required that He not hasten for them what they requested, because of what would follow from that.

The word ﴿hastening﴾ (*istiʿjalahum*) is in the accusative as a *masdar* (verbal noun) used as a *mushabbah bihi* (the element to which something is compared). Al-Zamakhshari said: Its original form is ﴿if God were to hasten evil for people in the manner of His hastening good for them﴾. So he placed *istiʿjalahum bil-khayr* (their seeking hastening of good) in place of *taʿjiluhu lahum al-khayr* (His hastening of good for them), to indicate the swiftness of His answering them and granting their request, as if their seeking the good were itself a hastening for them. Al-Hawfi and Ibn Atiyya said: The estimate is "like their hastening," and Abu al-Baqa' also estimated it this way.

The meaning of *ʿajjala* (to hasten, causative) is not the same as the meaning of *istaʿjala* (to seek to hasten), because *ʿajjala* indicates occurrence, while *istaʿjala* indicates (p. 129) seeking hastening. The former is from God, and the latter is attributed to them. Therefore the estimate cannot be as al-Zamakhshari stated. It admits two possibilities. The first is that the estimate is "hastening like their seeking of good," so the hastening is compared to the seeking, because their seeking of good and the occurrence of His hastening were, in their view, prior to everything else. The second is that there is an omitted element indicated by the verbal noun, its estimate being: "if God were to hasten evil for people when they seek it, [as He hastens] their seeking of good," because they used to seek evil and its occurrence mockingly, just as they used to seek good.

Ibn Amir read ﴿*la-qudiya*﴾ (it would have been decreed) with the active verb and ﴿*ajalahum*﴾ (their term) in the accusative. Al-A'mash read ﴿*la-qadayna*﴾ (We would have decreed). The rest of the seven readers read it in the passive, with ﴿*ajaluhum*﴾ (their term) in the nominative. *Qadā* (decree) is more complete. The *fa* in ﴿*fa-nadhar*﴾ (So We leave) is the answer to what He reported about them, in the manner of a resumptive clause (*istiʾnaf*). Its estimate is "So We leave," as al-Hawfi said. Abu al-Baqa' said: ﴿*fa-nadhar*﴾ is conjoined to an omitted verb, whose estimate is: "But We give them respite, so We leave [them]."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit, "The Surrounding Sea") on surah 10, verse 12:

﴿When harm touches man, he calls upon Us, lying on his side, or sitting, or standing. But when We remove his harm from him, he passes on as though he had never called upon Us against a harm that had touched him. Thus is what they used to do made attractive to the extravagant.﴾

The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that when the disbelievers sought to have evil befall them, and that He, exalted is He, does not act according to their demand but leaves those who do not hope for His meeting to persist in their transgression, He made clear the great need people have for Him and their dependence on seeking the rain of His beneficence, both the wrongdoer and the good-doer. Whoever does not hope for His meeting is nonetheless compelled to Him when harm touches him. So all turn to Him at that time and single Him out as the one capable of removing harm.

The apparent meaning is that "man" (al-insan) here does not refer to a specific individual. It has been said that it is Abu Hudhayfah Hashim ibn al-Mughirah ibn 'Abd Allah al-Makhzumi, related by Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil. It has also been said that it is 'Uqbah ibn Rabi'ah, and that it is al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah. It has been said that it refers to all of them, related by 'Ata'. It has been said that it is al-Nadr ibn al-Harith. The word does not refer only to the disbeliever; rather the intended meaning is man as such, whether he is a disbeliever or a sinner in matters other than disbelief. These three opinions allow that they refer to one person, and they allow that they refer to several persons, since "man" is a genus (jins). The meaning is that the one who has been struck by harm continues to call upon, seek refuge in, and turn with desire to God in all his states, every one of them.

He began with the most difficult state, which is lying down and being unable to rise, and this is greater and more emphatic in supplication. Then he mentioned what follows it, which is the state of sitting, the state of being unable to stand. Then he mentioned what follows that, which is standing, and this is the state of being unable to walk, so you see him struggling and not rising to walk, like the condition of the decrepit old man.

"Li-janbihi" (for his side) is a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning "lying on his side." For this reason the two circumstances after it are conjoined to it. The lam is in its original function according to the Basran grammarians, and the implied meaning is "laid down on his side," not that it means "upon" ('ala), contrary to what he claimed. The one whose state is described (dhu al-hal) is the pronoun in "da'ana" (he called upon Us), and the governing element is "da'ana," meaning: he called upon Us while in one of these states.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: It is also permissible for it to be a circumstance of "al-insan," with "massa" (touched) as its governing element. It is also permissible for it to be a circumstance of the subject in "da'ana," with "da'a" (called) as its governing element. These are two distinct meanings.

"Al-Durr" (harm) is a general term for all illnesses and calamities concerning the self, wealth, and loved ones. This is the view of the lexicographers. It has been said that it is specific to bodily calamities: emaciation and sickness. End of quotation. The first view is the view of al-Zajjaj.

Abu al-Baqa' considered it weak for "li-janbihi" and what follows it to be circumstances of "al-insan," with "massa" as the governing element. He said, for two reasons. The first: the circumstance on this reading occurs after the response of "idha" (when), and this is not the proper arrangement. The second: the meaning is the abundance of his supplication in all his states, not that the harm that befalls him is in all his states. Many verses in the Qur'an support this. End of quotation.

This second point entails that whoever is touched by harm in these states supplicates in these states, because it is the response to the condition in which these states are mentioned. So the qualifier within the conditional clause is a qualifier of the response, as when you say: "If Zayd came to us poor, we showed him kindness," meaning: we showed him kindness in his state of poverty. Thus the qualifier in the condition is a qualifier of the consequence.

The meaning of "removing harm" (kashf al-durr) is lifting it and taking it away, as if it had been a covering over the person, concealing him.

The author of the composition (Sahib al-Nazm) said: "And when harm touches man" is described in the future tense, and "then when We removed from him" is in the past tense. This arrangement indicates that the meaning of the verse is that he was thus in the past and thus will be in the future. So the future verb in the verse indicates its future meaning, and the past verb indicates its past meaning. End of quotation.

"Al-Murur" (passing on) here is a metaphor for continuing on in his former way, without mention of the affliction and harm he had been under. Muqatil said: he turned away from supplication. It has been said: he passed on from the place of earnest entreaty and humble petition, not returning to it, as if he had no prior relationship with it. This is close to the preceding view.

The clause "as though he had never called upon Us against a harm that had touched him" is in the position of a circumstance, meaning: calling upon Us for the removal of a harm that had touched him.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: His saying "passed on" requires that the revelation of the verse was concerning the disbelievers. Then it extends, after taking in everyone who falls under its meaning, whether disbeliever or sinner. That is, the verse applies to passing on in associating partners with God and in having little reliance upon Him. End of quotation.

The "ka" in "kadhalika" (thus) is in the accusative position, meaning: like that. "Dhalika" is a reference to the making attractive of turning away from earnest supplication to God when harm is removed, and of not thanking Him and not remembering Him for it. "Zuyyina" (was made attractive) is in the passive voice, so its agent may be God, either by way of creating and originating that in their hearts, as Ahl al-Sunnah (the People of the Sunnah) say, or by way of abandoning them and forsaking them, as the Mu'tazilah (the Mu'tazilites) say. Or the agent may be Satan, by his whisperings and deception. It has been said: or the self (nafs).

"Al-Musrifun" (the extravagant) is interpreted as the disbelievers. The disbeliever is extravagant because he wastes eternal happiness for base, transient desire, just as the spender wastes his wealth by going beyond the limit in it.

﴿What they used to do﴾: from turning away from the presence of God and from following desires.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 10, verse 13–14:

﴿And We destroyed the generations before you when they committed wrong, and their messengers came to them with clear proofs, but they were not going to believe. Thus do We recompense the criminal folk.﴾ ﴿Then We made you successors in the land after them, that We might see how you act.﴾: This is information addressed to the contemporaries of the Messenger (ﷺ), and an address to them about the destruction of the nations that preceded them, because of their wrongdoing, which is disbelief. It is for the purpose of deterring them, reminding them of the condition of the disbelievers who came before, warning them, and setting forth examples: just as He did to those, He will do to you. The word "lamma" (when/since, indicating causation) implies causality, and it is a particle of conditional linkage in the past. As for one who holds that it is an adverbial temporal clause governed by (ahlaknā), as az-Zamakhshari did following others, then it indicates only that the action occurred at the time of the wrongdoing, and so it would then carry no implication of causation. If you say, "I came when Zayd stood," your coming is not caused by Zayd's standing. You see that wherever "lamma" occurs, its answer, or what takes its place, is caused by what follows it, and this confirms the correctness of Sibawayh's view that it is a particle of necessity for necessity. (Wa-jā'at-hum): its apparent sense is that it is coordinated with (ẓalamū), meaning: when these two matters occurred, the coming of the messengers with clear proofs and their wrongdoing, they were destroyed.

Az-Zamakhshari said: The waw in (wa-jā'at-hum) is for the circumstantial state, meaning: they wronged by denying, while their messengers had already come to them with arguments and evidences of their truthfulness, which are the miracles. End of quotation. Muqatil said: "al-bayyinat" means things that warn of punishment. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in His saying (wa-mā kānū) refers back to "al-qurun," and that it is coordinated with His saying (ẓalamū). Az-Zamakhshari permitted that it be a parenthetical clause rather than a coordinated one, saying: The lam is for emphasizing the negation, in the sense of: "and they were not going to believe truly," an emphasis on the negation of their faith, and that God, exalted is He, knew that they were persisting in their disbelief, and that faith was improbable from them. The meaning is that the cause of their destruction was their persecution of the messengers, and God knew that there was no benefit in granting them respite after the proof had been established against them by the sending of the messengers. End of quotation. Muqatil said: the pronoun in His saying ﴿wa-mā kānū li-yu'minū﴾ refers to the people of Makkah; according to his view it is an iltifat (shift), since it moves from the second-person pronoun to the third-person pronoun, and it is consistent with His saying: ﴿And when Our clear verses are recited to them﴾ [Yunus: 15]. The kaf in (kadhālika) is in the accusative position, meaning: "like that recompense," which is the destruction.

﴿Thus do We recompense the criminal folk﴾: this is a severe warning to whoever commits crime, and it includes the people of Makkah and others. A group read (yajzī) with the yā', meaning: God recompenses, and this is an iltifat. The address in (ja'alnākum) is to those to whom the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was sent. It has been said that it is an address to the polytheists of Makkah, and the meaning is: We made you successors in the land after the destroyed generations, that We might see whether you will act with good or with evil, so that We may deal with you according to your deeds. The meaning of (li-nanẓura) is: that We might make evident in existence what We had known beforehand, so "seeing" is a metaphor for this.

Az-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, how is seeing permissible for God, exalted is He, when it implies confrontation? I say: it is used metaphorically for certain knowledge, which is knowledge of a thing as existing, resembling the seeing of the one who looks and the witnessing of the eyewitness in its reality. End of quotation. In this there is a hidden trace of Mu'tazilism, for seeing necessitates confrontation, and in it is a denial of describing Him, exalted is He, as "the All-Seeing" and a reduction of this to the sense of knowledge. It has also been said that (li-nanẓura) is with an elided noun, meaning: "that Our messengers and Our allies might see," and seeing is attributed to God metaphorically, while it belongs to others. Yahya ibn al-Harith al-Zammari read (linaẓẓara) with a single nun and a shadda on the ẓā', and he said: "I saw it thus in the Mushaf of Uthman ibn Affan, may God be pleased with him." He means that he saw it written with a single nun, because the dots, vowel marks and shaddas came into use only after Uthman. Writing it with a single nun does not indicate the omission of the nun from the pronunciation, nor its assimilation into the ẓā', because assimilating the nun into the ẓā' is not permissible. What justifies its omission is that it has no effect on the nasal sound, so Yahya's reading should be understood as his having exaggerated the concealment of the ghunna, so that the listener supposed it was an assimilation, and thus it was attributed to him. The interrogative "kayfa" is governed by (ta'malūn), and the clause is in the accusative position after (linanẓura), because it is a suspended clause. Suspension is permitted with (naẓara), even though it is not one of the verbs of the heart, because it is a link to the heart-verb which is knowledge.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 10, verse 15:

﴿When Our clear verses are recited to them, those who do not expect to meet Us say: "Bring a Qur'an other than this, or change it." Say: "It is not for me to change it on my own accord. I only follow what is revealed to me. Indeed, I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a tremendous day."﴾ Ibn 'Abbas and al-Kalbi said: it was revealed concerning the mockers of the Qur'an among the people of Makkah, who said: "O Muhammad, bring a Qur'an other than this, one in which there is nothing that we ask of you." Mujahid and Qatada said: it was revealed concerning a group of the polytheists of Makkah. Muqatil said: it was revealed concerning five men: 'Abd Allah ibn Umayya al-Makhzumi, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, Mikraz ibn Hafs, 'Amr ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Qays al-'Amiri, and al-'As ibn Wa'il. It has also been said that the five were: al-Walid, al-'As, al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib, al-Aswad ibn 'Abd Yaghuth, and al-Harith ibn Handhala. This was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas.

Al-Zamakhshari said: what angered them was the condemnation in the Qur'an of the worship of idols and the threat to the polytheists, so they said: "Bring another Qur'an in which there is nothing that angers us about this, and we will follow you." Ibn 'Atiyya said: it was revealed concerning the Quraysh, because some of the disbelievers of the Quraysh made this statement with the meaning: "Be lenient with us, O Muhammad, and make this speech that comes from you a matter of our choice: permit what it prohibits and prohibit what it permits, so that our affair becomes one and our word unified." End of quote. 

Allah, exalted is He, pointed out the attribute that moved them to this statement, which is that they do not believe in the Resurrection and the requital for what they have committed. The meaning is: when the verses of the Qur'an are recited to them, clear and luminous with no ambiguity in them, they say such-and-such. The verses are attributed to Him, exalted, because they are His speech, mighty and majestic. 

Tabdil (substitution, alteration) may occur in the essence, by making one essence into another essence, or in the attribute. The substitution here is in the attribute: some of its arrangement is removed by putting a verse of mercy in place of a verse of punishment. Substitution in the essence is not intended here, because that would require that the thing which necessitates difference be the very same thing; substitution in the essence is the bringing of "a Qur'an other than this." Since bringing a Qur'an other than this is not within human capacity, there was no need to negate it or to negate what is within human capacity, even though it is impossible in regard to him, peace and blessings be upon him. Therefore it was said to him: ﴿Say: It is not for me to change it on my own accord.﴾ The negation of "it is for me" here is like His saying: ﴿You could not have made its trees grow﴾ [al-Naml: 60], meaning that such a thing is impossible.

It is possible that substitution in the essence is intended, in that his words ﴿Bring a Qur'an other than this﴾ imply the continuation of this Qur'an while another Qur'an is brought in its place. Thus "or change it" would mean "remove it entirely and bring a replacement for it." So the demand would be one of two things: either its complete removal, which is substitution in the essence, or bringing something else while it remains, so that the two demands differ.

"Tilqa'" is a verbal noun like "tibyan," and no other noun of the form tif'al came from it. It is used as an adverb of place meaning "in front of" or "opposite"; you say: "Zayd is opposite you." It has also been read with a fatha on the ta', which is the measure of intensive verbal nouns such as tawaf, tajwal, and tardad. The meaning is: "on my own part, to follow in what I command you and forbid you, without addition, subtraction, or alteration, except what its report comes to me from the heavens."

Using His words ﴿I only follow what is revealed to me﴾ as evidence, scholars have concluded the negation of judgment by ijtihad (independent reasoning) and the negation of qiyas (analogical reasoning). They said ﴿Bring a Qur'an other than this, or change it﴾ because they did not acknowledge that the Qur'an is inimitable (mu'jiz), or because they were unable to produce its like. Do you not see their saying ﴿If we wished, we could say the like of this﴾ [al-Anfal: 31], and their saying ﴿He has invented a lie against Allah﴾ [Yunus: 17]? It is not possible that they meant "Bring a Qur'an other than this, or change it" from the standpoint of revelation, given his words ﴿Indeed, I fear﴾.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask: what was their purpose, when they were the most cunning and the most deceitful of people in this proposal? I say: it was scheming and plotting. As for the proposal to replace one Qur'an with another, it implies that it is from you, and that you are capable of its like, so replace it with another. As for the proposal of substitution and alteration, it was out of greed and to test the situation: if some alteration came from him, either Allah would destroy him and we would be saved from him, or He would not destroy him and they would mock him, and they would make the alteration a proof against him and a confirmation of his fabrication against Allah, exalted is He. End of quote.

﴿If I disobey﴾ by altering it on my own accord, and the following of revelation has preceded, and my abandonment of acting upon it. This is a conditional clause whose answer is omitted, indicated by what precedes it. The Great Day is the Day of Resurrection, and it is described as great either because of its length, or because of the abundance of its hardships, or both together.

Consider the excellence of this answer. Since one of the two demands was the alteration, it began with it in the answer. Then it followed with a general matter that includes the negation of alteration and other things. Then it mentioned the cause that moves one to that, which is fear, and linked it to mere disobedience in general, so that with even the slightest disobedience, fear is brought about.

(p. 132)

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 10, verse 16:

﴿Say: "Had Allah willed, I would not have recited it to you, nor would He have made you aware of it. I lived among you a lifetime before it. Will you not then reason?"﴾ This is an emphatic declaration of innocence from what they asked of him. That is, his reciting this Qur'an to them is by the will of Allah the Exalted and His bringing about a wondrous matter that is outside the normal course of habits: that a man who is unlettered, who had not studied, had not listened to, and had not seen the scholars for a single hour of his life, and who did not grow up in a town where there were scholars, should recite to you a book of eloquence whose speech overwhelms every eloquent person, rises above every prose and verse, is filled with sciences of the usul (principles) and furu' (branches) of religion, reports of what has happened and what will happen, and speaks of the unseen matters that no one knows except Allah the Exalted. He had lived among you for forty years, during which you observed his conditions, and nothing of his secrets was hidden from you, and you had not heard from him a single letter of that, nor had anyone of the closest people to him and most attached to him informed him of it.

The object of (shā'a, "willed") is omitted, meaning: "Say: Had Allah willed that I not recite it..." The answer to (law, "had") came in the familiar manner without the lam, because it was negated by (mā, "not"). It is said: dartu bihi and adraytu Zaydan bihi, and the meaning is: "nor would I inform you of it through my tongue."

Qunbul and al-Bazzi, through the transmission of al-Naqqash from Abu Rabi'ah from him, read (wa la-adrākum bihi, "nor would He have made you aware of it") with a lam that entered upon an affirmative verb coordinated with a negated one. The meaning is: "and He would have informed you of it by means other than me and through the tongue of another. But He bestows His favour upon whomever He wills of His servants, so He singled me out with this honour and saw me as worthy of it above the people."

The recitation of the majority is ﴿wa la adrākum bihi﴾. Here "la" is emphasizing and clarifying that the verb is negated, because it is coordinated with a negated verb. The "la" is not the particle by which the verb is negated, because it is not valid to negate the verb with "la" when it comes as an answer to a conditional, and what is coordinated with an answer is also an answer. You do not say: "Had it been so, it would not have been so," rather it is: "Had it been so, it would have been so."

Ibn Abbas, Ibn Sirin, al-Hasan and Abu Raja' read (wa la adra'tukum bihi) with a quiescent hamzah. This reading is explained in two ways. One: the original form is adraytukum with a ya', which was changed to a hamzah according to the dialect of those who say labba'tu bil-hajj and ra'athtu zawji bi-abyat, meaning labbaytu and rataytu. This substitution was permitted because the alif and the hamzah are of the same category, and for this reason, when the alif is vocalized it turns into a hamzah, as they said al-'alim becomes al-'a'lim, and al-mushtaq becomes al-mushta'q. The second way: the hamzah is original, and the verb is from al-dar', which is repelling, as it is said: dara'tuhu, "I pushed him away," as He said: ﴿wa yadra'u 'anha al-'adhab﴾ [al-Nur: 8], "and it would avert from her the punishment." And dara'tuhu also means "I made him a dari'" (one who repels). The meaning is: "and I would make you adversaries by his recitation, repelling me with argument and denying me."

Abu al-Fath (Ibn Jinni) claimed that it is only adraytukum, and he changed the ya' into an alif because the letter before it is open. This is a dialect of 'Uqayl, transmitted by Qutrub, who say in a'taytuka: a'ta'tuka. Abu Hatim said: al-Hasan changed the ya' into an alif as in the dialect of Bani al-Harith ibn Ka'b: al-salamu 'alak. It was said: there is a hamzah in it according to the dialect of one who says al-'a'lim for al-'alim.

Shahr ibn Hawshab and al-A'mash read (wa la andhartukum bihi, "nor would I have warned you of it") with a nun and a dhal, from al-indhar (warning). It is likewise in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud. He drew attention to the fact that this is a revelation from Allah the Exalted, through His having me live among them for a lifetime, which is forty years, before the Qur'an was revealed upon my tongue, as a youth and as a mature man. You did not test me in a lie, nor did I engage in any of this, nor did I undertake any occupation. So how can I be accused of fabricating it? Will you not reason that whoever is in this manner, having remained for such long periods without learning, without discipleship, without reading a book, and without the practice of disputation, then brings what it is not possible for anyone to bring, and is not but truthful in what he brings, conveying from his Lord what was revealed to him and what He singled him out with? As came in the hadith of Heraclius: "Did you test him for a lie?" He said: "No." He said: "One who does not leave lying about people would not lie about Allah."

Abu Amr assimilated the tha' of (labithtu, "I lived") into the following letter, while the rest of the seven readers made it clear.

al-A'mash read (umuran) with a sukun on the mim. The apparent reading is that the pronoun in (min qablihi, "before it") returns to the Qur'an. Al-Kirmani permitted that it return to the recitation, and to the revelation, and to the time, meaning: the time of its revelation.

(p-133)

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 10, verses 17–19:**

﴿Who is more wrongdoing than one who fabricates a lie against God, or denies His signs? Indeed, the criminals will not prosper.﴾ The explanation of this kind of statement has already passed (in the *tafsir*, interpretation), and its purpose here is according to two considerations. The first: when they said, "Bring a Qur'an other than this, or change it," it implied that they were attributing it to not being from God, and that it was only fabrication. So the wrongdoing of one who fabricates a lie against God was emphasised, as in His words: ﴿And who is more wrongdoing than one who fabricates a lie against God, or says, "It has been revealed to me," when nothing has been revealed to him, or who says, "I will send down the like of what God has sent down"?﴾ [al-An'am: 93]. The conclusive proof has already been established that this Qur'an is from God, and you have denied His signs, so no one is more wrongdoing than you. The second consideration: this is a preface to what comes after it of the worship of idols, meaning: no one is more wrongdoing than you in your fabrication against God that He has a partner, that He has a son, and in what you attribute to Him of permitting and forbidding.

﴿And they worship, besides God, that which neither harms them nor benefits them, and they say, "These are our intercessors with God." Say: "Will you inform God of something He does not know in the heavens or on the earth? Glory be to Him, and exalted is He above what they associate with Him."﴾ The pronoun in (they worship) refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh whose dialogue has preceded. ﴿That which neither harms them nor benefits them﴾ refers to the idols, inanimate objects that have no power to benefit or harm. It was said: if they worship them, they will not benefit them, and if they abandon worshipping them, they will not harm them. It is the right of the worshipped that it rewards obedience and punishes disobedience. The people of al-Ta'if worshipped al-Lat, and the people of Makkah worshipped al-'Uzza, Manat, Asaf, Na'ilah and Hubal. The report of this about the disbelievers is in the manner of ignorance-attribution and belittling of them and of what they worship, and an alert that they worshipped one who does not deserve worship. In His saying (besides God) there is an indication that they worshipped idols and did not worship God. Ibn Ishaq said: they mean in the Hereafter. Al-Nadr ibn al-Harith said: "When the Day of Resurrection comes, I will be given intercession concerning al-Lat and al-'Uzza." Al-Hasan said: "Our intercessors are for the setting right of our livelihoods in this world." [p. 134] because they do not affirm the resurrection. And (Will you inform) is an interrogative in the manner of mockery, regarding what they claimed of the impossible, which is the intercession of idols, and an announcement that what they informed of is false and not included under correctness. So it is as if they were informing Him of something to which His knowledge does not relate. And *ma* (what) is a relative pronoun meaning "that which."

Al-Zamakhshari said: "[It is] by their being intercessors with Him, and this is the informing of something that is not known to God, the Exalted; and if it is not known to Him, while He is the Knower of the essence, encompassing all the known things, then it is not a thing, because a thing is that which is known and reported about. So it was a report that has no reporter about it." End of quote. Thus *ma* refers to the intercession, the agent of (knows) is God, and the object is the omitted pronoun referring to *ma*. His saying ﴿in the heavens, nor on the earth﴾ is an emphasis of its negation, because what does not exist in them is non-existent and absent, as he said. In al-Tahrir: (Will you inform) means mockery, reproach, rebuke and denial, and the meaning according to this is: "Will you inform God of what He knows to be otherwise in the heavens and the earth?" For the attributes of the essence do not admit negation. It was said: "Will you inform God of what He does not know to exist in the heavens and the earth? How can the existence of what God does not know be valid?" It is like saying to a man, "You have said such-and-such," and he replies, "God did not know this from me," meaning this never happened, since if it had, God would have known it. End of quote.

What appears evident is that *ma* is a relative pronoun intended to refer to the idols, not to the intercession they claimed, and the agent of (knows) is a pronoun referring to *ma*, not to God. That is by omitting a modifier, and the meaning is: "Say: Will you inform God of the intercession of idols, whose knowledge is negated in the heavens and the earth?" That is, they are not characterised by knowledge at all. Thus this would be a refutation of their claim that they intercede with God, because whoever lacks knowledge, how can he intercede when he does not know whom he intercedes for, nor what he intercedes for, nor to whom he intercedes? Just as He refuted them concerning worship by His saying: ﴿that which neither harms them nor benefits them﴾. The negation of harm and benefit undermines worship, and the negation of knowledge undermines intercession, so worship and the claim of intercession are both invalid. His saying (in the heavens and on the earth) according to this is an alert to the places of the worshipped whose intercession they claim, since among the heavenly worshipped are the stars, such as the sun and Sirius. It was read ﴿Tunabbi'unahu﴾ (Will you inform) with lightening, from *anba'a*. When the Exalted mentioned their worship of what neither harms nor benefits, and that this was association, He resumed with purification by His saying, "Glory be to Him, and exalted is He." *Ma* may be a relative pronoun, or a verbal-noun (masdariyyah), meaning: their partners whom they associate with Him, or concerning their association. The two Iraqi readers, the two Meccan-Medinan readers, and 'Asim read (yushrikun) with *ya'* as third person here, and in the two passages of al-Nahl, and one passage in al-Rum. Abu Hatim mentioned that al-Hasan, al-A'raj, Ibn al-Qa'qa', Shaybah, Humayd, Talhah and al-A'mash read it likewise. Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read in al-Naml only with *ya'* as second person, while 'Asim and Abu 'Amr read with *ya'* as third person. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and the five read with *ta'* as second person, and used the present tense, and did not use the past tense (*ashraku*) to indicate the continuation of their state, just as they came worshipping, and indeed they are upon association in the future, as they were upon it in the past.

﴿And mankind was but one community, then they differed. And had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord, it would have been decided between them concerning that in which they differ.﴾ When the Exalted mentioned the proof of the corruption of worshipping idols, He mentioned the motive for it, which is the difference that arose among people. The apparent meaning is the generality of people, and it can be conceived of as Adam and his children until the difference occurred after one of his two sons killed the other. This was said by Ubayy ibn Ka'b. Al-Dahhak said: the intended ones are the people of Noah's ship, who agreed upon the *hanifiyyah* (primordial monotheism) and the religion of Islam. From Ibn 'Abbas: whoever was among the children of Adam until the time of Ibrahim. This was refuted by saying that idols such as Wadd and Suwa' were worshipped in the time of Noah, peace be upon him. Ibn al-Qushayri related that the people were the people of Ibrahim until 'Amr ibn Luhayy changed the religion. Ibn Zayd said: they are those upon whom the covenant was taken on the day of ﴿Am I not your Lord?﴾ [al-A'raf: 172]; they were not one community other than on that day. Al-Asamm said: they are the newborn children, who were upon the *fitrah* (natural disposition), then differed after puberty. The most remote is the view of one who held that the intended meaning of "people" here is Adam alone, which is narrated from Mujahid and al-Suddi, and he was described as a community because he gathered all kinds of good. These sayings are (p. 135) based on the meaning of ﴿one community﴾ being in Islam and faith. It was also said: in polytheism. And it is intended: the people of Ibrahim were gathered upon disbelief, then some of them believed, and some persisted in disbelief. Or those who were before the Resurrection among the Arabs and the People of the Book were upon disbelief, alteration and distortion, until the Messenger of God ﷺ was sent, and some of them believed. Or the Arabs in particular. These are sayings, the third of which is that of al-Zajjaj. The apparent meaning is that the intended meaning of His saying ﴿one community﴾ is in Islam, because this statement came after the refutation of idol worship, so it is not suitable that it should strengthen the idol worshippers. For people were upon the religion of disbelief; rather, what is suitable is to say that they were upon Islam until aversion arises from following other than what people were upon. Also, His saying ﴿And had it not been for a word﴾ is a threat, so directing it to the nearest previously mentioned thing, which is the difference, is the correct view. The difference due to disbelief is what necessitates the threat, not the difference that is due to faith, since it is not fit to be a cause for the threat. The discussion of this kind has already passed in al-Baqarah in His saying: ﴿Mankind was one community﴾ [al-Baqarah: 213], but we have repeated the discussion of it here because it is far off.

The word here is the decree, and the estimate is: for the children of Adam until fixed terms. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: It is possible that it intends the word concerning the matter of the Resurrection, and that punishment and reward occur only then. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is the postponement of the judgement between them until the Day of Resurrection, when He judges between them immediately concerning what they differed about, and distinguishes the righteous from the falsifier. The word of God preceded with postponement for a wisdom that required that this abode be an abode of obligation, and that abode be an abode of reward and punishment. Al-Kalbi said: the word is that God informed this community that He would not destroy them with punishment in this world until the Day of Resurrection; so had it not been for this postponement, He would have judged between them by sending down punishment, or by establishing the Hour. It was said: the preceding word is that He would not seize anyone except with proof, which is the sending of messengers. It was said: the word is His saying: "My mercy has preceded My wrath," and had it not been for that, He would not have delayed the disobedient until repentance.

It was said: the preceding word is that He would not seize anyone except with proof, which is the sending of messengers. It was said: the word is His saying: "My mercy has preceded My wrath," and had it not been for that, He would not have delayed the disobedient until repentance.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 10, verses 17–19:**

﴿Who is more wrongdoing than one who fabricates a lie against God, or denies His signs? Indeed, the criminals will not prosper.﴾ The explanation of this kind of statement has already passed (in the *tafsir*, interpretation), and its purpose here is according to two considerations. The first: when they said, "Bring a Qur'an other than this, or change it," it implied that they were attributing it to not being from God, and that it was only fabrication. So the wrongdoing of one who fabricates a lie against God was emphasised, as in His words: ﴿And who is more wrongdoing than one who fabricates a lie against God, or says, "It has been revealed to me," when nothing has been revealed to him, or who says, "I will send down the like of what God has sent down"?﴾ [al-An'am: 93]. The conclusive proof has already been established that this Qur'an is from God, and you have denied His signs, so no one is more wrongdoing than you. The second consideration: this is a preface to what comes after it of the worship of idols, meaning: no one is more wrongdoing than you in your fabrication against God that He has a partner, that He has a son, and in what you attribute to Him of permitting and forbidding.

﴿And they worship, besides God, that which neither harms them nor benefits them, and they say, "These are our intercessors with God." Say: "Will you inform God of something He does not know in the heavens or on the earth? Glory be to Him, and exalted is He above what they associate with Him."﴾ The pronoun in (they worship) refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh whose dialogue has preceded. ﴿That which neither harms them nor benefits them﴾ refers to the idols, inanimate objects that have no power to benefit or harm. It was said: if they worship them, they will not benefit them, and if they abandon worshipping them, they will not harm them. It is the right of the worshipped that it rewards obedience and punishes disobedience. The people of al-Ta'if worshipped al-Lat, and the people of Makkah worshipped al-'Uzza, Manat, Asaf, Na'ilah and Hubal. The report of this about the disbelievers is in the manner of ignorance-attribution and belittling of them and of what they worship, and an alert that they worshipped one who does not deserve worship. In His saying (besides God) there is an indication that they worshipped idols and did not worship God. Ibn Ishaq said: they mean in the Hereafter. Al-Nadr ibn al-Harith said: "When the Day of Resurrection comes, I will be given intercession concerning al-Lat and al-'Uzza." Al-Hasan said: "Our intercessors are for the setting right of our livelihoods in this world." [p. 134] because they do not affirm the resurrection. And (Will you inform) is an interrogative in the manner of mockery, regarding what they claimed of the impossible, which is the intercession of idols, and an announcement that what they informed of is false and not included under correctness. So it is as if they were informing Him of something to which His knowledge does not relate. And *ma* (what) is a relative pronoun meaning "that which."

Al-Zamakhshari said: "[It is] by their being intercessors with Him, and this is the informing of something that is not known to God, the Exalted; and if it is not known to Him, while He is the Knower of the essence, encompassing all the known things, then it is not a thing, because a thing is that which is known and reported about. So it was a report that has no reporter about it." End of quote. Thus *ma* refers to the intercession, the agent of (knows) is God, and the object is the omitted pronoun referring to *ma*. His saying ﴿in the heavens, nor on the earth﴾ is an emphasis of its negation, because what does not exist in them is non-existent and absent, as he said. In al-Tahrir: (Will you inform) means mockery, reproach, rebuke and denial, and the meaning according to this is: "Will you inform God of what He knows to be otherwise in the heavens and the earth?" For the attributes of the essence do not admit negation. It was said: "Will you inform God of what He does not know to exist in the heavens and the earth? How can the existence of what God does not know be valid?" It is like saying to a man, "You have said such-and-such," and he replies, "God did not know this from me," meaning this never happened, since if it had, God would have known it. End of quote.

What appears evident is that *ma* is a relative pronoun intended to refer to the idols, not to the intercession they claimed, and the agent of (knows) is a pronoun referring to *ma*, not to God. That is by omitting a modifier, and the meaning is: "Say: Will you inform God of the intercession of idols, whose knowledge is negated in the heavens and the earth?" That is, they are not characterised by knowledge at all. Thus this would be a refutation of their claim that they intercede with God, because whoever lacks knowledge, how can he intercede when he does not know whom he intercedes for, nor what he intercedes for, nor to whom he intercedes? Just as He refuted them concerning worship by His saying: ﴿that which neither harms them nor benefits them﴾. The negation of harm and benefit undermines worship, and the negation of knowledge undermines intercession, so worship and the claim of intercession are both invalid. His saying (in the heavens and on the earth) according to this is an alert to the places of the worshipped whose intercession they claim, since among the heavenly worshipped are the stars, such as the sun and Sirius. It was read ﴿Tunabbi'unahu﴾ (Will you inform) with lightening, from *anba'a*. When the Exalted mentioned their worship of what neither harms nor benefits, and that this was association, He resumed with purification by His saying, "Glory be to Him, and exalted is He." *Ma* may be a relative pronoun, or a verbal-noun (masdariyyah), meaning: their partners whom they associate with Him, or concerning their association. The two Iraqi readers, the two Meccan-Medinan readers, and 'Asim read (yushrikun) with *ya'* as third person here, and in the two passages of al-Nahl, and one passage in al-Rum. Abu Hatim mentioned that al-Hasan, al-A'raj, Ibn al-Qa'qa', Shaybah, Humayd, Talhah and al-A'mash read it likewise. Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read in al-Naml only with *ya'* as second person, while 'Asim and Abu 'Amr read with *ya'* as third person. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and the five read with *ta'* as second person, and used the present tense, and did not use the past tense (*ashraku*) to indicate the continuation of their state, just as they came worshipping, and indeed they are upon association in the future, as they were upon it in the past.

﴿And mankind was but one community, then they differed. And had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord, it would have been decided between them concerning that in which they differ.﴾ When the Exalted mentioned the proof of the corruption of worshipping idols, He mentioned the motive for it, which is the difference that arose among people. The apparent meaning is the generality of people, and it can be conceived of as Adam and his children until the difference occurred after one of his two sons killed the other. This was said by Ubayy ibn Ka'b. Al-Dahhak said: the intended ones are the people of Noah's ship, who agreed upon the *hanifiyyah* (primordial monotheism) and the religion of Islam. From Ibn 'Abbas: whoever was among the children of Adam until the time of Ibrahim. This was refuted by saying that idols such as Wadd and Suwa' were worshipped in the time of Noah, peace be upon him. Ibn al-Qushayri related that the people were the people of Ibrahim until 'Amr ibn Luhayy changed the religion. Ibn Zayd said: they are those upon whom the covenant was taken on the day of ﴿Am I not your Lord?﴾ [al-A'raf: 172]; they were not one community other than on that day. Al-Asamm said: they are the newborn children, who were upon the *fitrah* (natural disposition), then differed after puberty. The most remote is the view of one who held that the intended meaning of "people" here is Adam alone, which is narrated from Mujahid and al-Suddi, and he was described as a community because he gathered all kinds of good. These sayings are (p. 135) based on the meaning of ﴿one community﴾ being in Islam and faith. It was also said: in polytheism. And it is intended: the people of Ibrahim were gathered upon disbelief, then some of them believed, and some persisted in disbelief. Or those who were before the Resurrection among the Arabs and the People of the Book were upon disbelief, alteration and distortion, until the Messenger of God ﷺ was sent, and some of them believed. Or the Arabs in particular. These are sayings, the third of which is that of al-Zajjaj. The apparent meaning is that the intended meaning of His saying ﴿one community﴾ is in Islam, because this statement came after the refutation of idol worship, so it is not suitable that it should strengthen the idol worshippers. For people were upon the religion of disbelief; rather, what is suitable is to say that they were upon Islam until aversion arises from following other than what people were upon. Also, His saying ﴿And had it not been for a word﴾ is a threat, so directing it to the nearest previously mentioned thing, which is the difference, is the correct view. The difference due to disbelief is what necessitates the threat, not the difference that is due to faith, since it is not fit to be a cause for the threat. The discussion of this kind has already passed in al-Baqarah in His saying: ﴿Mankind was one community﴾ [al-Baqarah: 213], but we have repeated the discussion of it here because it is far off.

The word here is the decree, and the estimate is: for the children of Adam until fixed terms. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: It is possible that it intends the word concerning the matter of the Resurrection, and that punishment and reward occur only then. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is the postponement of the judgement between them until the Day of Resurrection, when He judges between them immediately concerning what they differed about, and distinguishes the righteous from the falsifier. The word of God preceded with postponement for a wisdom that required that this abode be an abode of obligation, and that abode be an abode of reward and punishment. Al-Kalbi said: the word is that God informed this community that He would not destroy them with punishment in this world until the Day of Resurrection; so had it not been for this postponement, He would have judged between them by sending down punishment, or by establishing the Hour. It was said: the preceding word is that He would not seize anyone except with proof, which is the sending of messengers. It was said: the word is His saying: "My mercy has preceded My wrath," and had it not been for that, He would not have delayed the disobedient until repentance.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 10, verses 20–21:

﴿They say, "Why has no sign been sent down to him from his Lord?" Say, "The unseen belongs only to Allah, so wait; I am with you among those who wait."﴾: This is part of their demands. Al-Zamakhshari said: They did not regard the great and numerous signs that were sent down to him, which had not been sent down to any of the prophets before him, nor did they count the Qur'an alone as a sufficient sign, one that remains for all time, unique and strange among the signs, subtle in its method among the miracles. They treated its descent as though it were no descent at all, as if nothing had ever been sent down to him, until they said, "Why has not one sign been sent down to him from his Lord?" This was due to the extremity of their obstinacy, their persistence in rebellion, and their immersion in error.

﴿So say, "The unseen belongs only to Allah"﴾, that is, He alone has exclusive knowledge of the unseen, and He alone holds it. I have no knowledge of it, nor does anyone else. The meaning is that what prevents the sending down of the signs you demand is a hidden matter that none knows but Him, glorified is He. (So wait) for the descent of what you have demanded, ﴿I am with you among those who wait﴾ for what Allah will do to you because of your obstinacy and your denial of the signs. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "A sign from his Lord" means a sign that compels people to faith. This kind of sign was never brought by any prophet, and compulsory miracles are not of this kind. Rather, signs are exposed to reflection, so that some people are guided and others go astray. So say, "The unseen belongs only to Allah. If He wills, He does it; if He wills, He does not. No one has access to His unseen in this matter." His saying "So wait" is a threat, and Allah fulfilled it by granting victory to Muhammad (ﷺ). It has also been said that the sign they demanded is what His saying, may He be exalted, includes: ﴿They said, "We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush forth for us"﴾ [al-Isra' 17:90], and so on. It has also been said that it is a sign like the signs of Musa and 'Isa, such as the staff, the white hand, and the raising of the dead. They asked for this out of perverse obstinacy.

﴿And when We let people taste mercy after adversity has touched them, behold, they have a scheme against Our signs. Say, "Allah is swifter in planning." Indeed Our messengers record what you plot﴾: (p-136) When He, may He be exalted, mentioned His saying, ﴿And when Our clear signs are recited to them, those who do not hope for meeting Us say﴾ [Yunus 10:15], and so on, and then mentioned His saying, ﴿They say, "Why has no sign been sent down to him?"﴾ [al-An'am 6:37], in the manner of obstinate challenge, He informed that these people only utter these statements when they are in ease of life and freedom from worry. They repay Allah's kindness with what is not permissible, namely seeking to scheme against His signs, though they should have been the first to believe in His signs. Their turning away from the signs is similar to His saying: ﴿So when We remove his harm, he passes on as though he had never called upon Us for a harm that touched him﴾ [Yunus 10:12].

The occasion of revelation was that when the Messenger (ﷺ) invoked a drought upon the people of Makka, they suffered famine for seven years. Abu Sufyan came to him and said, "Pray for us for abundance, and if we are blessed with abundance we will believe." So he asked Allah on their behalf, and they received rain, but they did not believe. Although this verse concerns the disbelievers, it also includes disobedient people who do not give thanks to Allah when the hardship is removed from them, and who are not restrained from their sins by it. This is very common among people. You find a person, when the harm touches him, resolving on repentance and on abandoning all sins; but when it is lifted from him, he returns to his worst habits. Mercy here means rain after drought, safety after fear, health after sickness, wealth after poverty, and whatever is similar to these. The meaning of "touched them" (massat-hum) is that it mixed with them until they felt the evil effect of it upon them. The meaning of ﴿a scheme against Our signs﴾ is denial of the Qur'an and doubt about it, as the majority said. Mujahid and Muqatil said it is mockery and denial. Abu 'Ubayda said it is rejection and repudiation. Al-Mawardi reported hypocrisy, because it is displaying faith and concealing disbelief. This is similar to what al-Zamakhshari said: that scheming (makr) is the most hidden of plots. Ibn 'Atiyya said: scheming is mockery and disparagement of them by the disbelievers, and abandoning gratitude and fear by the disobedient. End of quotation. Here "letting taste" (adhaqa) and "touching" (massa) are both figurative. In this sentence there is evidence of how swiftly the son of Adam shifts from a state of good to a state of evil. This is conveyed by the word "We let taste," as if it were said: the first taste of mercy, before one persists in relishing it, is followed by something hateful. The word "min" (from), which indicates the starting point, shows that the scheme arises immediately after the removal of the harm; there is no delay. And by the word "idha" (behold), the sudden conditional particle that is the answer to the conditional "idha" (when), meaning that at the moment of letting taste mercy, they are suddenly confronted with scheming. Since this sentence, as we have said, includes the swiftness of their scheming, it is said: ﴿Say, "Allah is swifter in planning,"﴾ so the comparative form (af'al al-tafdil) is used. The meaning of describing scheming with swiftness is that before they plan their stratagems, He, may He be exalted, has already decreed your punishment, and He is the one who will bring it upon you, and He has led you on gradually by granting you respite. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Aswara" is from "sara'a" (to be swift), and not from "asra'a yusri'u" (to hasten). He said: Abu 'Ali reported this. If it were from "asra'a," it would be irregular, but the Prophet (ﷺ) said about the fire of Hell: "It is blacker than tar," and what is transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ) is not irregular. End of quotation. It has also been said that "aswara" here is not comparative, and this is reported from Abu 'Ali. It is a valid opinion. Regarding the formation of the exclamative and of the comparative from "af'ala," there are three views: a prohibition absolutely, and whatever occurs of that is irregular; permission absolutely; and a distinction between whether the hamza in it is for transitivity (naql), in which case it is forbidden, or not for transitivity, in which case it is permitted, as in "ashkala al-amr" (the matter became unclear) and "azlama al-layl" (the night became dark). The correct statement on this is in the science of grammar. As for comparing "aswadu min al-qar" (blacker than tar) with "aswara," it is unsound, because "aswad" does not have a verb of the form "af'ala." Rather, it is of the form "fa'ula," like "sawuda," so "fa huwa aswad." The exclamative and the comparative form from "af'ala" were not prohibited according to the Basrans, except because it is a colour, and some Kufans permitted that for colours in general, and some only for black and white.

The messengers here are the recording angels, without disagreement. The meaning is that what you think is hidden and concealed from Allah is not hidden from Him, and He will take vengeance upon you. Al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq, and Abu 'Amr read "rusulana" with a lightened pronunciation. Al-Hasan, Qatada, Mujahid, al-A'raj, and something reported from Nafi' read "yamkurun" (they scheme) in the third person, following what preceded. Abu Raja', Shayba, Abu Ja'far, Ibn Abi Ishaq, 'Isa, Talha, al-A'mash, al-Jahdari, Ayyub ibn al-Mutawakkil, Ibn Muhaysin, Shibl, the people of Makka, and the Seven (al-Sab'a, the seven canonical readers) read it with the letter "ta" in the second person, as an emphasis upon them in informing them of the state of their scheming, and as a shift (iltifat) to His saying "Say, 'Allah'," that is, say to them, so the address fits. In His saying ﴿Indeed Our messengers﴾ there is also a shift, since it did not come as "Indeed His messengers." Ayyub ibn al-Mutawakkil said, in the codex (mushaf) of Ubayy: "O people, indeed Allah is swifter in planning, and indeed His messengers are with you, recording what you scheme." This should be understood as an explanation, because it contradicts what the Muslims have agreed upon in the written text of the mushaf. What is transmitted from Ubayy is the recitation and teaching according to the written text of the mushaf.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 10, verse 22:

﴿He it is Who enables you to travel on land and sea; until, when you are in the ships and they sail with them by a good wind and they rejoice therein, there comes upon them a violent wind, and the waves come upon them from every place, and they think they are encompassed, they call upon Allah, making their religion sincerely His: "If You deliver us from this, we will surely be among the thankful."﴾: The connection (munasabah) of this verse with what precedes it is that when He, exalted is He, mentioned that when harm touches people they turn to Allah, the Exalted, but when He lets them taste mercy, they return to their habit of neglecting the side of Allah and scheming against His signs. Before that, He had mentioned something similar in His saying: ﴿And when harm touches man﴾ [Yunus: 12], and so on. What was mentioned in the two verses was a general matter, and Allah, the Exalted, clarified that general matter with a clear example that reveals the reality of that general meaning, in which a person's hope is cut off from every attachment except Allah, the Exalted; so he sincerely makes supplication to Him alone to remove this calamity, which none removes but He, the Exalted, and the invalidity of worshipping what neither harms nor benefits, and the claim that it is their intercessor with Allah, becomes evident. Then, after the removal of this calamity, they return to their habit of transgression on the earth. So His, the Exalted, deliverance of them is an example of one whom He has let taste mercy, and what they were in before, of being on the brink of destruction, is an example of the harm that touched them. Zayd ibn Thabit, al-Hasan, Abu al-'Aliyah, Zayd ibn 'Ali, Abu Ja'far, 'Abdullah ibn Jubayr, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, Shaybah, and Ibn 'Amir read (yanshurukum) from al-nashr (spreading) and al-bath (dispersing). Al-Hasan also read (yunshirukum) from al-inshar, which is giving life, and this is the reading of 'Abdullah. Some of the Syrians read (yunashshirukum) with the doubled letter, for intensiveness, from al-nashr, which is the reflexive of al-intishar. The rest of the Seven and the majority read (yusayyirukum) from al-taysir. Abu 'Ali said: it is a doubling for intensification (mubalaghah), not a doubling for transitivity, because the Arabs say: sirtu al-rajula and sayyartuhu, and from it is the saying of the Hudhali:

﴿So do not grieve over a custom that you have traveled, for the first to be content with a custom is the one who travels it.﴾

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: there is an objection to this verse so that it would not be evidence for this, namely that the pronoun is like the adverbial noun, as you say: sirtu al-tariq (I traveled the road). End of quotation. What Abu 'Ali mentioned is not necessarily so; rather, the apparent meaning is that the doubling in it is for transitivity, because (sara al-rajulu) intransitive is more common than (sirtu al-rajula) transitive, so taking it as derived from the more common is better than taking it as derived from the less common. As for Ibn 'Atiyyah's view that the pronoun is like the adverbial noun, saying "as you say: sirtu al-tariq," this is not permissible according to the majority, because al-tariq for them is a restricted adverbial noun like al-dar and al-masjid, so the verb does not reach it except with ghayr (dakhaltu according to Sibawayh, and intalaqtu and dhahabat according to al-Farra') without the mediation of "fi," except in cases of necessity. If that is so, then its pronoun is even more deserving of not having the verb reach it directly. And if the adverbial noun to which the verb reaches directly reaches it through the mediation of "fi" unless it is used in a broader sense, then it is more fitting that the pronoun to which the verb reaches its apparent form through "fi" should reach it through the mediation of "fi." Ibn al-Tarawah claimed that (al-tariq) is an unrestricted adverbial noun, so the verb reaches it without the mediation of "fi," and this claim is rejected in grammar.

The meaning of (yusayyirukum) is: makes you travel, and travel is well known. In His saying (wal-bahr) there is an indication of the permissibility of sailing the sea. Since fear at sea is more prevalent for a person than on land, the example for that general meaning, namely the servant turning to his Lord, the Exalted, in a state of hardship and neglecting Him in a state of ease, was given through it. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say, how did He make being in the ships the goal (ghayah) of the travel at sea, when travel at sea is only by being in the ships? I say: He did not make being in the ships the goal of the travel, but the content of the conditional clause that follows "hatta" is with its predicate; as if He said: He makes you travel until, when this event occurs and there is such-and-such from the coming of the violent wind, the piling up of the waves, the thought of destruction, and the calling for deliverance. End of quotation. This is good. Abu al-Darda' and Umm al-Darda' read (fi al-fulkiyy) with the addition of the nisbah ya', and this is explained by its addition, as they added it in adjectives such as ahmariyy and zawariyy, and in proper nouns as in the saying of al-Saltan:

﴿I am al-Saltani, whom you know well.﴾

And with the intention of the nisbah meaning al-lujj (the deep sea), as if it were said "fi al-lujj al-fulkiyy," which is the abundant water in which ships alone sail. The pronoun in (wa-jarayna) refers to (al-fulk), in terms of its plural sense, since al-fulk, as was mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah, may be singular and plural. The pronoun in "bihim" refers to those who are in the ships. This is a shift (iltifat), since it is a movement from address (khitab) to third person (ghaybah). The purpose of turning the speech from address to third person, al-Zamakhshari said: exaggeration, as if He is describing their condition to others so as to amaze them and to invite from them denunciation and reproach. End of quotation. What appears, and Allah knows best, is that the wisdom of the shift here is that His saying: ﴿He it is Who enables you to travel on land and sea﴾ is an address containing favour and the display of a blessing to those addressed, and those who travel on land and sea are both believers and disbelievers, and the address is inclusive; so it is fitting to address them with this so that the righteous may persist in thankfulness, and perhaps the wicked may remember this blessing and return. When a state was mentioned whose outcome concerns the one involved in it being one who transgresses on the earth without right, He turned away from address to third person, so that the believers would not be addressed with the occurrence of such a state whose end is transgression. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "bihim" is a movement from presence to third person, and this is good because His saying: ﴿while you are in the ships﴾ is in the intelligible sense, until some of you have come to be in the boats; so it is as if he assumed a singular absent noun to which the pronoun refers, and it becomes like His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿or like darknesses in a deep sea which is covered by a wave﴾ [al-Nur: 40], i.e., or like one in darknesses, so the pronoun returned third person to a third-person noun, and therefore this is not from the category of shift. The "bi" in "bihim" and in (bi-rih) — al-'Ukbari said: both "ba's" are connected to (jarayna). End of quotation. What appears is that the "ba'" in "bihim" is connected to (jarayna) in the manner of connection to the object, as in: marartu bi-Zayd, and that the "ba'" in (bi-rih) may be causal, so the meanings of the two "ba's" differ, and so it is permissible that both connect to a single verb. It may also be that the "ba'" is of state, i.e., "and they ran with them while being accompanied by a good wind," so it is connected to an omitted element, as you say: "Zayd came with his garments," i.e., accompanied by them. As for ﴿and they rejoiced therein﴾ [al-Rum: 36], it may be conjoined to His saying: ﴿and they ran with them﴾, and it may be a state, i.e., "and they had rejoiced therein." Just as His saying (wa-jarayna) may be conjoined to (kuntum), and may be a state. The apparent meaning is that His saying: ﴿there comes upon them a violent wind﴾ is the response (jawab) of "idha". The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in (ja'atha) refers to the ships, because it is what is spoken of in His saying: ﴿and they ran with them﴾. Mujahid said so, and they permitted that it refers to the good wind, as al-Farra' said, and al-Zamakhshari began with it. The meaning of the goodness of the wind is the gentleness of its blowing and its being favourable. Ibn Abi 'Abla read (ja'atahum). The meaning of ﴿from every place﴾ is from the places of the waves. The word "zann" here is in its original sense of preponderance of one of two possibilities. It was said: its meaning is certainty. The meaning of ﴿they are encompassed﴾ is: for destruction, as an enemy encompasses one whom he wishes to destroy, and it is a metaphor for the seizing of the causes of destruction. Zayd ibn 'Ali read (huyita bihim), as a triliteral. The clause from His saying (da'awu Allah) — Abu al-Baqa' said: it is the answer to what the meaning contains of the sense of a condition, its estimate being: when they thought they were encompassed, they called upon Allah. End of quotation, and it is a statement from which nothing is attained. Al-Tabari said: the answer to ﴿until, when you are in the ships﴾ is ﴿there comes upon them a violent wind﴾, and the answer to His saying ﴿and they thought they were encompassed﴾ is (da'awu Allah). End of quotation. This contradicts the apparent meaning, because His saying (wa-zannu) apparently is conjoined to the answer of "idha", since it is conjoined to (kuntum), but it is open to possibility, as you say: "If so-and-so visits you, honour him, and if Khalid comes to you, treat him well," as if the conditional particle were mentioned. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is a substitute (badal) for "zannu," because their claim is among the necessary consequences of their thinking of destruction, so it is connected to it. End of quotation. Our teacher Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr used to derive this verse otherwise than what they mentioned, and he would say: it is the answer to an implied question, as if it were said: "What was their state at that time?" So it was said: they called upon Allah, making their religion sincerely His. End of quotation. The meaning of sincerity (ikhlas) is singling Him out in supplication without associating idols or anything else, as Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Zayd said. Al-Hasan said: "mukhlisin" means not sincerity of faith, but out of knowledge that none will deliver them from that except Allah, so that would be like involuntary faith. End of quotation. Acknowledgment of Allah is inherent in the natures of the world, and they are naturally inclined to hold that He is the one who disposes of things; therefore, when realities become clear, they all return to Him, believer and disbeliever alike.

﴿If You deliver us﴾: there is an omitted oath, and that oath and what follows it are reported by a verb of saying, i.e., saying. Or (da'aw) is treated as (qalu), since it is a kind of speech. The demonstrative "hadhihi" refers to the hardships in which they are. Al-Kalbi said: it refers to the violent wind.

(p-140) ﴿So when He had delivered them, behold, they committed outrage in the earth without right. O mankind, your outrage is only against yourselves—the enjoyment of the worldly life. Then to Us is your return, and We will inform you of what you used to do.﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas said: "They commit outrage by calling to the worship of other than Allah, and by acting in disobedience and corruption." Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you say, what is the meaning of His words ﴿without right﴾, when outrage cannot be with right? I say: Yes, it can be; it is the Muslims' seizing of the land of the disbelievers, demolishing their homes, burning their crops, and cutting down their trees, as the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did to the Banu Qurayza." End of quote. It seems that he explained His words "they outrage" (yabghūna) as meaning that they cause corruption, and are sent forth, proceeding in it and going to excess in it, from baghā al-jurḥ (the wound spread) when it progresses toward corruption. End of quote. Al-Zajjaj said: "Al-baghy is progression in corruption." Al-Asmaʿi said: "The wound baghā, meaning it progressed toward corruption, and the woman baghat, meaning she committed fornication." End of quote. It is not correct to say of the Muslims that they are transgressors against the disbelievers, unless it is mentioned that the原 root meaning of al-baghy is seeking in general and does not include corruption; then it is divided into seeking with right and seeking without right. When Ibn ʿAtiyya understood al-baghy here as corruption, he said: "He emphasized that by His words ﴿without right﴾."

The answer to "lamma" (when) is "idha" al-fujaʾiyya (the sudden "idha") and what follows it. The coming of "idha" and what follows it as its answer is evidence that it is a particle which orders what follows, as answer, upon what precedes it, the verb that comes after "lamma"; and that it conveys sequence and conditionality in the past. As Sibawayh said, it is a particle (ḥarf). The view of others is that it is an adverb (ẓarf), and we have clarified this in what we wrote on the science of grammar. The answer with the sudden "idha" is evidence that their outrage was not delayed after their deliverance; rather, at the very moment the deliverance occurred, the outrage occurred. As for the address "O mankind" (yā ayyuhā al-nās): the majority said it is addressed to the people of Mecca. What appears is that it is addressed to those whom Allah delivered and who then committed outrage, and it may, as they said, carry generality, so that those people are included within it; and this is a censure of outrage in the most concise wording. The meaning of "against yourselves" ('alā anfusikum): the burden of the outrage falls upon you, and none gathers its fruit except you. Thus His words "against yourselves" are the predicate of the subject which is "your outrage" (baghyukum), and it is connected to an omitted element. On this reading, "matāʿa" was put in the accusative in the reading of Zayd ibn ʿAli, Hafs, Ibn Abi Ishaq, and Harun, from Ibn Kathir: as a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial (ḥāl), meaning "enjoying," or remaining as a verbal noun, meaning "they enjoy it as enjoyment," or in the accusative as an adverb of time, like "maqdim al-ḥājj," meaning "at the time of the enjoyment of the worldly life." All these interpretations are transmitted. The governing element of "matāʿa," when it is a circumstantial or adverb, is what is connected to the predicate of "your outrage," meaning "being upon yourselves"; they are not in the accusative governed by "baghyukum," because it is a verbal noun separated from its complement by the predicate, which is not permissible. "Matāʿu" was put in the nominative in the reading of the majority, as the predicate of an omitted subject. Al-Nahhas permitted, and al-Zamakhshari followed him, that ﴿upon yourselves﴾ be connected to His words "your outrage," as it was connected in His words ﴿so he transgressed against them﴾ [al-Qasas: 76], and the predicate would be "matāʿ" if you put it in the nominative. The meaning of ﴿upon yourselves﴾: upon your like, and those whose kind is your kind, meaning: the outrage of some of you against others is the enjoyment of the worldly life. Ibn Abi Ishaq also read: "matāʿan al-ḥayāta al-dunyā," with "matāʿan" in the accusative and tanwin, and "al-ḥayāta" in the accusative.
