Sufyan ibn ʿUyayna said regarding this clause: "Its punishment will be hastened for you in the worldly life." A group read "fa-yunabbi'ukum" with the yāʾ, in the third person, and the intended referent is Allah the Exalted.

(p-141) The occasion of revelation of this verse in relation to what precedes it: when He, exalted is He, said, ﴿O people, your rebellion is only against yourselves; it is the enjoyment of the life of this world﴾ [Yunus: 23], He struck a wondrous and strange parable for the life of this world, depicting one who rebels in it, the swiftness of its passing and its ending, and that it is, at the very moment it is most honoured and most pleasing, dwindling, and its affair ends in annihilation.

Al-Zamakhshari said: This is from the compound comparison (al-tashbih al-murakkab, a comparison in which the whole image is likened to another whole image). The state of the world, in the swiftness of its passing and the extinction of its delights after they have come, is likened to the state of the earth's vegetation (p-142) in its drying and its going away as crumbled debris, after it had grown thick and dense and had adorned the earth with its greenness and its shimmering. End of quote.

Here, "innama" is not restrictive, neither in its lexical form nor in its usage, because He, exalted is He, struck other parables for the life of this world besides this one. The word "mathal" here may mean a description (sifa), or it may mean a well-known saying in which the state of the second is likened to the state of the first.

The apparent meaning is the comparison of the attribute of the life of this world to water, in respect of what it is by way of benefit, and what follows from it of benefit and then of cessation. It has been said: the life of this world is likened to vegetation, with these same attributes, so the sense is "like the vegetation of water," and the word for "water" is elided (al-mudaf mahdhuf, the elision of the genitive-governing noun). 

It has been said: the life of this world is likened to a hypothetical life (p-143) with these attributes, so the sense is "like the life of a people, [with] water which We sent down from the sky." It has been said: this is strengthened by His words, "and its people thought that they were able to control it."

As for "al-sama'" (the sky/heaven), it may mean the clouds, or it may mean the direction of the sky. The apparent meaning is that the vegetation mingled with the water. The meaning of "ikhtilat" (mingling) is its clinging to the water, its taking hold of it, and its receiving it, because it serves for it as nourishment; so the "ba'" here is for accompaniment (li-l-musahaba).

Of any two things that mingle, it is correct to say of each of them that it mingled with its companion. For this reason some of them explained it with the words: the water mixed with it and entered into it, so that it nourished every part of it. Al-Karmani said: "fa-ikhtalata bihi" means mingling of proximity (ikhtilat mujawara, mingling by contiguity), because ikhtilat is the interpenetration of things one within another. End of quote.

It is not impossible for the vegetation to mingle with the water by way of interpenetration, so one should not say that it is mere mingling by proximity.

It has been said: "ikhtalata" means it differed and varied with the water; but the wording "ikhtalata" does not naturally bear this interpretation. It has been said: the meaning of "ikhtalata" is that it was compounded; it has been said: it stretched out and lengthened. Al-Zamakhshari said: so it became intertwined because of it, until some of it mixed with some of it. Ibn 'Atiyya said: a group joined the vegetation to His words "fa-ikhtalata," meaning: the vegetation mingled one part with another because of the water. End of quote.

On these views, the "ba'" in "bi-ma'" is causal (li-l-sababiyya, indicating cause). The one who went furthest astray was the one who held that the subject of "fa-ikhtalata" is a pronoun referring to the water, meaning: "the water mingled with the earth." This person would stop at "fa-ikhtalata" and begin afresh with "bihi nabatu" as a new sentence, with the predicate placed first.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: on this view it is possible that the pronoun in "bihi" refers to the water and to the mingling that is contained in the verb. End of quote.

Stopping at "fa-ikhtalata" is not permitted, especially in the Qur'an, because it dismembers a connected and sound speech, eloquent in its wording, and it leads to riddle, convolution, and weak meaning. Consider: if one were to state explicitly the noun which the pronoun stands for, saying "with the mingling, the vegetation of the earth," or "with the water, the vegetation of the earth," the sentence would scarcely form a complete subject and predicate, because this predication is weak and close to not conveying meaning. Had Ibn 'Atiyya not mentioned it and interpreted it as we have reported from him, we would not have mentioned it in our book.

Since vegetation divides into what is eaten and what is not, He clarified that the intended meaning is one of the two categories, by using "min" (of/from), saying: "of what men eat," such as grains, fruits and herbs; "and livestock," such as grass and all that is grazed.

Al-Hawfi said: "min" is related to "ikhtalata." Abu al-Baqa' said: "mimma ya'kulu" is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the vegetation. The statement of Abu al-Baqa' implies that the operator of the circumstantial clause is elided, because when a prepositional phrase and an adverbial phrase occur as circumstantial clauses, the operator is elided.

Abu al-Baqa's statement is the apparent one, and its estimate is: "being of what men eat." "Hatta" (until) is a limit (ghaya, a terminal point), so the verb that precedes it must be extended for the limit to be valid. Either something elided is supposed before it, meaning: "it continued to grow until, when," or the verb "fa-ikhtalata" is used figuratively, and its meaning is: "the mingling of the vegetation with the water continued until, when."

His words, "the earth took on its adornment and became beautiful," form a wondrous phrase: the earth is made to be one taking its finery and adorning itself. This is by way of imagery of a bride, when she takes fine garments of every colour and clothes herself and adorns herself with various kinds of jewellery. The verb "akhadha" (to take), which is grasping with the hand, is used metaphorically for the vegetation of the earth's containing brilliance, freshness, and garments of varied colours; and the word "zukhruf," which is gold, is used metaphorically for that brilliance, freshness, and varied colours, since it is among things pleasing to look at and delightful to souls.

"Wazzayyanat": that is, with its vegetation and what was deposited in it of grains, fruits and blossoms. It is possible that His words "wazzayyanat" are an emphasis of His words "the earth took its adornment." It is also possible that it is not an emphasis, since taking adornment may occur without the intention of beautifying; so "wazzayyanat" was said to make clear that it intended beautification.

Attributing the taking to the earth and the beautifying is a wondrous metaphor (isti'ara, metaphor). The majority read "wazzayyanat," whose original form is "tazayyanat." The "ta'" was assimilated into the "zay," so a connecting hamza was brought in because the "zay" needed to be made quiescent at the point of assimilation.

Ubayy, 'Abd Allah, Zayd ibn 'Ali, and al-A'mash read "wa-tazayyanat," on the pattern of "tafa''alat."

Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, Ibn Ya'mar, al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi, Abu al-'Aliya, Qatada, Nasr ibn 'Asim, Ibn Hurmuz, and 'Isa al-Thaqafi read "wa-azyanat," on the pattern of "af'alat" (p-144), like "ahsada al-zar'u," meaning its adornment appeared and drew near.

The "ya'" is sound here by way of rarity, as in "a'balat al-mar'a" (the woman became fat/plump). The analogical form would be "wa-azanat," like your saying "wa-abanat." Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi read with a fatha on the hamza in the pattern of "if'a'allat," as reported from him by the author of al-Lawami'. He said: as if it had originally been in the pattern of "ihmarrat," but they disliked the joining of two quiescent letters, so the alif was moved and became a fatha-marked hamza. Ibn 'Atiyya ascribed this reading to a group, saying: a group read "wazyan'nat," and it is a dialect of theirs; the poet said:

"When the front ranks reddened with fresh blood."

Shaykhs of 'Awf ibn Abi Jamila read "wazyanna't," with a doubled nun and a quiescent alif before it. Ibn 'Atiyya said: this is the reading of Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi.

A group read "wazzaya-nat," and the original is "tazayyanat," which was assimilated. The verb "zann" here retains its original sense, being the preference of one of two permissible options. It has been said: it means "they were certain," but this is not correct. The meaning of "power over it" is the ability to obtain its produce and its benefit and to raise its yield, and this is because of the goodness of its growth and its freedom from blights.

The pronoun in "ahliha" refers back to the earth, and it is by elision of a genitive noun, meaning: the people of its vegetation. It has been said: the pronoun refers back to the yield. It has been said: it refers back to the adornment, but this is weak.

The answer to "idha" is His words, "Our command came to it," such as the wind, the freezing blast, the scorching wind, and other calamities like mice and locusts. It has been said: "Our command came to it" means its destruction; and it is left indefinite in His words "by night or by day," although God, exalted is He, knows when His command comes to it. "Aw" (or) here is for variety (li-l-tanwi', indicating distribution), because some of the earth has His command come to it by night and some by day, and no existent thing is outside its occurring in one of these two.

"Al-hasid" is on the pattern "fa'il" in the sense of "maf'ul," meaning "that which is reaped," and it is not feminized, just as "jarih" is not feminized for a wounded woman. Abu 'Ubayda said: "al-hasid" is that which has been uprooted. End of quote.

He expressed "hasid" (harvested) for "sparse" as a metaphor: He made what perished of the crop through blight before its time a harvest, because of the connection between them through being cast down on the earth.

It has been said: it is permissible for it to be a comparison without a particle of comparison, and the sense is: "so We made it like the harvest." His words, "as if it had not flourished yesterday," are hyperbole about the destruction and ruin, to the extent that it is as if it had not existed before, and no brilliance, greenness or freshness remained on the earth to gladden its people.

Al-Hasan and Qatada read "ka'an lam yaghna" with the "ya'" in the masculine. It has been said: it refers back to the elided genitive noun, which is "the crop"; the elided noun was dropped and the feminine "ha'" took its place in His words "'alayha" and in His words "atahа" and "fa-ja'alnaha." It has been said: it refers back to the finery, but the better view is that it refers back to "al-hasid," meaning: "as if the harvest had not flourished."

Marwan ibn al-Hakam used to read from the pulpit "ka'an lam tatagħgħan" with two "ta's," like "tatafa''al." Al-A'sha said: "long in staying, long in its flourishing." It derives from "ghaniya bi-kadha," meaning "he stayed in it." Al-Zamakhshari said: "al-amsu" (yesterday) is a figure for a time. As if it were said: "as if it had not flourished just now." End of quote.

"Al-amsu" is not an expression for an absolute time, nor is it synonymous with "a'nifan" (just now), because "a'nifan" means "the present hour," whereas the meaning here is: "as if it had had no existence in the time that has passed."

Were someone to say outside the Qur'an, "as if it had had no existence this hour," this meaning would not be sound, because it has no existence this hour. How can something that has no real existence be compared to something that has no real existence? What is compared is something whose existence is now non-existent to something whose non-existence is assumed in past time, because of how swiftly it passes from the state of existence to the state of non-existence, so that it is as if the state of existence never preceded it.

In the codex of Ubayy: "as if it had not flourished yesterday, and We did not destroy it except for the sins of its people." In al-Tahrir: "We detail the signs," which Ibn 'Abbas transmitted from him. It has also been said that in his codex: "and God would not destroy it except for the sins of its people," and in al-Tahrir.

Abu Salama ibn 'Abd al-Rahman used to read, in Ubayy's reading: "as if it had not flourished yesterday, and We did not destroy it except for the sins of its people." It is not fitting for anyone to recite with this reading, because it contradicts the written text of the codex on which the Companions and the Successors agreed. End of quote.

﴿Thus do We detail the signs for a people who give thought﴾: that is, like this detailing which We have set forth in the past, We will detail in the future.

Abu al-Darda' read "li-qawmin yatadhakkarun" with a dhal in place of the fa'.

(p-145) Having mentioned the parable of the life of this world, and what it comes to in the end of perishing and vanishing, and the calamities and defects it contains, God, exalted is He, mentioned that He calls to the abode of safety, health and security, which is Paradise, since its people are safe from every hateful thing.

It is permissible that God, exalted is He, attributed the abode to His noble Name as a means of magnifying and honouring it, as it is said: "the House of God" and "the she-camel of God." It is also permissible that the abode is attributed to salam (safety) in the sense of greeting, because greeting was widespread among them, and because of the angels' greeting upon them, as He said: ﴿They will not hear therein any idle talk or sinful speech﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 25] ﴿except the word "Peace, peace"﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 26].

Al-Hasan said: Peace (salam) never ceases for the people of Paradise, and it is their greeting, as God, exalted is He, said: (Their greeting therein will be "Peace"). Traditions have also been transmitted concerning God's call to His servants.

Qatadah said: It has been related to us that in the Torah it is written: "O seeker of good, come forward; O seeker of evil, desist."

Since the call is general, it was not restricted by the will (of God), and since guidance is specific, it was restricted by the will, so He said: ﴿and guides whom He wills﴾.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "and guides" means: grants success to whom He wills, and they are those whom He knows that divine grace (lutf) will benefit, because His will follows His wisdom.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 10, verse 26–31 (part 1 of 3):

﴿For those who did good is the best (reward) and more. Neither dust nor humiliation will cover their faces. Those are the companions of the Garden; therein they will abide forever.﴾ ﴿As for those who earned evil deeds, the recompense of an evil deed is its like, and humiliation will cover them. They will have no protector from Allah. It is as if their faces were covered with pieces of the dark night. Those are the companions of the Fire; therein they will abide forever.﴾ ﴿And (remember) the Day We will gather them all together, then We will say to those who associated others with Allah: "Stay in your place, you and your partners." Then We will separate them, and their partners will say: "You did not worship us."﴾ ﴿So Allah is sufficient as a witness between us and you; we were indeed unaware of your worship.﴾ ﴿There every soul will experience what it has sent ahead, and they will be returned to Allah, their true Master, and what they used to fabricate will be lost from them.﴾ ﴿Say: "Who provides for you from the heaven and the earth? Or who controls hearing and sight? And who brings forth the living from the dead and brings forth the dead from the living? And who arranges the affair?" They will say: "Allah." Say: "Will you not then fear (Him)?"﴾ ﴿So that is Allah, your true Lord. What is there after the truth except error? So how are you turned away?﴾ ﴿Thus the word of your Lord has been justified against those who defied, that they will not believe.﴾ ﴿Say: "Is there any of your partners who originates creation then repeats it?" Say: "Allah originates creation then repeats it, so how are you deluded?"﴾ ﴿Say: "Is there any of your partners who guides to the truth?" Say: "Allah guides to the truth. Is then He who guides to the truth more worthy to be followed, or he who does not guide unless he is guided? What is wrong with you? How do you judge?"﴾ ﴿Most of them follow nothing but conjecture. Indeed, conjecture avails nothing against the truth. Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what they do.﴾ ﴿And this Qur'an could not have been fabricated other than by Allah, but it is a confirmation of what was before it and a detailed explanation of the Book, about which there is no doubt, from the Lord of the worlds.﴾ ﴿Or do they say, "He has fabricated it"? Say: "Then bring a surah like it, and call upon whomever you can besides Allah, if you are truthful."﴾ ﴿Rather, they denied that which they did not encompass in knowledge, and its interpretation had not yet come to them. Likewise denied those before them. So observe how was the end of the wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿And among them are those who believe in it, and among them are those who do not believe in it. Your Lord is most knowing of the corrupters.﴾ ﴿And if they deny you, say: "For me is my deed, and for you is your deed. You are disassociated from what I do, and I am disassociated from what you do."﴾ ﴿And among them are those who listen to you. Can you make the deaf hear, even if they do not reason?﴾ ﴿And among them are those who look at you. Can you guide the blind, even if they do not see?﴾ ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong the people at all, but the people wrong themselves.﴾ ﴿And (remember) the Day He will gather them, (it will be) as if they had not remained but an hour of the day, recognizing one another. Those have lost who denied the meeting with Allah, and they were not guided.﴾ ﴿And whether We show you part of what We promise them, or We cause you to die, to Us is their return; then Allah is Witness over what they do.﴾ ﴿And for every nation is a messenger. When their messenger comes, the matter will be judged between them with justice, and they will not be wronged.﴾ ﴿And they say, "When is this promise, if you are truthful?"﴾ ﴿Say: "I do not control for myself any harm or benefit, except what Allah wills. For every nation is a term. When their term comes, they will not remain behind it an hour, nor will they precede it."﴾ ﴿Say: "Tell me, if His punishment comes to you by night or by day, what is it that the criminals would hasten?"﴾ ﴿Then, when it has occurred, will you believe in it? Now? And you were (once) asking for it hastily!﴾ ﴿Then it will be said to those who wronged: "Taste the punishment of eternity. Are you recompensed except for what you used to earn?"﴾ ﴿And they ask you, "Is it true?" Say: "Yes, by my Lord, indeed it is true, and you cannot escape (it)."﴾ ﴿And if every soul that wronged had all that is on earth, it would surely offer it for ransom. And they will conceal their regret when they see the punishment. And it will be judged between them with justice, and they will not be wronged.﴾ ﴿Unquestionably, to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth. Unquestionably, the promise of Allah is true, but most of them do not know.﴾ ﴿He gives life and causes death, and to Him you will be returned.﴾ ﴿O mankind, there has come to you an admonition from your Lord and a healing for what is in the breasts, and guidance and mercy for the believers.﴾ ﴿Say: "In the bounty of Allah and His mercy, in that let them rejoice; it is better than what they accumulate."﴾ ﴿Say: "Have you considered what Allah has sent down to you of provision, and you made from it lawful and unlawful?" Say: "Has Allah permitted you, or do you fabricate against Allah?"﴾ ﴿And what will be the thought of those who fabricate against Allah the lie on the Day of Resurrection? Indeed, Allah is full of bounty toward the people, but most of them do not give thanks.﴾ ﴿And you are not engaged in any matter, nor recite from it any Qur'an, nor do you do any deed, but We are witness over you when you are involved in it. And not absent from your Lord is any part of an atom's weight within the earth or within the heaven, nor anything smaller than that or greater, but it is in a clear register.﴾ (p-146) Rahiqa: he covered him, and it is said: he reached him. From it (comes) the verse: ﴿And do not burden me with difficulty in my affair﴾ [al-Kahf: 73]. A man who is murhaq is one whom the guests overwhelm. Al-Azhari said: ar-rahaq is a noun derived from al-irhaq, which is for a person to impose upon himself what he cannot bear.
It is said: arhaqtuhu an yusalliya, if you hurry him away from the prayer. It is also said: the origin of rahaq is closeness; one says: ghulam muraahiq, meaning he has approached puberty. In a hadith: "Arhiqu al-qiblah," meaning: draw near to it. It is said: rahiqat al-kilab as-sayd, when the dogs reached the prey; and arhaqna as-salah, we delayed the prayer until it approached the next.
Al-qatar and al-qatarah: dust accompanied by blackness. Ibn Arafah said: dust. Al-Farazdaq said:
Crowned with the robe of kingship, followed by a wave, above which you see the banners and the qatar.
That is, the dust of the army. Ibn Bahr said: the origin of qatar is the smoke of fire, and from it comes qutar al-qidr (the aroma of the cooking pot), end of quote.
It is also said: qatr, with a sukun on the ta', means matter or affair, its plural is shu'un. Its origin is hamz, meaning intention, from sha'ani sha'nahu, when you intended his intention.
Ghaaba (ya'zubu and ya'zibu, with kasra or damma on the zay): to be absent until hidden, from which comes ar-rawd al-'azib (the pasture far from people). Abu Tammam said:
Qalqal, a distance from Khurasan, its heart (trembling); so I said: be calm, the most blooming of the meadows is what is far from it.
It is said of one absent from his family that he is 'azib, to the point that they say it of one who has no wife.
﴿For those who did good is the best (reward) and more. Neither dust nor humiliation will cover their faces. Those are the companions of the Garden; therein they will abide forever.﴾: "Those who did good" — Ibn Abbas said: they remembered the words "There is no god but Allah." Al-Asamm said: they did good in everything they were worshipped through, i.e., they carried out what was commanded as it should be, and avoided what was forbidden.
It is said: they did good in dealing with people. Anas narrated from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Do good in deeds in this world." And in the Sahih: "What is ihsan? He said: That you worship Allah as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, then He sees you." And from Jesus, peace be upon him: "Ihsan is not that you do good to one who has done good to you; that is repayment! Rather, ihsan is that you do good to one who has wronged you."
As for "al-husna," most of them said it is the Garden, and this was narrated from the Messenger (ﷺ); and if it is authentic, it is obligatory to adopt it.
Al-Tabari said: al-husna is general for every good thing, so it encompasses everything promised by Allah, and in all of it there is an increase. This is also supported by His saying: ﴿Those are the companions of the Garden﴾. If the meaning of al-husna were the Garden, there would be repetition in the statement. Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabit said: it is an-nadrah (radiance).
Ibn Zayd said: the reward in the Hereafter. It is said: the hope/wish; this was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari. Al-Zamakhshari said: the reward is "the best" and "more," and what exceeds the reward is the favour (tafaddul), and this is indicated by His saying: ﴿And He will increase them of His bounty﴾ [an-Nisa': 173]. From Ali: the increase is one pearl-chamber.
From Ibn Abbas: al-husna is the good deed, and the increase is ten times its like. From al-Hasan: ten times its like up to seven hundred fold.
From Mujahid: the increase is forgiveness from Allah and pleasure. From Ziyad ibn Shajarah: the increase is that a cloud passes over the people of the Garden and says: "What do you want me to rain upon you?" They want nothing, except that it rains it upon them.
The Mushabbihah and the Mujbirah claimed that the increase is looking at the Face of Allah, the Exalted, and they brought a fabricated hadith: "When the people of the Garden enter the Garden, they will be called: O people of the Garden! Then they will uncover the veil and look at Him; by Allah, Allah the Exalted has given them nothing more beloved to them than that." End of quote.
As for his interpretation at first and his transmission from those who mentioned the interpretation of the increase, that is the text of al-Jubba'i and his transmission. As for his statement, "it came with a fabricated hadith," it is not fabricated; rather Muslim recorded it in his Sahih from Suhayb, and an-Nasa'i from him from the Messenger (ﷺ). Ibn al-Mubarak recorded it in his Daqa'iq as a mawquf (halted) report from Abu Musa, and he said that the increase is the looking at Allah, the Exalted.
Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, and Ali ibn Abi Talib in one narration, and Hudhayfah, and Ubadah ibn al-Samit, and Ka'b ibn Ujrah, and Abu Musa, and Suhayb, and Ibn Abbas in one narration, and it is the view of a group of the Successors.
The question of the vision is discussed in the principles of religion (usul al-din). Mujahid said: He meant that disgrace will not reach them, and disgrace is what changes the face and makes it blacken.
Ibn Abbas said: "dhillah" is sorrow (al-ka'abah). Others said: humiliation. It was said: failure. He negated for the virtuous what He affirmed for the disbelievers in His saying: ﴿And humiliation will cover them﴾ and His saying: ﴿Upon them will be dust﴾ [Abasa: 40] ﴿Covered by darkness﴾ [Abasa: 41]. And He referred to the face as the whole, because it is the noblest part, and because the traces of joy and sorrow appear in it. Al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Isa ibn Umar, and al-A'mash read qatr with a sukun on the ta', and it is a dialect like qadar and qadr. And they were called "companions of the Garden" because of their disposal within it, as owners dispose of their property according to their choice.
﴿As for those who earned evil deeds, the recompense of an evil deed is its like, and humiliation will cover them. They will have no protector from Allah. It is as if their faces were covered with pieces of the dark night. Those are the companions of the Fire; therein they will abide forever.﴾: When He mentioned what He prepared for those who did good, their state on the Day of Resurrection, and their destination to the Garden, He mentioned what He prepared for their opposites, their state and their destination. The relative clause for the believers is "did good," and the relative clause for the disbelievers is "earned evil deeds," as an indication that the believer, since he was created upon the fitrah and perfected it through ihsan, and the disbeliever, since he was created upon the fitrah but departed from it and earned evil deeds, the one is made a doer of good, and this one an earner of evil, so that it shows the believer followed what is fitting, and this one followed what is not fitting.
The apparent view is that "those who" is a subject (mubtada'), and they permitted several possibilities for the predicate. The first: that the predicate is the clause following it, which is "the recompense of an evil deed is its like," and "recompense" is a subject whose predicate is affirmed as "bi-mithliha" (by its like). They differed about the ba'. It is said it is extra (za'idah), said by Ibn Kaysan, meaning: the recompense of an evil deed is its like, as He said: "and the recompense of an evil deed is an evil deed like it," just as it is added in the predicate in the verse: "So He prevented it with something that can be done," meaning: something that can be done. It is also said: it is not extra, and the estimate is: "determined by its like" or "established by its like." It is also said: it is omitted; al-Hawfi estimated it as: "For them is the recompense of an evil deed," and he said: the indication of the estimate "for them" is His saying: ﴿For those who did good is the best reward﴾, so that this may correspond with that.
Abu al-Baqa' estimated it as: "recompense of an evil deed by its like is due," and the ba' in both their statements is related to the word "recompense," and the returning pronoun from this clause which is the predicate of "those who" is omitted, its estimate being: "recompense of an evil deed from them," as it is omitted in their saying: "Samn manawan bi-dirham" (ghee, two manas for a dirham), meaning: two manas of it for a dirham. And according to al-Hawfi's estimate: "for them is recompense," which serves as the returning pronoun ("for them").
The second: that the predicate is His saying: "They will have no protector from Allah," and it would be that a separation occurred between the subject and the predicate by two clauses in the manner of parenthesis (i'tiraD). This is not permitted according to Abu Ali al-Farisi, and the correct view is that it is permitted.
The third: that the predicate is: "It is as if their faces were covered with pieces of the dark night."

**The fourth: that the predicate is "Those" and what follows it.** In this case, the sentence has four intervening clauses between the subject and predicate. In the third opinion, there are three. The correct view is that inserting three or four clauses between them is not permitted. Ibn 'Atiyya permitted that *alladhina* (those who) be in the genitive position, in apposition to the phrase *lilladhina ahsanu* (for those who did good), with *jaza'* (recompense) as the subject, and *alladhina* as its predicate, with the preposition dropped. The meaning would be: "and for those who earned evil deeds is the recompense of an evil deed like it." Thus the division is balanced, just as you say: *fi al-dar Zayd, wal-qasr 'Amr*, meaning *wa-fi al-qasr 'Amr* (in the house is Zayd, and in the palace is 'Amr).

This construction is attested in the speech of the Arabs. al-Akhfash interpreted it as coordination between two governing elements ('atf 'ala 'amilayn).

The majority (al-Jumhur) interpreted it as a case in which the preposition has been omitted, with the noun governed by that deleted preposition, not by coordination with the preceding genitive noun. This is a matter of disagreement and detail that is discussed in the science of grammar (*'ilm al-nahw*).

The apparent meaning is that *al-sayyi'at* (the evil deeds) here refers to the evil deeds of disbelief, as indicated by the mention of their attributes afterwards. It has been said that *al-sayyi'at* refers to sins, so that disbelief and other sins are included. For this reason Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Here *al-sayyi'at* encompasses both disbelief and sins. The like of the evil deed of disbelief is eternal abiding in the Fire, while the like of the evil deeds of sins is subject to the will of God, the Exalted. The meaning of *bi-mithlaha* (with its like) is that nothing is added to it."

al-Zamakhshari said: "In this there is evidence that the intended meaning of 'increase' is grace (*fadl*), because by not adding to the evil deed He indicated His justice, and by affirming an increase in the reward He indicated His grace."

It has also been said: the meaning of *bi-mithlaha* is: with what befits it of punishments. Punishments are proportioned to the magnitude of evil deeds, and for this reason Hell has levels (*darakat*), and the hypocrites were in the lowest level (*al-darak al-asfal*) because of the ugliness of their disobedience.

It was read *wa-yarhaquhum* with the *ya'* (third person masculine), because the feminization of *al-dhilla* (humiliation) is metaphorical. In the description of the hypocrites there is a negation of *qatar* (dust/gloom) and humiliation from their faces, and here humiliation has covered them. An exaggeration is made regarding what is the opposite of *qatar*, so it is said: "as if their faces had been covered with pieces of the night, dark." This is an exaggeration of the blackness of the faces.

This has been stated explicitly in His saying: ﴿And faces will turn black﴾ [Al 'Imran: 106]. *Min Allah* (from God) means from His wrath and His punishment, or from His direction, and from Him is the one who protects them, just as it is for the believers. *Ughshiyat* means "were covered," from the same root as *al-ghita'* (covering). That their faces are blackened is a literal, not a metaphorical, reality, so their complexions are blackened.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: "Know that the sages of Islam said: the intended meaning of this blackness here is the blackness of ignorance and the darkness of misguidance, for ignorance by its nature is the nature of darkness. So His saying: ﴿Faces that day will be bright﴾ [Abasa: 38], ﴿laughing, rejoicing﴾ [Abasa: 39], the intended meaning is the light of knowledge, its spirit, its joy and its good news. (p-149) ﴿And faces that day will have dust upon them﴾ [Abasa: 40], ﴿darkness will cover them﴾ [Abasa: 41], the intended meaning is the darkness of ignorance and the murkiness of error." End of quote.

This man often transmits from the sages of Islam in tafsir, and sometimes he quotes their words attributed to them, and sometimes he relies on them. By "sages of Islam" he means the philosophers (*hukama' al-falasifa*) who arose during the period of the Islamic religion. They deserve to be called foolish and ignorant rather than sages, for they are enemies of the prophets and distorters of the Islamic Shari'a, and they are more harmful to Muslims than Jews and Christians. If the Commander of the Faithful 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) forbade reading the Torah despite it being a divine book, then forbidding the reading of the words of the philosophers is more deserving. In this era, and shortly before it, occupation with the ignorance of the philosophers has overcome most people, and they call it wisdom (*al-hikma*). They consider those who are free of it to be ignorant, and they believe themselves to be the perfect of men. They devote themselves to studying it, and you can hardly find any of them who memorizes a Qur'an or a hadith from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Once I belittled Ibn Sina and attributed ignorance to him, and one of them said to me, showing amazement at someone belittling Ibn Sina: "How can the most knowledgeable of people about God be attributed to ignorance?" When the judge of the community, Abu al-Walid Muhammad ibn Abi al-Qasim Ahmad ibn Abi al-Walid ibn Rushd, displayed concern for the sayings of the philosophers and reverence for them, the scholars of Islam in al-Andalus incited against him al-Mansur, the ruler of the Almohads, Ya'qub ibn Yusuf ibn 'Abd al-Mu'min ibn 'Ali, king of the Maghrib and al-Andalus, until he inflicted upon him what is well known: beating, cursing, and humiliation, and the humiliation of a group of them, publicly before the eyes of the crowds. Among what was addressed to al-Mansur concerning them was the saying of one of the scholar-poets:

O our Caliph, may Allah reward you with good
on behalf of Islam and your noble striving.
You have struggled in it with the struggle due to it
until you attained the mighty victory.
You have made the people, by good guidance,
to follow the path of the straight way.
So strive against a people who have led astray
the path of the Shari'a with ancient knowledge.
Burn their books in east and west,
for within them lies hidden the worst of sciences.
Their harm creeps into beliefs
like poisons, and beliefs are like bodies.
In such cases, when there is no cure,
the sword becomes the antidote to poisons.

And he said:

O desolation of Islam from a sect
occupied with its own folly,
it has cast the religion of guidance behind it
and claimed wisdom and philosophy.

And he said:

A sect has appeared in our era
whose appearance is a bad omen for the age.
Do not follow in religion except what
Ibn Sina or Abu Nasr has laid down.

When I arrived in the land of Egypt and saw many of its people occupied openly with the ignorance of the philosophers, without anyone denouncing it, I was amazed at this, for we had grown up in the island of al-Andalus disavowing it and denouncing it. When a book on logic (*al-mantiq*) was sold, it was sold secretly, and no one dared to utter the word *mantiq*; they called it *al-maf'al* (the act). Even our friend, the minister of the king Ibn al-Ahmar, Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Rahman known as Ibn al-Hakim, wrote to us a letter from al-Andalus asking me to buy or copy a book by one of our shaykhs on logic. He did not dare to utter the word logic, though he was a minister, so in his letter to me he called it *al-maf'al*.

When their faces were clothed in blackness, He said: "as if their faces had been covered." And since the darkness of night is the ultimate in blackness, the blackness of their faces was likened to pieces of the night at the height of its darkness.

Ibn Kathir and al-Kisa'i read *qit'an* with the *ta'* sukun. It is a singular noun denoting the thing that is cut off. al-Akhfash, regarding His saying ﴿with a portion of the night﴾ [Hud: 81], said: "with a blackness of the night." The lexicographers say: *al-qit'* is the darkness of the last part of the night.

Some said: "a portion of the night." In this reading, *muzlliman* (dark) is an attribute of *qit'an*, as is attested in the reading of Ubayy: "as if there covered their faces a dark portion of the night." Ibn Abi 'Abla read it likewise, except that he made the *ta'* a fatha.

It has also been said: *qit'* is the plural of *qit'a*, like *sidr* and *sidra*, so it is permissible in that case to describe it with the masculine, as in *nakhl munqa'ir* (uprooted palms), and with the feminine, as in *nakhl khawiya* (fallen palms). It is also permissible in this case for *muzlliman* to be a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from *al-layl* (the night), as they parsed it in the reading of the rest of the seven: "as if their faces had been covered with pieces (*qita'an*) of the night, with a fatha on the *ta'*, dark (*muzlliman*) in the accusative."

al-Zamakhshari said: "If you say: when you make *muzlliman* a circumstantial clause from *al-layl*, what is its governing element? I say: it is either that *ughshiyat* (were covered) governs it, because *min al-layl* is an attribute of *qit'an*, so its governance reaches the modified noun as it reaches the attribute; or that it is the meaning of the verb in *min al-layl*. End of quote."

As for the first possibility, it is remote, because the principle is that the governing element of the circumstantial clause should be the governing element of the head noun (*dhu al-hal*), while the governing element of *al-layl* is the stable element reached by *min* (*mustaqarr*), and *ughshiyat* governs *qit'an*, which is described by *min al-layl*. So they differ, and for this reason the last possibility is preferable, namely: *qit'an* (pieces) stationed from the night, or existing from the night in the state of its darkening.

It has also been said: *muzlliman* is a circumstantial clause from *qit'an*, or an attribute. These two analyses were mentioned because *qit'an* has the meaning of "many," so the singular and masculine were taken into account. They also permitted, in the reading of the one who made the *ta'* sukun, that *muzlliman* be a circumstantial clause from *qit'in* and also a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in *min*.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "If it is an attribute, meaning *muzlliman* is an attribute of *qit'in*, then its proper place would be before the clause, but it may come after this, and the estimated clause is: *qit'an istaqarra min al-layl muzlliman*, in the manner of His saying: ﴿And this is a Book We have sent down, blessed﴾ [An'am: 92]. End of quote."

The governing element of the genitive noun is not required to be a verb, making it a clause; rather, the apparent view is that it be estimated as an active participle (*ism al-fa'il*), making it of the type of a descriptive singular, and the estimate is: *qit'an ka'inan min al-layl muzlliman* (pieces existing from the night, dark).

﴿And on the day We gather them all together, then We will say to those who associated partners: "Stay in your place, you and your partners." Then We will separate them, and their partners will say: "You did not used to worship us."﴾ ﴿"Sufficient is God as witness between us and you; we were indeed unaware of your worship."﴾

The pronoun in *nahshuruhum* (We will gather them) refers to those previously mentioned from "those who did good" and "those who earned evil deeds." Al-Hasan, Shayba, and the seven readers read *nahshuruhum* with the *nun*, and a group read it with the *ya'*.

It has been said: the pronoun refers to those who earned evil deeds, among whom are the worshippers of other than God and those who worship nothing. *Yawma* (the day) is in the accusative by an omitted verb, meaning: "remind them," or "warn them," or the like.

*Jami'an* (all together) is a circumstantial clause. *Al-shuraka'* (the partners) are: the devils, or the angels, or the idols, or whoever is worshipped besides God, whatever he may be: four opinions. Whoever said "the idols" said: the spirit is breathed into them, and God makes them speak in that, in place of the intercession on which they set their hopes.

It is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ): "When the disbelievers see the punishment and their means are cut off, it is said to them: 'Follow what you used to worship.' They will say: 'By God, we used to worship you.' Then the gods will say: 'Sufficient is God as witness,' etc."

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "The apparent meaning of this verse is that their dialogue is only with the idols, not with the angels, 'Isa son of Maryam, as indicated by the saying to them: ﴿Stay in your place, you and your partners﴾, nor with Pharaoh and those among the jinn who were worshipped, as indicated by their saying: ﴿we were indeed unaware of your worship﴾. These did not ever become unaware of the worship of those who worshipped them."

*Makanakum* (stay in your place) has been counted by the grammarians among the *asma' al-af'al* (nouns functioning as verbs), and it is estimated as *uthbutu* (remain firm), as in the saying of the poet:

And my saying, whenever she stirs and agitates:
"Stay in your place, you will be praised or you will rest."

That is: "remain firm." Because it has the meaning of "remain firm," *tuhmadi* is apocopated (jussive), and it bears a pronoun, which was emphasized and coordinated with in His saying: *antum wa-shuraka'ukum* (you and your partners).

As for the vowel on *makanaka* and *dunaka*, is it an inflectional vowel (*harakat i'rab*), or a built vowel (*harakat bina'*) that is grounded in the dispute among the grammarians regarding the nouns functioning as verbs: do they have a place in inflection or not? Whoever says: "it is in the accusative position," makes the vowel inflectional; whoever says: "it has no place in inflection," makes it a built vowel. Az-Zamakhshari relied on the first, saying: "*Makanakum*: keep to your place; do not move until you see what will be done to you."

They differed regarding *antum*. The apparent view is what we mentioned, that it is an emphasis of the pronoun concealed in *makanakum*, and *shuraka'ukum* is coordinated with that concealed pronoun. This is az-Zamakhshari's view. He said: "*Antum* emphasizes the pronoun in *makanakum*, because it takes the place of His saying: *ilzamu* (keep to), and *shuraka'ukum* is coordinated with it." End of quote.

He means coordination with the concealed pronoun, and its estimate is: *ilzamu* (keep to), and that *makanakum* has taken its place. The pronoun that is in *ilzamu* is then carried... This is not good, for if it were so, then *makanaka*, which is a noun functioning as a verb, would be transitive just as *ilzamu* is transitive.

Do you not see that when the verbal noun (*ism al-fi'l*, a noun that functions as a verb) stands for an intransitive verb, it is itself intransitive, and when it stands for a transitive verb, it is transitive? An example is *ʿalayka Zaydan* (lit. "upon you, Zayd"): since it takes the place of *ilzam* ("keep to"), it is transitive. And *ilayka*, since it takes the place of *tanaḥḥa* ("step aside"), is not transitive. Because *makānaka* is not transitive, the grammarians estimated it as *uthbut* ("stand firm"), and *uthbut* is not transitive.

Al-Ḥawfī said: *makānakum* is in the accusative by an implied verb, meaning: "Keep to your place," or "Stand firm." Abu al-Baqa' said: *makānakum* is an indeclinable adverb of place, because it occupies the position of an imperative, meaning: "Keep to (your place)." End of quotation.

I have already shown that estimating *ilzamū* ("keep to") is not sound, since the Arabs did not say *makānaka Zaydan* so as to make it transitive, as *ilzam* is transitive. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: *antum* is in the nominative as the subject (*mubtada'*), and its predicate is *makhziyyūn* ("disgraced") or *muhānūn* ("humiliated") or the like. End of quotation.

So *makānakum* would be a complete phrase, and then He informs that they are such-and-such. This is weak, because it severs the apparent flow of speech whose parts are joined together, and because it posits an implied element for which there is no necessity. It also conflicts with His saying: *So We separated them* (*fa-zayyalnā baynahum*), since that indicates that they and their partners stood together in one place until the separation took place between them, which is the parting.

As for the reading of those who read *antum wa-shurakā'akum* with the accusative, it is taken as an object of accompaniment (*maf'ūl maʿahu*), with the verbal noun as its governing element. But if *antum* were a subject (*mubtada'*) whose predicate had been omitted, it would not be permissible for an object of accompaniment to follow it. You say *kull rajul wa-ḍay'atuhu* with the nominative, and the accusative is not permitted there.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya also said: "It is permissible for *antum* to be an emphasis (*taʾkīd*) of the pronoun within the implied verb, which is *qifū* ("stop!") or the like." End of quotation.

This is not sound. If it were an emphasis of that pronoun attached to the verb, it would be permissible to place it before the adverb, since the adverb does not, on this view, bear a pronoun, so it would be necessary to place it after the adverb, which is not permissible. You do not say *anta makānaka*, and it is not transmitted from their speech.

The more correct view is that it is not permissible to omit the emphasized word in a semantic emphasis (*taʾkīd maʿnawī*), and likewise here, because emphasis contradicts omission. It is not from their speech to say *anta Zaydan* to someone you see brandishing a sword, meaning *uḍrib anta Zaydan* ("you, strike Zayd"). Rather, the speech of the Arabs is *Zaydan turīdu uḍrib Zaydan* ("Zayd, you want: strike Zayd").

It is said: *zil al-shay' ʿan makānihi, uzīluhu* ("I removed the thing from its place"). Al-Farrāʾ said: The Arabs say *zil al-ḍaʾn min al-maʿz fa-lam tazul* ("separate the sheep from the goats, but it did not separate"). Al-Wāḥidī said: *al-tazyīl*, *al-tazayyul* and *al-muzāyalah* all mean distinguishing and separating. End of quotation.

*Zayyala* is the intensive form (*mudaʿʿaf*) for intensification. It means separating what is mixed, and its root is from the *ya'* category (*dhawāt al-yā'*), unlike *zāla yazūlu*, so their root letters differ. Ibn Qutayba claimed that *zayyalnā* is from the root of *zāla yazūlu*, and Abu al-Baqa' followed him.

Abu al-Baqa' said: In *fa-zayyalnā*, the middle radical is a *wāw*, because it is from *zāla yazūlu*. It was changed to a *yā'* because the pattern of the word is *fayʿala* (i.e., *zaywalna*), like *bayṭara* and *bayqara*. When the *wāw* and *yā'* came together under the known condition, the *wāw* was changed to a *yā'*. End of quotation.

This is not sound, because *faʿʿala* is more common than *fayʿala*, and because its verbal noun is *tazyīl*. Had it been *fayʿala*, its verbal noun would have been *fayʿalah*, so it would have been *zayyalah* like *bayṭarah*, since *fayʿala* is assimilated to *faʿlala*. Also, for a word close in meaning they say *zāyala* ("separated"), but they did not say *zāwala* with the meaning of separating. *Zāwala* is used in the sense of *ḥāwala* ("tried"), *khālaṭa* ("mixed with"), and *sharaḥa* ("explained").

So *fa-zayyalnā* means: We separated them, cut off their connections, and severed the bonds that existed between them in the world. Or it means: We drove them apart after gathering them together at the place of standing, and between them and their partners, as in His saying: ﴿Where are your partners whom you used to claim?﴾ (Al-Anʿām: 22). They say: "They strayed from us." A group read *fa-zāyalnā*, related by al-Farrāʾ. Al-Zamakhsharī said: It is like your saying *ṣāʿara khaddahu* and *ṣaʿʿara*, and *kālamtuhu* and *kallamtuhu*. End of quotation.

He means that *fāʿala* has the meaning of *faʿʿala*, and *zāyala* in the language of the Arabs means *fāraqa* ("separated"). He said:

*"The young women said: 'You are only our uncle,' while youth was like a companion that departs from him."*

Another said:

*"By my life, for a death with no punishment after it, for one with sorrow—the one who loves does not depart from it, even more than the one who is healed."*

The apparent meaning is that *al-tazyīl* or *al-muzāyalah* is the separation of bodies and their distancing. It has also been said: He separated them in argument and doctrine, as Ibn ʿAṭiyya said. He said: Here "*fa-zayyalnā*" are two verbs in the past tense in form, but the meaning is future: "So We will separate them, and say," because they are coordinated with a future verb. The denial of partners is a rejection of the worship of the polytheists, as their saying: ﴿By God, we were indeed in clear error, when we equated you with the Lord of the worlds﴾ (Al-Shuʿarāʾ: 97–98) ... *(the reference is their saying: "By God, we were in manifest error..." — here the text simply says: "their saying: 'By God, we used to worship you.'")* Its meaning is: You used to worship those who ordered you to take equals to God, and you obeyed them. When they disputed, the partners called God as witness. *Shahīd* is in the accusative. It was said it is a circumstantial accusative (*ḥāl*), but the more correct view is that it is a specificative accusative (*tamyīz*), because it is preceded by *min*.

The discussion of *kafā* and of the *yā'* has preceded, and *in* is the light form of the heavy *inna*. According to the readers, it is the negating particle, and the *lām* has the sense of *illā* ("except"), which has been discussed previously. Their being content with God's testimony is based on the negation that they worshipped them. Then they began a declarative sentence: that they were unaware of their worship, meaning: we have no awareness of that. This supports that the partners are idols, as Ibn ʿAṭiyya said, because if the partners were rational beings, whether human, jinn, or angel, they would have awareness of their worship. Nothing is a greater cause of heedlessness than inanimacy, since it neither perceives nor is aware of anything at all.

﴿There, every soul will be tested for what it sent forth before. And they will be returned to God, their true Master, and what they used to fabricate will be lost to them.﴾

*Hunālika* is an adverb of place, meaning: in that position and standing that calls for bewilderment and astonishment. It has also been said that it refers to time, the place-adverb being used for time, meaning: at that time.

Al-Akhawān (Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī) and Zayd ibn ʿAlī read *tatlū* with two *tā'*s, meaning: it follows and seeks what it sent forth of its deeds, as related from al-Suddī. From this is the poet's saying:

*"Indeed the doubter follows the doubter, as you see the wolf follows the wolf."*

It has been said that it may come from *tilāwah*, meaning recitation: it reads its books that are handed to it. The rest of the seven read *tabluw* with *tā'* and *bā'*, meaning: it tests what it sent forth of deeds, so it knows what they are like: Are they ugly or good? Beneficial or harmful? Accepted or rejected? As a person comes to know a thing through testing it. It is related from ʿĀṣim: *nabluw* with *nūn* and *bā'*, meaning: we test. *Kull nafs* is in the accusative, and *mā aslafat* is an apposition (*badal*) of *kull nafs*, or it is in the accusative by omission of the preposition, meaning: *mā aslafat*. Or *nabluw* may be from *balāʾ*, meaning punishment, meaning: We afflict every disobedient soul with affliction because of what it sent forth of evil deeds. It is related from al-Ḥasan: *tabluw* means: *tatasallamu* ("receives"). From al-Kalbī: *taʿlamu* ("knows"). It has been said: *tadhūfu* ("tastes").

Yaḥyā ibn Wathhāb read *wa-ruddū* with a *kasra* on the *rā'*. When it is made quiescent for assimilation, the vowel of the *dāl* is transferred to the *rā'* after its own vowel is dropped. The meaning of *ilā Allāh* ("to God") is: to His punishment. It has also been said: to the place of His recompense.

*(mawlāhumu al-ḥaqq)* — not what they claimed of their idols, since He is the one who takes charge of their reckoning. He is their master in ownership and encompassing, not in victory and mercy. It is also read *al-ḥaqqa* with the accusative as praise, like: *al-ḥamdu lillāhi ahla al-ḥamd* ("praise belongs to God, deserving of praise"). Al-Zamakhsharī said: Like your saying "This is ʿAbd Allāh the true, not the false," as an emphasis of His saying "returned to God." End of quotation. Abū ʿAbd Allāh al-Rāzī said: "They were returned to God" means they were compelled to acknowledge His divinity, after having worshipped other than God in the world, and for this reason He said: "their true Master." *Ḍalla ʿanhum* means: what they used to fabricate, of falsehood, or of their claim that their idols were partners of God who would intercede for them with Him, was nullified and went away.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 10, verse 26–31 (part 1 of 3):

﴿For those who did good is the best (reward) and more. Neither dust nor humiliation will cover their faces. Those are the companions of the Garden; therein they will abide forever.﴾ ﴿As for those who earned evil deeds, the recompense of an evil deed is its like, and humiliation will cover them. They will have no protector from Allah. It is as if their faces were covered with pieces of the dark night. Those are the companions of the Fire; therein they will abide forever.﴾ ﴿And (remember) the Day We will gather them all together, then We will say to those who associated others with Allah: "Stay in your place, you and your partners." Then We will separate them, and their partners will say: "You did not worship us."﴾ ﴿So Allah is sufficient as a witness between us and you; we were indeed unaware of your worship.﴾ ﴿There every soul will experience what it has sent ahead, and they will be returned to Allah, their true Master, and what they used to fabricate will be lost from them.﴾ ﴿Say: "Who provides for you from the heaven and the earth? Or who controls hearing and sight? And who brings forth the living from the dead and brings forth the dead from the living? And who arranges the affair?" They will say: "Allah." Say: "Will you not then fear (Him)?"﴾ ﴿So that is Allah, your true Lord. What is there after the truth except error? So how are you turned away?﴾ ﴿Thus the word of your Lord has been justified against those who defied, that they will not believe.﴾ ﴿Say: "Is there any of your partners who originates creation then repeats it?" Say: "Allah originates creation then repeats it, so how are you deluded?"﴾ ﴿Say: "Is there any of your partners who guides to the truth?" Say: "Allah guides to the truth. Is then He who guides to the truth more worthy to be followed, or he who does not guide unless he is guided? What is wrong with you? How do you judge?"﴾ ﴿Most of them follow nothing but conjecture. Indeed, conjecture avails nothing against the truth. Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what they do.﴾ ﴿And this Qur'an could not have been fabricated other than by Allah, but it is a confirmation of what was before it and a detailed explanation of the Book, about which there is no doubt, from the Lord of the worlds.﴾ ﴿Or do they say, "He has fabricated it"? Say: "Then bring a surah like it, and call upon whomever you can besides Allah, if you are truthful."﴾ ﴿Rather, they denied that which they did not encompass in knowledge, and its interpretation had not yet come to them. Likewise denied those before them. So observe how was the end of the wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿And among them are those who believe in it, and among them are those who do not believe in it. Your Lord is most knowing of the corrupters.﴾ ﴿And if they deny you, say: "For me is my deed, and for you is your deed. You are disassociated from what I do, and I am disassociated from what you do."﴾ ﴿And among them are those who listen to you. Can you make the deaf hear, even if they do not reason?﴾ ﴿And among them are those who look at you. Can you guide the blind, even if they do not see?﴾ ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong the people at all, but the people wrong themselves.﴾ ﴿And (remember) the Day He will gather them, (it will be) as if they had not remained but an hour of the day, recognizing one another. Those have lost who denied the meeting with Allah, and they were not guided.﴾ ﴿And whether We show you part of what We promise them, or We cause you to die, to Us is their return; then Allah is Witness over what they do.﴾ ﴿And for every nation is a messenger. When their messenger comes, the matter will be judged between them with justice, and they will not be wronged.﴾ ﴿And they say, "When is this promise, if you are truthful?"﴾ ﴿Say: "I do not control for myself any harm or benefit, except what Allah wills. For every nation is a term. When their term comes, they will not remain behind it an hour, nor will they precede it."﴾ ﴿Say: "Tell me, if His punishment comes to you by night or by day, what is it that the criminals would hasten?"﴾ ﴿Then, when it has occurred, will you believe in it? Now? And you were (once) asking for it hastily!﴾ ﴿Then it will be said to those who wronged: "Taste the punishment of eternity. Are you recompensed except for what you used to earn?"﴾ ﴿And they ask you, "Is it true?" Say: "Yes, by my Lord, indeed it is true, and you cannot escape (it)."﴾ ﴿And if every soul that wronged had all that is on earth, it would surely offer it for ransom. And they will conceal their regret when they see the punishment. And it will be judged between them with justice, and they will not be wronged.﴾ ﴿Unquestionably, to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth. Unquestionably, the promise of Allah is true, but most of them do not know.﴾ ﴿He gives life and causes death, and to Him you will be returned.﴾ ﴿O mankind, there has come to you an admonition from your Lord and a healing for what is in the breasts, and guidance and mercy for the believers.﴾ ﴿Say: "In the bounty of Allah and His mercy, in that let them rejoice; it is better than what they accumulate."﴾ ﴿Say: "Have you considered what Allah has sent down to you of provision, and you made from it lawful and unlawful?" Say: "Has Allah permitted you, or do you fabricate against Allah?"﴾ ﴿And what will be the thought of those who fabricate against Allah the lie on the Day of Resurrection? Indeed, Allah is full of bounty toward the people, but most of them do not give thanks.﴾ ﴿And you are not engaged in any matter, nor recite from it any Qur'an, nor do you do any deed, but We are witness over you when you are involved in it. And not absent from your Lord is any part of an atom's weight within the earth or within the heaven, nor anything smaller than that or greater, but it is in a clear register.﴾ (p-146) Rahiqa: he covered him, and it is said: he reached him. From it (comes) the verse: ﴿And do not burden me with difficulty in my affair﴾ [al-Kahf: 73]. A man who is murhaq is one whom the guests overwhelm. Al-Azhari said: ar-rahaq is a noun derived from al-irhaq, which is for a person to impose upon himself what he cannot bear.
It is said: arhaqtuhu an yusalliya, if you hurry him away from the prayer. It is also said: the origin of rahaq is closeness; one says: ghulam muraahiq, meaning he has approached puberty. In a hadith: "Arhiqu al-qiblah," meaning: draw near to it. It is said: rahiqat al-kilab as-sayd, when the dogs reached the prey; and arhaqna as-salah, we delayed the prayer until it approached the next.
Al-qatar and al-qatarah: dust accompanied by blackness. Ibn Arafah said: dust. Al-Farazdaq said:
Crowned with the robe of kingship, followed by a wave, above which you see the banners and the qatar.
That is, the dust of the army. Ibn Bahr said: the origin of qatar is the smoke of fire, and from it comes qutar al-qidr (the aroma of the cooking pot), end of quote.
It is also said: qatr, with a sukun on the ta', means matter or affair, its plural is shu'un. Its origin is hamz, meaning intention, from sha'ani sha'nahu, when you intended his intention.
Ghaaba (ya'zubu and ya'zibu, with kasra or damma on the zay): to be absent until hidden, from which comes ar-rawd al-'azib (the pasture far from people). Abu Tammam said:
Qalqal, a distance from Khurasan, its heart (trembling); so I said: be calm, the most blooming of the meadows is what is far from it.
It is said of one absent from his family that he is 'azib, to the point that they say it of one who has no wife.
﴿For those who did good is the best (reward) and more. Neither dust nor humiliation will cover their faces. Those are the companions of the Garden; therein they will abide forever.﴾: "Those who did good" — Ibn Abbas said: they remembered the words "There is no god but Allah." Al-Asamm said: they did good in everything they were worshipped through, i.e., they carried out what was commanded as it should be, and avoided what was forbidden.
It is said: they did good in dealing with people. Anas narrated from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Do good in deeds in this world." And in the Sahih: "What is ihsan? He said: That you worship Allah as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, then He sees you." And from Jesus, peace be upon him: "Ihsan is not that you do good to one who has done good to you; that is repayment! Rather, ihsan is that you do good to one who has wronged you."
As for "al-husna," most of them said it is the Garden, and this was narrated from the Messenger (ﷺ); and if it is authentic, it is obligatory to adopt it.
Al-Tabari said: al-husna is general for every good thing, so it encompasses everything promised by Allah, and in all of it there is an increase. This is also supported by His saying: ﴿Those are the companions of the Garden﴾. If the meaning of al-husna were the Garden, there would be repetition in the statement. Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabit said: it is an-nadrah (radiance).
Ibn Zayd said: the reward in the Hereafter. It is said: the hope/wish; this was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari. Al-Zamakhshari said: the reward is "the best" and "more," and what exceeds the reward is the favour (tafaddul), and this is indicated by His saying: ﴿And He will increase them of His bounty﴾ [an-Nisa': 173]. From Ali: the increase is one pearl-chamber.
From Ibn Abbas: al-husna is the good deed, and the increase is ten times its like. From al-Hasan: ten times its like up to seven hundred fold.
From Mujahid: the increase is forgiveness from Allah and pleasure. From Ziyad ibn Shajarah: the increase is that a cloud passes over the people of the Garden and says: "What do you want me to rain upon you?" They want nothing, except that it rains it upon them.
The Mushabbihah and the Mujbirah claimed that the increase is looking at the Face of Allah, the Exalted, and they brought a fabricated hadith: "When the people of the Garden enter the Garden, they will be called: O people of the Garden! Then they will uncover the veil and look at Him; by Allah, Allah the Exalted has given them nothing more beloved to them than that." End of quote.
As for his interpretation at first and his transmission from those who mentioned the interpretation of the increase, that is the text of al-Jubba'i and his transmission. As for his statement, "it came with a fabricated hadith," it is not fabricated; rather Muslim recorded it in his Sahih from Suhayb, and an-Nasa'i from him from the Messenger (ﷺ). Ibn al-Mubarak recorded it in his Daqa'iq as a mawquf (halted) report from Abu Musa, and he said that the increase is the looking at Allah, the Exalted.
Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, and Ali ibn Abi Talib in one narration, and Hudhayfah, and Ubadah ibn al-Samit, and Ka'b ibn Ujrah, and Abu Musa, and Suhayb, and Ibn Abbas in one narration, and it is the view of a group of the Successors.
The question of the vision is discussed in the principles of religion (usul al-din). Mujahid said: He meant that disgrace will not reach them, and disgrace is what changes the face and makes it blacken.
Ibn Abbas said: "dhillah" is sorrow (al-ka'abah). Others said: humiliation. It was said: failure. He negated for the virtuous what He affirmed for the disbelievers in His saying: ﴿And humiliation will cover them﴾ and His saying: ﴿Upon them will be dust﴾ [Abasa: 40] ﴿Covered by darkness﴾ [Abasa: 41]. And He referred to the face as the whole, because it is the noblest part, and because the traces of joy and sorrow appear in it. Al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Isa ibn Umar, and al-A'mash read qatr with a sukun on the ta', and it is a dialect like qadar and qadr. And they were called "companions of the Garden" because of their disposal within it, as owners dispose of their property according to their choice.
﴿As for those who earned evil deeds, the recompense of an evil deed is its like, and humiliation will cover them. They will have no protector from Allah. It is as if their faces were covered with pieces of the dark night. Those are the companions of the Fire; therein they will abide forever.﴾: When He mentioned what He prepared for those who did good, their state on the Day of Resurrection, and their destination to the Garden, He mentioned what He prepared for their opposites, their state and their destination. The relative clause for the believers is "did good," and the relative clause for the disbelievers is "earned evil deeds," as an indication that the believer, since he was created upon the fitrah and perfected it through ihsan, and the disbeliever, since he was created upon the fitrah but departed from it and earned evil deeds, the one is made a doer of good, and this one an earner of evil, so that it shows the believer followed what is fitting, and this one followed what is not fitting.
The apparent view is that "those who" is a subject (mubtada'), and they permitted several possibilities for the predicate. The first: that the predicate is the clause following it, which is "the recompense of an evil deed is its like," and "recompense" is a subject whose predicate is affirmed as "bi-mithliha" (by its like). They differed about the ba'. It is said it is extra (za'idah), said by Ibn Kaysan, meaning: the recompense of an evil deed is its like, as He said: "and the recompense of an evil deed is an evil deed like it," just as it is added in the predicate in the verse: "So He prevented it with something that can be done," meaning: something that can be done. It is also said: it is not extra, and the estimate is: "determined by its like" or "established by its like." It is also said: it is omitted; al-Hawfi estimated it as: "For them is the recompense of an evil deed," and he said: the indication of the estimate "for them" is His saying: ﴿For those who did good is the best reward﴾, so that this may correspond with that.
Abu al-Baqa' estimated it as: "recompense of an evil deed by its like is due," and the ba' in both their statements is related to the word "recompense," and the returning pronoun from this clause which is the predicate of "those who" is omitted, its estimate being: "recompense of an evil deed from them," as it is omitted in their saying: "Samn manawan bi-dirham" (ghee, two manas for a dirham), meaning: two manas of it for a dirham. And according to al-Hawfi's estimate: "for them is recompense," which serves as the returning pronoun ("for them").
The second: that the predicate is His saying: "They will have no protector from Allah," and it would be that a separation occurred between the subject and the predicate by two clauses in the manner of parenthesis (i'tiraD). This is not permitted according to Abu Ali al-Farisi, and the correct view is that it is permitted.
The third: that the predicate is: "It is as if their faces were covered with pieces of the dark night."

**The fourth: that the predicate is "Those" and what follows it.** In this case, the sentence has four intervening clauses between the subject and predicate. In the third opinion, there are three. The correct view is that inserting three or four clauses between them is not permitted. Ibn 'Atiyya permitted that *alladhina* (those who) be in the genitive position, in apposition to the phrase *lilladhina ahsanu* (for those who did good), with *jaza'* (recompense) as the subject, and *alladhina* as its predicate, with the preposition dropped. The meaning would be: "and for those who earned evil deeds is the recompense of an evil deed like it." Thus the division is balanced, just as you say: *fi al-dar Zayd, wal-qasr 'Amr*, meaning *wa-fi al-qasr 'Amr* (in the house is Zayd, and in the palace is 'Amr).

This construction is attested in the speech of the Arabs. al-Akhfash interpreted it as coordination between two governing elements ('atf 'ala 'amilayn).

The majority (al-Jumhur) interpreted it as a case in which the preposition has been omitted, with the noun governed by that deleted preposition, not by coordination with the preceding genitive noun. This is a matter of disagreement and detail that is discussed in the science of grammar (*'ilm al-nahw*).

The apparent meaning is that *al-sayyi'at* (the evil deeds) here refers to the evil deeds of disbelief, as indicated by the mention of their attributes afterwards. It has been said that *al-sayyi'at* refers to sins, so that disbelief and other sins are included. For this reason Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Here *al-sayyi'at* encompasses both disbelief and sins. The like of the evil deed of disbelief is eternal abiding in the Fire, while the like of the evil deeds of sins is subject to the will of God, the Exalted. The meaning of *bi-mithlaha* (with its like) is that nothing is added to it."

al-Zamakhshari said: "In this there is evidence that the intended meaning of 'increase' is grace (*fadl*), because by not adding to the evil deed He indicated His justice, and by affirming an increase in the reward He indicated His grace."

It has also been said: the meaning of *bi-mithlaha* is: with what befits it of punishments. Punishments are proportioned to the magnitude of evil deeds, and for this reason Hell has levels (*darakat*), and the hypocrites were in the lowest level (*al-darak al-asfal*) because of the ugliness of their disobedience.

It was read *wa-yarhaquhum* with the *ya'* (third person masculine), because the feminization of *al-dhilla* (humiliation) is metaphorical. In the description of the hypocrites there is a negation of *qatar* (dust/gloom) and humiliation from their faces, and here humiliation has covered them. An exaggeration is made regarding what is the opposite of *qatar*, so it is said: "as if their faces had been covered with pieces of the night, dark." This is an exaggeration of the blackness of the faces.

This has been stated explicitly in His saying: ﴿And faces will turn black﴾ [Al 'Imran: 106]. *Min Allah* (from God) means from His wrath and His punishment, or from His direction, and from Him is the one who protects them, just as it is for the believers. *Ughshiyat* means "were covered," from the same root as *al-ghita'* (covering). That their faces are blackened is a literal, not a metaphorical, reality, so their complexions are blackened.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: "Know that the sages of Islam said: the intended meaning of this blackness here is the blackness of ignorance and the darkness of misguidance, for ignorance by its nature is the nature of darkness. So His saying: ﴿Faces that day will be bright﴾ [Abasa: 38], ﴿laughing, rejoicing﴾ [Abasa: 39], the intended meaning is the light of knowledge, its spirit, its joy and its good news. (p-149) ﴿And faces that day will have dust upon them﴾ [Abasa: 40], ﴿darkness will cover them﴾ [Abasa: 41], the intended meaning is the darkness of ignorance and the murkiness of error." End of quote.

This man often transmits from the sages of Islam in tafsir, and sometimes he quotes their words attributed to them, and sometimes he relies on them. By "sages of Islam" he means the philosophers (*hukama' al-falasifa*) who arose during the period of the Islamic religion. They deserve to be called foolish and ignorant rather than sages, for they are enemies of the prophets and distorters of the Islamic Shari'a, and they are more harmful to Muslims than Jews and Christians. If the Commander of the Faithful 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) forbade reading the Torah despite it being a divine book, then forbidding the reading of the words of the philosophers is more deserving. In this era, and shortly before it, occupation with the ignorance of the philosophers has overcome most people, and they call it wisdom (*al-hikma*). They consider those who are free of it to be ignorant, and they believe themselves to be the perfect of men. They devote themselves to studying it, and you can hardly find any of them who memorizes a Qur'an or a hadith from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Once I belittled Ibn Sina and attributed ignorance to him, and one of them said to me, showing amazement at someone belittling Ibn Sina: "How can the most knowledgeable of people about God be attributed to ignorance?" When the judge of the community, Abu al-Walid Muhammad ibn Abi al-Qasim Ahmad ibn Abi al-Walid ibn Rushd, displayed concern for the sayings of the philosophers and reverence for them, the scholars of Islam in al-Andalus incited against him al-Mansur, the ruler of the Almohads, Ya'qub ibn Yusuf ibn 'Abd al-Mu'min ibn 'Ali, king of the Maghrib and al-Andalus, until he inflicted upon him what is well known: beating, cursing, and humiliation, and the humiliation of a group of them, publicly before the eyes of the crowds. Among what was addressed to al-Mansur concerning them was the saying of one of the scholar-poets:

O our Caliph, may Allah reward you with good
on behalf of Islam and your noble striving.
You have struggled in it with the struggle due to it
until you attained the mighty victory.
You have made the people, by good guidance,
to follow the path of the straight way.
So strive against a people who have led astray
the path of the Shari'a with ancient knowledge.
Burn their books in east and west,
for within them lies hidden the worst of sciences.
Their harm creeps into beliefs
like poisons, and beliefs are like bodies.
In such cases, when there is no cure,
the sword becomes the antidote to poisons.

And he said:

O desolation of Islam from a sect
occupied with its own folly,
it has cast the religion of guidance behind it
and claimed wisdom and philosophy.

And he said:

A sect has appeared in our era
whose appearance is a bad omen for the age.
Do not follow in religion except what
Ibn Sina or Abu Nasr has laid down.

When I arrived in the land of Egypt and saw many of its people occupied openly with the ignorance of the philosophers, without anyone denouncing it, I was amazed at this, for we had grown up in the island of al-Andalus disavowing it and denouncing it. When a book on logic (*al-mantiq*) was sold, it was sold secretly, and no one dared to utter the word *mantiq*; they called it *al-maf'al* (the act). Even our friend, the minister of the king Ibn al-Ahmar, Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Rahman known as Ibn al-Hakim, wrote to us a letter from al-Andalus asking me to buy or copy a book by one of our shaykhs on logic. He did not dare to utter the word logic, though he was a minister, so in his letter to me he called it *al-maf'al*.

When their faces were clothed in blackness, He said: "as if their faces had been covered." And since the darkness of night is the ultimate in blackness, the blackness of their faces was likened to pieces of the night at the height of its darkness.

Ibn Kathir and al-Kisa'i read *qit'an* with the *ta'* sukun. It is a singular noun denoting the thing that is cut off. al-Akhfash, regarding His saying ﴿with a portion of the night﴾ [Hud: 81], said: "with a blackness of the night." The lexicographers say: *al-qit'* is the darkness of the last part of the night.

Some said: "a portion of the night." In this reading, *muzlliman* (dark) is an attribute of *qit'an*, as is attested in the reading of Ubayy: "as if there covered their faces a dark portion of the night." Ibn Abi 'Abla read it likewise, except that he made the *ta'* a fatha.

It has also been said: *qit'* is the plural of *qit'a*, like *sidr* and *sidra*, so it is permissible in that case to describe it with the masculine, as in *nakhl munqa'ir* (uprooted palms), and with the feminine, as in *nakhl khawiya* (fallen palms). It is also permissible in this case for *muzlliman* to be a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from *al-layl* (the night), as they parsed it in the reading of the rest of the seven: "as if their faces had been covered with pieces (*qita'an*) of the night, with a fatha on the *ta'*, dark (*muzlliman*) in the accusative."

al-Zamakhshari said: "If you say: when you make *muzlliman* a circumstantial clause from *al-layl*, what is its governing element? I say: it is either that *ughshiyat* (were covered) governs it, because *min al-layl* is an attribute of *qit'an*, so its governance reaches the modified noun as it reaches the attribute; or that it is the meaning of the verb in *min al-layl*. End of quote."

As for the first possibility, it is remote, because the principle is that the governing element of the circumstantial clause should be the governing element of the head noun (*dhu al-hal*), while the governing element of *al-layl* is the stable element reached by *min* (*mustaqarr*), and *ughshiyat* governs *qit'an*, which is described by *min al-layl*. So they differ, and for this reason the last possibility is preferable, namely: *qit'an* (pieces) stationed from the night, or existing from the night in the state of its darkening.

It has also been said: *muzlliman* is a circumstantial clause from *qit'an*, or an attribute. These two analyses were mentioned because *qit'an* has the meaning of "many," so the singular and masculine were taken into account. They also permitted, in the reading of the one who made the *ta'* sukun, that *muzlliman* be a circumstantial clause from *qit'in* and also a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in *min*.
