Al-Hawfi said: "the seeing" is of the heart's seeing which means knowledge, because it enters upon the interrogative clause, and its meaning is affirmation (taqrir).

The answer to the condition is omitted, and the construction of the sentence is: "Ara'aytum what the criminals seek to hasten of the punishment, if His punishment comes upon you." End of quote.

The apparent sense of al-Hawfi's words is that "ara'aytum" remains on its original meaning, not carrying the sense of "inform me," that it means "a'lamtum" (did you know), that the interrogative clause fills the place of the two objects, and that it is an interrogative whose meaning is affirmation; al-Hawfi did not explain what the omitted answer of the condition conveys.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you say: with what is the interrogative connected, and where is the answer to the condition?" I say: it is connected to "ara'aytum," because the meaning is: inform me what the criminals seek to hasten of it; the answer to the condition is omitted, and it is: you would regret the hastening and recognize the error in it. End of quote.

What al-Zamakhshari estimated is not permissible, because the answer is only estimated from what precedes it, either verbally or by implication. You say: "You are a wrongdoer if you do it," so the estimate is: "if you do it, then you are a wrongdoer." Likewise: ﴿And indeed we, if God wills, will be guided﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 70], the estimate being: "if God wills, we will be guided." So what permits being estimated here is: "If His punishment comes upon you, then inform me what the criminal seeks to hasten?"

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also possible that "what is it that the criminals seek to hasten of it" is a parenthetical clause, and the meaning: if His punishment comes upon you, do you believe in it after its occurrence, when belief will not benefit you? End of quote.

As for his permitting that "mādhā" be the answer to the condition, this is not valid, because when the answer to the condition is an interrogative, it must have the "fa" (fa'), you say: "If so-and-so visits us, then what kind of man is he?" and "If so-and-so visits us, then what hand does he have in that?" and it is not permissible to omit it except in a case of necessity (darura). The example he mentioned, namely: "If I come to you, what will you feed me?", is from his own illustration, not from the speech of the Arabs.

As for his saying that the clause is connected to "ara'aytum," if by the clause he means "what does he seek to hasten?", this is not valid, because he has made it the answer to the condition; and if by the clause he means the clause of the condition, then he has explained "ara'aytum" with the meaning of "inform me," and "inform me" requires an object complement, and the clause of the condition does not occupy the position of the object of "inform me."

As for his permitting that "a-thumma idha ma waqa'a amantum bihi" be the answer to the condition, and "mādhā yasta'jilu minhu al-mujrimun" a parenthetical clause, this is also not valid, for the reason we have mentioned, that an interrogative clause does not serve as the answer to a condition except with the answer-particle "fa" accompanying it.

Also, "thumma" here is a conjunctive particle, which links the clause following it to what precedes it, so the interrogative clause is conjoined; and when it is conjoined it cannot be the answer to a condition. Also, "ara'aytum" in the sense of "inform me" needs an object, and the conditional clause does not occupy its place.

The discussion of "bayatan" has preceded in al-A'raf, both its meaning and its grammatical analysis. The meaning is: if His punishment comes upon you while you are heedless and unaware, either by sleep or by preoccupation with livelihood and earning. This is like His saying: "suddenly" (baghtatan), because when punishment overtakes one without any awareness of it, it is more severe and harder, unlike when one has prepared for it and readied oneself for its arrival. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿by night while they are sleeping﴾ [Al-A'raf: 97] ﴿in the forenoon while they are playing﴾ [Al-A'raf: 98].

It is also permissible for "mādhā" that "mā" be a subject and "dhā" its predicate, in the sense of "alladhi" (that which), and "yasta'jilu" its relative clause, with the pronoun returning to the relative omitted; the estimate: "what thing does the criminals seek to hasten of the punishment?"

It is also permissible for "mādhā" that the whole be an object, as if it were said: "what thing do the criminals seek to hasten of the punishment?" Some have permitted that the whole "mādhā" be a subject, with the clause after it as its predicate. Abu 'Ali held this weak, because the clause would be devoid of a pronoun returning to the subject. The apparent reading is that the pronoun in "minhu" returns to the punishment, and by it the connection of the interrogative clause to the omitted object of "ara'aytum," which is originally a subject, is achieved. It was said: it returns to God, exalted is He. The criminals are the ones addressed in "ara'aytum in atakum." He drew attention to the attribute that requires not hastening, which is criminality, because it is the right of the criminal to fear punishment for his crime, and to die of fright at its coming even if it is delayed; how then would he seek to hasten it?

"Thumma" is a conjunctive particle, and the interrogative hamza has been placed before it, as it was placed before the waw and fa in: ﴿Have they not travelled?﴾ [Yusuf: 109] and in ﴿Have they not travelled?﴾ [Ar-Rum: 9]. The discussion of this has preceded.

Al-Zamakhshari's disagreement with the majority in claiming that between the hamza and the conjunctive particle there is an omitted clause to which the clause after the conjunction is conjoined.

Al-Tabari said, regarding His saying "athumma" with a damma on the tha, that its meaning is "hunalika" (there), and said: "This 'thumma' is not the one that comes meaning conjunction," end of quote. What al-Tabari said, that "thumma" here is not for conjunction, is a claim; as for his saying that the meaning is "hunalika," what should be meant is that this is an explanation of meaning, not that "thumma" with a damma has the meaning of "hunalika."

Talha ibn Musarrif read "athamma" with a fatha on the tha, and this agrees with al-Tabari's explanation "hunalika." The majority read "ālān" with the interrogative and the madd, and likewise "ālān wa-qad 'asayta" (Now? And you had disobeyed). Talha and al-A'raj read with the hamza of interrogation without madd, and this is on the supposition of an implied saying: it is said to them when they believe after the punishment has fallen: "Now you believe in it?" So the governing element of "ālān" is "amantum bihi," which is omitted; it is said that the angels say this to them, and it is said God does. The interrogation is by way of rebuke.

In the book al-Lawami', 'Isa al-Basri and Talha read "amantum bihi al-an" with the hamza connected and without interrogation, but as a statement, so its accusative is as an adverb of time governed by the mentioned "amantum bihi." As for the common reading, its accusative is by an implied verb indicated by the mentioned "amantum bihi," because the interrogation has taken the beginning of the sentence, so what precedes it prevents it from governing what follows, end of quote. "Wa-qad kuntum" is a circumstantial clause. Al-Zamakhshari said: "and you were seeking to hasten it" means: you were denying it, because your hastening was by way of denial and rejection. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "you were seeking to hasten" as deniers of it.

Then it will be said to those who did wrong, "Taste the punishment of eternity. Are you being recompensed except for what you used to earn?"

This means that the keepers of Hell (khazanat Jahannam) say these words to them. The wrongdoing here is the wrongdoing of disbelief (zulm al-kufr), not the wrongdoing of disobedience (zulm al-ma'siyah), because whoever among the sinful believers enters the Fire does not remain in it forever. As for "thumma qila" (then it was said), it is a conjunction coordinating with the pronoun implied before "al-an" (now).

As for the one who reads with wasl (connecting) the alif of "al-an," then it is a resumed statement reporting what will be said to them on the Day of Resurrection. And "hal tujzawna" (are you being recompensed) is a rebuke to them and a clarification that the recompense is according to the servant's earning (kasb).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 10, verse 38–52 (part 1 of 4):

﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"? Say, "Then bring a surah like it, and call upon whomever you can besides Allah, if you are truthful."﴾ When Allah, the Exalted, negated that the Qur'an is fabricated, and that it instead came confirming what is before it of the Scriptures and as an explanation of what is in them, He mentioned the greatest proof that it is from Allah, which is the inimitability (i'jaz) it contains, thereby refuting their claim that it is a fabrication. The discussion of this has already been covered in full detail in al-Baqarah, in His saying: ﴿And if you are in doubt﴾ [al-Baqarah: 23], and so on. "Am" (أم) here implies the meaning of "bal" (بل), and the hamzah, according to the view of Sibawayh, is (for the sense of) "Do they say He invented it?"

The hamzah is for affirming the obligation of the proof upon them, or for denouncing their claim and expressing disbelief in it. A group said: this "am" has the status of the interrogative hamzah. Abu 'Ubaydah said: "am" means "wa" (و), and its sense is: "and they say, 'He invented it.'" It was also said: the mim is a redundant particle, and the estimate is: "Do they say...?"

It was also said: "am" is the one corresponding to the hamzah, and the sentence before it has been omitted, the estimate being: "Do they acknowledge it, or do they say, 'He invented it'?" Al-Zamakhshari made "Say, 'Then bring'" an omitted conditional clause, and said: "Say: If the matter is as you claim, then you yourselves, by way of fabrication, bring a surah like it, for you are its equal in Arabic, eloquence, and sharpness of intellect. So bring a surah similar to it, resembling it in eloquence and beauty of composition," end of quote.

The pronoun in "mithlihi" (مثله) refers to the Qur'an, meaning: a surah comparable to the Qur'an. We have already discussed what the inimitability consists of.

'Amr ibn Qa'id read "bi-surati mithlihi" (بسورة مثله) with an idafah, meaning: "a surah of a book or speech like it," i.e., like the Qur'an. The author of al-Lawami said: this is one of the cases where the modified noun is omitted and the adjective takes its place, meaning: "with the form of a human like it," so the pronoun in that reading refers to the Prophet ﷺ, while in the common reading it refers to the Qur'an. "And call upon whomever you can" means: whomever you are able to call upon from among Allah's creation, to seek help in producing its like, "besides Allah," i.e., other than Allah, because no one is able to produce its like except Allah. So do not seek help from Him alone, but seek help from everyone else besides Him, if you are truthful in that He invented it.

The Mu'tazilah have held to this verse as proof that the Qur'an is created. They said: because He challenged with it and demanded that they produce its like, and they were unable; this is only possible if producing its like is genuinely possible in principle. If it were eternal, then producing the like of the eternal would be impossible in reality, and so the challenge with it would not be valid.

Abu 'Abdullah al-Razi said: the levels of the challenge with the Qur'an are six: a challenge with the entire Qur'an, in His saying: ﴿Say: If mankind and the jinn gathered together﴾ [al-Isra': 88], etc.; a challenge with ten surahs; a challenge with one surah; and a challenge with a discourse like it, in His saying: ﴿Then let them produce a discourse like it﴾ [al-Tur: 34]. In these four, He demanded that a man equal to the Messenger in not having been a student or taught, be matched; and a challenge in which He demanded that a surah be matched from any human whatsoever, whether he had learned the sciences or not. In these five levels, He challenged every single one of creation. And a challenge in which He demanded from the collective the assistance of some with others. End of summary.

﴿Nay, they denied what they did not encompass in knowledge, and its interpretation had not yet come to them. Likewise denied those before them. So see how was the end of the wrongdoers.﴾ Al-Zamakhshari said: "Nay, they denied" — nay, they hastened to deny the Qur'an, and were taken aback by it at first hearing, before they understood it and knew its true nature, and before they contemplated it and grasped its interpretation and meanings, and that was due to their extreme aversion to what contradicts their religion and their fleeing from abandoning the religion of their fathers.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this expression may bear two meanings. One: that by "what" he means the threat that Allah promised them for disbelief, and its "interpretation" on this view means what its matter will come to, as in His saying: ﴿Do they await but its interpretation?﴾ [al-A'raf: 53]. The verse, on this interpretation, includes a threat. The second meaning: that He meant "Nay, they denied this mighty Qur'an, which informs of the unseen, of which they had no prior knowledge, nor did they encompass knowledge of its unseen matters or the beauty of its composition, and nor had its explanation and clarification come to them." Abu 'Abdullah al-Razi said: it may bear several aspects. The first: whenever they heard some narrative, they said "fables of the ancients" (al-An'am: 25), and did not realize that the purpose of these narratives is not the story itself, but His power to dispose of this world, to transfer its people from honor to humiliation and from humiliation to honor, and the perishing of the world, so that one may take warning from that. And that these narratives are by revelation from Allah, since He informed of them through the tongue of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ without distortion, despite his not having learned or been a student. The second: whenever they heard the disjointed letters and did not understand anything from them, their suspicion grew, and Allah has answered this with His saying: ﴿In it are clear signs﴾ [Al 'Imran: 97], etc. The third: the Qur'an appeared gradually, so their suspicion grew and they said: ﴿Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?﴾ [al-Furqan: 32]. Allah has answered and explained this in its place. The fourth: the Qur'an is full of the gathering (on the Day of Resurrection), and they had become accustomed to sensible things, so they found the return of life after death improbable, and Allah demonstrated the truth of the Resurrection with many proofs. The fifth: that it is full of commands to acts of worship, and they used to say: the God of the worlds is independent of our obedience, and is too exalted to command us with what has no benefit in it. Allah answered with His saying: ﴿If you do good, you do good for yourselves﴾ [al-Isra': 7], etc. In sum, the resemblances among the disbelievers are many; when they saw the Qur'an containing matters whose realities they did not know and whose wisdom they had not grasped, they denied the Qur'an. So His saying "what they did not encompass in knowledge" points to their lack of knowledge of these matters, and His saying "and its interpretation had not yet come to them" points to their lack of effort and striving in seeking the secrets of what the Qur'an contains. End of summary.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: what is the sense of expectation in His saying, 'and its interpretation had not yet come to them'?" I say: its meaning is that they denied it instantly before reflection, and before knowing its interpretation, by blind imitation of their fathers; and they denied it after reflection out of obstinacy and stubbornness. So He blamed them for their haste to deny before knowledge of it, and He used the word of expectation (lamma) to indicate that they came to know, after the elevation of its status and its inimitability, when He repeatedly challenged them and they exhausted their strength in trying to produce its like, and became certain of their inability to match it; yet they denied it out of insolence and envy. End of quote.

His statement needs scrutiny. He also said: it is possible that the meaning is: "and its interpretation had not yet come to them, and its interpretation of what it contains of informing of the unseen had not yet come to them, i.e., its outcome, until it becomes clear to them whether it is a lie or the truth?" He means: it is a Book inimitable from two angles: from the angle of the inimitability of its composition, and from the angle of what it contains of informing of the unseen. So they hastened to deny it before they looked into its composition and its reaching the limit of inimitability, and before they were informed of its reports of the unseen matters, and its truth or falsehood. End of quote.

The sentence of "encompassing" is introduced with "lam" (لم), and the sentence of "its interpretation coming to them" with "lamma" (لما), and this requires a subtle distinction. The kaf (ك) is in the accusative position, meaning: like that denial, those before them denied, i.e., before considering the miracles of the prophets and before reflecting upon them, without being fair to themselves; rather they imitated their fathers and were obstinate.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: al-Zajjaj said: "kayfa" (كيف) is in the accusative position as the predicate of "kana" (كان); "unzur" (انظر) cannot govern it, because what precedes the interrogative does not govern it. This is the rule of the grammarians, for they treated "kayfa" everywhere as a pure interrogative, as in your saying: "How is Zayd?" And "kayfa" has other usages beyond this, in which it takes the place of the verbal noun meaning "manner," and the sense of interrogation is dissolved; this position may be one of these, and among its usages is their saying: "Be however you wish," and consider al-Bukhari's words: "How the beginning of revelation was," for it did not ... end of quote.

Al-Zajjaj's statement, "it cannot be governed by unzur," and his reasoning: he means that the word "unzur" cannot govern it verbally, but the clause is in the accusative position as an object of "unzur" in suspended form, and it is from the seeing of the heart.

Ibn 'Atiyyah's statement, "this is the rule of the grammarians," through to the end of his reasoning, is not as he stated. Rather "kayfa" has two meanings: one, the pure interrogative, which is a question about the state, except when you suspend the governing verb from it, in which case its meaning is that of the nouns used for interrogation when the governing verb is suspended. The second: the conditional, as in the Arabs' saying: "However you become, I will become." And his statement, "and kayfa has other usages, in which it takes the place of the verbal noun," and so on, is not correct: "kayfa" does not take the place of a verbal noun, and the word "kayfiyyah" is not a verbal noun; rather that is an attribution to "kayfa."

His statement, "it may be that this position is among them and among its usages, the saying: 'Be however you wish'," is not admissible, because he did not establish for it the meaning he mentioned of "kayfa" being in the sense of "kayfiyyah" and the claim of a verbal noun "kayfiyyah." As for "Be however you wish," "kayfa" here does not mean "kayfiyyah"; rather it is conditional, and that is the second meaning it has.

Its answer is omitted; the estimate is: "However you wish, then be," just as you say: "Stand whenever you wish," where "mata" is a conditional noun of time, governing nothing, and the answer is omitted, its estimate being: "Whenever you wish, then stand." The answer is omitted because what precedes it indicates it, like the saying: "Strike Zayd if he wrongs you," the estimate: "If he wrongs you, then strike him," and "strike him" is omitted because of the indication of the earlier "strike." As for al-Bukhari's words, "How was the beginning of revelation?" it is a pure interrogative, either by way of narration, as if a questioner asked him and said: "How was the beginning of revelation?" and he answered with the hadith that contains the manner of it.

As for "the wrongdoers" (al-zalimin): the apparent meaning is that it refers to those before them; it is possible that it refers to those to whom the pronoun of "Nay, they denied" refers.

﴿And among them are those who believe in it, and among them are those who do not believe in it. And your Lord is most knowing of the corrupters.﴾ The apparent meaning is that it is an announcement that among the disbelievers of Quraysh there will be someone who will believe in it, namely one for whom happiness has preceded, and among them is one who does not believe in it and will die upon disbelief.

It was also said: this is a division among the disbelievers who remain upon their disbelief: among them is one who believes in it inwardly and knows that it is true, but denies out of obstinacy; and among them is one who does not believe in it neither inwardly nor outwardly, either because of the swiftness of his denial and his not having contemplated it, or because he looked into it but doubts overcame him and he lacked the understanding to repel them. In it is a splitting of the word of the disbelievers, and that they are not uniform in their beliefs; rather they are in turmoil, even if denial and disbelief encompass them.

It was also said: the pronoun in "among them" refers to the People of the Book, while the apparent reference is to those to whom the pronoun of "Do they say" refers. Attaching knowledge to "the corrupters" alone is a great threat to them.

﴿And if they deny you, say: "For me is my work, and for you is your work. You are free of what I do, and I am free of what you do."﴾ That is: and if they persist in denying you, then disassociate yourself from them; you have already given excuse and delivered (the message), as in His saying: ﴿So if they disobey you, say: "I am free of what you do"﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 216]. The meaning of "for me is my work" is: the recompense of my work, and for you is the recompense of your work.

The meaning of "my work" is the righteous work comprising faith and obedience, and "your work" is that comprising association and disobedience. The apparent sense is that it is a verse of disassociation and disengagement from them, and it includes a threat, as in His saying: ﴿Say: "O disbelievers"﴾ [al-Kafirun: 1], the whole surah. It was also said: the intent of this is to win them over and attract their hearts.

Some, including Ibn Zayd, said: it is abrogated by fighting, because it is Meccan; this is the view of Mujahid, al-Kalbi and Muqatil. But the verifiers said: it is not abrogated, and its implication is that each one is singled out for his own actions and their fruits of reward and punishment, and the verse of the sword did not lift anything of this.

He began with the commanded part, saying "for me is my deed," because it is more emphatic in dissociating them, and he began the disavowal with "you are free from what I do," because this sentence comes as an emphasis and completion of what precedes it. So it suited to follow "and for you is your deed." It also serves the fawasil (verse endings). Had the mention of disavowal come first, as the mention of "for me is my deed" did, the sentence would not have fallen as a verse ending, since the construction would have been "and you are free from what I do."

(p-161)﴿And among them are those who listen to you. Can you make the deaf hear, even though they do not understand?﴾ ﴿And among them are those who look at you. Can you guide the blind, even though they do not see?﴾ ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong people at all, but people wrong themselves.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: the two verses were revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith and others among the mockers. Ibn al-Anbari said: concerning a group of Jews. (end of quotation)

This verse contains a division of the disbelievers who do not believe into these two categories, after the division of the deniers into those who believe and those who do not. The pronoun in "yastami'una" (they listen) refers to the meaning of "man" (whoever), and referring back to the meaning rather than the wording is permissible in the plural. It is like His saying: ﴿And among the devils are those who dive for him﴾ (21:82). The meaning is: those who listen to you when you recite the Qur'an and teach the laws. Then he negated the benefit of that listening by saying: "Can you make the deaf hear?" That is, they are deaf to grasping what you convey to them; even if they listen to you, they have no awareness and no acceptance. Especially since, added to their deafness, is the absence of reason. So the lack of hearing and reason, with "min" (among) before them, means they have no perception of anything whatsoever. This is unlike a deaf person who is rational, for by his reason he can be guided to things.

In His saying "And among them are those who look at you," he repeated the pronoun in the singular masculine according to the wording of "man," which is the most common usage in the Arabic language. The meaning is that they are blind, so you cannot guide them, because the means by which one is guided to seeing the proofs they have lost. Moreover, along with the loss of sight, they have lost insight, for whoever is blind is guided by the light of his insight to things by intuition, whereas these have combined the loss of sight and insight. This is a great exaggeration of their total non-acceptance of what is conveyed to them, since they combined deafness with absence of reason, and blindness with lack of insight.

His saying "Can you [...]" is a consolation to the Messenger (ﷺ), and a means to ensure that he does not grieve over their non-acceptance, since guidance belongs only to Allah. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "He came with 'yanzuru' according to the wording of 'man.' When the verb comes according to its wording, it is permissible for another verb to be conjoined to it according to the meaning. But when it first comes according to its meaning, it is not permissible to conjoin to it another according to the wording, because the speech would then become confused." (end of quotation)

This is not as he said. Rather, it is permissible to observe the meaning first, and to refer the pronoun according to what you intend of the meaning in terms of feminine, dual, or plural, and then to observe the wording, referring the pronoun in the singular masculine. This has detailed treatment in the science of grammar. The purpose of the two verses is to inform him, peace be upon him, that these disbelievers have reached such a degree of aversion, enmity and intense hatred that no treatment whatsoever will benefit them. For whoever is deaf, foolish, blind, and lacking insight cannot comprehend the excellences of speech or the inimitability contained within it, nor can he see the marvels that Allah performed through His Messenger. Thus, guidance for these people has been despaired of. The poet said:

"And if I am hidden from the dullard, it is excusable that a blind eye does not see me."

When the Exalted mentioned these wretched people, He mentioned that He does not wrong them at all, since He has removed their excuses by sending the Messengers and warning them of His punishment. Rather, they wronged themselves by disbelief and denial.

This negation of wronging could mean in this world, that is, He does not wrong them in any of their interests. It could also mean in the Hereafter, and that the punishment that befalls them is justice from Him, because they are the ones who caused it by earning their sins, as He decreed for them: "He is not questioned about what He does."

The readers' disagreement regarding "wa-lakinna al-nas" (but people) has been mentioned before: the nun being doubled with "al-nas" in the accusative, the nun being lightened, and with "al-nas" in the nominative.

(And the day He gathers them, as if they had not remained but an hour of the day, recognizing one another among themselves. Those who denied the meeting with Allah have indeed lost, and they were not guided.) Al-A'mash and Hafs recited "yahshuruhum" with the yā' (y), the pronoun referring in the third person to Allah, since "Indeed, Allah does not wrong people at all" preceded it. When He mentioned those wretched people, He followed it with the warning and the description of their state on the Day of Resurrection. The meaning: "as if they had not remained" in the world or in the graves; that is, their stay was brief. This is due to the horror of what they witness of the severe trials of the Resurrection, or due to the length of the Day of Resurrection and their standing for reckoning.

Ibn 'Abbas said: they saw that the length of their lives, compared with eternity, was like an hour. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "'Yawma' (the day) is an adverbial accusative (zarf), and its accusative may be correct by a hidden verb, whose estimation is: 'and remember.' It may also be in the accusative by the verb that is implied in His saying: 'as if they had not remained but an hour of the day.' It may also be in the accusative by 'yata'arafuna' (recognizing one another). The kaf in His saying 'ka-anna' may be in the position of a description of the day, and it may be in the position of a description of a verbal noun (masdar), as if he said: 'and the day We gather them with a gathering as if they had not remained.' It may also be that His saying 'ka-anna lam yalbathu' (as if they had not remained) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in 'nahshuruhum' (We gather them)." (end of quotation)

As for his saying "It may be in the accusative by the verb implied in 'ka-anna lam yalbathu,'" this is a vague statement, for he did not specify the verb that is implied in "ka-anna lam yalbathu." Perhaps he meant what al-Haufi said: that the kaf is in the accusative position governed by the sense of the speech contained in it, which is speed. (end of quotation)

Thus the estimate would be: "And the day We gather them, they hasten as if they had not remained." As for his saying "The kaf in 'ka-anna' may be in the position of a description of the day," this is not correct, because "yawma nahshuruhum" is definite, while the clauses are indefinite, and a definite noun is not described by an indefinite one.

It cannot be said that the clause following time nouns is indefinite in every case. For if it is in estimation resolved into a definite, then what it is attached to becomes definite; and if it is resolved into an indefinite, then what it is attached to is indefinite. You say: "I passed on the day that Zayd arrived, the past one," so you describe "yawm" with the definite. And you say: "I came on the night that Zayd arrived, the blessed one upon us."

Moreover, "ka-anna lam yalbathu" cannot be a description of the day in meaning, because that is a description of the ones gathered, not a description of the day of their gathering. Some have burdened themselves with estimating an omitted linking element, estimating: "as if they had not remained before it," so "before it" was omitted, that is, before the day. But the omission of such a linking element is not permissible.

Therefore, the apparent reading is that it is a circumstantial clause from the object of "nahshuruhum," as Ibn 'Atiyya said last, and Abu al-Baqa' and al-Zamakhshari likewise parsed it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: 'ka-anna lam yalbathu' and 'yata'arafuna' — what is their position? I say: as for the first, it is a circumstantial clause from them, meaning: We gather them, likened to those who did not remain but an hour. As for the second, it is either attached to the adverb of time, meaning it is a circumstantial clause, or it is explanatory of His saying 'ka-anna lam yalbathu illa sa'atan,' because recognition remains with the long passage of time and turns into mutual denial." (end of quotation)

Al-Haufi said: "yata'arafuna" is a imperfect verb in the position of a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "yalbathu," and it is the governing element. As if he said: "gathered recognizing one another." The meaning: they gathered recognizing one another. It is also permissible that it be a circumstantial clause from the "ha" and "mim" in "nahshuruhum," and it is the governing element. (end of quotation)

As for Ibn 'Atiyya's statement: "It may be in the accusative position of the verbal noun, as if he said: 'and the day We gather them with a gathering as if they had not remained,'" this was reported by Abu al-Baqa', who said: "It was also said it is a description of an omitted verbal noun, that is, a gathering as if they had not remained before it." (end of quotation)

We have already mentioned that the omission of such a linking element is not permissible. They also permitted that "yata'arafuna" be a circumstantial clause, according to what was mentioned earlier of the disagreement regarding the one with the circumstance and its governing element, and that it be a resumptive sentence (istinaf), in which Allah informs that recognition takes place among them.

Al-Kalbi said: "Each one recognizes the other as they knew one another in the world when they came out of their graves. It is a recognition of rebuke and exposure. One says to another: 'You misled me and led me astray.' It is not a recognition of compassion and tenderness. Then recognition ceases when they witness the horrors of the Resurrection, as the Exalted said: ﴿And no intimate friend asks after an intimate friend﴾ (70:10), ﴿though they are made to see one another﴾ (70:11). It was also said: each one informs the other of the error and disbelief they were upon."

Al-Dahhak said: "It is the recognition of the affection of believers, while the disbelievers have no kinship among them." It was also said: the Resurrection has stages; in one stage they recognize one another, and in another stage they do not recognize one another.

The apparent reading is that His saying "Those who [...] have indeed lost" to the end is a resumptive sentence, in which Allah informs of the loss of those who denied meeting Him. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is a resumption carrying the meaning of wonder, as if it were said: 'How great is their loss!'" (end of quotation)

He also said: "He began with 'qad khasira' with the intention of saying, that is: they recognize one another among themselves, saying this." (end of quotation) Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It was also said it is the report of the gathered ones in the manner of rebuke against themselves." (end of quotation)

This may be as al-Zamakhshari said: "they recognize one another among themselves, saying that," or as others said: "We gather them, saying: 'they have indeed lost.'" The implied element may be governed by "yata'arafuna" or by "nahshuruhum." He also pointed out the cause that necessitates the loss, which is their denial of meeting Allah.

(And they were not guided.) The apparent reading is that it is conjoined to His saying "qad khasira," so it would be part of the speech of the gathered ones, if we say that "qad khasira" is part of their speech. They report about themselves their loss in the Hereafter and the absence of their guidance in this world. It may also be conjoined to the relative clause "alladhina" (those who), meaning: they denied meeting Allah, and their guidance in this world was negated. It may also be that the sentence is like an emphasis of the relative clause, because whoever denies meeting Allah is one who is not guided. It was also said: "they were not guided to the utmost of the interests of trade." It was also said: "to faith." It was also said: "in the knowledge of Allah," rather, they are among those whose misguidance He decreed and judged.

(Whether We show you some of what We promise them, or We cause you to die, to Us is their return. Then Allah is witness over what they do.) The word "imma" is the conditional "in" (if) with what Ibn 'Atiyya added to it, and because of it the heavy nun was permitted. If "in" alone were used, it would not be permitted. (end of quotation)

He means that the entry of the nun for emphasis only occurs with the addition of "ma" after "in." This that he mentioned contradicts the apparent statement of Sibawayh. Ibn Kharuf said: Sibawayh permitted bringing "ma," and not bringing it, and bringing the nun with "ma" and not bringing it. The seeing here is visual, and for this reason the verb is transitive to two objects. The kaf is an address to the Messenger (ﷺ).

"Some of what We promise them," that is: of the punishment in this world. Allah has shown him kinds of punishment of the disbelievers in this world: killing, captivity, plunder of wealth, taking of women and children as captives, imposing the jizya (poll tax), and scattering of their community through exile away from their lands. What befalls them in the Hereafter is greater, because it is the lasting punishment that does not end.

The apparent reading is that the answer to the condition is His saying "to Us is their return," and so Haufi and Ibn 'Atiyya said.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "The meaning of this verse is a warning of the return to Allah, blessed and exalted: that is, whether We show you their punishment or do not show it to you, they are in every case returning to Us for reckoning and punishment. Then, along with that, Allah is witness from the first of their being obligated over all their deeds." (end of quotation)

Therefore "thumma" here marks the sequence of reports, not the sequence of the stories themselves. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Then to Us is their return" is the answer to "natawaffayannaka" (Whether We take you in death), and the answer to "nurayannaka" (Whether We show you) is omitted, as if it were said: "And if We show you part of what We promise them, so be it; or We take you in death before We show it to you, and We show you in the Hereafter." End of quote. So al-Zamakhshari made the statement into two conditionals, each with its own answer, and there is no need to assume an omitted answer, because His saying "then to Us is their return" is suitable to be the answer both to the condition and to what is conjoined to it.

Also, al-Zamakhshari's saying "fa-dhalika" (so be it) is a single noun, from which no conditional answer can be formed. He should have brought a sentence from which the answer to the condition would become clear, since from his words "fa-dhalika" one does not understand the omitted element, the thing by which the benefit of predication is achieved.

Ibn Abi Abla read "thamma Allahu" with a fatha on the tha, meaning "there" (hunalika). The meaning of God's witnessing over what they do, its requirement and its consequence, is punishment; it is as if He said: "Then God will punish them." Otherwise, He, exalted is He, is a witness over their deeds in this world and the Hereafter.

It is also possible that the meaning is: He, exalted is He, will render His testimony over their deeds on the Day of Resurrection, until their skins, tongues and hands and feet speak as witnesses against them.

﴿And for every nation there is a messenger; when their messenger comes, judgment is passed between them with justice, and they are not wronged.﴾ When He explained the state of the Messenger ﷺ among his people, He explained the state of the prophets, peace be upon them, with their peoples, as consolation for him and reassurance for his heart.

The verse indicates that God did not neglect any nation, but sent a messenger to it, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And there was no nation but that a warner had passed among them﴾ [Fatir: 24]. His saying: ﴿when their messenger comes﴾ may either be a report about a past state, in which case it refers to this world, and the meaning is: He sent to every nation a messenger calling them to the religion of God and informing them of His unity; when he came to them with clear proofs, they denied him, and judgment was passed between them, that is, between the messenger and his nation, so the messenger was saved and those who denied were punished. Or it may refer to a future state, that is: when their messenger comes to them on the Day of Resurrection to bear witness against them, judgment is passed between them, that is, between the nations, with justice, so some go to Paradise and some to Hell; this is the judgment between them, as said by Mujahid and others. It would be like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the prophets and the witnesses are brought, and judgment is passed between them﴾ [Az-Zumar: 69].

﴿And they say: When is this promise, if you are truthful?﴾ The pronoun in "wa-yaqulun" refers to the polytheists of Quraysh and those who followed them among the deniers of resurrection. They sought to hasten what they were promised of punishment, by way of disbelief in it or by way of mockery, and for this reason they said: "if you are truthful," that is, you are not truthful in what you promised, so nothing of it will happen.

Their saying "this" supports the first view regarding the previous verse, that it is a narration of a past state, and that the meaning of that is: when the messenger came to them and they denied him, judgment was passed between them in this world, and that every messenger promised his nation punishment in this world if it denied him.

﴿Say: I have no power over harm or benefit for myself except what God wills. For every nation there is a term; when their term comes, they will not delay it an hour, nor will they hasten it.﴾ When they asked for the hastening of the punishment or the hastening of the Hour, he, peace be upon him, was commanded to say to them: That is not up to me; it is up to God, exalted is He.

And if I have no power over benefit or harm for myself, how would I have power over it for others? Or how would I know what God has not informed me of? Rather, "for every nation there is a term" belongs to His knowledge alone, exalted is He. The discussion of the like of His saying "for every nation there is a term" to the end of the verse has preceded in al-A'raf. Ibn Sirin read "ajaluhum" in the plural.

As for "except what God wills," its apparent meaning is that it is a connected exception: except what God wills that I should possess and have power over. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is a disconnected exception, that is: but what God wills of that is occurring, so how could I possess for you harm and the bringing of punishment? "For every nation there is a term" means: your punishment has an appointed term with God.

﴿Say: Tell me, if His punishment comes upon you by night or by day, what is it that the criminals seek to hasten?﴾ ﴿Is it then, when it has befallen, that you believe in it? Now? And you were seeking to hasten it!﴾

The discussion of "arayitum" has been given in Surat al-An'am, and there we established that the Arabs make "ara'ayta" carry the meaning of "inform me" (akhbirni), and that it then takes two objects, and that the second object is most often an interrogative clause, from which what precedes it forms a subject and predicate, as in the Arab saying: "Ara'ayta Zaydan ma sana'a?" meaning: inform me about Zayd, what he did.

Before "ara'ayta" entered, the sentence was: "Zayd, what did he do?" Given this, the first object of "arayitum" here is omitted, and the matter is one of the cases of double government (tanazu'). "Ara'aytum" and "in atakum" compete for "adhabuhu," so the second was made to govern, since it is preferred according to the school of the Basrans, and it is what the usage attested more than making the first govern.

When the second governed, the first's object was omitted and not pronounced, because pronouncing it is restricted to poetry, or is rare in speech, according to the grammarians' disagreement on this. The meaning: say to them, O Muhammad: inform me about God's punishment, if it comes upon you, what is it that you seek to hasten of it? There is no part of punishment that a sane person would seek to hasten, since all punishment is bitter to taste and causes the nature to recoil from it; so the interrogative clause has come as a gentle address to them and an alert that punishment should not be hastened.

It is also possible that the clause came by way of wonder and magnifying the punishment, that is: what a severe thing is it that you seek to hasten? That is: how great and how terrible is what you seek to hasten of punishment! Al-Hawfi said: "the seeing" is of the heart's seeing which means knowledge, because it enters upon the interrogative clause, and its meaning is affirmation (taqrir).

The answer to the condition is omitted, and the construction of the sentence is: "Ara'aytum what the criminals seek to hasten of the punishment, if His punishment comes upon you." End of quote.

The apparent sense of al-Hawfi's words is that "ara'aytum" remains on its original meaning, not carrying the sense of "inform me," that it means "a'lamtum" (did you know), that the interrogative clause fills the place of the two objects, and that it is an interrogative whose meaning is affirmation; al-Hawfi did not explain what the omitted answer of the condition conveys.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you say: with what is the interrogative connected, and where is the answer to the condition?" I say: it is connected to "ara'aytum," because the meaning is: inform me what the criminals seek to hasten of it; the answer to the condition is omitted, and it is: you would regret the hastening and recognize the error in it. End of quote.

What al-Zamakhshari estimated is not permissible, because the answer is only estimated from what precedes it, either verbally or by implication. You say: "You are a wrongdoer if you do it," so the estimate is: "if you do it, then you are a wrongdoer." Likewise: ﴿And indeed we, if God wills, will be guided﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 70], the estimate being: "if God wills, we will be guided." So what permits being estimated here is: "If His punishment comes upon you, then inform me what the criminal seeks to hasten?"

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also possible that "what is it that the criminals seek to hasten of it" is a parenthetical clause, and the meaning: if His punishment comes upon you, do you believe in it after its occurrence, when belief will not benefit you? End of quote.

As for his permitting that "mādhā" be the answer to the condition, this is not valid, because when the answer to the condition is an interrogative, it must have the "fa" (fa'), you say: "If so-and-so visits us, then what kind of man is he?" and "If so-and-so visits us, then what hand does he have in that?" and it is not permissible to omit it except in a case of necessity (darura). The example he mentioned, namely: "If I come to you, what will you feed me?", is from his own illustration, not from the speech of the Arabs.

As for his saying that the clause is connected to "ara'aytum," if by the clause he means "what does he seek to hasten?", this is not valid, because he has made it the answer to the condition; and if by the clause he means the clause of the condition, then he has explained "ara'aytum" with the meaning of "inform me," and "inform me" requires an object complement, and the clause of the condition does not occupy the position of the object of "inform me."

As for his permitting that "a-thumma idha ma waqa'a amantum bihi" be the answer to the condition, and "mādhā yasta'jilu minhu al-mujrimun" a parenthetical clause, this is also not valid, for the reason we have mentioned, that an interrogative clause does not serve as the answer to a condition except with the answer-particle "fa" accompanying it.

Also, "thumma" here is a conjunctive particle, which links the clause following it to what precedes it, so the interrogative clause is conjoined; and when it is conjoined it cannot be the answer to a condition. Also, "ara'aytum" in the sense of "inform me" needs an object, and the conditional clause does not occupy its place.

The discussion of "bayatan" has preceded in al-A'raf, both its meaning and its grammatical analysis. The meaning is: if His punishment comes upon you while you are heedless and unaware, either by sleep or by preoccupation with livelihood and earning. This is like His saying: "suddenly" (baghtatan), because when punishment overtakes one without any awareness of it, it is more severe and harder, unlike when one has prepared for it and readied oneself for its arrival. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿by night while they are sleeping﴾ [Al-A'raf: 97] ﴿in the forenoon while they are playing﴾ [Al-A'raf: 98].

It is also permissible for "mādhā" that "mā" be a subject and "dhā" its predicate, in the sense of "alladhi" (that which), and "yasta'jilu" its relative clause, with the pronoun returning to the relative omitted; the estimate: "what thing does the criminals seek to hasten of the punishment?"

It is also permissible for "mādhā" that the whole be an object, as if it were said: "what thing do the criminals seek to hasten of the punishment?" Some have permitted that the whole "mādhā" be a subject, with the clause after it as its predicate. Abu 'Ali held this weak, because the clause would be devoid of a pronoun returning to the subject. The apparent reading is that the pronoun in "minhu" returns to the punishment, and by it the connection of the interrogative clause to the omitted object of "ara'aytum," which is originally a subject, is achieved. It was said: it returns to God, exalted is He. The criminals are the ones addressed in "ara'aytum in atakum." He drew attention to the attribute that requires not hastening, which is criminality, because it is the right of the criminal to fear punishment for his crime, and to die of fright at its coming even if it is delayed; how then would he seek to hasten it?

"Thumma" is a conjunctive particle, and the interrogative hamza has been placed before it, as it was placed before the waw and fa in: ﴿Have they not travelled?﴾ [Yusuf: 109] and in ﴿Have they not travelled?﴾ [Ar-Rum: 9]. The discussion of this has preceded.

Al-Zamakhshari's disagreement with the majority in claiming that between the hamza and the conjunctive particle there is an omitted clause to which the clause after the conjunction is conjoined.

Al-Tabari said, regarding His saying "athumma" with a damma on the tha, that its meaning is "hunalika" (there), and said: "This 'thumma' is not the one that comes meaning conjunction," end of quote. What al-Tabari said, that "thumma" here is not for conjunction, is a claim; as for his saying that the meaning is "hunalika," what should be meant is that this is an explanation of meaning, not that "thumma" with a damma has the meaning of "hunalika."

Talha ibn Musarrif read "athamma" with a fatha on the tha, and this agrees with al-Tabari's explanation "hunalika." The majority read "ālān" with the interrogative and the madd, and likewise "ālān wa-qad 'asayta" (Now? And you had disobeyed). Talha and al-A'raj read with the hamza of interrogation without madd, and this is on the supposition of an implied saying: it is said to them when they believe after the punishment has fallen: "Now you believe in it?" So the governing element of "ālān" is "amantum bihi," which is omitted; it is said that the angels say this to them, and it is said God does. The interrogation is by way of rebuke.

In the book al-Lawami', 'Isa al-Basri and Talha read "amantum bihi al-an" with the hamza connected and without interrogation, but as a statement, so its accusative is as an adverb of time governed by the mentioned "amantum bihi." As for the common reading, its accusative is by an implied verb indicated by the mentioned "amantum bihi," because the interrogation has taken the beginning of the sentence, so what precedes it prevents it from governing what follows, end of quote. "Wa-qad kuntum" is a circumstantial clause. Al-Zamakhshari said: "and you were seeking to hasten it" means: you were denying it, because your hastening was by way of denial and rejection. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "you were seeking to hasten" as deniers of it.

Then it will be said to those who did wrong, "Taste the punishment of eternity. Are you being recompensed except for what you used to earn?"

This means that the keepers of Hell (khazanat Jahannam) say these words to them. The wrongdoing here is the wrongdoing of disbelief (zulm al-kufr), not the wrongdoing of disobedience (zulm al-ma'siyah), because whoever among the sinful believers enters the Fire does not remain in it forever. As for "thumma qila" (then it was said), it is a conjunction coordinating with the pronoun implied before "al-an" (now).

As for the one who reads with wasl (connecting) the alif of "al-an," then it is a resumed statement reporting what will be said to them on the Day of Resurrection. And "hal tujzawna" (are you being recompensed) is a rebuke to them and a clarification that the recompense is according to the servant's earning (kasb).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 10, verse 38–52 (part 1 of 4):

﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"? Say, "Then bring a surah like it, and call upon whomever you can besides Allah, if you are truthful."﴾ When Allah, the Exalted, negated that the Qur'an is fabricated, and that it instead came confirming what is before it of the Scriptures and as an explanation of what is in them, He mentioned the greatest proof that it is from Allah, which is the inimitability (i'jaz) it contains, thereby refuting their claim that it is a fabrication. The discussion of this has already been covered in full detail in al-Baqarah, in His saying: ﴿And if you are in doubt﴾ [al-Baqarah: 23], and so on. "Am" (أم) here implies the meaning of "bal" (بل), and the hamzah, according to the view of Sibawayh, is (for the sense of) "Do they say He invented it?"

The hamzah is for affirming the obligation of the proof upon them, or for denouncing their claim and expressing disbelief in it. A group said: this "am" has the status of the interrogative hamzah. Abu 'Ubaydah said: "am" means "wa" (و), and its sense is: "and they say, 'He invented it.'" It was also said: the mim is a redundant particle, and the estimate is: "Do they say...?"

It was also said: "am" is the one corresponding to the hamzah, and the sentence before it has been omitted, the estimate being: "Do they acknowledge it, or do they say, 'He invented it'?" Al-Zamakhshari made "Say, 'Then bring'" an omitted conditional clause, and said: "Say: If the matter is as you claim, then you yourselves, by way of fabrication, bring a surah like it, for you are its equal in Arabic, eloquence, and sharpness of intellect. So bring a surah similar to it, resembling it in eloquence and beauty of composition," end of quote.

The pronoun in "mithlihi" (مثله) refers to the Qur'an, meaning: a surah comparable to the Qur'an. We have already discussed what the inimitability consists of.

'Amr ibn Qa'id read "bi-surati mithlihi" (بسورة مثله) with an idafah, meaning: "a surah of a book or speech like it," i.e., like the Qur'an. The author of al-Lawami said: this is one of the cases where the modified noun is omitted and the adjective takes its place, meaning: "with the form of a human like it," so the pronoun in that reading refers to the Prophet ﷺ, while in the common reading it refers to the Qur'an. "And call upon whomever you can" means: whomever you are able to call upon from among Allah's creation, to seek help in producing its like, "besides Allah," i.e., other than Allah, because no one is able to produce its like except Allah. So do not seek help from Him alone, but seek help from everyone else besides Him, if you are truthful in that He invented it.

The Mu'tazilah have held to this verse as proof that the Qur'an is created. They said: because He challenged with it and demanded that they produce its like, and they were unable; this is only possible if producing its like is genuinely possible in principle. If it were eternal, then producing the like of the eternal would be impossible in reality, and so the challenge with it would not be valid.

Abu 'Abdullah al-Razi said: the levels of the challenge with the Qur'an are six: a challenge with the entire Qur'an, in His saying: ﴿Say: If mankind and the jinn gathered together﴾ [al-Isra': 88], etc.; a challenge with ten surahs; a challenge with one surah; and a challenge with a discourse like it, in His saying: ﴿Then let them produce a discourse like it﴾ [al-Tur: 34]. In these four, He demanded that a man equal to the Messenger in not having been a student or taught, be matched; and a challenge in which He demanded that a surah be matched from any human whatsoever, whether he had learned the sciences or not. In these five levels, He challenged every single one of creation. And a challenge in which He demanded from the collective the assistance of some with others. End of summary.

﴿Nay, they denied what they did not encompass in knowledge, and its interpretation had not yet come to them. Likewise denied those before them. So see how was the end of the wrongdoers.﴾ Al-Zamakhshari said: "Nay, they denied" — nay, they hastened to deny the Qur'an, and were taken aback by it at first hearing, before they understood it and knew its true nature, and before they contemplated it and grasped its interpretation and meanings, and that was due to their extreme aversion to what contradicts their religion and their fleeing from abandoning the religion of their fathers.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this expression may bear two meanings. One: that by "what" he means the threat that Allah promised them for disbelief, and its "interpretation" on this view means what its matter will come to, as in His saying: ﴿Do they await but its interpretation?﴾ [al-A'raf: 53]. The verse, on this interpretation, includes a threat. The second meaning: that He meant "Nay, they denied this mighty Qur'an, which informs of the unseen, of which they had no prior knowledge, nor did they encompass knowledge of its unseen matters or the beauty of its composition, and nor had its explanation and clarification come to them." Abu 'Abdullah al-Razi said: it may bear several aspects. The first: whenever they heard some narrative, they said "fables of the ancients" (al-An'am: 25), and did not realize that the purpose of these narratives is not the story itself, but His power to dispose of this world, to transfer its people from honor to humiliation and from humiliation to honor, and the perishing of the world, so that one may take warning from that. And that these narratives are by revelation from Allah, since He informed of them through the tongue of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ without distortion, despite his not having learned or been a student. The second: whenever they heard the disjointed letters and did not understand anything from them, their suspicion grew, and Allah has answered this with His saying: ﴿In it are clear signs﴾ [Al 'Imran: 97], etc. The third: the Qur'an appeared gradually, so their suspicion grew and they said: ﴿Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?﴾ [al-Furqan: 32]. Allah has answered and explained this in its place. The fourth: the Qur'an is full of the gathering (on the Day of Resurrection), and they had become accustomed to sensible things, so they found the return of life after death improbable, and Allah demonstrated the truth of the Resurrection with many proofs. The fifth: that it is full of commands to acts of worship, and they used to say: the God of the worlds is independent of our obedience, and is too exalted to command us with what has no benefit in it. Allah answered with His saying: ﴿If you do good, you do good for yourselves﴾ [al-Isra': 7], etc. In sum, the resemblances among the disbelievers are many; when they saw the Qur'an containing matters whose realities they did not know and whose wisdom they had not grasped, they denied the Qur'an. So His saying "what they did not encompass in knowledge" points to their lack of knowledge of these matters, and His saying "and its interpretation had not yet come to them" points to their lack of effort and striving in seeking the secrets of what the Qur'an contains. End of summary.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: what is the sense of expectation in His saying, 'and its interpretation had not yet come to them'?" I say: its meaning is that they denied it instantly before reflection, and before knowing its interpretation, by blind imitation of their fathers; and they denied it after reflection out of obstinacy and stubbornness. So He blamed them for their haste to deny before knowledge of it, and He used the word of expectation (lamma) to indicate that they came to know, after the elevation of its status and its inimitability, when He repeatedly challenged them and they exhausted their strength in trying to produce its like, and became certain of their inability to match it; yet they denied it out of insolence and envy. End of quote.

His statement needs scrutiny. He also said: it is possible that the meaning is: "and its interpretation had not yet come to them, and its interpretation of what it contains of informing of the unseen had not yet come to them, i.e., its outcome, until it becomes clear to them whether it is a lie or the truth?" He means: it is a Book inimitable from two angles: from the angle of the inimitability of its composition, and from the angle of what it contains of informing of the unseen. So they hastened to deny it before they looked into its composition and its reaching the limit of inimitability, and before they were informed of its reports of the unseen matters, and its truth or falsehood. End of quote.

The sentence of "encompassing" is introduced with "lam" (لم), and the sentence of "its interpretation coming to them" with "lamma" (لما), and this requires a subtle distinction. The kaf (ك) is in the accusative position, meaning: like that denial, those before them denied, i.e., before considering the miracles of the prophets and before reflecting upon them, without being fair to themselves; rather they imitated their fathers and were obstinate.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: al-Zajjaj said: "kayfa" (كيف) is in the accusative position as the predicate of "kana" (كان); "unzur" (انظر) cannot govern it, because what precedes the interrogative does not govern it. This is the rule of the grammarians, for they treated "kayfa" everywhere as a pure interrogative, as in your saying: "How is Zayd?" And "kayfa" has other usages beyond this, in which it takes the place of the verbal noun meaning "manner," and the sense of interrogation is dissolved; this position may be one of these, and among its usages is their saying: "Be however you wish," and consider al-Bukhari's words: "How the beginning of revelation was," for it did not ... end of quote.

Al-Zajjaj's statement, "it cannot be governed by unzur," and his reasoning: he means that the word "unzur" cannot govern it verbally, but the clause is in the accusative position as an object of "unzur" in suspended form, and it is from the seeing of the heart.

Ibn 'Atiyyah's statement, "this is the rule of the grammarians," through to the end of his reasoning, is not as he stated. Rather "kayfa" has two meanings: one, the pure interrogative, which is a question about the state, except when you suspend the governing verb from it, in which case its meaning is that of the nouns used for interrogation when the governing verb is suspended. The second: the conditional, as in the Arabs' saying: "However you become, I will become." And his statement, "and kayfa has other usages, in which it takes the place of the verbal noun," and so on, is not correct: "kayfa" does not take the place of a verbal noun, and the word "kayfiyyah" is not a verbal noun; rather that is an attribution to "kayfa."

His statement, "it may be that this position is among them and among its usages, the saying: 'Be however you wish'," is not admissible, because he did not establish for it the meaning he mentioned of "kayfa" being in the sense of "kayfiyyah" and the claim of a verbal noun "kayfiyyah." As for "Be however you wish," "kayfa" here does not mean "kayfiyyah"; rather it is conditional, and that is the second meaning it has.

Its answer is omitted; the estimate is: "However you wish, then be," just as you say: "Stand whenever you wish," where "mata" is a conditional noun of time, governing nothing, and the answer is omitted, its estimate being: "Whenever you wish, then stand." The answer is omitted because what precedes it indicates it, like the saying: "Strike Zayd if he wrongs you," the estimate: "If he wrongs you, then strike him," and "strike him" is omitted because of the indication of the earlier "strike." As for al-Bukhari's words, "How was the beginning of revelation?" it is a pure interrogative, either by way of narration, as if a questioner asked him and said: "How was the beginning of revelation?" and he answered with the hadith that contains the manner of it.

As for "the wrongdoers" (al-zalimin): the apparent meaning is that it refers to those before them; it is possible that it refers to those to whom the pronoun of "Nay, they denied" refers.

﴿And among them are those who believe in it, and among them are those who do not believe in it. And your Lord is most knowing of the corrupters.﴾ The apparent meaning is that it is an announcement that among the disbelievers of Quraysh there will be someone who will believe in it, namely one for whom happiness has preceded, and among them is one who does not believe in it and will die upon disbelief.

It was also said: this is a division among the disbelievers who remain upon their disbelief: among them is one who believes in it inwardly and knows that it is true, but denies out of obstinacy; and among them is one who does not believe in it neither inwardly nor outwardly, either because of the swiftness of his denial and his not having contemplated it, or because he looked into it but doubts overcame him and he lacked the understanding to repel them. In it is a splitting of the word of the disbelievers, and that they are not uniform in their beliefs; rather they are in turmoil, even if denial and disbelief encompass them.

It was also said: the pronoun in "among them" refers to the People of the Book, while the apparent reference is to those to whom the pronoun of "Do they say" refers. Attaching knowledge to "the corrupters" alone is a great threat to them.

﴿And if they deny you, say: "For me is my work, and for you is your work. You are free of what I do, and I am free of what you do."﴾ That is: and if they persist in denying you, then disassociate yourself from them; you have already given excuse and delivered (the message), as in His saying: ﴿So if they disobey you, say: "I am free of what you do"﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 216]. The meaning of "for me is my work" is: the recompense of my work, and for you is the recompense of your work.

The meaning of "my work" is the righteous work comprising faith and obedience, and "your work" is that comprising association and disobedience. The apparent sense is that it is a verse of disassociation and disengagement from them, and it includes a threat, as in His saying: ﴿Say: "O disbelievers"﴾ [al-Kafirun: 1], the whole surah. It was also said: the intent of this is to win them over and attract their hearts.

Some, including Ibn Zayd, said: it is abrogated by fighting, because it is Meccan; this is the view of Mujahid, al-Kalbi and Muqatil. But the verifiers said: it is not abrogated, and its implication is that each one is singled out for his own actions and their fruits of reward and punishment, and the verse of the sword did not lift anything of this.

He began with the commanded part, saying "for me is my deed," because it is more emphatic in dissociating them, and he began the disavowal with "you are free from what I do," because this sentence comes as an emphasis and completion of what precedes it. So it suited to follow "and for you is your deed." It also serves the fawasil (verse endings). Had the mention of disavowal come first, as the mention of "for me is my deed" did, the sentence would not have fallen as a verse ending, since the construction would have been "and you are free from what I do."

(p-161)﴿And among them are those who listen to you. Can you make the deaf hear, even though they do not understand?﴾ ﴿And among them are those who look at you. Can you guide the blind, even though they do not see?﴾ ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong people at all, but people wrong themselves.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: the two verses were revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith and others among the mockers. Ibn al-Anbari said: concerning a group of Jews. (end of quotation)

This verse contains a division of the disbelievers who do not believe into these two categories, after the division of the deniers into those who believe and those who do not. The pronoun in "yastami'una" (they listen) refers to the meaning of "man" (whoever), and referring back to the meaning rather than the wording is permissible in the plural. It is like His saying: ﴿And among the devils are those who dive for him﴾ (21:82). The meaning is: those who listen to you when you recite the Qur'an and teach the laws. Then he negated the benefit of that listening by saying: "Can you make the deaf hear?" That is, they are deaf to grasping what you convey to them; even if they listen to you, they have no awareness and no acceptance. Especially since, added to their deafness, is the absence of reason. So the lack of hearing and reason, with "min" (among) before them, means they have no perception of anything whatsoever. This is unlike a deaf person who is rational, for by his reason he can be guided to things.

In His saying "And among them are those who look at you," he repeated the pronoun in the singular masculine according to the wording of "man," which is the most common usage in the Arabic language. The meaning is that they are blind, so you cannot guide them, because the means by which one is guided to seeing the proofs they have lost. Moreover, along with the loss of sight, they have lost insight, for whoever is blind is guided by the light of his insight to things by intuition, whereas these have combined the loss of sight and insight. This is a great exaggeration of their total non-acceptance of what is conveyed to them, since they combined deafness with absence of reason, and blindness with lack of insight.

His saying "Can you [...]" is a consolation to the Messenger (ﷺ), and a means to ensure that he does not grieve over their non-acceptance, since guidance belongs only to Allah. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "He came with 'yanzuru' according to the wording of 'man.' When the verb comes according to its wording, it is permissible for another verb to be conjoined to it according to the meaning. But when it first comes according to its meaning, it is not permissible to conjoin to it another according to the wording, because the speech would then become confused." (end of quotation)

This is not as he said. Rather, it is permissible to observe the meaning first, and to refer the pronoun according to what you intend of the meaning in terms of feminine, dual, or plural, and then to observe the wording, referring the pronoun in the singular masculine. This has detailed treatment in the science of grammar. The purpose of the two verses is to inform him, peace be upon him, that these disbelievers have reached such a degree of aversion, enmity and intense hatred that no treatment whatsoever will benefit them. For whoever is deaf, foolish, blind, and lacking insight cannot comprehend the excellences of speech or the inimitability contained within it, nor can he see the marvels that Allah performed through His Messenger. Thus, guidance for these people has been despaired of. The poet said:

"And if I am hidden from the dullard, it is excusable that a blind eye does not see me."

When the Exalted mentioned these wretched people, He mentioned that He does not wrong them at all, since He has removed their excuses by sending the Messengers and warning them of His punishment. Rather, they wronged themselves by disbelief and denial.

This negation of wronging could mean in this world, that is, He does not wrong them in any of their interests. It could also mean in the Hereafter, and that the punishment that befalls them is justice from Him, because they are the ones who caused it by earning their sins, as He decreed for them: "He is not questioned about what He does."

The readers' disagreement regarding "wa-lakinna al-nas" (but people) has been mentioned before: the nun being doubled with "al-nas" in the accusative, the nun being lightened, and with "al-nas" in the nominative.

(And the day He gathers them, as if they had not remained but an hour of the day, recognizing one another among themselves. Those who denied the meeting with Allah have indeed lost, and they were not guided.) Al-A'mash and Hafs recited "yahshuruhum" with the yā' (y), the pronoun referring in the third person to Allah, since "Indeed, Allah does not wrong people at all" preceded it. When He mentioned those wretched people, He followed it with the warning and the description of their state on the Day of Resurrection. The meaning: "as if they had not remained" in the world or in the graves; that is, their stay was brief. This is due to the horror of what they witness of the severe trials of the Resurrection, or due to the length of the Day of Resurrection and their standing for reckoning.

Ibn 'Abbas said: they saw that the length of their lives, compared with eternity, was like an hour. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "'Yawma' (the day) is an adverbial accusative (zarf), and its accusative may be correct by a hidden verb, whose estimation is: 'and remember.' It may also be in the accusative by the verb that is implied in His saying: 'as if they had not remained but an hour of the day.' It may also be in the accusative by 'yata'arafuna' (recognizing one another). The kaf in His saying 'ka-anna' may be in the position of a description of the day, and it may be in the position of a description of a verbal noun (masdar), as if he said: 'and the day We gather them with a gathering as if they had not remained.' It may also be that His saying 'ka-anna lam yalbathu' (as if they had not remained) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in 'nahshuruhum' (We gather them)." (end of quotation)

As for his saying "It may be in the accusative by the verb implied in 'ka-anna lam yalbathu,'" this is a vague statement, for he did not specify the verb that is implied in "ka-anna lam yalbathu." Perhaps he meant what al-Haufi said: that the kaf is in the accusative position governed by the sense of the speech contained in it, which is speed. (end of quotation)

Thus the estimate would be: "And the day We gather them, they hasten as if they had not remained." As for his saying "The kaf in 'ka-anna' may be in the position of a description of the day," this is not correct, because "yawma nahshuruhum" is definite, while the clauses are indefinite, and a definite noun is not described by an indefinite one.

It cannot be said that the clause following time nouns is indefinite in every case. For if it is in estimation resolved into a definite, then what it is attached to becomes definite; and if it is resolved into an indefinite, then what it is attached to is indefinite. You say: "I passed on the day that Zayd arrived, the past one," so you describe "yawm" with the definite. And you say: "I came on the night that Zayd arrived, the blessed one upon us."

Moreover, "ka-anna lam yalbathu" cannot be a description of the day in meaning, because that is a description of the ones gathered, not a description of the day of their gathering. Some have burdened themselves with estimating an omitted linking element, estimating: "as if they had not remained before it," so "before it" was omitted, that is, before the day. But the omission of such a linking element is not permissible.

Therefore, the apparent reading is that it is a circumstantial clause from the object of "nahshuruhum," as Ibn 'Atiyya said last, and Abu al-Baqa' and al-Zamakhshari likewise parsed it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: 'ka-anna lam yalbathu' and 'yata'arafuna' — what is their position? I say: as for the first, it is a circumstantial clause from them, meaning: We gather them, likened to those who did not remain but an hour. As for the second, it is either attached to the adverb of time, meaning it is a circumstantial clause, or it is explanatory of His saying 'ka-anna lam yalbathu illa sa'atan,' because recognition remains with the long passage of time and turns into mutual denial." (end of quotation)

Al-Haufi said: "yata'arafuna" is a imperfect verb in the position of a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "yalbathu," and it is the governing element. As if he said: "gathered recognizing one another." The meaning: they gathered recognizing one another. It is also permissible that it be a circumstantial clause from the "ha" and "mim" in "nahshuruhum," and it is the governing element. (end of quotation)

As for Ibn 'Atiyya's statement: "It may be in the accusative position of the verbal noun, as if he said: 'and the day We gather them with a gathering as if they had not remained,'" this was reported by Abu al-Baqa', who said: "It was also said it is a description of an omitted verbal noun, that is, a gathering as if they had not remained before it." (end of quotation)

We have already mentioned that the omission of such a linking element is not permissible. They also permitted that "yata'arafuna" be a circumstantial clause, according to what was mentioned earlier of the disagreement regarding the one with the circumstance and its governing element, and that it be a resumptive sentence (istinaf), in which Allah informs that recognition takes place among them.

Al-Kalbi said: "Each one recognizes the other as they knew one another in the world when they came out of their graves. It is a recognition of rebuke and exposure. One says to another: 'You misled me and led me astray.' It is not a recognition of compassion and tenderness. Then recognition ceases when they witness the horrors of the Resurrection, as the Exalted said: ﴿And no intimate friend asks after an intimate friend﴾ (70:10), ﴿though they are made to see one another﴾ (70:11). It was also said: each one informs the other of the error and disbelief they were upon."

Al-Dahhak said: "It is the recognition of the affection of believers, while the disbelievers have no kinship among them." It was also said: the Resurrection has stages; in one stage they recognize one another, and in another stage they do not recognize one another.

The apparent reading is that His saying "Those who [...] have indeed lost" to the end is a resumptive sentence, in which Allah informs of the loss of those who denied meeting Him. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is a resumption carrying the meaning of wonder, as if it were said: 'How great is their loss!'" (end of quotation)

He also said: "He began with 'qad khasira' with the intention of saying, that is: they recognize one another among themselves, saying this." (end of quotation) Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It was also said it is the report of the gathered ones in the manner of rebuke against themselves." (end of quotation)
