Al-Zamakhshari's disagreement with the majority in claiming that between the hamza and the conjunctive particle there is an omitted clause to which the clause after the conjunction is conjoined.

Al-Tabari said, regarding His saying "athumma" with a damma on the tha, that its meaning is "hunalika" (there), and said: "This 'thumma' is not the one that comes meaning conjunction," end of quote. What al-Tabari said, that "thumma" here is not for conjunction, is a claim; as for his saying that the meaning is "hunalika," what should be meant is that this is an explanation of meaning, not that "thumma" with a damma has the meaning of "hunalika."

Talha ibn Musarrif read "athamma" with a fatha on the tha, and this agrees with al-Tabari's explanation "hunalika." The majority read "ālān" with the interrogative and the madd, and likewise "ālān wa-qad 'asayta" (Now? And you had disobeyed). Talha and al-A'raj read with the hamza of interrogation without madd, and this is on the supposition of an implied saying: it is said to them when they believe after the punishment has fallen: "Now you believe in it?" So the governing element of "ālān" is "amantum bihi," which is omitted; it is said that the angels say this to them, and it is said God does. The interrogation is by way of rebuke.

In the book al-Lawami', 'Isa al-Basri and Talha read "amantum bihi al-an" with the hamza connected and without interrogation, but as a statement, so its accusative is as an adverb of time governed by the mentioned "amantum bihi." As for the common reading, its accusative is by an implied verb indicated by the mentioned "amantum bihi," because the interrogation has taken the beginning of the sentence, so what precedes it prevents it from governing what follows, end of quote. "Wa-qad kuntum" is a circumstantial clause. Al-Zamakhshari said: "and you were seeking to hasten it" means: you were denying it, because your hastening was by way of denial and rejection. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "you were seeking to hasten" as deniers of it.

Then it will be said to those who did wrong, "Taste the punishment of eternity. Are you being recompensed except for what you used to earn?"

This means that the keepers of Hell (khazanat Jahannam) say these words to them. The wrongdoing here is the wrongdoing of disbelief (zulm al-kufr), not the wrongdoing of disobedience (zulm al-ma'siyah), because whoever among the sinful believers enters the Fire does not remain in it forever. As for "thumma qila" (then it was said), it is a conjunction coordinating with the pronoun implied before "al-an" (now).

As for the one who reads with wasl (connecting) the alif of "al-an," then it is a resumed statement reporting what will be said to them on the Day of Resurrection. And "hal tujzawna" (are you being recompensed) is a rebuke to them and a clarification that the recompense is according to the servant's earning (kasb).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 10, verses 53–60 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And they ask you, "Is it true?" Say, "Yes, by my Lord, it is indeed true, and you cannot escape it."﴾ That is, they ask you for information. The pronoun in "Is it true?" refers to the punishment. It has also been said that it refers to the Law and the Qur'an, or to the threat, or to the matter of the Hour. The clause is in a position of accusative (naṣb). Al-Zamakhshari said: the verb "yaqūlūna" (they say) is implied, so the sentence is "They say, 'Is it true?'" and so "yastanbi'ūnaka" (they ask you) takes one object. Ibn 'Atiyya said: its meaning is "yastakhbirūnaka" (they ask you for information), and on this view it takes two objects: the first is the kāf (you), and the second is the clause of the interrogative (the subject and predicate). According to what he said, "yastanbi'ūnaka" is then a suspended verb (mu'allaqah). The original use of "istanba'a" is that it takes two objects, the first with "'an" (about). You say "istanba'tu Zaydan 'an 'Amrin" (I asked Zayd about 'Amr), meaning I asked him to inform me about 'Amr. The apparent view is that the verb is suspended from the second object.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: It has also been said that it means "yasta'limūnaka" (they seek to know from you). On this view it requires three objects: the first is the kāf, and the inceptive and predicate together stand in place of the two objects. [End of his words.] But this is not as he stated, because "ista'lama" is not known to take three objects. One does not say "ista'lamtu Zaydan 'Amran qā'iman" so that the interrogative clause would stand in place of the two objects. Its meaning being "yasta'limūnaka" does not require that it take three objects, because "ista'lama" does not take three objects as we have mentioned. "Huwa" is in the nominative as the subject, and "ḥaqq" is its predicate.

Al-Hawfi and Abu al-Baqa' permitted that "ḥaqq" be the subject (mubtada') and that "huwa" be the agent of it, standing in place of the predicate. "Ḥaqq" is not an active or passive participle; it is in origin a verbal noun (maṣdar), and it is not far-fetched that it be in the nominative because it has the meaning of something established. This question from them was by way of mockery and denial.

Al-A'mash read "al-ḥaqq" (with the definite article). Al-Zamakhshari said: This is more suited to mockery, because it contains an implication of insinuation that it is false, for the lām is for the category, as if it were said: "Is it the truth, not falsehood? Or is it that which you named 'the truth'?" [End of his words.]

Almighty God commanded His Prophet to say in reply to them: ﴿Say, "Yes, by my Lord."﴾ That is: yes, by my Lord. "Ay" is used only in an oath, just as "hal" is used with the meaning of "qad" (indeed) only in that context. Al-Zamakhshari said this and said: I have heard them say in affirmation "ay," and they connect it to the particle of oath "wāw," and they do not pronounce it alone. [End of his words.] But what al-Zamakhshari heard from them is no proof, because his speech is not authoritative as evidence, owing to the corruption of the Arabic speech of that time and of the many periods before it. (p-169) Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is a word that precedes an oath and has the meaning of "na'am" (yes), and after it comes the particle of oath, though it may not come. You say "ay rabbī" or "ay wa-rabbī." [End of his words.]

The answer could have been limited to "ay wa-rabbī," but it was emphasized by stating the clause that was implied after "ay wa-rabbī," introduced with "inna" and the lām, as an intensification of emphasis in the answer. Since their question "Is it true?" contained a question about the punishment, and it was a question about the punishment that would befall them, not about any punishment that befalls whomever it befalls, it was said: ﴿And you cannot escape it,﴾ that is, you cannot escape the punishment asked about; rather, it will overtake you.

This clause may be included in the answer to the oath, so that it is conjoined to the answer before it. It may also be understood as an assertion, conjoined to the clause that was said and not to the answer to the oath. The hamza in "a'jaza" is for transitivity, as in His saying: ﴿And we will never make Him unable [to escape] by flight﴾ [al-Jinn: 12]. But its object is frequently omitted, to the point that the Arabs say "a'jaza fulānun" (so-and-so was unable) when he went off into the land and was not reached. Al-Zajjaj said: That is, you are not among those who can frustrate those who punish you.

﴿And if every soul that wronged had all that is on earth, it would surely offer it for ransom. And they will conceal the regret when they see the punishment. And it will be judged between them with justice, and they will not be wronged.﴾ When He mentioned the punishment and swore to its reality, and that they would not escape from it, He mentioned some of the states of the wrongdoers in the Hereafter.

"Wronged" is an attribute of "soul." The wrongdoing here is polytheism and disbelief. "Iftada" comes as the reflexive of "fada," so it is intransitive: you say "fadaytuhu fa-iftada" (I ransomed him, so he ransomed himself). And it can have the meaning of "fada," in which case it is transitive. Here it may bear either of the two meanings.

"What is on earth" means: what it possessed in the world of treasures, wealth, and benefits. "Asarru" is among the words with opposite meanings and comes with the meaning of "azhara" (to reveal). Al-Farazdaq said:

When al-Hajjaj drew his sword,
the Kharijite who had been showing himself concealed himself.

And another said:

So I concealed the regret the day the caller called out
for the return of the camels of Ghadira, the caller.

It also comes with the meaning of "akhfa" (to conceal), which is the best known meaning of it, as in His saying: ﴿He knows what they keep secret and what they make public﴾ [Hud: 5]. Here it may bear both meanings. As for revealing, it is not a day for patience or fortitude, and the disbeliever cannot in it hide what befalls him. And because at the moment of seeing the punishment a person is overcome with grief over the sin that caused it, and he shows regret over what he has missed of success and of deliverance from the punishment. They have indeed said: ﴿Our Lord, our wretchedness overcame us﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 106].

As for concealing the regret, it has been said: their leaders concealed the regret from their followers out of shame before them and fear of their reproach. This is far-fetched, because one who beholds the punishment is occupied with what he suffers from it, so how could he have thought about shame or about the reproach coming from the lowly? Also, "wa-asarru" refers to "every soul that wronged" according to meaning, and it is general, applying to leaders and followers alike.

It has also been said: the concealing of regret results from their being stunned at seeing what they had not expected and had not occurred to them, and from their witnessing what weakened their strength, so that at that moment they were unable to cry out or wail, and could do nothing that the one who is distressed does except hide the regret and grief in their hearts, as happens to one who is brought to the cross and hardly says a word, remaining stunned and motionless. As for him who said that the meaning of His saying "and they concealed the regret" is that they were sincere to God in that regret, or that the faces of their foreheads showed the regret, that is, the wrinkles of their brows, this is far from the context of the verse.

The apparent view is that His saying ﴿And it will be judged between them with justice﴾ is a separate, new clause of information, and is not conjoined to what is within the scope of "lammā," and that the pronoun in "baynahum" refers to "every soul that wronged." Al-Zamakhshari said: "between the wrongdoers and the wronged" is indicated by the mention of wrongdoing. [End of his words.]

It has been said that it refers to the believer and the disbeliever. It has also been said that it refers to the leaders and the followers.

﴿Surely to God belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth. Surely the promise of God is true, but most of them do not know.﴾ ﴿He gives life and causes death, and to Him you will be returned.﴾ It has been said: the connection of this verse to what came before is that He supposed that the wrongdoing soul, if it had what is on earth, would ransom itself with it, while it has absolutely nothing, because all things entirely belong to God Almighty, and He is the one who disposes of them, for to Him belong the dominion and the ownership. And the connection of it (p-170) to what came before appears to be this: when they asked about what they had been promised of punishment, "Is it true?", and they were answered that it was indeed true beyond doubt, that answer was sufficient for one whom God Almighty had granted success in faith, just as it was an answer to the bedouin when he asked the Messenger (ﷺ): "Did God send you?" He (peace be upon him) said: "O God, yes," and he was content with that from him, upon his (ﷺ) informing him, since he knew that he would say nothing but the truth and what is right, as Heraclius said: "He would not leave off lying to people and then lie about God."

He moved from this answer to mentioning the decisive proof for his argument and the establishment that belief in prophethood and the return rests on establishing a God who is powerful and wise, and that whatever is other than Him is His dominion and property. On this basis (comes) this verse, and he had fully surveyed the proofs of this in this surah in His saying: ﴿Indeed in the alternation of night and day﴾ [Yunus: 6], and His saying: ﴿He it is who made the sun a radiance﴾ [Yunus: 5]. So he was content here to omit mentioning them.

And if everything in the world is His dominion and property, then He is capable of all possibilities, knowing of all knowables, free of need for all needs, exalted above all deficiencies and defects. And by His being capable of possibilities, He is capable of sending down punishment upon the disbelievers in this world and the Hereafter, and capable of supporting His messenger with proofs and exalting His religion, so mockery and challenge are void.

And by His being exalted above deficiencies, He is exalted above breaking promises and lying. Thus it is established that His saying ﴿Surely to God belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ is a premise that necessitates the certainty of the truth of His saying: "Surely the promise of God is true." The word "alā" (surely) is a particle of alerting, which entered upon both clauses as an alert for the heedless, since they were occupied with looking at the apparent causes, from attributing things to be owned by one to whom some disposal and succession over them was granted. For this reason Almighty God said: ﴿But most of them do not know,﴾ meaning: because of their neglect of these proofs. Then He followed that with mention of His power over giving life and causing death.

It must be that He is capable of bringing them back to life a second time, and for this reason He said: ﴿And to Him you will be returned,﴾ so you will see what He promised. Al-Hasan, in one report from him, and 'Isa ibn 'Umar read "yurja'ūna" with the "yā'" in the third person. The majority read it with the "tā'" in the second person.

﴿O mankind, there has come to you an admonition from your Lord, and a healing for what is in the breasts, and guidance and mercy for the believers.﴾ It has been said: it was revealed concerning the Quraysh who asked the Messenger (ﷺ), "Is it true?" So "mankind" refers to the disbelieving Quraysh. Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is an address to all the world.

The connection of this verse to what came before is that when He mentioned the proofs of divinity, oneness, and power, He mentioned the proofs indicating the validity of prophethood and the path leading to it, which is the Qur'an, and the one characterized by these noble attributes is the Qur'an. Al-Zamakhshari said: That is, there has come to you a book comprehensive of these benefits, of admonition and warning concerning monotheism. It is a healing, that is, a remedy for what is in your breasts of corrupt beliefs, and a call to the truth, and a mercy for whoever among you believes in it. [End of his words.]

"Min rabbikum" may be connected to "jā'atkum," so "min" indicates the starting point. It may also be in a position of description, meaning: from the admonitions of your Lord, in which case it is connected to an implied element, and "min" is partitive. In His saying "min rabbikum" there is an indication that it is from God and not from anyone else.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: He made it an admonition according to all people, and He made it guidance and mercy according to the believers. This is a division that is sound in meaning if it is interpreted by directing it so. [End of his words.] Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi mentioned here much speech mixed with what they call wisdom. We know for certain that the Arabs would not understand what he established from the words of the Qur'an. He elaborated on that and gave sensible examples that are to be understood from his exegesis. Then he said at the end of his speech: The sum is that admonition is an indication of purifying the outward forms of creation from what is not fitting, which is the Law; healing is an indication of purifying the spirits from corrupt beliefs and blameworthy character traits, which is the Path; guidance is an indication of the appearance of the light of truth in the hearts of the truthful, which is the Reality; and mercy is an indication of its being perfect in completeness, and the radiance, to the point where it completes the deficient, which is prophethood. These are rational degrees and demonstrative stages indicated by these Qur'anic words, and it is not possible for what was mentioned first to come later, nor for what was mentioned last to come first.

(p-171) ﴿Say, "In the grace of God and in His mercy, in that let them rejoice; it is better than what they amass."﴾ Al-Zamakhshari said, citing Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited: ﴿Say, 'In the grace of God and in His mercy,'﴾ and said: 'By the Book of God and Islam. Its grace is Islam, and its mercy is what He promised for it.'" [End of his words.]

If this hadith is sound, its contrary cannot be allowed. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatadah, and Hilal ibn Yasaf said: The grace of God is Islam, and His mercy is the Qur'an. Al-Dahhak and Zayd ibn Aslam said the opposite of this. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri said: The grace is the Qur'an, and the mercy is that He made them among its people.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 10, verses 53–60 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn ʿAbbas said, as transmitted by al-Dahhak from him: "The grace (al-fadl) is knowledge, and the mercy (al-rahma) is Muhammad (ﷺ)." Ibn ʿUmar said: "The grace is Islam, and the mercy is its adornment in the hearts." Mujahid said: "The grace and the mercy are the Qur'an," and al-Zajjaj chose this view.

Khalid ibn Maʿdan said: "The grace is the Qur'an, and the mercy is the Sunnah." He also said, on another report: "The grace is Islam, and the mercy is concealment (of sins)." ʿAmr ibn ʿUthman said: "The grace of Allah is the lifting of the veil, and His mercy is the vision and the meeting (with Him)." Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: "The grace is faith (al-iman), and the mercy is Paradise."

It was also said: "The grace is divine success (al-tawfiq), and the mercy is protection (from sin) (al-ʿisma)." It was said: "The grace is His outward blessings, and the mercy is His inward blessings." Al-Sadiq said: "The grace is forgiveness, and the mercy is divine success." Dhu al-Nun said: "The grace is the gardens (of Paradise), and His mercy is deliverance from the Fires."

These are specifications that require evidence, and it should be understood that they are examples (tamthilat), because "grace" and "mercy" are intended to refer to what has been mentioned, not to restrict them to it.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: "What the wording indicates and necessarily implies is that the grace is Allah's guidance to His religion and His granting of success in following the sharʿ (sacred law, here meaning divine law), and the mercy is His pardon and dwelling in His Paradise, which He made a reward for following Islam and faith." End of quotation.

The meaning of the verse: Say, O Muhammad, to all people: "By the grace of Allah and His mercy, let them rejoice, not by worldly affairs and what is gathered of its trash." So the believers are told: "Let them rejoice," while they are connected to the cause and reason of joy, sincere toward the grace of Allah, and awaiting His mercy. As for the disbelievers, it is said to them: "By the grace of Allah and His mercy, let them rejoice," in the sense of: "If it happened to you, or if you were made happy by being guided to attaining that." End of quotation.

The apparent reading is that His saying, "Say: By the grace of Allah and His mercy, so by that let them rejoice," consists of two clauses, and the element to which the preposition "bi-" (by) relates has been omitted. The meaning is: "Say: By the grace of Allah and His mercy, that they may rejoice." Then the second clause is conjoined to the first for the sake of emphasis. Al-Zamakhshari said: "The repetition is for affirmation and emphasis, and for making the rejoicing specific to the grace and mercy, excluding what is other than them of the benefits of this world. So one of the two verbs is omitted because the mentioned verb indicates it, and the fa' (so) carries the sense of a condition, as if it were said: 'If they rejoice at something, let them restrict their rejoicing to these two, for there is nothing rejoiced at that is more worthy than them.' It is also permissible that it means: 'By the grace of Allah and His mercy, let them take care of that, so let them rejoice.'" End of quotation.

It is also permissible that it means: "Indeed there has come to you an admonition by the grace of Allah and His mercy, so by that (i.e., by the coming of these two), let them rejoice." End of quotation.

As for the supposition of the verb "let them take care" (fa-l-yaʿtanu), there is no evidence for it. As for linking "bi-" to His saying, "There has come to you," that would require the phrase to be understood as omitted after "qul" (say), and it cannot be linked to the first "jaʾatkum" because of the separation between them by "qul."

Al-Hawfi said: "The preposition 'bi-' is related to what indicates the meaning, i.e., 'the admonition has come to you by the grace of Allah.'" It was also said: "The first fa' is extra (ziyada), and by that (bi-dhalika) is a substitute (badal) placed before it, and it refers to the two, the grace and the mercy." It was also said: "The second fa' is repeated for emphasis. On this view, the first fa' is not extra, and the original structure is 'bi-dhalika li-yafrahu' (by that, that they may rejoice). In the previous statement, the original structure would be 'bi-dhalika fa-l-yafrahu' (by that, let them rejoice)." There is no contradiction between the command to rejoice here and the prohibition in His saying: ﴿Do not exult; indeed Allah does not love the exultant﴾ [al-Qasas: 76], because the object of the joy differs. The thing commanded here is rejoicing in the grace of Allah and His mercy, while the thing forbidden there is rejoicing in the gathering of wealth for worldly leadership, the desire for dominance through it, and corruption. For this reason, what follows is His saying: ﴿But seek, through what Allah has given you, the Home of the Hereafter, and do not forget your share of this world﴾ [al-Qasas: 77], and what precedes it is: ﴿Indeed, Qarun was of the people of Moses, but he oppressed them﴾ [al-Qasas: 76]. And His saying: ﴿Surely he is exultant and boastful﴾ [Hud: 10] came in the manner of censure, for his joy at receiving blessings after hardship, and his despair and ingratitude for blessings when they were taken from him. This is a blameworthy trait, and such conduct is not among the acts of the Hereafter.

As for the view of one who says: "When rejoicing (al-faraḥ) is stated without qualification, it is blameworthy, and when it is qualified, it is not blameworthy, as in His saying: ﴿rejoicing in what Allah has given them of His grace﴾ [Al ʿImran: 170]," this is not a consistent rule, since it came qualified in censure in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿until, when they rejoiced in what they had been given, We seized them suddenly﴾ [al-Anʿam: 44]. Rejoicing is praised or blamed according to its object. When it is over attaining the reward of the Hereafter and deeds of righteousness, it is praiseworthy, and when it is over attaining the pleasures of this world and its trash, it is blameworthy.

ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan, Ubayy, Anas, al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Ibn Hurmuz, Ibn Sirin, Abu Jaʿfar al-Madani, al-Sulami, Qatada, al-Jahdari, Hilal ibn Yasaf, al-Aʿmash, ʿAmr ibn Qaʾid, and al-ʿAbbas ibn al-Fadl al-Ansari read: "falta-farahu" with the taʾ (second person, addressing the audience: "so let you rejoice") as a form of address, and this was transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ).

The author of al-Lawamih (Sahib al-Lawamih, Ibn Mihran's Kitab al-Lawami' or related work on readings) said: "And he said..., and it has come down from Yaʿqub likewise." End of quotation.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: "Ubayy, Ibn al-Qaʿqaʿ, Ibn ʿAmir, and al-Hasan read (it so), according to what Harun claimed. It was transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ): 'falta-farahu' and 'tajmaʿuna' with the taʾ in both, in address. This is the reading of a large group of the early generations (al-salaf), though most of them differ on it." End of quotation.

The majority read it with the yaʾ (third person), as a command to the absent party. What Ibn ʿAtiyya reported, that Ibn ʿAmir read "falta-farahu" with the taʾ, is not what is well known from him. Rather, his reading in the famous seven readings is with the yaʾ, as a command to the absent party. However, he read "tajmaʿuna" with the taʾ in address, while the rest of the seven read it with the taʾ in address.

In the Mushaf of Ubayy it is: "bi-dhalika fa-farihu" (by that, rejoice), and this is the common, well-known usage for commanding the addressee.

As for "fa-l-yafrahu" with the yaʾ, it is a rare dialect form. In a hadith: "Let you take your rows (li-taʾkhudhu masaffakum)." Abu al-Tayyah and al-Hasan read "fa-l-yafrahu" with a kasra on the lam (fa-li-yafrahu). The fact that the reference is to a single thing is shown by the pronoun returning to it in the singular in His saying: "it is better than what they gather." So what is most appropriate is that His saying, "by the grace of Allah and His mercy," treats them as one thing, expressed by two names for emphasis. For this reason it is referred to as "dhalika" (that), and the pronoun returns to it in the singular. His saying, "what they gather," means from the trash and goods of this world.

﴿Say: Have you considered what Allah has sent down to you of provision, and you made some of it unlawful and some lawful? Say: Did Allah permit you, or do you invent against Allah?﴾

The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that when He, exalted is He, mentioned: ﴿O mankind, there has come to you an admonition from your Lord﴾, and the intended meaning of that was the Book of Allah, which includes the permitting and forbidding, He then clarified the corruption of their laws and rulings concerning the lawful and unlawful, without any basis for them in revelation.

"Arayitum" here means "inform me." They allowed that "ma anzala" be a relative pronoun (mawsula) as the first object of "arayitum," with a returning pronoun omitted, and the second object is His saying, "Did Allah permit you?" The pronoun referring back from the predicate to the subject is omitted; its estimated form is: "Did Allah permit you in it?" "Qul" (say) was repeated before the predicate for emphasis.

"Ma" may also be an interrogative noun (ism istifhamiyya) in the accusative, governed by "anzala." This was said by al-Hawfi and al-Zamakhshari. It was also said: "ma" is an interrogative noun in the nominative (mubtada'), and the pronoun from the predicate is omitted; its estimated form is: "Did Allah permit you in it, or by it?" This is weak, because of the omission of this returning pronoun. Making "ma" a relative pronoun is the preferable view, because it keeps "arayita" in its proper function, of transitivity to the first object so that it governs it, unlike making it interrogative, in which case "arayita" would be suspended (mu'allaqa) and "ma" would fill the place of both objects. The apparent reading is that "am" (or) is conjunctive, and the meaning is: "Inform me: Did Allah permit you to permit and forbid? So do you do that by His permission, or do you lie against Allah in attributing that to Him?" By making them face one of the two alternatives, and since they cannot claim that Allah permitted that, their fabrication is established.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is also permissible that the hamza be for denial, and 'am' be disjunctive (munqati'a), meaning 'bal' (rather), 'Do you invent against Allah?' affirming the fabrication." End of quotation.

Here, "anzala" has been said to mean "created," like His saying: ﴿And We sent down iron﴾ [al-Hadid: 25], and ﴿He sent down for you eight pairs of livestock﴾ [al-Zumar: 6]. It was also said: "anzala" keeps its original sense, with an omitted noun, meaning: "from a cause of provision," which is rain.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: "'Anzala' is a word with figurative usage (tajawwuz). The sending down of provision is either within the sending down of rain by way of outcome (bi-l-maʾal), and the descent of the command concerning it, which is the appearance of the effect in the created thing from which it is produced, the invented thing, and the thing made unlawful and lawful." End of quotation.

Mujahid said: "It refers to what they ruled concerning the forbidding of the bahira, the sa'iba, the wasila, and the ham." Al-Dahhak said: "It refers to His saying: (p-173) ﴿And they assigned to Allah a share of what He created of the crops and livestock﴾ [al-Anʿam: 136]."

﴿And what will be the thought of those who invent lies against Allah on the Day of Resurrection? Indeed, Allah is full of grace to the people, but most of them do not give thanks.﴾

"Ma" here is an interrogative noun in the nominative (mubtada'), and its predicate is "zann" (thought). The meaning is: "What thought will those who fabricate have on the Day of Resurrection?" The matter is left vague as a threat and a warning, on the day when the recompense will be for good and evil. "Yawm" (day) is in the accusative, governed by "zann." The object of "zann" has been said to be estimated as: "What will their thought be, that Allah will do to them: will He save them, or will He punish them?" Isa ibn ʿAmr read "ma zanna" as a past verb, making it: "What kind of thought did those who fabricate think?" So "ma" is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), and the interrogative "ma" may stand in place of the verbal noun. You say: "Ma tadribu Zaydan?" meaning: "What kind of striking do you strike Zayd?"

The poet said:

What does the wailing of the two daughters of Rabʿ change for them?
They do not sleep, nor is there misery for one who slept.

The verb "zann" came in the past tense because it is certain to happen, as if it had already occurred. The better view is that "zann" has the meaning of "yazunnu" (present), because it governs "yawm al-qiyama," which is a future time. His grace upon people is that He bestowed blessings upon them and showed them mercy, so He sent the messengers to them, and He explained to them the lawful and the unlawful. Most of them do not give thanks for this blessing.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 10, verses 53–60 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And they ask you, "Is it true?" Say, "Yes, by my Lord, it is indeed true, and you cannot escape it."﴾ That is, they ask you for information. The pronoun in "Is it true?" refers to the punishment. It has also been said that it refers to the Law and the Qur'an, or to the threat, or to the matter of the Hour. The clause is in a position of accusative (naṣb). Al-Zamakhshari said: the verb "yaqūlūna" (they say) is implied, so the sentence is "They say, 'Is it true?'" and so "yastanbi'ūnaka" (they ask you) takes one object. Ibn 'Atiyya said: its meaning is "yastakhbirūnaka" (they ask you for information), and on this view it takes two objects: the first is the kāf (you), and the second is the clause of the interrogative (the subject and predicate). According to what he said, "yastanbi'ūnaka" is then a suspended verb (mu'allaqah). The original use of "istanba'a" is that it takes two objects, the first with "'an" (about). You say "istanba'tu Zaydan 'an 'Amrin" (I asked Zayd about 'Amr), meaning I asked him to inform me about 'Amr. The apparent view is that the verb is suspended from the second object.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: It has also been said that it means "yasta'limūnaka" (they seek to know from you). On this view it requires three objects: the first is the kāf, and the inceptive and predicate together stand in place of the two objects. [End of his words.] But this is not as he stated, because "ista'lama" is not known to take three objects. One does not say "ista'lamtu Zaydan 'Amran qā'iman" so that the interrogative clause would stand in place of the two objects. Its meaning being "yasta'limūnaka" does not require that it take three objects, because "ista'lama" does not take three objects as we have mentioned. "Huwa" is in the nominative as the subject, and "ḥaqq" is its predicate.

Al-Hawfi and Abu al-Baqa' permitted that "ḥaqq" be the subject (mubtada') and that "huwa" be the agent of it, standing in place of the predicate. "Ḥaqq" is not an active or passive participle; it is in origin a verbal noun (maṣdar), and it is not far-fetched that it be in the nominative because it has the meaning of something established. This question from them was by way of mockery and denial.

Al-A'mash read "al-ḥaqq" (with the definite article). Al-Zamakhshari said: This is more suited to mockery, because it contains an implication of insinuation that it is false, for the lām is for the category, as if it were said: "Is it the truth, not falsehood? Or is it that which you named 'the truth'?" [End of his words.]

Almighty God commanded His Prophet to say in reply to them: ﴿Say, "Yes, by my Lord."﴾ That is: yes, by my Lord. "Ay" is used only in an oath, just as "hal" is used with the meaning of "qad" (indeed) only in that context. Al-Zamakhshari said this and said: I have heard them say in affirmation "ay," and they connect it to the particle of oath "wāw," and they do not pronounce it alone. [End of his words.] But what al-Zamakhshari heard from them is no proof, because his speech is not authoritative as evidence, owing to the corruption of the Arabic speech of that time and of the many periods before it. (p-169) Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is a word that precedes an oath and has the meaning of "na'am" (yes), and after it comes the particle of oath, though it may not come. You say "ay rabbī" or "ay wa-rabbī." [End of his words.]

The answer could have been limited to "ay wa-rabbī," but it was emphasized by stating the clause that was implied after "ay wa-rabbī," introduced with "inna" and the lām, as an intensification of emphasis in the answer. Since their question "Is it true?" contained a question about the punishment, and it was a question about the punishment that would befall them, not about any punishment that befalls whomever it befalls, it was said: ﴿And you cannot escape it,﴾ that is, you cannot escape the punishment asked about; rather, it will overtake you.

This clause may be included in the answer to the oath, so that it is conjoined to the answer before it. It may also be understood as an assertion, conjoined to the clause that was said and not to the answer to the oath. The hamza in "a'jaza" is for transitivity, as in His saying: ﴿And we will never make Him unable [to escape] by flight﴾ [al-Jinn: 12]. But its object is frequently omitted, to the point that the Arabs say "a'jaza fulānun" (so-and-so was unable) when he went off into the land and was not reached. Al-Zajjaj said: That is, you are not among those who can frustrate those who punish you.

﴿And if every soul that wronged had all that is on earth, it would surely offer it for ransom. And they will conceal the regret when they see the punishment. And it will be judged between them with justice, and they will not be wronged.﴾ When He mentioned the punishment and swore to its reality, and that they would not escape from it, He mentioned some of the states of the wrongdoers in the Hereafter.

"Wronged" is an attribute of "soul." The wrongdoing here is polytheism and disbelief. "Iftada" comes as the reflexive of "fada," so it is intransitive: you say "fadaytuhu fa-iftada" (I ransomed him, so he ransomed himself). And it can have the meaning of "fada," in which case it is transitive. Here it may bear either of the two meanings.

"What is on earth" means: what it possessed in the world of treasures, wealth, and benefits. "Asarru" is among the words with opposite meanings and comes with the meaning of "azhara" (to reveal). Al-Farazdaq said:

When al-Hajjaj drew his sword,
the Kharijite who had been showing himself concealed himself.

And another said:

So I concealed the regret the day the caller called out
for the return of the camels of Ghadira, the caller.

It also comes with the meaning of "akhfa" (to conceal), which is the best known meaning of it, as in His saying: ﴿He knows what they keep secret and what they make public﴾ [Hud: 5]. Here it may bear both meanings. As for revealing, it is not a day for patience or fortitude, and the disbeliever cannot in it hide what befalls him. And because at the moment of seeing the punishment a person is overcome with grief over the sin that caused it, and he shows regret over what he has missed of success and of deliverance from the punishment. They have indeed said: ﴿Our Lord, our wretchedness overcame us﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 106].

As for concealing the regret, it has been said: their leaders concealed the regret from their followers out of shame before them and fear of their reproach. This is far-fetched, because one who beholds the punishment is occupied with what he suffers from it, so how could he have thought about shame or about the reproach coming from the lowly? Also, "wa-asarru" refers to "every soul that wronged" according to meaning, and it is general, applying to leaders and followers alike.

It has also been said: the concealing of regret results from their being stunned at seeing what they had not expected and had not occurred to them, and from their witnessing what weakened their strength, so that at that moment they were unable to cry out or wail, and could do nothing that the one who is distressed does except hide the regret and grief in their hearts, as happens to one who is brought to the cross and hardly says a word, remaining stunned and motionless. As for him who said that the meaning of His saying "and they concealed the regret" is that they were sincere to God in that regret, or that the faces of their foreheads showed the regret, that is, the wrinkles of their brows, this is far from the context of the verse.

The apparent view is that His saying ﴿And it will be judged between them with justice﴾ is a separate, new clause of information, and is not conjoined to what is within the scope of "lammā," and that the pronoun in "baynahum" refers to "every soul that wronged." Al-Zamakhshari said: "between the wrongdoers and the wronged" is indicated by the mention of wrongdoing. [End of his words.]

It has been said that it refers to the believer and the disbeliever. It has also been said that it refers to the leaders and the followers.

﴿Surely to God belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth. Surely the promise of God is true, but most of them do not know.﴾ ﴿He gives life and causes death, and to Him you will be returned.﴾ It has been said: the connection of this verse to what came before is that He supposed that the wrongdoing soul, if it had what is on earth, would ransom itself with it, while it has absolutely nothing, because all things entirely belong to God Almighty, and He is the one who disposes of them, for to Him belong the dominion and the ownership. And the connection of it (p-170) to what came before appears to be this: when they asked about what they had been promised of punishment, "Is it true?", and they were answered that it was indeed true beyond doubt, that answer was sufficient for one whom God Almighty had granted success in faith, just as it was an answer to the bedouin when he asked the Messenger (ﷺ): "Did God send you?" He (peace be upon him) said: "O God, yes," and he was content with that from him, upon his (ﷺ) informing him, since he knew that he would say nothing but the truth and what is right, as Heraclius said: "He would not leave off lying to people and then lie about God."

He moved from this answer to mentioning the decisive proof for his argument and the establishment that belief in prophethood and the return rests on establishing a God who is powerful and wise, and that whatever is other than Him is His dominion and property. On this basis (comes) this verse, and he had fully surveyed the proofs of this in this surah in His saying: ﴿Indeed in the alternation of night and day﴾ [Yunus: 6], and His saying: ﴿He it is who made the sun a radiance﴾ [Yunus: 5]. So he was content here to omit mentioning them.

And if everything in the world is His dominion and property, then He is capable of all possibilities, knowing of all knowables, free of need for all needs, exalted above all deficiencies and defects. And by His being capable of possibilities, He is capable of sending down punishment upon the disbelievers in this world and the Hereafter, and capable of supporting His messenger with proofs and exalting His religion, so mockery and challenge are void.

And by His being exalted above deficiencies, He is exalted above breaking promises and lying. Thus it is established that His saying ﴿Surely to God belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ is a premise that necessitates the certainty of the truth of His saying: "Surely the promise of God is true." The word "alā" (surely) is a particle of alerting, which entered upon both clauses as an alert for the heedless, since they were occupied with looking at the apparent causes, from attributing things to be owned by one to whom some disposal and succession over them was granted. For this reason Almighty God said: ﴿But most of them do not know,﴾ meaning: because of their neglect of these proofs. Then He followed that with mention of His power over giving life and causing death.

It must be that He is capable of bringing them back to life a second time, and for this reason He said: ﴿And to Him you will be returned,﴾ so you will see what He promised. Al-Hasan, in one report from him, and 'Isa ibn 'Umar read "yurja'ūna" with the "yā'" in the third person. The majority read it with the "tā'" in the second person.

﴿O mankind, there has come to you an admonition from your Lord, and a healing for what is in the breasts, and guidance and mercy for the believers.﴾ It has been said: it was revealed concerning the Quraysh who asked the Messenger (ﷺ), "Is it true?" So "mankind" refers to the disbelieving Quraysh. Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is an address to all the world.

The connection of this verse to what came before is that when He mentioned the proofs of divinity, oneness, and power, He mentioned the proofs indicating the validity of prophethood and the path leading to it, which is the Qur'an, and the one characterized by these noble attributes is the Qur'an. Al-Zamakhshari said: That is, there has come to you a book comprehensive of these benefits, of admonition and warning concerning monotheism. It is a healing, that is, a remedy for what is in your breasts of corrupt beliefs, and a call to the truth, and a mercy for whoever among you believes in it. [End of his words.]

"Min rabbikum" may be connected to "jā'atkum," so "min" indicates the starting point. It may also be in a position of description, meaning: from the admonitions of your Lord, in which case it is connected to an implied element, and "min" is partitive. In His saying "min rabbikum" there is an indication that it is from God and not from anyone else.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: He made it an admonition according to all people, and He made it guidance and mercy according to the believers. This is a division that is sound in meaning if it is interpreted by directing it so. [End of his words.] Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi mentioned here much speech mixed with what they call wisdom. We know for certain that the Arabs would not understand what he established from the words of the Qur'an. He elaborated on that and gave sensible examples that are to be understood from his exegesis. Then he said at the end of his speech: The sum is that admonition is an indication of purifying the outward forms of creation from what is not fitting, which is the Law; healing is an indication of purifying the spirits from corrupt beliefs and blameworthy character traits, which is the Path; guidance is an indication of the appearance of the light of truth in the hearts of the truthful, which is the Reality; and mercy is an indication of its being perfect in completeness, and the radiance, to the point where it completes the deficient, which is prophethood. These are rational degrees and demonstrative stages indicated by these Qur'anic words, and it is not possible for what was mentioned first to come later, nor for what was mentioned last to come first.

(p-171) ﴿Say, "In the grace of God and in His mercy, in that let them rejoice; it is better than what they amass."﴾ Al-Zamakhshari said, citing Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited: ﴿Say, 'In the grace of God and in His mercy,'﴾ and said: 'By the Book of God and Islam. Its grace is Islam, and its mercy is what He promised for it.'" [End of his words.]

If this hadith is sound, its contrary cannot be allowed. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatadah, and Hilal ibn Yasaf said: The grace of God is Islam, and His mercy is the Qur'an. Al-Dahhak and Zayd ibn Aslam said the opposite of this. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri said: The grace is the Qur'an, and the mercy is that He made them among its people.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 10, verses 53–60 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn ʿAbbas said, as transmitted by al-Dahhak from him: "The grace (al-fadl) is knowledge, and the mercy (al-rahma) is Muhammad (ﷺ)." Ibn ʿUmar said: "The grace is Islam, and the mercy is its adornment in the hearts." Mujahid said: "The grace and the mercy are the Qur'an," and al-Zajjaj chose this view.

Khalid ibn Maʿdan said: "The grace is the Qur'an, and the mercy is the Sunnah." He also said, on another report: "The grace is Islam, and the mercy is concealment (of sins)." ʿAmr ibn ʿUthman said: "The grace of Allah is the lifting of the veil, and His mercy is the vision and the meeting (with Him)." Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: "The grace is faith (al-iman), and the mercy is Paradise."

It was also said: "The grace is divine success (al-tawfiq), and the mercy is protection (from sin) (al-ʿisma)." It was said: "The grace is His outward blessings, and the mercy is His inward blessings." Al-Sadiq said: "The grace is forgiveness, and the mercy is divine success." Dhu al-Nun said: "The grace is the gardens (of Paradise), and His mercy is deliverance from the Fires."

These are specifications that require evidence, and it should be understood that they are examples (tamthilat), because "grace" and "mercy" are intended to refer to what has been mentioned, not to restrict them to it.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: "What the wording indicates and necessarily implies is that the grace is Allah's guidance to His religion and His granting of success in following the sharʿ (sacred law, here meaning divine law), and the mercy is His pardon and dwelling in His Paradise, which He made a reward for following Islam and faith." End of quotation.

The meaning of the verse: Say, O Muhammad, to all people: "By the grace of Allah and His mercy, let them rejoice, not by worldly affairs and what is gathered of its trash." So the believers are told: "Let them rejoice," while they are connected to the cause and reason of joy, sincere toward the grace of Allah, and awaiting His mercy. As for the disbelievers, it is said to them: "By the grace of Allah and His mercy, let them rejoice," in the sense of: "If it happened to you, or if you were made happy by being guided to attaining that." End of quotation.

The apparent reading is that His saying, "Say: By the grace of Allah and His mercy, so by that let them rejoice," consists of two clauses, and the element to which the preposition "bi-" (by) relates has been omitted. The meaning is: "Say: By the grace of Allah and His mercy, that they may rejoice." Then the second clause is conjoined to the first for the sake of emphasis. Al-Zamakhshari said: "The repetition is for affirmation and emphasis, and for making the rejoicing specific to the grace and mercy, excluding what is other than them of the benefits of this world. So one of the two verbs is omitted because the mentioned verb indicates it, and the fa' (so) carries the sense of a condition, as if it were said: 'If they rejoice at something, let them restrict their rejoicing to these two, for there is nothing rejoiced at that is more worthy than them.' It is also permissible that it means: 'By the grace of Allah and His mercy, let them take care of that, so let them rejoice.'" End of quotation.

It is also permissible that it means: "Indeed there has come to you an admonition by the grace of Allah and His mercy, so by that (i.e., by the coming of these two), let them rejoice." End of quotation.

As for the supposition of the verb "let them take care" (fa-l-yaʿtanu), there is no evidence for it. As for linking "bi-" to His saying, "There has come to you," that would require the phrase to be understood as omitted after "qul" (say), and it cannot be linked to the first "jaʾatkum" because of the separation between them by "qul."

Al-Hawfi said: "The preposition 'bi-' is related to what indicates the meaning, i.e., 'the admonition has come to you by the grace of Allah.'" It was also said: "The first fa' is extra (ziyada), and by that (bi-dhalika) is a substitute (badal) placed before it, and it refers to the two, the grace and the mercy." It was also said: "The second fa' is repeated for emphasis. On this view, the first fa' is not extra, and the original structure is 'bi-dhalika li-yafrahu' (by that, that they may rejoice). In the previous statement, the original structure would be 'bi-dhalika fa-l-yafrahu' (by that, let them rejoice)." There is no contradiction between the command to rejoice here and the prohibition in His saying: ﴿Do not exult; indeed Allah does not love the exultant﴾ [al-Qasas: 76], because the object of the joy differs. The thing commanded here is rejoicing in the grace of Allah and His mercy, while the thing forbidden there is rejoicing in the gathering of wealth for worldly leadership, the desire for dominance through it, and corruption. For this reason, what follows is His saying: ﴿But seek, through what Allah has given you, the Home of the Hereafter, and do not forget your share of this world﴾ [al-Qasas: 77], and what precedes it is: ﴿Indeed, Qarun was of the people of Moses, but he oppressed them﴾ [al-Qasas: 76]. And His saying: ﴿Surely he is exultant and boastful﴾ [Hud: 10] came in the manner of censure, for his joy at receiving blessings after hardship, and his despair and ingratitude for blessings when they were taken from him. This is a blameworthy trait, and such conduct is not among the acts of the Hereafter.

As for the view of one who says: "When rejoicing (al-faraḥ) is stated without qualification, it is blameworthy, and when it is qualified, it is not blameworthy, as in His saying: ﴿rejoicing in what Allah has given them of His grace﴾ [Al ʿImran: 170]," this is not a consistent rule, since it came qualified in censure in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿until, when they rejoiced in what they had been given, We seized them suddenly﴾ [al-Anʿam: 44]. Rejoicing is praised or blamed according to its object. When it is over attaining the reward of the Hereafter and deeds of righteousness, it is praiseworthy, and when it is over attaining the pleasures of this world and its trash, it is blameworthy.

ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan, Ubayy, Anas, al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Ibn Hurmuz, Ibn Sirin, Abu Jaʿfar al-Madani, al-Sulami, Qatada, al-Jahdari, Hilal ibn Yasaf, al-Aʿmash, ʿAmr ibn Qaʾid, and al-ʿAbbas ibn al-Fadl al-Ansari read: "falta-farahu" with the taʾ (second person, addressing the audience: "so let you rejoice") as a form of address, and this was transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ).

The author of al-Lawamih (Sahib al-Lawamih, Ibn Mihran's Kitab al-Lawami' or related work on readings) said: "And he said..., and it has come down from Yaʿqub likewise." End of quotation.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: "Ubayy, Ibn al-Qaʿqaʿ, Ibn ʿAmir, and al-Hasan read (it so), according to what Harun claimed. It was transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ): 'falta-farahu' and 'tajmaʿuna' with the taʾ in both, in address. This is the reading of a large group of the early generations (al-salaf), though most of them differ on it." End of quotation.

The majority read it with the yaʾ (third person), as a command to the absent party. What Ibn ʿAtiyya reported, that Ibn ʿAmir read "falta-farahu" with the taʾ, is not what is well known from him. Rather, his reading in the famous seven readings is with the yaʾ, as a command to the absent party. However, he read "tajmaʿuna" with the taʾ in address, while the rest of the seven read it with the taʾ in address.

In the Mushaf of Ubayy it is: "bi-dhalika fa-farihu" (by that, rejoice), and this is the common, well-known usage for commanding the addressee.

As for "fa-l-yafrahu" with the yaʾ, it is a rare dialect form. In a hadith: "Let you take your rows (li-taʾkhudhu masaffakum)." Abu al-Tayyah and al-Hasan read "fa-l-yafrahu" with a kasra on the lam (fa-li-yafrahu). The fact that the reference is to a single thing is shown by the pronoun returning to it in the singular in His saying: "it is better than what they gather." So what is most appropriate is that His saying, "by the grace of Allah and His mercy," treats them as one thing, expressed by two names for emphasis. For this reason it is referred to as "dhalika" (that), and the pronoun returns to it in the singular. His saying, "what they gather," means from the trash and goods of this world.

﴿Say: Have you considered what Allah has sent down to you of provision, and you made some of it unlawful and some lawful? Say: Did Allah permit you, or do you invent against Allah?﴾

The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that when He, exalted is He, mentioned: ﴿O mankind, there has come to you an admonition from your Lord﴾, and the intended meaning of that was the Book of Allah, which includes the permitting and forbidding, He then clarified the corruption of their laws and rulings concerning the lawful and unlawful, without any basis for them in revelation.

"Arayitum" here means "inform me." They allowed that "ma anzala" be a relative pronoun (mawsula) as the first object of "arayitum," with a returning pronoun omitted, and the second object is His saying, "Did Allah permit you?" The pronoun referring back from the predicate to the subject is omitted; its estimated form is: "Did Allah permit you in it?" "Qul" (say) was repeated before the predicate for emphasis.

"Ma" may also be an interrogative noun (ism istifhamiyya) in the accusative, governed by "anzala." This was said by al-Hawfi and al-Zamakhshari. It was also said: "ma" is an interrogative noun in the nominative (mubtada'), and the pronoun from the predicate is omitted; its estimated form is: "Did Allah permit you in it, or by it?" This is weak, because of the omission of this returning pronoun. Making "ma" a relative pronoun is the preferable view, because it keeps "arayita" in its proper function, of transitivity to the first object so that it governs it, unlike making it interrogative, in which case "arayita" would be suspended (mu'allaqa) and "ma" would fill the place of both objects. The apparent reading is that "am" (or) is conjunctive, and the meaning is: "Inform me: Did Allah permit you to permit and forbid? So do you do that by His permission, or do you lie against Allah in attributing that to Him?" By making them face one of the two alternatives, and since they cannot claim that Allah permitted that, their fabrication is established.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is also permissible that the hamza be for denial, and 'am' be disjunctive (munqati'a), meaning 'bal' (rather), 'Do you invent against Allah?' affirming the fabrication." End of quotation.

Here, "anzala" has been said to mean "created," like His saying: ﴿And We sent down iron﴾ [al-Hadid: 25], and ﴿He sent down for you eight pairs of livestock﴾ [al-Zumar: 6]. It was also said: "anzala" keeps its original sense, with an omitted noun, meaning: "from a cause of provision," which is rain.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: "'Anzala' is a word with figurative usage (tajawwuz). The sending down of provision is either within the sending down of rain by way of outcome (bi-l-maʾal), and the descent of the command concerning it, which is the appearance of the effect in the created thing from which it is produced, the invented thing, and the thing made unlawful and lawful." End of quotation.

Mujahid said: "It refers to what they ruled concerning the forbidding of the bahira, the sa'iba, the wasila, and the ham." Al-Dahhak said: "It refers to His saying: (p-173) ﴿And they assigned to Allah a share of what He created of the crops and livestock﴾ [al-Anʿam: 136]."

﴿And what will be the thought of those who invent lies against Allah on the Day of Resurrection? Indeed, Allah is full of grace to the people, but most of them do not give thanks.﴾

"Ma" here is an interrogative noun in the nominative (mubtada'), and its predicate is "zann" (thought). The meaning is: "What thought will those who fabricate have on the Day of Resurrection?" The matter is left vague as a threat and a warning, on the day when the recompense will be for good and evil. "Yawm" (day) is in the accusative, governed by "zann." The object of "zann" has been said to be estimated as: "What will their thought be, that Allah will do to them: will He save them, or will He punish them?" Isa ibn ʿAmr read "ma zanna" as a past verb, making it: "What kind of thought did those who fabricate think?" So "ma" is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), and the interrogative "ma" may stand in place of the verbal noun. You say: "Ma tadribu Zaydan?" meaning: "What kind of striking do you strike Zayd?"

The poet said:

What does the wailing of the two daughters of Rabʿ change for them?
They do not sleep, nor is there misery for one who slept.

The verb "zann" came in the past tense because it is certain to happen, as if it had already occurred. The better view is that "zann" has the meaning of "yazunnu" (present), because it governs "yawm al-qiyama," which is a future time. His grace upon people is that He bestowed blessings upon them and showed them mercy, so He sent the messengers to them, and He explained to them the lawful and the unlawful. Most of them do not give thanks for this blessing.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 10, verses 53–60 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And they ask you, "Is it true?" Say, "Yes, by my Lord, it is indeed true, and you cannot escape it."﴾ That is, they ask you for information. The pronoun in "Is it true?" refers to the punishment. It has also been said that it refers to the Law and the Qur'an, or to the threat, or to the matter of the Hour. The clause is in a position of accusative (naṣb). Al-Zamakhshari said: the verb "yaqūlūna" (they say) is implied, so the sentence is "They say, 'Is it true?'" and so "yastanbi'ūnaka" (they ask you) takes one object. Ibn 'Atiyya said: its meaning is "yastakhbirūnaka" (they ask you for information), and on this view it takes two objects: the first is the kāf (you), and the second is the clause of the interrogative (the subject and predicate). According to what he said, "yastanbi'ūnaka" is then a suspended verb (mu'allaqah). The original use of "istanba'a" is that it takes two objects, the first with "'an" (about). You say "istanba'tu Zaydan 'an 'Amrin" (I asked Zayd about 'Amr), meaning I asked him to inform me about 'Amr. The apparent view is that the verb is suspended from the second object.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: It has also been said that it means "yasta'limūnaka" (they seek to know from you). On this view it requires three objects: the first is the kāf, and the inceptive and predicate together stand in place of the two objects. [End of his words.] But this is not as he stated, because "ista'lama" is not known to take three objects. One does not say "ista'lamtu Zaydan 'Amran qā'iman" so that the interrogative clause would stand in place of the two objects. Its meaning being "yasta'limūnaka" does not require that it take three objects, because "ista'lama" does not take three objects as we have mentioned. "Huwa" is in the nominative as the subject, and "ḥaqq" is its predicate.

Al-Hawfi and Abu al-Baqa' permitted that "ḥaqq" be the subject (mubtada') and that "huwa" be the agent of it, standing in place of the predicate. "Ḥaqq" is not an active or passive participle; it is in origin a verbal noun (maṣdar), and it is not far-fetched that it be in the nominative because it has the meaning of something established. This question from them was by way of mockery and denial.

Al-A'mash read "al-ḥaqq" (with the definite article). Al-Zamakhshari said: This is more suited to mockery, because it contains an implication of insinuation that it is false, for the lām is for the category, as if it were said: "Is it the truth, not falsehood? Or is it that which you named 'the truth'?" [End of his words.]

Almighty God commanded His Prophet to say in reply to them: ﴿Say, "Yes, by my Lord."﴾ That is: yes, by my Lord. "Ay" is used only in an oath, just as "hal" is used with the meaning of "qad" (indeed) only in that context. Al-Zamakhshari said this and said: I have heard them say in affirmation "ay," and they connect it to the particle of oath "wāw," and they do not pronounce it alone. [End of his words.] But what al-Zamakhshari heard from them is no proof, because his speech is not authoritative as evidence, owing to the corruption of the Arabic speech of that time and of the many periods before it. (p-169) Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is a word that precedes an oath and has the meaning of "na'am" (yes), and after it comes the particle of oath, though it may not come. You say "ay rabbī" or "ay wa-rabbī." [End of his words.]

The answer could have been limited to "ay wa-rabbī," but it was emphasized by stating the clause that was implied after "ay wa-rabbī," introduced with "inna" and the lām, as an intensification of emphasis in the answer. Since their question "Is it true?" contained a question about the punishment, and it was a question about the punishment that would befall them, not about any punishment that befalls whomever it befalls, it was said: ﴿And you cannot escape it,﴾ that is, you cannot escape the punishment asked about; rather, it will overtake you.

This clause may be included in the answer to the oath, so that it is conjoined to the answer before it. It may also be understood as an assertion, conjoined to the clause that was said and not to the answer to the oath. The hamza in "a'jaza" is for transitivity, as in His saying: ﴿And we will never make Him unable [to escape] by flight﴾ [al-Jinn: 12]. But its object is frequently omitted, to the point that the Arabs say "a'jaza fulānun" (so-and-so was unable) when he went off into the land and was not reached. Al-Zajjaj said: That is, you are not among those who can frustrate those who punish you.

﴿And if every soul that wronged had all that is on earth, it would surely offer it for ransom. And they will conceal the regret when they see the punishment. And it will be judged between them with justice, and they will not be wronged.﴾ When He mentioned the punishment and swore to its reality, and that they would not escape from it, He mentioned some of the states of the wrongdoers in the Hereafter.

"Wronged" is an attribute of "soul." The wrongdoing here is polytheism and disbelief. "Iftada" comes as the reflexive of "fada," so it is intransitive: you say "fadaytuhu fa-iftada" (I ransomed him, so he ransomed himself). And it can have the meaning of "fada," in which case it is transitive. Here it may bear either of the two meanings.

"What is on earth" means: what it possessed in the world of treasures, wealth, and benefits. "Asarru" is among the words with opposite meanings and comes with the meaning of "azhara" (to reveal). Al-Farazdaq said:

When al-Hajjaj drew his sword,
the Kharijite who had been showing himself concealed himself.

And another said:

So I concealed the regret the day the caller called out
for the return of the camels of Ghadira, the caller.

It also comes with the meaning of "akhfa" (to conceal), which is the best known meaning of it, as in His saying: ﴿He knows what they keep secret and what they make public﴾ [Hud: 5]. Here it may bear both meanings. As for revealing, it is not a day for patience or fortitude, and the disbeliever cannot in it hide what befalls him. And because at the moment of seeing the punishment a person is overcome with grief over the sin that caused it, and he shows regret over what he has missed of success and of deliverance from the punishment. They have indeed said: ﴿Our Lord, our wretchedness overcame us﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 106].

As for concealing the regret, it has been said: their leaders concealed the regret from their followers out of shame before them and fear of their reproach. This is far-fetched, because one who beholds the punishment is occupied with what he suffers from it, so how could he have thought about shame or about the reproach coming from the lowly? Also, "wa-asarru" refers to "every soul that wronged" according to meaning, and it is general, applying to leaders and followers alike.

It has also been said: the concealing of regret results from their being stunned at seeing what they had not expected and had not occurred to them, and from their witnessing what weakened their strength, so that at that moment they were unable to cry out or wail, and could do nothing that the one who is distressed does except hide the regret and grief in their hearts, as happens to one who is brought to the cross and hardly says a word, remaining stunned and motionless. As for him who said that the meaning of His saying "and they concealed the regret" is that they were sincere to God in that regret, or that the faces of their foreheads showed the regret, that is, the wrinkles of their brows, this is far from the context of the verse.

The apparent view is that His saying ﴿And it will be judged between them with justice﴾ is a separate, new clause of information, and is not conjoined to what is within the scope of "lammā," and that the pronoun in "baynahum" refers to "every soul that wronged." Al-Zamakhshari said: "between the wrongdoers and the wronged" is indicated by the mention of wrongdoing. [End of his words.]

It has been said that it refers to the believer and the disbeliever. It has also been said that it refers to the leaders and the followers.

﴿Surely to God belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth. Surely the promise of God is true, but most of them do not know.﴾ ﴿He gives life and causes death, and to Him you will be returned.﴾ It has been said: the connection of this verse to what came before is that He supposed that the wrongdoing soul, if it had what is on earth, would ransom itself with it, while it has absolutely nothing, because all things entirely belong to God Almighty, and He is the one who disposes of them, for to Him belong the dominion and the ownership. And the connection of it (p-170) to what came before appears to be this: when they asked about what they had been promised of punishment, "Is it true?", and they were answered that it was indeed true beyond doubt, that answer was sufficient for one whom God Almighty had granted success in faith, just as it was an answer to the bedouin when he asked the Messenger (ﷺ): "Did God send you?" He (peace be upon him) said: "O God, yes," and he was content with that from him, upon his (ﷺ) informing him, since he knew that he would say nothing but the truth and what is right, as Heraclius said: "He would not leave off lying to people and then lie about God."

He moved from this answer to mentioning the decisive proof for his argument and the establishment that belief in prophethood and the return rests on establishing a God who is powerful and wise, and that whatever is other than Him is His dominion and property. On this basis (comes) this verse, and he had fully surveyed the proofs of this in this surah in His saying: ﴿Indeed in the alternation of night and day﴾ [Yunus: 6], and His saying: ﴿He it is who made the sun a radiance﴾ [Yunus: 5]. So he was content here to omit mentioning them.

And if everything in the world is His dominion and property, then He is capable of all possibilities, knowing of all knowables, free of need for all needs, exalted above all deficiencies and defects. And by His being capable of possibilities, He is capable of sending down punishment upon the disbelievers in this world and the Hereafter, and capable of supporting His messenger with proofs and exalting His religion, so mockery and challenge are void.

And by His being exalted above deficiencies, He is exalted above breaking promises and lying. Thus it is established that His saying ﴿Surely to God belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ is a premise that necessitates the certainty of the truth of His saying: "Surely the promise of God is true." The word "alā" (surely) is a particle of alerting, which entered upon both clauses as an alert for the heedless, since they were occupied with looking at the apparent causes, from attributing things to be owned by one to whom some disposal and succession over them was granted. For this reason Almighty God said: ﴿But most of them do not know,﴾ meaning: because of their neglect of these proofs. Then He followed that with mention of His power over giving life and causing death.

It must be that He is capable of bringing them back to life a second time, and for this reason He said: ﴿And to Him you will be returned,﴾ so you will see what He promised. Al-Hasan, in one report from him, and 'Isa ibn 'Umar read "yurja'ūna" with the "yā'" in the third person. The majority read it with the "tā'" in the second person.

﴿O mankind, there has come to you an admonition from your Lord, and a healing for what is in the breasts, and guidance and mercy for the believers.﴾ It has been said: it was revealed concerning the Quraysh who asked the Messenger (ﷺ), "Is it true?" So "mankind" refers to the disbelieving Quraysh. Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is an address to all the world.

The connection of this verse to what came before is that when He mentioned the proofs of divinity, oneness, and power, He mentioned the proofs indicating the validity of prophethood and the path leading to it, which is the Qur'an, and the one characterized by these noble attributes is the Qur'an. Al-Zamakhshari said: That is, there has come to you a book comprehensive of these benefits, of admonition and warning concerning monotheism. It is a healing, that is, a remedy for what is in your breasts of corrupt beliefs, and a call to the truth, and a mercy for whoever among you believes in it. [End of his words.]

"Min rabbikum" may be connected to "jā'atkum," so "min" indicates the starting point. It may also be in a position of description, meaning: from the admonitions of your Lord, in which case it is connected to an implied element, and "min" is partitive. In His saying "min rabbikum" there is an indication that it is from God and not from anyone else.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: He made it an admonition according to all people, and He made it guidance and mercy according to the believers. This is a division that is sound in meaning if it is interpreted by directing it so. [End of his words.] Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi mentioned here much speech mixed with what they call wisdom. We know for certain that the Arabs would not understand what he established from the words of the Qur'an. He elaborated on that and gave sensible examples that are to be understood from his exegesis. Then he said at the end of his speech: The sum is that admonition is an indication of purifying the outward forms of creation from what is not fitting, which is the Law; healing is an indication of purifying the spirits from corrupt beliefs and blameworthy character traits, which is the Path; guidance is an indication of the appearance of the light of truth in the hearts of the truthful, which is the Reality; and mercy is an indication of its being perfect in completeness, and the radiance, to the point where it completes the deficient, which is prophethood. These are rational degrees and demonstrative stages indicated by these Qur'anic words, and it is not possible for what was mentioned first to come later, nor for what was mentioned last to come first.

(p-171) ﴿Say, "In the grace of God and in His mercy, in that let them rejoice; it is better than what they amass."﴾ Al-Zamakhshari said, citing Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited: ﴿Say, 'In the grace of God and in His mercy,'﴾ and said: 'By the Book of God and Islam. Its grace is Islam, and its mercy is what He promised for it.'" [End of his words.]

If this hadith is sound, its contrary cannot be allowed. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatadah, and Hilal ibn Yasaf said: The grace of God is Islam, and His mercy is the Qur'an. Al-Dahhak and Zayd ibn Aslam said the opposite of this. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri said: The grace is the Qur'an, and the mercy is that He made them among its people.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 10, verses 53–60 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn ʿAbbas said, as transmitted by al-Dahhak from him: "The grace (al-fadl) is knowledge, and the mercy (al-rahma) is Muhammad (ﷺ)." Ibn ʿUmar said: "The grace is Islam, and the mercy is its adornment in the hearts." Mujahid said: "The grace and the mercy are the Qur'an," and al-Zajjaj chose this view.

Khalid ibn Maʿdan said: "The grace is the Qur'an, and the mercy is the Sunnah." He also said, on another report: "The grace is Islam, and the mercy is concealment (of sins)." ʿAmr ibn ʿUthman said: "The grace of Allah is the lifting of the veil, and His mercy is the vision and the meeting (with Him)." Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: "The grace is faith (al-iman), and the mercy is Paradise."

It was also said: "The grace is divine success (al-tawfiq), and the mercy is protection (from sin) (al-ʿisma)." It was said: "The grace is His outward blessings, and the mercy is His inward blessings." Al-Sadiq said: "The grace is forgiveness, and the mercy is divine success." Dhu al-Nun said: "The grace is the gardens (of Paradise), and His mercy is deliverance from the Fires."

These are specifications that require evidence, and it should be understood that they are examples (tamthilat), because "grace" and "mercy" are intended to refer to what has been mentioned, not to restrict them to it.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: "What the wording indicates and necessarily implies is that the grace is Allah's guidance to His religion and His granting of success in following the sharʿ (sacred law, here meaning divine law), and the mercy is His pardon and dwelling in His Paradise, which He made a reward for following Islam and faith." End of quotation.

The meaning of the verse: Say, O Muhammad, to all people: "By the grace of Allah and His mercy, let them rejoice, not by worldly affairs and what is gathered of its trash." So the believers are told: "Let them rejoice," while they are connected to the cause and reason of joy, sincere toward the grace of Allah, and awaiting His mercy. As for the disbelievers, it is said to them: "By the grace of Allah and His mercy, let them rejoice," in the sense of: "If it happened to you, or if you were made happy by being guided to attaining that." End of quotation.

The apparent reading is that His saying, "Say: By the grace of Allah and His mercy, so by that let them rejoice," consists of two clauses, and the element to which the preposition "bi-" (by) relates has been omitted. The meaning is: "Say: By the grace of Allah and His mercy, that they may rejoice." Then the second clause is conjoined to the first for the sake of emphasis. Al-Zamakhshari said: "The repetition is for affirmation and emphasis, and for making the rejoicing specific to the grace and mercy, excluding what is other than them of the benefits of this world. So one of the two verbs is omitted because the mentioned verb indicates it, and the fa' (so) carries the sense of a condition, as if it were said: 'If they rejoice at something, let them restrict their rejoicing to these two, for there is nothing rejoiced at that is more worthy than them.' It is also permissible that it means: 'By the grace of Allah and His mercy, let them take care of that, so let them rejoice.'" End of quotation.

It is also permissible that it means: "Indeed there has come to you an admonition by the grace of Allah and His mercy, so by that (i.e., by the coming of these two), let them rejoice." End of quotation.

As for the supposition of the verb "let them take care" (fa-l-yaʿtanu), there is no evidence for it. As for linking "bi-" to His saying, "There has come to you," that would require the phrase to be understood as omitted after "qul" (say), and it cannot be linked to the first "jaʾatkum" because of the separation between them by "qul."

Al-Hawfi said: "The preposition 'bi-' is related to what indicates the meaning, i.e., 'the admonition has come to you by the grace of Allah.'" It was also said: "The first fa' is extra (ziyada), and by that (bi-dhalika) is a substitute (badal) placed before it, and it refers to the two, the grace and the mercy." It was also said: "The second fa' is repeated for emphasis. On this view, the first fa' is not extra, and the original structure is 'bi-dhalika li-yafrahu' (by that, that they may rejoice). In the previous statement, the original structure would be 'bi-dhalika fa-l-yafrahu' (by that, let them rejoice)." There is no contradiction between the command to rejoice here and the prohibition in His saying: ﴿Do not exult; indeed Allah does not love the exultant﴾ [al-Qasas: 76], because the object of the joy differs. The thing commanded here is rejoicing in the grace of Allah and His mercy, while the thing forbidden there is rejoicing in the gathering of wealth for worldly leadership, the desire for dominance through it, and corruption. For this reason, what follows is His saying: ﴿But seek, through what Allah has given you, the Home of the Hereafter, and do not forget your share of this world﴾ [al-Qasas: 77], and what precedes it is: ﴿Indeed, Qarun was of the people of Moses, but he oppressed them﴾ [al-Qasas: 76]. And His saying: ﴿Surely he is exultant and boastful﴾ [Hud: 10] came in the manner of censure, for his joy at receiving blessings after hardship, and his despair and ingratitude for blessings when they were taken from him. This is a blameworthy trait, and such conduct is not among the acts of the Hereafter.

As for the view of one who says: "When rejoicing (al-faraḥ) is stated without qualification, it is blameworthy, and when it is qualified, it is not blameworthy, as in His saying: ﴿rejoicing in what Allah has given them of His grace﴾ [Al ʿImran: 170]," this is not a consistent rule, since it came qualified in censure in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿until, when they rejoiced in what they had been given, We seized them suddenly﴾ [al-Anʿam: 44]. Rejoicing is praised or blamed according to its object. When it is over attaining the reward of the Hereafter and deeds of righteousness, it is praiseworthy, and when it is over attaining the pleasures of this world and its trash, it is blameworthy.
