Ibn al-'Arabi al-Ta'i has statements about the wali and other matters from which we seek refuge in Allah.

It is related from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Among the servants of Allah are servants who are neither prophets nor martyrs, yet the prophets and martyrs will envy them for their station with Allah." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, who are they?" He said: "People who love one another by the Spirit of Allah, without ties of kinship or wealth exchanged between them. By Allah, their faces will be radiant, and they will be upon pulpits of light. They will not fear when people fear, and they will not grieve when people grieve." Then he recited: ﴿Indeed, the awliya' of Allah﴾ to the end of the verse.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 10, verses 65–66:**

﴿And let not their saying grieve you. Indeed, all might belongs to Allah. He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿Unquestionably, to Allah belongs whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth. And those who invoke other than Allah as partners do not follow [anything real]. They follow only assumption, and they are merely guessing.﴾: Either their saying refers to some of its instances, namely the denial and the threats, and what they conspire about concerning the matter of the Messenger ﷺ. In that case it is the use of a general term to mean a specific one.

Or it is a case in which the qualifying attribute has been omitted, meaning: their saying that indicates their denial of you and their opposition to you. Then He resumed with His words, "Indeed, all might belongs to Allah," meaning: they have no might and no protection. They are not able to do anything to you, nor can they harm you. Indeed, dominance and subjugation belong to Allah, and He is able to take vengeance upon them. Nothing overpowers Him, and nothing prevails over Him.

It is as if someone said: "Why does their saying not grieve him, when it is of the kind that causes grief?" So it was said: "Indeed, all might belongs to Allah," and they have no share of it. Abu Haywah read (أنَّ العِزَّةَ) with a fathah on the hamzah. In this reading, it is not governed by "their saying," because that would not grieve the Messenger ﷺ, since it is a true statement. This reading has been explained as causal, meaning: no grief comes from you concerning what they say, because all might belongs to Allah. It has also been construed as "Indeed, all might" being an apposition (badal) to "their saying," but this construal is not evident.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Whoever makes it an apposition to their saying and then rejects it, the thing rejected is his interpretation, not what he rejected from the Qur'an." Al-Qadi said: "Its fathah is an anomalous reading (shadh) that comes close to disbelief. If it is kasrah, it is a new resumptive sentence (istinaf). This shows the virtue of the science of grammar (ʿilm al-iʿrab, the science of Arabic inflection)." Ibn Qutaybah said: "It is not permissible to make the hamzah fathah in this place, and it is disbelief and exaggeration." Al-Qadi and Ibn Qutaybah spoke on the basis that (إنَّ) is governed by "their saying." We have already mentioned the explanation of that as causal, and it is a correct explanation. "He is the All-Hearing": of what they say. "The All-Knowing": of what they intend.

In this verse there is an assurance to the Messenger ﷺ from the harm of the disbelievers, and that Allah, exalted is He, will grant him victory over them and support him.

﴿Allah has decreed: "I and My messengers will surely prevail."﴾ ﴿Indeed, We will surely support Our messengers.﴾ Al-Asamm said: "They used to take pride in the multitude of their servants and their wealth. So He informed that He is able to strip them of ownership of things, to grant you victory, and to transfer to you their wealth and their homes." End of quotation.

There is no contradiction between His words, "Indeed, all might belongs to Allah," and His words, "Might belongs to Allah, to His Messenger, and to the believers" (al-Munafiqun: 8), because their might is only through Allah, so all of it belongs to Allah.

﴿Unquestionably, to Allah belongs whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth. And those who invoke other than Allah as partners do not follow [anything real]. They follow only assumption, and they are merely guessing.﴾

The connection is evident in this verse. When He mentioned that might belongs to Him, exalted is He, and that might is dominance and subjugation, He mentioned what is consistent with dominance, which is that the created beings are His possession, exalted is He. Originally, the expression "whoever" (man) is used for rational beings, but here it includes them and other beings by way of taghlib (the prevailing of the majority category over the minority). This is used because most created beings are not rational.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "It means the rational, discerning beings, who are the angels and the two weighty ones (jinn and humans). He singled them out to indicate that if these are in His possession, they are all servants. None of them is fit for lordship, nor to be a partner in it. So whatever is less than them, which is non-rational, is more deserving of not being a rival and a partner." It also indicates that whoever takes other than Him as a lord, whether an angel or a human, let alone an idol or other than that, is a falsifier who follows what imitation (taqlid) and abandoning reflection have led him to.

It is apparent that (ما) is negative, (شُرَكاءَ) is the object of (يَتَّبِعُ), and the object of (يَدْعُونَ) is omitted because the meaning is understood. Its estimated form is: "gods or partners." That is, those who made them gods and associated them with Allah in lordship are not truly partners, since partnership in divinity is impossible, even though they applied the name of partners to them. Some allowed that (ما) could be interrogative in a position of accusative case governed by (يَتَّبِعُ), with (شُرَكاءَ) in the accusative governed by (يَدْعُونَ). The meaning would be: "And what do they follow?" in order to belittle what is followed, as if it were said: "Whoever calls upon a partner of Allah does not follow anything." Al-Zamakhshari allowed that (ما) be a relative pronoun (موصولة) coordinated with "whoever" (من), with the returning pronoun omitted, meaning: "And what they follow, those who invoke other than Allah as partners," that is, "and He has their partners."(p-177) Others allowed that (ما) be a relative pronoun in the nominative position as a beginning (مبتدأ), with the predicate omitted, its estimated form being: "And what the polytheists follow is falsehood."

As-Sulami read (تَدْعُونَ) with a taʾ, in the second person address. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: "This reading is not well-founded." Al-Zamakhshari said: "ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, read (تَدْعُونَ) with a taʾ. Its construal is that (وما يتبع) is taken as an interrogative, meaning: 'And what do those whom you call partners, from among the angels and the prophets, follow?' That is, they follow Allah, exalted is He, and obey Him. So why do you not do the same as their action, as in His words: 'Those whom they call upon seek a means of access to their Lord' (al-Isra': 57)." End of quotation.

(إنْ) is negative, meaning: they follow only their assumption that they are partners. (يَخْرُصُونَ) means: they guess.

For whoever reads (تَدْعُونَ) with a taʾ, His words "they follow" (إنْ يَتَّبِعُونَ) constitute an iltifat (a shift in grammatical person), since it is a departure from address (second person) to the third person (absence).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 10, verse 67:

﴿He is the One who made the night for you that you may rest therein, and the day to see by. Indeed in that are signs for a people who listen.﴾: This is a reminder from Him, exalted is He, of the greatness of His power and the comprehensiveness of His blessing upon His servants. He is therefore the one deserving to be singled out for worship, "that you may rest therein" from what you suffer of movement and toil in seeking livelihood and other things during the day. He attributed "the sight" (al-absar) to the day metaphorically, because sight occurs in it, as the poet said:

"I slept, though the night of the riding camels was not sleeping"

That is: they see therein the objects of their livelihoods.

Qutrub said: It is said: "adhlama al-layl" (the night became dark), meaning it became possessed of darkness; and "ada'a al-nahar wa absar" (the day became bright and clear-sighted), meaning it became possessed of light and sight. End of quotation.

He mentioned the cause for the creation of the night, which is His saying ﴿that you may rest therein﴾, and omitted it for the day; and he mentioned the description of the day and omitted it for the night. Each of the omitted elements is indicated by its counterpart. The implied meaning is: He made the night dark so that you may rest therein, and the day seeing (bright) so that you may move about in it, in your earning and in what you need that requires movement. The meaning of "yasma'un" (they listen) is attentive hearing (sama' mu'tabar).

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 10, verses 68–70:**

﴿They say: "God has taken a son." Glory be to Him! He is the Self-Sufficient. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. You have no authority for this. Do you say about God what you do not know?﴾ ﴿Say: "Indeed, those who invent lies against God will not prosper."﴾ ﴿A little enjoyment in this world; then to Us is their return; then We will make them taste the severe punishment because they used to disbelieve.﴾

The pronoun in (qalu, "they said") refers to those who attributed a son to God, among them those who said: "The angels are God's daughters," or "Uzayr is the son of God," or "The Messiah is the son of God." The word (subhanahu, "Glory be to Him") is a declaration of His transcendence above taking a son, and an expression of amazement at those who say such a thing.

(Huwa al-Ghaniyy, "He is the Self-Sufficient"): this is the reason for negating a son, because taking a son happens only from need for him, and God, exalted is He, has no need of anything. Therefore a son is negated of Him, and whatever is in the heavens and the earth is His possession, so He is free of need for taking a son. (In) is negating, and (sultan) means proof, meaning: you have no proof for this statement. Al-Hawfi said: (bihadha, "for this") is connected to the sense of settledness, meaning the element to which the adverbial phrase is attached.

Al-Zamakhshari followed him and said: the preposition (ba') should properly be connected to the phrase (inna 'indakum, "you have"), with the statement made in place of the authority, as when you say: "What you have in your land is light," as if it were said: "You have, in what you say, an authority." Abu al-Baqa' said: (bihadha) is connected to (sultan), or is a qualifier of it. The phrase (ataqulun, "Do you say") is an interrogative of denial and reproach directed at those who follow what they do not know. This is used as an argument for refuting (taqlid, blind imitation) in the foundations of religion, and those who deny analogy (qiyas) and solitary reports (akhbar al-ahad) have used it as evidence.

When God negated proof from them, He made them people who do not know. This indicates that every statement for which its speaker has no proof is ignorance and not knowledge.

﴿Those who invent lies against God﴾ [Yunus: 60] is general, encompassing whoever attributes a son to God, and whoever says about God and His attributes something without knowledge. It is included in the threat of the negation of prosperity. When He negated prosperity from them, and they had a share of prosperity in this world, through their portions in it of wealth, status and other things, it was said: ﴿a little enjoyment﴾ [Al 'Imran: 197]. This is an answer based on an assumed question, as if someone said: "How do they not prosper when they prosper in this world through kinds of things they enjoy?" So it was said: that is an enjoyment in this world, or they have an enjoyment in this world that is passing and has no permanence. Then they will meet everlasting misery in the Hereafter. [p. 178]

Al-Hawfi said: (bihadha, "for this") is connected to the sense of settledness, meaning the element to which the adverbial phrase is attached.

Al-Zamakhshari followed him and said: the preposition (ba') should properly be connected to the phrase (inna 'indakum, "you have"), with the statement made in place of the authority, as when you say: "What you have in your land is light," as if it were said: "You have, in what you say, an authority." Abu al-Baqa' said: (bihadha) is connected to (sultan), or is a qualifier of it. The phrase (ataqulun, "Do you say") is an interrogative of denial and reproach directed at those who follow what they do not know. This is used as an argument for refuting (taqlid, blind imitation) in the foundations of religion, and those who deny analogy (qiyas) and solitary reports (akhbar al-ahad) have used it as evidence.

When God negated proof from them, He made them people who do not know. This indicates that every statement for which its speaker has no proof is ignorance and not knowledge.

﴿Those who invent lies against God﴾ [Yunus: 60] is general, encompassing whoever attributes a son to God, and whoever says about God and His attributes something without knowledge. It is included in the threat of the negation of prosperity. When He negated prosperity from them, and they had a share of prosperity in this world, through their portions in it of wealth, status and other things, it was said: ﴿a little enjoyment﴾ [Al 'Imran: 197]. This is an answer based on an assumed question, as if someone said: "How do they not prosper when they prosper in this world through kinds of things they enjoy?" So it was said: that is an enjoyment in this world, or they have an enjoyment in this world that is passing and has no permanence. Then they will meet everlasting misery in the Hereafter. [p. 178]

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 10, verses 71–74 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And recite to them the news of Noah, when he said to his people: "O my people, if my standing (among you) and my reminding you of the signs of God is burdensome to you, then in God I have put my trust. So resolve upon your affair, and (gather) your partners, then let not your affair be a concealed matter for you. Then carry out your decision against me, and give me no respite."﴾ ﴿But if you turn away, I have not asked you for any reward. My reward is only from God, and I have been commanded to be among the Muslims.﴾ ﴿So they denied him, and We delivered him and those with him in the ship, and We made them successors, and We drowned those who denied Our signs. So look at how was the end of those who were warned.﴾ ﴿Then after him We sent messengers to their peoples, and they brought them clear proofs, but they were not going to believe in what they had denied before. Thus do We seal the hearts of the transgressors.﴾ ﴿Then after them We sent Moses and Aaron to Pharaoh and his chiefs with Our signs, but they were arrogant, and they were a criminal people.﴾ [Yunus: 75] ﴿So when the truth came to them from Us, they said: "Indeed this is clear magic."﴾ [Yunus: 76] ﴿Moses said: "Do you say of the truth when it has come to you, 'Is this magic?' And magicians do not prosper."﴾ [Yunus: 77] ﴿They said: "Have you come to us to turn us away from what we found our fathers upon, and that you two may have greatness in the land? We are not going to believe you two."﴾ [Yunus: 78]

Laftha ʿunuqahu (لَفَتَ عُنُقَهُ): he twisted his neck, i.e., turned it and redirected it.

Al-Azhari said: laftha al-shay' wa-fatalahu means he twisted it. This is from the inverted form (al-maqlub), and the passage ends. The reflexive verb of laftha is iltafta (التفت), and it was said: infatala.

﴿And recite to them the news of Noah, when he said to his people: "O my people, if my standing (among you) and my reminding you of the signs of God is burdensome to you, then in God I have put my trust. So resolve upon your affair, and (gather) your partners, then let not your affair be a concealed matter for you. Then carry out your decision against me, and give me no respite."﴾: When the Exalted mentioned the proofs of His oneness, and mentioned what took place between the Messenger and the disbelievers, He mentioned stories from the stories of the prophets and what happened to them with their peoples of disagreement. This is a consolation for the Messenger (ﷺ), so that he may take the prophets before him as an example, and so that what he suffers from them of denial and scarcity of followers may become lighter for him. It is also so that those to whom this story is recited may know the end of those who denied the prophets, and (so that they may know) what God granted His Prophet of knowledge of this story, although he had not studied any book nor accompanied any scholar, and that it corresponds exactly to what he reported. This indicates that God revealed it to him and informed him of it, and that he is a prophet without doubt. The pronoun in ʿalayhim (عَلَيْهِمْ) refers to the people of Mecca, who were mentioned earlier.

Kabura (كَبُرَ) means: "my standing was great," i.e., the length of my standing among you, or my standing up for admonition, as is related of Jesus, peace be upon him, that he used to admonish the Disciples while standing so that they would see him while they were seated, and like the standing of the preacher so that people may hear and see him. Or it is attributed to his standing while the intended meaning is himself, as you say: "I did such-and-such because of the position (makan) of so-and-so," and "so-and-so is heavy in shadow," meaning because of so-and-so, and "so-and-so is heavy." Ibn ʿAtiyya said: It was not read here with a dammah on the mim. This is not as he mentioned; rather Abu Majlaz, Abu Raja' and Abu al-Jawza read muqami with a dammah on the mim. Al-muqam is the act of residing in a place, and al-maqam is the place of standing. Al-tadhkir is his admonishing them and deterring them from sins. The response of the conditional clause is omitted, its estimate being: "then do whatever you wish." It was also said: the response is "then in God I have put my trust." "Fa-ajmiʿu" (فَأجْمِعُوا) is coordinated with the response, but this does not appear, because he always relied upon God.

Most scholars said: the response is "fa-ajmiʿu," and "fa-ʿala Allahi tawakkaltu" is a parenthetical sentence between the condition and its answer, like the verse of the poet:

"Do you not see that I have become thin, and whoever becomes a target for the points of spears will become thin?"

"Then many a bright-faced one, like your heavy one, a stout, large one on the back of a horse, bare-backed (mahbal)."

The majority read fa-ajmiʿu from ajmaʿa al-rajulu al-shay' (أجْمَعَ الرَّجُلُ الشَّيْءَ), meaning he resolved upon it and intended it. The poet said:

"They resolved their affair at night, but when they became morning, their clamor became (evident) to them."

Another said:(p-179)

"Would that I knew, while desires do not benefit, whether you ever gave an excuse, while my affair is resolved."

Abu Qayd al-Sadusi said: ajmaʿtu al-amr is more eloquent than ajmaʿtu ʿalayhi. Abu al-Haytham said: ajmaʿa amrahu means he made it gathered after it had been scattered. He said: its distinction is that he says once, "I will do such-and-such," and once, "I will do such-and-such," but when he resolves upon one matter, he has made it; that is, he has made it all together. This is the origin of ijmaʿ (إجماع), then it came to mean resolve, until it was connected with ʿala, so it was said: ajmaʿtu ʿala al-amr, meaning ʿazamtu ʿalayhi (I resolved upon it), while the original is ajmaʿtu al-amr. End quote.

On this reading, "wa-shurakaʾakum" (وَشُرَكاءَكم) is coordinated with "amrakum" (أمْرَكم) by omitting a modifier, meaning: "and the affair of your partners," or it is coordinated with "amrakum" without considering an omitted element, because it is also said: ajmaʿtu shurakaʾi (I gathered my partners). Or it is in the accusative by an implied verb, meaning: "and call your partners," on the basis that one does not say ajmaʿtu shurakaʾi, in the majority of usage, so it is like the verse:

"So I fed her straw and cold water, until her eyes shed tears of flowing."

Here "wa-saqaytuha" (and I gave her to drink) is the sense, according to one of the two positions. Likewise it is in the codex of Ubayy: "wa-diʿu shurakaʾakum" (and call your partners). Abu ʿAli said: the partners may be put in the accusative by the waw of accompaniment (wāw maʿa, واو مع), as they said: "the rain came with the tayalisa" (a garment). Al-Zamakhshari did not mention for the accusative of "wa-shurakaʾakum" any view other than the reading of Ubayy, that it is accusative by the waw of accompaniment. This construction should be understood as an object of accompaniment (mafʿul maʿahu) from the subject, which is the pronoun in "fa-ajmiʿu," not from the object which is "amrakum," and this is according to the more common of the two usages, because one says: "the partners gathered (ajmaʿa al-shurakaʾu)," and one does not say "they gathered their affair" except rarely, nor "the partners gathered" (ajmaʿat al-shurakaʾu) except rarely.

Regarding the condition for the validity of coordination in what is an object of accompaniment, there is a difference of opinion. When we make it from the subject, it is preferable.

Al-Zuhri, al-Aʿmash, al-Jahdari, Abu Raja', al-Aʿraj, and al-Asmaʿi from Nafiʿ and Yaʿqub with a variant from him read: "fa-jmaʿu" (فَاجْمَعُوا) with a connecting alif and a fatḥa on the mim, from jamaʿa, and "shurakaʾakum" is coordinated with "amrakum," because one says: "my partners" (shurakaʾi), or it is an object of accompaniment, or by omitting a modifier, meaning: "those in authority among you," so what applies to the genitive would apply to the noun if it were present. This was said by Abu ʿAli.

In the Kitab al-Lawamih: ajmaʿtu al-amr means I made it all together, and jamaʿtu al-amwal jamiʿan (I gathered the wealth all together). So ijmaʿ is used for events and jamʿ for physical things, and each may be used in place of the other. In the Revelation: "fa-jamaʿa kaydahu" (so he gathered his plot) [Taha: 60]. End quote.

Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman, al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq, ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar, Sallam and Yaʿqub, as related from him, read: "wa-shurakaʾukum" (وَشُرَكاؤُكم) with a nominative, which is justified as coordinated with the pronoun in "fa-ajmiʿu," and the separation by the object makes it acceptable. And it is also justified as the subject of an elided predicate, indicated by what precedes it, meaning: "and your partners, let them resolve their affair." A group read: "wa-shurakaʾikum" (وَشُرَكائِكم) with a genitive, coordinated with the pronoun in "amrakum," meaning "and the affair of your partners," the modifier being omitted, as in the saying of another:

"Do you, who think a man is a man, and a fire that is kindled by night is a fire?"

meaning: "and every fire," with "kull" omitted because the preceding words indicate it. The partners intended here are the rivals besides God. He attributed them to them, since they make them partners by their own claim. He attributed the resolving to the partners in the manner of mockery, like the saying of the Exalted: "Say: call your partners, then plot against me" [al-Araf: 195]. Or the partners intended are those who share their religion and way. Ibn al-Anbari said: What is meant by the affair here is the existence of their plot and scheming. So the estimate is: do not leave anything of your affair without bringing it forth. End quote.

His command to them to resolve their affair is evidence of his indifference to them, because of his confidence in what his Lord had promised him of protection and safeguarding. "Then let not your affair be a concealed matter for you" (ثُمَّ لا يَكُنْ أمْرُكم عَلَيْكم غُمَّةً): that is, your situation with me and your companionship with me should be a grief and a worry; that is, "then destroy me, so that your life will not be a choking because of me, and your situation will not be a concealment against you." Ghamm (غَمّ) and ghumma (غُمَّة) are like karb (كَرْب) and kurba (كُرْبَة). Abu al-Haytham said: it comes from their saying: "the crescent was concealed from us (ghamma ʿalaynaa al-hilal), so it is maghmum (concealed) if it is sought and not seen." Tarafa said:

"By your life, my affair is not concealed from me, neither my day nor my night is an everlasting darkness upon me."

(p-180) Al-Layth said: it is said: "he is in ghumma about his affair" if it has not become clear to him. Al-Zajjaj said: your affair is apparent and open. Al-Zamakhshari praised this, saying: he mentioned the first view, in which by "amr" is meant the sense used here, and the second is that by it is meant the same as the first "amr."

Al-ghumma means a covering, from ghammahu, when he covered it. From it is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "There is no concealment in the obligations of God the Exalted." That is: they are not to be hidden, but are to be proclaimed openly. That is, do not let your intent to destroy me be hidden from you, but rather let it be open and well-known, which you proclaim. End quote.

The meaning of "iqḍū ilayya" (اقْضُوا إلَيَّ) is: carry out your decision toward me. The object of "iqḍū" is omitted, meaning: "carry out that matter against me, and proceed in yourselves, and cut off what is between me and you." Al-Sarri ibn Yanʿum read: "thumma afḍū" (ثُمَّ أفْضُوا) with a fāʾ and cutting the alif, meaning: "reach me with your evil," from afḍā bi-kadhā (أفضى بكذا), meaning: it reached him.

It was said: its meaning is "hasten." It was said: from afḍā, when one goes out to the open space (faḍāʾ), meaning: "so bring it out before me and make it manifest." From it is the saying of the poet:

"He refused humiliation, while al-Numan's fang burns against him, so he brought it out, and the swords were his refuges."

"Wa-la tunẓirūni" (وَلا تُنْظِرُونِ): that is, do not delay me. The nazra (النَّظِرَة) is a postponement.

﴿But if you turn away, I have not asked you for any reward. My reward is only from God, and I have been commanded to be among the Muslims.﴾: That is: if your turning away from what I have brought to you, of the oneness of God and the rejection of your gods, continues, then I am not concerned about you, because your turning away does not harm me personally, nor has it cut off from me any connection with you. Since what I called you to, reminded you of, and admonished you with, I did not ask you for any reward for it. It is God the Exalted who rewards me for it. That is, I have advised you only for the sake of God the Exalted, not for any aim of worldly purposes. Then He informed that He commanded him to be among the Muslims, meaning among those submitting to the command of God, obedient to Him. "So they denied him," and they persisted in their denial of him, and that was when destruction was approaching them, by the Flood.

"Fi al-Fulk" (فِي الفُلْكِ) is connected to the settled element (al-istiqrar) that is connected with it, or to "fa-najjaynahu." "Wa-jaʿalnahum" (وَجَعَلْناهم): the pronoun of the object was made plural according to the sense of "min" (those). "Khalaʾif" (خَلائِفَ) means: they succeed those who perished and were destroyed.

Then He commanded them to look at the end of those warned with punishment, and at what their condition came to. In this report there is a threat to the disbelievers regarding Muhammad (ﷺ), and an example for them that they are in the same condition of denial as those, so their condition will be like theirs in punishment.

The address in "fa-unẓur" (فانْظُرْ) is to the hearer of this story. In this there is magnification of what befell them, a warning to those whom the Messenger warned, and a consolation for him (ﷺ).

﴿Then after him We sent messengers to their peoples, and they brought them clear proofs, but they were not going to believe in what they had denied before. Thus do We seal the hearts of the transgressors.﴾: "Min baʿdihi" (مِن بَعْدِهِ) means: after Noah, messengers to their peoples, meaning Hud, Salih, Lut, Ibrahim and Shuʿayb. "Al-bayyinat" (الْبَيِّنات) are the miracles and the clear proofs establishing what they brought.

The negation came with the lam of denial (lam al-juhud, لامُ الجُحُود) to indicate that their belief was in the category of impossibility and refusal. The pronoun in "kadhdhabu" (كَذَّبُوا) refers to those to whom the pronoun in "kanu" (كانُوا) refers, namely the people of the messengers. The meaning is: before the sending of the messengers they were people of ignorance and denial of the truth, so their condition before the sending and after it was the same, as if no one had been sent to them.

"Min qablu" (مِن قَبْلُ) is connected with "kadhdhabu," meaning: before the sending of the messengers. It was also said: the meaning is that they rushed to deny their messengers whenever a messenger came, then they persisted in disbelief and continued in it, so they would not believe in what their denial had preceded, before their persistence and continuation in disbelief. Yahya ibn Salam said: "min qabl" means before the punishment, and this view is far-fetched. It was also said: the pronoun in "kadhdhabu" refers to the people of Noah, meaning: the people of the messengers would not believe in what the people of Noah denied, meaning: their disposition in denial is one.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "The wording, in my view, may also bear another meaning, namely that mā is a verbal noun (maṣdariyya), and the meaning is: 'So they denied their messengers, and their punishment from God was that they would not believe because of their denial before, i.e., because of its cause and as its consequence.' This interpretation is supported by 'thus do We seal' (kadhālika naṭbaʿu)." End of quote.

The apparent reading is that mā is a relative pronoun (mawṣūla), and for this reason the pronoun returns to it in His words: "by what they had denied before" (bimā kadhdhabū bihi). Had it been a verbal noun, the pronoun would have no antecedent that has been mentioned, and one would have to contrive something for it to refer back to.

The reading of the majority (al-Jumhūr) is naṭbaʿu with the nūn, while al-ʿAbbās ibn al-Faḍl read yaṭbaʿu with the yāʾ. The kāf is for comparison, meaning: "Like that firm seal, which cannot be removed, We seal upon the hearts of the transgressors (al-muʿtadīn), those who exceed their bounds (al-mujāwizīna ṭawrahum) and who go to extremes in disbelief (al-mubālighīna fī al-kufr)."

This was said by Abu ʿAli.

In the Kitab al-Lawamih: ajmaʿtu al-amr means I made it all together, and jamaʿtu al-amwal jamiʿan (I gathered the wealth all together). So ijmaʿ is used for events and jamʿ for physical things, and each may be used in place of the other. In the Revelation: "fa-jamaʿa kaydahu" (so he gathered his plot) [Taha: 60]. End quote.

Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman, al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq, ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar, Sallam and Yaʿqub, as related from him, read: "wa-shurakaʾukum" (وَشُرَكاؤُكم) with a nominative, which is justified as coordinated with the pronoun in "fa-ajmiʿu," and the separation by the object makes it acceptable. And it is also justified as the subject of an elided predicate, indicated by what precedes it, meaning: "and your partners, let them resolve their affair." A group read: "wa-shurakaʾikum" (وَشُرَكائِكم) with a genitive, coordinated with the pronoun in "amrakum," meaning "and the affair of your partners," the modifier being omitted, as in the saying of another:

"Do you, who think a man is a man, and a fire that is kindled by night is a fire?"

meaning: "and every fire," with "kull" omitted because the preceding words indicate it. The partners intended here are the rivals besides God. He attributed them to them, since they make them partners by their own claim. He attributed the resolving to the partners in the manner of mockery, like the saying of the Exalted: "Say: call your partners, then plot against me" [al-Araf: 195]. Or the partners intended are those who share their religion and way. Ibn al-Anbari said: What is meant by the affair here is the existence of their plot and scheming. So the estimate is: do not leave anything of your affair without bringing it forth. End quote.

His command to them to resolve their affair is evidence of his indifference to them, because of his confidence in what his Lord had promised him of protection and safeguarding. "Then let not your affair be a concealed matter for you" (ثُمَّ لا يَكُنْ أمْرُكم عَلَيْكم غُمَّةً): that is, your situation with me and your companionship with me should be a grief and a worry; that is, "then destroy me, so that your life will not be a choking because of me, and your situation will not be a concealment against you." Ghamm (غَمّ) and ghumma (غُمَّة) are like karb (كَرْب) and kurba (كُرْبَة). Abu al-Haytham said: it comes from their saying: "the crescent was concealed from us (ghamma ʿalaynaa al-hilal), so it is maghmum (concealed) if it is sought and not seen." Tarafa said:

"By your life, my affair is not concealed from me, neither my day nor my night is an everlasting darkness upon me."

(p-180) Al-Layth said: it is said: "he is in ghumma about his affair" if it has not become clear to him. Al-Zajjaj said: your affair is apparent and open. Al-Zamakhshari praised this, saying: he mentioned the first view, in which by "amr" is meant the sense used here, and the second is that by it is meant the same as the first "amr."

Al-ghumma means a covering, from ghammahu, when he covered it. From it is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "There is no concealment in the obligations of God the Exalted." That is: they are not to be hidden, but are to be proclaimed openly. That is, do not let your intent to destroy me be hidden from you, but rather let it be open and well-known, which you proclaim. End quote.

The meaning of "iqḍū ilayya" (اقْضُوا إلَيَّ) is: carry out your decision toward me. The object of "iqḍū" is omitted, meaning: "carry out that matter against me, and proceed in yourselves, and cut off what is between me and you." Al-Sarri ibn Yanʿum read: "thumma afḍū" (ثُمَّ أفْضُوا) with a fāʾ and cutting the alif, meaning: "reach me with your evil," from afḍā bi-kadhā (أفضى بكذا), meaning: it reached him.

It was said: its meaning is "hasten." It was said: from afḍā, when one goes out to the open space (faḍāʾ), meaning: "so bring it out before me and make it manifest." From it is the saying of the poet:

"He refused humiliation, while al-Numan's fang burns against him, so he brought it out, and the swords were his refuges."

"Wa-la tunẓirūni" (وَلا تُنْظِرُونِ): that is, do not delay me. The nazra (النَّظِرَة) is a postponement.

﴿But if you turn away, I have not asked you for any reward. My reward is only from God, and I have been commanded to be among the Muslims.﴾: That is: if your turning away from what I have brought to you, of the oneness of God and the rejection of your gods, continues, then I am not concerned about you, because your turning away does not harm me personally, nor has it cut off from me any connection with you. Since what I called you to, reminded you of, and admonished you with, I did not ask you for any reward for it. It is God the Exalted who rewards me for it. That is, I have advised you only for the sake of God the Exalted, not for any aim of worldly purposes. Then He informed that He commanded him to be among the Muslims, meaning among those submitting to the command of God, obedient to Him. "So they denied him," and they persisted in their denial of him, and that was when destruction was approaching them, by the Flood.

"Fi al-Fulk" (فِي الفُلْكِ) is connected to the settled element (al-istiqrar) that is connected with it, or to "fa-najjaynahu." "Wa-jaʿalnahum" (وَجَعَلْناهم): the pronoun of the object was made plural according to the sense of "min" (those). "Khalaʾif" (خَلائِفَ) means: they succeed those who perished and were destroyed.

Then He commanded them to look at the end of those warned with punishment, and at what their condition came to. In this report there is a threat to the disbelievers regarding Muhammad (ﷺ), and an example for them that they are in the same condition of denial as those, so their condition will be like theirs in punishment.

The address in "fa-unẓur" (فانْظُرْ) is to the hearer of this story. In this there is magnification of what befell them, a warning to those whom the Messenger warned, and a consolation for him (ﷺ).

﴿Then after him We sent messengers to their peoples, and they brought them clear proofs, but they were not going to believe in what they had denied before. Thus do We seal the hearts of the transgressors.﴾: "Min baʿdihi" (مِن بَعْدِهِ) means: after Noah, messengers to their peoples, meaning Hud, Salih, Lut, Ibrahim and Shuʿayb. "Al-bayyinat" (الْبَيِّنات) are the miracles and the clear proofs establishing what they brought.

The negation came with the lam of denial (lam al-juhud, لامُ الجُحُود) to indicate that their belief was in the category of impossibility and refusal. The pronoun in "kadhdhabu" (كَذَّبُوا) refers to those to whom the pronoun in "kanu" (كانُوا) refers, namely the people of the messengers. The meaning is: before the sending of the messengers they were people of ignorance and denial of the truth, so their condition before the sending and after it was the same, as if no one had been sent to them.

"Min qablu" (مِن قَبْلُ) is connected with "kadhdhabu," meaning: before the sending of the messengers. It was also said: the meaning is that they rushed to deny their messengers whenever a messenger came, then they persisted in disbelief and continued in it, so they would not believe in what their denial had preceded, before their persistence and continuation in disbelief. Yahya ibn Salam said: "min qabl" means before the punishment, and this view is far-fetched. It was also said: the pronoun in "kadhdhabu" refers to the people of Noah, meaning: the people of the messengers would not believe in what the people of Noah denied, meaning: their disposition in denial is one.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "The wording, in my view, may also bear another meaning, namely that mā is a verbal noun (maṣdariyya), and the meaning is: 'So they denied their messengers, and their punishment from God was that they would not believe because of their denial before, i.e., because of its cause and as its consequence.' This interpretation is supported by 'thus do We seal' (kadhālika naṭbaʿu)." End of quote.

The apparent reading is that mā is a relative pronoun (mawṣūla), and for this reason the pronoun returns to it in His words: "by what they had denied before" (bimā kadhdhabū bihi). Had it been a verbal noun, the pronoun would have no antecedent that has been mentioned, and one would have to contrive something for it to refer back to.

The reading of the majority (al-Jumhūr) is naṭbaʿu with the nūn, while al-ʿAbbās ibn al-Faḍl read yaṭbaʿu with the yāʾ. The kāf is for comparison, meaning: "Like that firm seal, which cannot be removed, We seal upon the hearts of the transgressors (al-muʿtadīn), those who exceed their bounds (al-mujāwizīna ṭawrahum) and who go to extremes in disbelief (al-mubālighīna fī al-kufr)."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 10, verses 71–74 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And recite to them the news of Noah, when he said to his people: "O my people, if my standing (among you) and my reminding you of the signs of God is burdensome to you, then in God I have put my trust. So resolve upon your affair, and (gather) your partners, then let not your affair be a concealed matter for you. Then carry out your decision against me, and give me no respite."﴾ ﴿But if you turn away, I have not asked you for any reward. My reward is only from God, and I have been commanded to be among the Muslims.﴾ ﴿So they denied him, and We delivered him and those with him in the ship, and We made them successors, and We drowned those who denied Our signs. So look at how was the end of those who were warned.﴾ ﴿Then after him We sent messengers to their peoples, and they brought them clear proofs, but they were not going to believe in what they had denied before. Thus do We seal the hearts of the transgressors.﴾ ﴿Then after them We sent Moses and Aaron to Pharaoh and his chiefs with Our signs, but they were arrogant, and they were a criminal people.﴾ [Yunus: 75] ﴿So when the truth came to them from Us, they said: "Indeed this is clear magic."﴾ [Yunus: 76] ﴿Moses said: "Do you say of the truth when it has come to you, 'Is this magic?' And magicians do not prosper."﴾ [Yunus: 77] ﴿They said: "Have you come to us to turn us away from what we found our fathers upon, and that you two may have greatness in the land? We are not going to believe you two."﴾ [Yunus: 78]

Laftha ʿunuqahu (لَفَتَ عُنُقَهُ): he twisted his neck, i.e., turned it and redirected it.

Al-Azhari said: laftha al-shay' wa-fatalahu means he twisted it. This is from the inverted form (al-maqlub), and the passage ends. The reflexive verb of laftha is iltafta (التفت), and it was said: infatala.

﴿And recite to them the news of Noah, when he said to his people: "O my people, if my standing (among you) and my reminding you of the signs of God is burdensome to you, then in God I have put my trust. So resolve upon your affair, and (gather) your partners, then let not your affair be a concealed matter for you. Then carry out your decision against me, and give me no respite."﴾: When the Exalted mentioned the proofs of His oneness, and mentioned what took place between the Messenger and the disbelievers, He mentioned stories from the stories of the prophets and what happened to them with their peoples of disagreement. This is a consolation for the Messenger (ﷺ), so that he may take the prophets before him as an example, and so that what he suffers from them of denial and scarcity of followers may become lighter for him. It is also so that those to whom this story is recited may know the end of those who denied the prophets, and (so that they may know) what God granted His Prophet of knowledge of this story, although he had not studied any book nor accompanied any scholar, and that it corresponds exactly to what he reported. This indicates that God revealed it to him and informed him of it, and that he is a prophet without doubt. The pronoun in ʿalayhim (عَلَيْهِمْ) refers to the people of Mecca, who were mentioned earlier.

Kabura (كَبُرَ) means: "my standing was great," i.e., the length of my standing among you, or my standing up for admonition, as is related of Jesus, peace be upon him, that he used to admonish the Disciples while standing so that they would see him while they were seated, and like the standing of the preacher so that people may hear and see him. Or it is attributed to his standing while the intended meaning is himself, as you say: "I did such-and-such because of the position (makan) of so-and-so," and "so-and-so is heavy in shadow," meaning because of so-and-so, and "so-and-so is heavy." Ibn ʿAtiyya said: It was not read here with a dammah on the mim. This is not as he mentioned; rather Abu Majlaz, Abu Raja' and Abu al-Jawza read muqami with a dammah on the mim. Al-muqam is the act of residing in a place, and al-maqam is the place of standing. Al-tadhkir is his admonishing them and deterring them from sins. The response of the conditional clause is omitted, its estimate being: "then do whatever you wish." It was also said: the response is "then in God I have put my trust." "Fa-ajmiʿu" (فَأجْمِعُوا) is coordinated with the response, but this does not appear, because he always relied upon God.

Most scholars said: the response is "fa-ajmiʿu," and "fa-ʿala Allahi tawakkaltu" is a parenthetical sentence between the condition and its answer, like the verse of the poet:

"Do you not see that I have become thin, and whoever becomes a target for the points of spears will become thin?"

"Then many a bright-faced one, like your heavy one, a stout, large one on the back of a horse, bare-backed (mahbal)."

The majority read fa-ajmiʿu from ajmaʿa al-rajulu al-shay' (أجْمَعَ الرَّجُلُ الشَّيْءَ), meaning he resolved upon it and intended it. The poet said:

"They resolved their affair at night, but when they became morning, their clamor became (evident) to them."

Another said:(p-179)

"Would that I knew, while desires do not benefit, whether you ever gave an excuse, while my affair is resolved."

Abu Qayd al-Sadusi said: ajmaʿtu al-amr is more eloquent than ajmaʿtu ʿalayhi. Abu al-Haytham said: ajmaʿa amrahu means he made it gathered after it had been scattered. He said: its distinction is that he says once, "I will do such-and-such," and once, "I will do such-and-such," but when he resolves upon one matter, he has made it; that is, he has made it all together. This is the origin of ijmaʿ (إجماع), then it came to mean resolve, until it was connected with ʿala, so it was said: ajmaʿtu ʿala al-amr, meaning ʿazamtu ʿalayhi (I resolved upon it), while the original is ajmaʿtu al-amr. End quote.

On this reading, "wa-shurakaʾakum" (وَشُرَكاءَكم) is coordinated with "amrakum" (أمْرَكم) by omitting a modifier, meaning: "and the affair of your partners," or it is coordinated with "amrakum" without considering an omitted element, because it is also said: ajmaʿtu shurakaʾi (I gathered my partners). Or it is in the accusative by an implied verb, meaning: "and call your partners," on the basis that one does not say ajmaʿtu shurakaʾi, in the majority of usage, so it is like the verse:

"So I fed her straw and cold water, until her eyes shed tears of flowing."

Here "wa-saqaytuha" (and I gave her to drink) is the sense, according to one of the two positions. Likewise it is in the codex of Ubayy: "wa-diʿu shurakaʾakum" (and call your partners). Abu ʿAli said: the partners may be put in the accusative by the waw of accompaniment (wāw maʿa, واو مع), as they said: "the rain came with the tayalisa" (a garment). Al-Zamakhshari did not mention for the accusative of "wa-shurakaʾakum" any view other than the reading of Ubayy, that it is accusative by the waw of accompaniment. This construction should be understood as an object of accompaniment (mafʿul maʿahu) from the subject, which is the pronoun in "fa-ajmiʿu," not from the object which is "amrakum," and this is according to the more common of the two usages, because one says: "the partners gathered (ajmaʿa al-shurakaʾu)," and one does not say "they gathered their affair" except rarely, nor "the partners gathered" (ajmaʿat al-shurakaʾu) except rarely.

﴿And recite to them the news of Noah, when he said to his people: "O my people, if my standing (among you) and my reminding you of the signs of God is burdensome to you, then in God I have put my trust. So resolve upon your affair, and (gather) your partners, then let not your affair be a concealed matter for you. Then carry out your decision against me, and give me no respite."﴾ ﴿But if you turn away, I have not asked you for any reward. My reward is only from God, and I have been commanded to be among the Muslims.﴾ ﴿So they denied him, and We delivered him and those with him in the ship, and We made them successors, and We drowned those who denied Our signs. So look at how was the end of those who were warned.﴾ ﴿Then after him We sent messengers to their peoples, and they brought them clear proofs, but they were not going to believe in what they had denied before. Thus do We seal the hearts of the transgressors.﴾ ﴿Then after them We sent Moses and Aaron to Pharaoh and his chiefs with Our signs, but they were arrogant, and they were a criminal people.﴾ [Yunus: 75] ﴿So when the truth came to them from Us, they said: "Indeed this is clear magic."﴾ [Yunus: 76] ﴿Moses said: "Do you say of the truth when it has come to you, 'Is this magic?' And magicians do not prosper."﴾ [Yunus: 77] ﴿They said: "Have you come to us to turn us away from what we found our fathers upon, and that you two may have greatness in the land? We are not going to believe you two."﴾ [Yunus: 78]

Laftha ʿunuqahu (لَفَتَ عُنُقَهُ): he twisted his neck, i.e., turned it and redirected it.

Al-Azhari said: laftha al-shay' wa-fatalahu means he twisted it. This is from the inverted form (al-maqlub), and the passage ends. The reflexive verb of laftha is iltafta (التفت), and it was said: infatala.

﴿And recite to them the news of Noah, when he said to his people: "O my people, if my standing (among you) and my reminding you of the signs of God is burdensome to you, then in God I have put my trust. So resolve upon your affair, and (gather) your partners, then let not your affair be a concealed matter for you. Then carry out your decision against me, and give me no respite."﴾: When the Exalted mentioned the proofs of His oneness, and mentioned what took place between the Messenger and the disbelievers, He mentioned stories from the stories of the prophets and what happened to them with their peoples of disagreement. This is a consolation for the Messenger (ﷺ), so that he may take the prophets before him as an example, and so that what he suffers from them of denial and scarcity of followers may become lighter for him. It is also so that those to whom this story is recited may know the end of those who denied the prophets, and (so that they may know) what God granted His Prophet of knowledge of this story, although he had not studied any book nor accompanied any scholar, and that it corresponds exactly to what he reported. This indicates that God revealed it to him and informed him of it, and that he is a prophet without doubt. The pronoun in ʿalayhim (عَلَيْهِمْ) refers to the people of Mecca, who were mentioned earlier.

Kabura (كَبُرَ) means: "my standing was great," i.e., the length of my standing among you, or my standing up for admonition, as is related of Jesus, peace be upon him, that he used to admonish the Disciples while standing so that they would see him while they were seated, and like the standing of the preacher so that people may hear and see him. Or it is attributed to his standing while the intended meaning is himself, as you say: "I did such-and-such because of the position (makan) of so-and-so," and "so-and-so is heavy in shadow," meaning because of so-and-so, and "so-and-so is heavy." Ibn ʿAtiyya said: It was not read here with a dammah on the mim. This is not as he mentioned; rather Abu Majlaz, Abu Raja' and Abu al-Jawza read muqami with a dammah on the mim. Al-muqam is the act of residing in a place, and al-maqam is the place of standing. Al-tadhkir is his admonishing them and deterring them from sins. The response of the conditional clause is omitted, its estimate being: "then do whatever you wish." It was also said: the response is "then in God I have put my trust." "Fa-ajmiʿu" (فَأجْمِعُوا) is coordinated with the response, but this does not appear, because he always relied upon God.

Most scholars said: the response is "fa-ajmiʿu," and "fa-ʿala Allahi tawakkaltu" is a parenthetical sentence between the condition and its answer, like the verse of the poet:

"Do you not see that I have become thin, and whoever becomes a target for the points of spears will become thin?"

"Then many a bright-faced one, like your heavy one, a stout, large one on the back of a horse, bare-backed (mahbal)."

The majority read fa-ajmiʿu from ajmaʿa al-rajulu al-shay' (أجْمَعَ الرَّجُلُ الشَّيْءَ), meaning he resolved upon it and intended it. The poet said:

"They resolved their affair at night, but when they became morning, their clamor became (evident) to them."

Another said:(p-179)

"Would that I knew, while desires do not benefit, whether you ever gave an excuse, while my affair is resolved."

Abu Qayd al-Sadusi said: ajmaʿtu al-amr is more eloquent than ajmaʿtu ʿalayhi. Abu al-Haytham said: ajmaʿa amrahu means he made it gathered after it had been scattered. He said: its distinction is that he says once, "I will do such-and-such," and once, "I will do such-and-such," but when he resolves upon one matter, he has made it; that is, he has made it all together. This is the origin of ijmaʿ (إجماع), then it came to mean resolve, until it was connected with ʿala, so it was said: ajmaʿtu ʿala al-amr, meaning ʿazamtu ʿalayhi (I resolved upon it), while the original is ajmaʿtu al-amr. End quote.

On this reading, "wa-shurakaʾakum" (وَشُرَكاءَكم) is coordinated with "amrakum" (أمْرَكم) by omitting a modifier, meaning: "and the affair of your partners," or it is coordinated with "amrakum" without considering an omitted element, because it is also said: ajmaʿtu shurakaʾi (I gathered my partners). Or it is in the accusative by an implied verb, meaning: "and call your partners," on the basis that one does not say ajmaʿtu shurakaʾi, in the majority of usage, so it is like the verse:

"So I fed her straw and cold water, until her eyes shed tears of flowing."

Here "wa-saqaytuha" (and I gave her to drink) is the sense, according to one of the two positions. Likewise it is in the codex of Ubayy: "wa-diʿu shurakaʾakum" (and call your partners). Abu ʿAli said: the partners may be put in the accusative by the waw of accompaniment (wāw maʿa, واو مع), as they said: "the rain came with the tayalisa" (a garment). Al-Zamakhshari did not mention for the accusative of "wa-shurakaʾakum" any view other than the reading of Ubayy, that it is accusative by the waw of accompaniment. This construction should be understood as an object of accompaniment (mafʿul maʿahu) from the subject, which is the pronoun in "fa-ajmiʿu," not from the object which is "amrakum," and this is according to the more common of the two usages, because one says: "the partners gathered (ajmaʿa al-shurakaʾu)," and one does not say "they gathered their affair" except rarely, nor "the partners gathered" (ajmaʿat al-shurakaʾu) except rarely.

Regarding the condition for the validity of coordination in what is an object of accompaniment, there is a difference of opinion. When we make it from the subject, it is preferable.

Al-Zuhri, al-Aʿmash, al-Jahdari, Abu Raja', al-Aʿraj, and al-Asmaʿi from Nafiʿ and Yaʿqub with a variant from him read: "fa-jmaʿu" (فَاجْمَعُوا) with a connecting alif and a fatḥa on the mim, from jamaʿa, and "shurakaʾakum" is coordinated with "amrakum," because one says: "my partners" (shurakaʾi), or it is an object of accompaniment, or by omitting a modifier, meaning: "those in authority among you," so what applies to the genitive would apply to the noun if it were present. This was said by Abu ʿAli.

In the Kitab al-Lawamih: ajmaʿtu al-amr means I made it all together, and jamaʿtu al-amwal jamiʿan (I gathered the wealth all together). So ijmaʿ is used for events and jamʿ for physical things, and each may be used in place of the other. In the Revelation: "fa-jamaʿa kaydahu" (so he gathered his plot) [Taha: 60]. End quote.

Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman, al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq, ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar, Sallam and Yaʿqub, as related from him, read: "wa-shurakaʾukum" (وَشُرَكاؤُكم) with a nominative, which is justified as coordinated with the pronoun in "fa-ajmiʿu," and the separation by the object makes it acceptable. And it is also justified as the subject of an elided predicate, indicated by what precedes it, meaning: "and your partners, let them resolve their affair." A group read: "wa-shurakaʾikum" (وَشُرَكائِكم) with a genitive, coordinated with the pronoun in "amrakum," meaning "and the affair of your partners," the modifier being omitted, as in the saying of another:

"Do you, who think a man is a man, and a fire that is kindled by night is a fire?"

meaning: "and every fire," with "kull" omitted because the preceding words indicate it. The partners intended here are the rivals besides God. He attributed them to them, since they make them partners by their own claim. He attributed the resolving to the partners in the manner of mockery, like the saying of the Exalted: "Say: call your partners, then plot against me" [al-Araf: 195]. Or the partners intended are those who share their religion and way. Ibn al-Anbari said: What is meant by the affair here is the existence of their plot and scheming. So the estimate is: do not leave anything of your affair without bringing it forth. End quote.

His command to them to resolve their affair is evidence of his indifference to them, because of his confidence in what his Lord had promised him of protection and safeguarding. "Then let not your affair be a concealed matter for you" (ثُمَّ لا يَكُنْ أمْرُكم عَلَيْكم غُمَّةً): that is, your situation with me and your companionship with me should be a grief and a worry; that is, "then destroy me, so that your life will not be a choking because of me, and your situation will not be a concealment against you." Ghamm (غَمّ) and ghumma (غُمَّة) are like karb (كَرْب) and kurba (كُرْبَة). Abu al-Haytham said: it comes from their saying: "the crescent was concealed from us (ghamma ʿalaynaa al-hilal), so it is maghmum (concealed) if it is sought and not seen." Tarafa said:

"By your life, my affair is not concealed from me, neither my day nor my night is an everlasting darkness upon me."

(p-180) Al-Layth said: it is said: "he is in ghumma about his affair" if it has not become clear to him. Al-Zajjaj said: your affair is apparent and open. Al-Zamakhshari praised this, saying: he mentioned the first view, in which by "amr" is meant the sense used here, and the second is that by it is meant the same as the first "amr."

Al-ghumma means a covering, from ghammahu, when he covered it. From it is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "There is no concealment in the obligations of God the Exalted." That is: they are not to be hidden, but are to be proclaimed openly. That is, do not let your intent to destroy me be hidden from you, but rather let it be open and well-known, which you proclaim. End quote.

The meaning of "iqḍū ilayya" (اقْضُوا إلَيَّ) is: carry out your decision toward me. The object of "iqḍū" is omitted, meaning: "carry out that matter against me, and proceed in yourselves, and cut off what is between me and you." Al-Sarri ibn Yanʿum read: "thumma afḍū" (ثُمَّ أفْضُوا) with a fāʾ and cutting the alif, meaning: "reach me with your evil," from afḍā bi-kadhā (أفضى بكذا), meaning: it reached him.

It was said: its meaning is "hasten." It was said: from afḍā, when one goes out to the open space (faḍāʾ), meaning: "so bring it out before me and make it manifest." From it is the saying of the poet:

"He refused humiliation, while al-Numan's fang burns against him, so he brought it out, and the swords were his refuges."

"Wa-la tunẓirūni" (وَلا تُنْظِرُونِ): that is, do not delay me. The nazra (النَّظِرَة) is a postponement.

﴿But if you turn away, I have not asked you for any reward. My reward is only from God, and I have been commanded to be among the Muslims.﴾: That is: if your turning away from what I have brought to you, of the oneness of God and the rejection of your gods, continues, then I am not concerned about you, because your turning away does not harm me personally, nor has it cut off from me any connection with you. Since what I called you to, reminded you of, and admonished you with, I did not ask you for any reward for it. It is God the Exalted who rewards me for it. That is, I have advised you only for the sake of God the Exalted, not for any aim of worldly purposes. Then He informed that He commanded him to be among the Muslims, meaning among those submitting to the command of God, obedient to Him. "So they denied him," and they persisted in their denial of him, and that was when destruction was approaching them, by the Flood.

"Fi al-Fulk" (فِي الفُلْكِ) is connected to the settled element (al-istiqrar) that is connected with it, or to "fa-najjaynahu." "Wa-jaʿalnahum" (وَجَعَلْناهم): the pronoun of the object was made plural according to the sense of "min" (those). "Khalaʾif" (خَلائِفَ) means: they succeed those who perished and were destroyed.

Then He commanded them to look at the end of those warned with punishment, and at what their condition came to. In this report there is a threat to the disbelievers regarding Muhammad (ﷺ), and an example for them that they are in the same condition of denial as those, so their condition will be like theirs in punishment.

The address in "fa-unẓur" (فانْظُرْ) is to the hearer of this story. In this there is magnification of what befell them, a warning to those whom the Messenger warned, and a consolation for him (ﷺ).

﴿Then after him We sent messengers to their peoples, and they brought them clear proofs, but they were not going to believe in what they had denied before. Thus do We seal the hearts of the transgressors.﴾: "Min baʿdihi" (مِن بَعْدِهِ) means: after Noah, messengers to their peoples, meaning Hud, Salih, Lut, Ibrahim and Shuʿayb. "Al-bayyinat" (الْبَيِّنات) are the miracles and the clear proofs establishing what they brought.

The negation came with the lam of denial (lam al-juhud, لامُ الجُحُود) to indicate that their belief was in the category of impossibility and refusal. The pronoun in "kadhdhabu" (كَذَّبُوا) refers to those to whom the pronoun in "kanu" (كانُوا) refers, namely the people of the messengers. The meaning is: before the sending of the messengers they were people of ignorance and denial of the truth, so their condition before the sending and after it was the same, as if no one had been sent to them.

"Min qablu" (مِن قَبْلُ) is connected with "kadhdhabu," meaning: before the sending of the messengers. It was also said: the meaning is that they rushed to deny their messengers whenever a messenger came, then they persisted in disbelief and continued in it, so they would not believe in what their denial had preceded, before their persistence and continuation in disbelief. Yahya ibn Salam said: "min qabl" means before the punishment, and this view is far-fetched. It was also said: the pronoun in "kadhdhabu" refers to the people of Noah, meaning: the people of the messengers would not believe in what the people of Noah denied, meaning: their disposition in denial is one.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "The wording, in my view, may also bear another meaning, namely that mā is a verbal noun (maṣdariyya), and the meaning is: 'So they denied their messengers, and their punishment from God was that they would not believe because of their denial before, i.e., because of its cause and as its consequence.' This interpretation is supported by 'thus do We seal' (kadhālika naṭbaʿu)." End of quote.

The apparent reading is that mā is a relative pronoun (mawṣūla), and for this reason the pronoun returns to it in His words: "by what they had denied before" (bimā kadhdhabū bihi). Had it been a verbal noun, the pronoun would have no antecedent that has been mentioned, and one would have to contrive something for it to refer back to.

The reading of the majority (al-Jumhūr) is naṭbaʿu with the nūn, while al-ʿAbbās ibn al-Faḍl read yaṭbaʿu with the yāʾ. The kāf is for comparison, meaning: "Like that firm seal, which cannot be removed, We seal upon the hearts of the transgressors (al-muʿtadīn), those who exceed their bounds (al-mujāwizīna ṭawrahum) and who go to extremes in disbelief (al-mubālighīna fī al-kufr)."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 10, verses 75–77:

﴿Then after them We sent Musa and Harun to Fir'awn (Pharaoh) and his chiefs with Our signs, but they were arrogant, and they were a guilty people.﴾ ﴿So when the truth came to them from Us, they said, "Indeed, this is manifest magic."﴾ ﴿Musa said, "Do you say this of the truth when it has come to you? Is this magic? Magicians do not prosper."﴾

That is: after those messengers, with Our signs, which are the miracles that appeared at his hands. His words "and his chiefs" are not restricted to the nobles; rather, they include all of the people of Fir'awn, its noble and its common folk.

"Fastakbaru" (they were arrogant) means they magnified themselves above accepting them. The greatest arrogance is that slaves magnify themselves above accepting the message of their Lord after it has become clear and evident. By committing great sins, they were arrogant and dared to reject it.

"Al-haqq" (the truth) refers to the staff and the hand. Out of their love for desires, they said: ﴿Indeed, this is manifest magic.﴾ while they knew that the truth is farthest from magic, which is nothing but deception and falsehood. They did not say ﴿Indeed, this is manifest magic﴾ except upon witnessing the staff turn into a serpent and the hand come out white, and they undertook only to oppose the staff, which is the miracle of Musa, in which the opponent's inability was manifest.

Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr and al-A'mash read: ﴿لَساحِرٌ مُبِينٌ﴾ [Yunus: 2], making the predicate of "inna" an active participle (ism fa'il) rather than a verbal noun (masdar), as in the reading of the majority. When they defied Musa regarding the truth he brought, they stated with certainty that what he brought was manifest magic. So Musa said to them, "Do you say?" as an interrogative in the sense of denial and rebuke, since they made the truth into magic. "Is this magic?" That is: a truth like this is not claimed to be magic.

He informed that one who is a magician does not prosper, based on His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And a magician does not prosper wherever he goes﴾ [Ta-Ha: 69]. The apparent view is that the object (ma'mul) of "ataqulun" (do you say) is omitted, its estimated form being what was previously mentioned, namely "inna hadha lasihrun" (indeed, this is magic). It is also permissible that the object of the verb of saying be omitted, because of the indication of it, as in the words of the poet:

*"We are those you spoke of, so how were you filled with terror at the sight of us before any concern for you?"*

As for the issue in al-Kitab (Sibawayh's grammar work): when you see or say "Zaydan munṭaliqan" (Zayd departing)... It was also said: the object of "ataqulun" is "a-sihrun hadha" (is this magic) and what follows it, as if they said: "Have you come with magic, seeking by it success, and magicians do not prosper?"

Just as Musa said to the magicians: ﴿What you have brought is magic; indeed, Allah will nullify it﴾ [Yunus: 81].

As for those who said that the sentence and the interrogation are reported speech (mahkiyyah) of a statement, they differed. Some of them said: they said that in the manner of magnifying the magic they had seen, according to their claim, just as you say to a horse that you see running well: "Is this a horse?" in the manner of wonder and amazement, although you know that it is a horse. So it is an interrogation whose meaning is wonder and magnification.

Others said: every ignorant person among them said it about the matter, so he asks: "Is it magic?" in response to some of them saying: "Indeed, this is magic."

Al-Zamakhshari permitted that the meaning of His saying "ataqulun lil-haqq" (do you say of the truth) is: "Do you find fault with it and attack it? You should have submitted to it and magnified it." He said: from their saying: "So-and-so fears al-qala (gossip)," and "Among the people there is taqawul (backbiting)," when some of them say to others what is hurtful. The word "al-qawl" (saying) here is like the word "al-dhikr" (mention) in His saying: "We heard a youth mentioning them," then he said: "Is this magic?" So he denied what they said in finding fault with it and attacking it.

*"We are those you spoke of, so how were you filled with terror at the sight of us before any concern for you?"*

As for the issue in al-Kitab (Sibawayh's grammar work): when you see or say "Zaydan munṭaliqan" (Zayd departing)... It was also said: the object of "ataqulun" is "a-sihrun hadha" (is this magic) and what follows it, as if they said: "Have you come with magic, seeking by it success, and magicians do not prosper?"

Some of them said: they said that in the manner of magnifying the magic they had seen, according to their claim, just as you say to a horse that you see running well: "Is this a horse?" in the manner of wonder and amazement, although you know that it is a horse. So it is an interrogation whose meaning is wonder and magnification.

Others said: every ignorant person among them said it about the matter, so he asks: "Is it magic?" in response to some of them saying: "Indeed, this is magic."

Al-Zamakhshari permitted that the meaning of His saying "ataqulun lil-haqq" (do you say of the truth) is: "Do you find fault with it and attack it? You should have submitted to it and magnified it." He said: from their saying: "So-and-so fears al-qala (gossip)," and "Among the people there is taqawul (backbiting)," when some of them say to others what is hurtful. The word "al-qawl" (saying) here is like the word "al-dhikr" (mention) in His saying: "We heard a youth mentioning them," then he said: "Is this magic?" So he denied what they said in finding fault with it and attacking it.

Indeed, Allah will nullify it. Indeed, Allah does not set right the work of corrupters."﴾ ﴿And Allah establishes the truth by His words, even if the criminals dislike it.﴾: "Have you come to us" is addressed to Musa alone, because it was he upon whose hands the miracles of the staff and the hand appeared. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, al-Dahhak and most of the commentators said: what is meant here is kingship (al-mulk), since kings are described as having pride (al-kibr), and for this reason a king is called jabbar (tyrant), and he is described as stubborn and fierce. "His kingship is a kingship of compassion, in which there is no tyranny from him nor kibriya'."

He means what kings possess of that. Ibn al-Ruqa' said:

"A lordship that is not shameful, which does not approach... of tyranny nor kibriya'."

Al-A'mash said: al-kibriya' is greatness (al-'azama). Ibn Zayd said: exaltation (al-'uluww). Al-Dahhak also said: obedience. "The land" here means the land of Egypt.

Ibn Mas'ud, Isma'il, al-Hasan, as reported by Kharija, Abu 'Amr and 'Asim (with variant transmissions from them) read "takunu" with the ta' (feminine), on account of the metaphorical feminine form of kibriya'. The majority read it with the ya' (yakuna), in consideration of the wording. The meaning is that they said: your aim in coming to us with what you have brought is that we should move from the religion of our fathers to what you command, and obey you, and that greatness and kingship over us should belong to you two through our obedience to you, so that we become your followers, abandoning the religion of our fathers. This is an aim we do not see, so we do not believe you in what you have brought, since your purpose is only to have us agree with what you are upon, and to dominate us.

Thus the first motive is imitation (taqlid), and the second is zeal for leadership, so that you will not be followers. These two motives, which they imagined to be the aim, required an explicit denial of faith, which is the cause of the occurrence of the two motives.

When they claimed that what Musa had brought was magic, they set about opposing it with kinds of magic, so that it would appear to all people that what Musa had brought was of the category of magic.

Ibn Musarrif, Ibn Wathhab, 'Isa, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "bi-kulli sahharin" (every great sorcerer), for emphasis. In His words "Throw what you are going to throw" there is an element of looking down upon them and disregard for them.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: how did he command them? Disbelief, magic, and commanding disbelief are disbelief. We say: peace be upon him commanded them to throw the ropes and staffs, so that he might show the creation that what they threw was corrupt work and vain effort, not in the sense that he commanded them to practice magic. End.

On the interrogative reading they said: it is permissible for "ma" to be an interrogative pronoun in the nominative as subject, with "al-siḥr" as its apposition, and it may be in the accusative governed by an implied verb whose explanation is "ji'tum bihi," with "al-siḥr" as the predicate of an omitted subject.

In my view, it is also permissible in this reading for "ma" to be a relative pronoun, the subject, and the interrogative clause to be the predicate, since the sense is: "Is it magic, or is it the magic? Thus the first motive is imitation (taqlid), and the second is zeal for leadership, so that you will not be followers. These two motives, which they imagined to be the aim, required an explicit denial of faith, which is the cause of the occurrence of the two motives.

It is also possible that they intended a reproach: that if the two of them ruled the land of Egypt, they would become arrogant and tyrannical, as the Copt said: ﴿You only want to be a tyrant in the land﴾ [al-Qasas: 19]. When they claimed that what Musa had brought was magic, they set about opposing it with kinds of magic, so that it would appear to all people that what Musa had brought was of the category of magic.

The addressees of "Bring me" are Pharaoh's servants and those who carry out his orders. Ibn Musarrif, Ibn Wathhab, 'Isa, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "bi-kulli sahharin" (every great sorcerer), for emphasis. In His words "Throw what you are going to throw" there is an element of looking down upon them and disregard for them.

In leaving "what you are going to throw" vague, there is a belittling of it and a minimizing, and an indication that there is nothing worth paying attention to. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: how did he command them? Disbelief, magic, and commanding disbelief are disbelief. We say: peace be upon him commanded them to throw the ropes and staffs, so that he might show the creation that what they threw was corrupt work and vain effort, not in the sense that he commanded them to practice magic. End.

Abu 'Amr, Mujahid and his companions, and Ibn al-Qa'qa' read "ālsiḥru" with the interrogative hamzah in his saying (p-183) "ālsiḥru" with madd, while the rest of the Seven and the majority read it with hamzat al-wasl. On the interrogative reading they said: it is permissible for "ma" to be an interrogative pronoun in the nominative as subject, with "al-siḥr" as its apposition, and it may be in the accusative governed by an implied verb whose explanation is "ji'tum bihi," with "al-siḥr" as the predicate of an omitted subject.

In my view, it is also permissible in this reading for "ma" to be a relative pronoun, the subject, and the interrogative clause to be the predicate, since the sense is: "Is it magic, or is it the magic? Is it he?" So the pronoun serves as the link, as you say: "The one who came to you, is it Zayd?" On the reading with hamzat al-wasl it is permissible for "ma" to be a relative pronoun, the subject, with "al-siḥr" as the predicate; this is supported by the reading of Abdullah and al-A'mash: "siḥrun" (magic). And the reading of Ubayy: "mā ataytum bihi siḥrun."

In my view, it is also permissible in this reading for it to be an interrogative in a position of nominative as subject, or in a position of accusative by way of ishtighal, and it is an interrogative for the purpose of belittling and of giving a reason for what they brought; "al-siḥr" is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "huwa al-siḥr" (it is magic).

Ibn 'Atiyya said: the definite article here in "al-siḥr" is more fitting, because it was previously mentioned indefinitely in their saying: "Indeed, this is magic (la-siḥrun)," so it comes here with the definite article of reference, as one says at the beginning of a letter, "Peace be upon you," and at its end, "and peace be upon you." End.

This he took from al-Farra'. Al-Farra' said: He said "al-siḥr" with the definite article because when an indefinite noun is repeated, it is repeated with the definite article; if he had said to him, "Who is a man?", it would not have occurred to him that he was asking about the man who had been mentioned to him. End.

What the two of them have stated here regarding "al-siḥr" is not of the category of an indefinite noun being mentioned first and then referred to afterwards, because the condition for this is that the definite article's referent must be the previously mentioned indefinite noun and not something else, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿As We sent to Pharaoh a messenger﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 15] ﴿But Pharaoh disobeyed the messenger﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 16]. And you say: "A man visited me, so I honoured the man," and since it is the same one, it is permissible to use a pronoun in its place, so you say: "So I honoured him."

The two referents differ: they spoke about Musa's miracle, and Musa spoke about what they had brought. It is read "bi-kalimatihi" in the singular, meaning by His command and His will.
