**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 10, verses 83–86:**

﴿But none believed in Moses except a few offspring of his people, out of fear of Pharaoh and their chiefs, lest he should persecute them. Indeed Pharaoh was haughty in the land, and indeed he was among the extravagant.﴾ ﴿Moses said, "O my people, if you have believed in God, then rely upon Him, if you are Muslims."﴾ ﴿They said, "In God we have put our trust. Our Lord, do not make us a trial for the wrongdoing people. And save us by Your mercy from the disbelieving people."﴾

The apparent meaning of the *fa'* (فاء, "so/then") is that it indicates sequence (al-ta'qib), namely that this belief issuing from the offspring did not come later than the story of the casting (of the staffs). The apparent meaning is also that the pronoun in "his people" (p. 184) refers to Moses and not to Pharaoh, because Moses is the one being spoken of in this verse and he is the nearest antecedent.

Furthermore, if it referred to Pharaoh, the name "Pharaoh" would not have appeared, and the construction would have been "out of fear of him and of their chiefs, lest he persecute them." Also, this belief of the offspring was at the very beginning of his mission, since the Children of Israel, his people, all believed in him. At first he called the fathers, but they did not answer him out of fear of Pharaoh, and a group of their sons answered him despite the fear.

Mujahid and al-A'mash said: the meaning of the verse is that Moses reached a people who did not believe, and only their descendants believed after their destruction, due to the long passage of time. Ibn 'Atiyya said: this is an incorrect opinion. If a people believed after the death of their fathers, there is no sense in singling them out with the name "offspring" (dhurriyyah).

Also, what has been transmitted of the reports about the Children of Israel does not support this and negates it, because His saying "so none believed" gives the sense of the few who believed in him, since He negated belief and then affirmed it for some of them. Had the majority been believers, He would have affirmed belief first and then negated it from the minority. On this basis, Ibn 'Abbas's statement about "offspring" is to be understood: that it means the few, not that the word "offspring" means "few," as Makki and others assumed.

A group said: they were called "offspring" only because their mothers were from the Children of Israel while their maidservants were Copts. This was narrated by Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas. Thus they were called the "offspring," just as the Persians of Yemen were called "the sons" (al-abna'), and they were the Persians who migrated with Wahuz by the agency of Sayf ibn Dhi Yazan.

Among those who held that the pronoun in "his people" refers to Moses was Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "They were six hundred thousand, because Ya'qub (peace be upon him) entered Egypt with seventy-two souls, and they multiplied in Egypt until they became six hundred thousand."

It was also said: the pronoun in "his people" refers to Pharaoh. It was narrated that the wife of Pharaoh, his treasurer, the wife of his treasurer, and some youths of his people believed. Ibn 'Abbas also said: the magicians as well, since they are counted among the people of Pharaoh.

Al-Suddi said: they were seventy households from the people of Pharaoh. Ibn 'Atiyya said: among what weakens the pronoun referring to Moses (peace be upon him) is that what is known from the reports about the Children of Israel is that they were a people among whom wrongdoings had spread, and during the period of Pharaoh they had suffered an extreme humiliation, and they hoped to be relieved of it at the hand of a child who would arise among them and would be a prophet. When Moses (peace be upon him) came to them, they united around him and pledged allegiance to him. It is never preserved that a group of the Children of Israel disbelieved in him. So how could this verse indicate that the smaller part of them were the ones who believed? According to this, what is more likely is that the pronoun refers to Pharaoh. This is also supported by the previous dialogue of Moses and his rejection of them, and his rebuke of them for their saying "this is magic." God related that about them, then said: "So none believed in Moses except a few offspring of the people of Pharaoh, whose sayings are these."

On this interpretation, the story would be after the appearance of the sign and the challenge with the staff, and the *fa'* would be arranging the meanings to which it is coordinated. End.

It is possible that the meaning of "so none believed" is: none openly displayed his belief and proclaimed it except a few offspring of the people of Moses, so this does not indicate that a group of the Children of Israel disbelieved in him. The apparent reference of the pronoun in His saying "and their chiefs" is to the offspring, and this was said by al-Akhfash and preferred by al-Tabari; that is: the ones most feared among the Children of Israel were the offspring, and they were the nobles of the Children of Israel, if the pronoun in "his people" refers to Moses, because they used to prevent their descendants out of fear of Pharaoh for their own selves. What indicates this is His saying, exalted is He: "lest he should persecute them," that is, torment them. Ibn 'Abbas said: "lest he kill them."

It was also said: it refers to "his people," meaning the chiefs of the people of Moses, or the people of Pharaoh. It was also said: it refers to a deleted annexed noun (al-mudaf al-mahdhuf), its estimated form being: "out of fear of the family of Pharaoh," said by al-Farra'. This is like what is deleted in "and ask the town" (Yusuf: 82). It was refuted by saying that fear can be from Pharaoh, but asking the town is impossible; so nothing is deleted except what is indicated by evidence.

It may be said: the plural pronoun in "their chiefs" indicates this deleted noun. It was also said: there is a deleted conjoined noun indicated by the fact that a king does not exist alone, but has a retinue and soldiers. It is as if it were said: "out of fear of Pharaoh, his people, and their chiefs," meaning the chiefs of Pharaoh and his people. This was also said by al-Farra'. It was said: since he was a tyrannical king, he was described with the verb of the whole group. It was said: the group was called "Pharaoh," like Hud. (p. 185)

"Lest he should persecute them" is a substitute for Pharaoh, a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal), meaning: "his persecution." It is then in the genitive position. It may also be in the accusative position, governed by "fear," either as a causal clause, or as in the position of the direct object, meaning: "out of fear for the sake of his persecution," or "out of fear of his persecution."

Al-Hasan, Jarrah, and Nubayh read *yaftinahum* (يَفْتِنَهُمْ) with a *damma* on the *ya'* from *afnata*. "Laʿalin" means: tyrannical, or transgressing and oppressive, or exalted, or dominating, as in the line of poetry:

*So aim at what you rise above, for you have no hands for what you cannot master of affairs.*

That is: for what you dominate. Similar sayings are close in meaning. His "extravagance" is that he was abundant in killing and torment. It was also said: that he was from the basest of slaves, and then claimed divinity. This statement explains the reason for those believers' fear of him.

In the verse there is consolation for the Messenger (ﷺ) regarding the small number who believed in Moses and who responded to him, despite the manifestation of that dazzling miracle, and only a few offspring of his people believed in him. Moses's address to those who believed with his words "O my people" is evidence that the believing offspring were from his people, and he addressed them thus when their fear had intensified because of what Pharaoh threatened them with: killing the fathers and slaughtering the offspring.

It was also said: he said this to them when they said: "Indeed we are overtaken." It was also said: when they said: "We were harmed before you came to us and after you came to us" (al-A'raf: 129). It was said: the first is the correct one, because the answer to each of the two statements is mentioned after it: "By no means! Indeed, my Lord is with me; He will guide me" (al-Shu'ara: 62), and His saying: "Perhaps your Lord will destroy your enemy" (al-A'raf: 129), and the verse. Their reliance was made conditional on two conditions: a preceding one and a following one.

When two conditions do not follow each other in existence, the second condition is a condition for the first. Since it is a condition for it, it must precede it. Islam is submission to the obligations issued by God, the manifestation of humility, and the abandonment of rebellion. Faith (iman) is the heart's recognition of God, His oneness, and His other attributes, and that all else is created, under His domination and governance. When these two conditions are fulfilled, the servant entrusts all his affairs to God, exalted is He, and relies upon Him in all circumstances.

The conditional verbs introduced by *in* (إنْ, "if") are, for the most part, used for what is not certain. Yet here it is used despite His knowledge of their belief, in order to establish the proof, awaken the souls, and stir up dignity, just as you say: "If you are a man, then fight," addressing a man whom you want to establish the evidence against.

Ibn 'Atiyya elaborated here on the matter of reliance (tawakkul) with what can be found in his book. They answered Moses (peace be upon him) with what he had commanded them, namely reliance upon God, because they were sincere in their faith and submission. Then they asked God, exalted is He, for two things. One of them: that He not make them a trial for the wrongdoing people.

Al-Zamakhshari said: that is, a place of trial for them, meaning a torment that you would inflict upon us, or that you would tempt us away from our religion; or a trial for them by which they would be tempted, saying: "If these were upon the truth, they would not have been afflicted."

Mujahid, Abu Mijlaz, Abu al-Duha and others said: the meaning of the other statement is: "He said: the meaning is: do not let (harm) descend upon us, our chiefs at their hands or otherwise, during the period of our fighting with them, so that they are tempted and believe that our destruction is only by your intent, due to the corruption of our religion and the soundness of theirs, and that they are the people of truth." Another group said the meaning is: "Do not let us tempt them or test them by our killing and harming, so that You would torment them for that in the Hereafter." Ibn 'Atiyya said: in this interpretation there is some unease. Ibn al-Kalbi said: "Do not make us a trial by restricting provision upon us and expanding it upon them." The other request is: that He save them from the disbelievers, that is, from their subjugation and enslavement.

What appears is that they asked God, exalted is He, that they not be tempted away from their religion and that they be delivered from the disbelievers. They placed first what was more important to them, namely the safety of their religion, and postponed the safety of their own selves, since concern for the interests of religion is more emphatic than concern for the interests of the bodies.

*So aim at what you rise above, for you have no hands for what you cannot master of affairs.*

That is: for what you dominate. Similar sayings are close in meaning. His "extravagance" is that he was abundant in killing and torment. It was also said: that he was from the basest of slaves, and then claimed divinity. This statement explains the reason for those believers' fear of him.

In the verse there is consolation for the Messenger (ﷺ) regarding the small number who believed in Moses and who responded to him, despite the manifestation of that dazzling miracle, and only a few offspring of his people believed in him. Moses's address to those who believed with his words "O my people" is evidence that the believing offspring were from his people, and he addressed them thus when their fear had intensified because of what Pharaoh threatened them with: killing the fathers and slaughtering the offspring.

Faith (iman) is the heart's recognition of God, His oneness, and His other attributes, and that all else is created, under His domination and governance. **Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 10, verses 83–86:**

﴿But none believed in Moses except a few offspring of his people, out of fear of Pharaoh and their chiefs, lest he should persecute them. Indeed Pharaoh was haughty in the land, and indeed he was among the extravagant.﴾ ﴿Moses said, "O my people, if you have believed in God, then rely upon Him, if you are Muslims."﴾ ﴿They said, "In God we have put our trust. Our Lord, do not make us a trial for the wrongdoing people. And save us by Your mercy from the disbelieving people."﴾

The apparent meaning of the *fa'* (فاء, "so/then") is that it indicates sequence (al-ta'qib), namely that this belief issuing from the offspring did not come later than the story of the casting (of the staffs). The apparent meaning is also that the pronoun in "his people" (p. 184) refers to Moses and not to Pharaoh, because Moses is the one being spoken of in this verse and he is the nearest antecedent.

Furthermore, if it referred to Pharaoh, the name "Pharaoh" would not have appeared, and the construction would have been "out of fear of him and of their chiefs, lest he persecute them." Also, this belief of the offspring was at the very beginning of his mission, since the Children of Israel, his people, all believed in him. At first he called the fathers, but they did not answer him out of fear of Pharaoh, and a group of their sons answered him despite the fear.

Mujahid and al-A'mash said: the meaning of the verse is that Moses reached a people who did not believe, and only their descendants believed after their destruction, due to the long passage of time. Ibn 'Atiyya said: this is an incorrect opinion. If a people believed after the death of their fathers, there is no sense in singling them out with the name "offspring" (dhurriyyah).

Also, what has been transmitted of the reports about the Children of Israel does not support this and negates it, because His saying "so none believed" gives the sense of the few who believed in him, since He negated belief and then affirmed it for some of them. Had the majority been believers, He would have affirmed belief first and then negated it from the minority. On this basis, Ibn 'Abbas's statement about "offspring" is to be understood: that it means the few, not that the word "offspring" means "few," as Makki and others assumed.

A group said: they were called "offspring" only because their mothers were from the Children of Israel while their maidservants were Copts. This was narrated by Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas. Thus they were called the "offspring," just as the Persians of Yemen were called "the sons" (al-abna'), and they were the Persians who migrated with Wahuz by the agency of Sayf ibn Dhi Yazan.

Among those who held that the pronoun in "his people" refers to Moses was Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "They were six hundred thousand, because Ya'qub (peace be upon him) entered Egypt with seventy-two souls, and they multiplied in Egypt until they became six hundred thousand."

Al-Suddi said: they were seventy households from the people of Pharaoh. Ibn 'Atiyya said: among what weakens the pronoun referring to Moses (peace be upon him) is that what is known from the reports about the Children of Israel is that they were a people among whom wrongdoings had spread, and during the period of Pharaoh they had suffered an extreme humiliation, and they hoped to be relieved of it at the hand of a child who would arise among them and would be a prophet. This is also supported by the previous dialogue of Moses and his rejection of them, and his rebuke of them for their saying "this is magic." God related that about them, then said: "So none believed in Moses except a few offspring of the people of Pharaoh, whose sayings are these."

On this interpretation, the story would be after the appearance of the sign and the challenge with the staff, and the *fa'* would be arranging the meanings to which it is coordinated. End.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 10, verse 87:

﴿And We revealed to Musa and his brother: "Settle your people in Egypt in houses, and make your houses into places of worship (qiblah), and establish the prayer, and give good tidings to the believers."﴾: He did not state the name of his brother, because it had already been mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿Then after them We sent Musa and Harun﴾ [Yunus: 75]. And "tabawwa" means: take as a dwelling (mubaah), that is, a place of return for worship and prayer, just as you say "tawattana" (he made a homeland): he took a homeland (mawtin). The apparent meaning is that they should take houses in Misr. Al-Dahhak said: it is Misr al-Mahrusah (the guarded Misr), and Misr extends from the sea to Aswan, and Alexandria is from the land of Egypt. Mujahid said: it is (p-186) Alexandria. Pharaoh had seized control over the Children of Israel, had destroyed their mosques and places of worship, prevented them from the prayers, and imposed heavy labors upon them.

At the beginning of their affair they were commanded to pray in their houses, in secret from the disbelievers, so that they would not be exposed to them, lest they turn them back and tempt them away from their religion, just as the believers were in this state at the beginning of Islam.

Hafs, in the transmission of Hubayrah, read "tabawwaya" with a ya', and this is a non-analogical facilitation (tashil ghayr qiyasi); had it followed analogy, it would have been between the hamzah and the alif. The apparent meaning is that the one commanded to make them a qiblah is the one commanded to settle them.

The meaning of "qiblah" is: masajid (places of prostration/mosques). They were commanded to take their houses as mosques; this was said by al-Nakha'i and Ibn Zayd. It is also narrated from Ibn Abbas: "make your houses facing the qiblah," and from him also: "facing Makkah." Mujahid, Qatadah, Muqatil and al-Farra' said: they were commanded to make them face the Ka'bah. From Ibn Abbas also, and Ibn Jubayr: qiblah in the sense that some of them face one another.

﴿And establish the prayer﴾: this was before the revelation of the Torah, because it was not revealed except after the crossing of the sea.

﴿And give good tidings to the believers﴾ means: of victory in this world and of Paradise in the Hereafter. This is a command to Musa, peace be upon him, that they should settle their people and choose these houses for worship, and that is among the matters entrusted to the prophets. Then He made the address general to both of them and to their people, regarding taking the mosques and praying in them, because that is obligatory upon the majority; then He singled out Musa, peace be upon him, with the giving of good tidings, which is the purpose, honoring him and the one with whom he is given good tidings.

And Moses said, "Our Lord, You have given Pharaoh and his chiefs adornment and wealth in the life of this world. Our Lord, that they may lead astray from Your way. Our Lord, obliterate their wealth and harden their hearts, so that they will not believe until they see the painful punishment." He said, "Your supplication has been answered, so remain steadfast and do not follow the way of those who do not know."

Abu Hayyan said: When Moses, peace be upon him, pushed hard in displaying the miracles while they persisted in obstinacy, and their harm toward him and toward those who believed with him intensified, and they added nothing to the presentation of the signs except disbelief, nor to the warning except arrogance, and he knew by experience and long companionship that nothing would come from them except error and misguidance (or he knew that by revelation from Allah the Exalted), he invoked Allah the Exalted against them with what he knew would not happen other than that, just as you say: "May Allah curse Iblis and disgrace the disbelievers." Likewise Noah invoked against his people when it was revealed to him: ﴿That none of your people will believe except those who have already believed﴾ [Hud: 36]. He preceded the supplication by mentioning the blessing Allah had given them in this world, and this was meant to be a cause for their faith in Him and for thankfulness for His blessings, but they made it a cause for denying Him and for ungratefulness for His blessings. Adornment (zinah) is an expression for what one beautifies and embellishes oneself with, of clothing, mounts and furnishings; and wealth (mal) is what exceeds that, of gold and silver (al-samit) and of livestock and goods (al-nategh).

The historians and exegetes said: Their domain extended from the city of Misr (Fustat) to the land of Abyssinia, with mountains containing mines of gold, silver, peridot and ruby. The repetition of "our Lord" serves as emphasis for the supplication and the appeal for help. The lam in "li-yudillu" (that they may lead astray) is apparently the lam of purpose (kay), meaning: You gave them what You gave them as a form of gradual enticement (istidraj), so the giving was for the purpose that they would go astray. It is also possible that it is the lam of outcome and consequence, as in His saying: ﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up, that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ [al-Qasas: 8], and as the poet said:

"For the fates, every nursing mother is raised, and for ruin people build up their lives."

Al-Hasan said: it is a supplication against them, and with this Zamakhshari began. He said: It is as if he said: so that they remain upon what they are upon of error, and so that they become misguided, and so that Allah seals their hearts and they do not believe. It is unlikely that it is a supplication according to the reading of one who read "li-yudillu" with a dammah on the yaa', since it is unlikely that he would supplicate that they become misleaders of others. This is the reading of the Kufans, Qatadah, al-A'mash, Isa, al-Hasan and al-A'raj, with a variant from the latter two.

The two Harams (Makkans and Medinans), the two Iraqi (Basran and Kufan) readers, Mujahid, Abu Rajaa, al-A'raj, Shaybah, Abu Ja'far and the people of Makkah read it with a fat-hah. Al-Sha'bi read it with a kasrah, and he joined the three kasrahs. It was said: the lam is elided, the estimate being: "lest they go astray from Your way," said by Abu Ali al-Jubba'i. Abu al-Fadl al-Raqqashi read: "a-innaka atayta" as an interrogative. Since the wealth had been mentioned, and it is the most precious of what is stored, he invoked obliteration upon it; and obliteration (tamsis) is effacement and alteration, or destruction. Ibn Abbas and Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: their dirhams became inscribed stones, whole, halved and quartered, and no mine remained except that Allah obliterated it, so no one benefited from them afterward. Qatadah said: It has reached us that their wealth and their crops became stones.

Mujahid and Atiyyah said: He destroyed it so that it could not be seen. Ibn Zayd said: their dinars, their dirhams, their carpets, and everything belonging to them became stones. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz asked me, and I mentioned that to him, so he called for a box that had been found in Misr, and he took out from it fruits, dirhams and dinars, and they were stones. Qatadah, al-Dahhak, Abu Salih and al-Qurtubi said: He made their sugar into stones. Al-Suddi said: Allah transformed the fruits, the palm trees and the foods into stones. Our shaykh Abu Abd Allah Muhammad ibn Sulayman al-Maqdisi, known as Ibn al-Naqib, who compiled the book al-Tahrir wa al-Tahbir in this discipline, said: A group of righteous people whose occupation was travelling told me that they had witnessed, in the mountains of Misr and its deserts, stones in the form of dinars and dirhams, bearing traces of the imprint, and in the form of fulus (copper coins), in the form of the Abdawi melon and the green melon, in the form of cucumber and qithha', and long, thin, curved stones in the form of carvings, and sometimes they saw them in the shape of trees.

"Shdud" (harden) refers to "upon their hearts." Ibn Abbas, Muqatil, al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: seal them and prevent them from faith. Ibn Abbas also said, as did al-Dahhak: destroy them as disbelievers.

Mujahid said: harden them upon misguidance. Ibn Qutaybah said: harden their hearts. Ibn Bahr said: harden them with death. Al-Kirmani said: meaning, you should not find consolation for their wealth, nor patience at its loss. Al-Sha'bi and a group read "ut-mus" with a dammah on the meem, which is a well-known dialect.

"Fa-la yu'minu" (so that they do not believe) is in the jussive according to al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' as a supplication. It is in the subjunctive as the answer to "shdud," as al-Zamakhshari began, and conjoined with "li-yudillu" on the view that it is in the subjunctive, said by al-Akhfash and others. What lies between them is a parenthetical clause. Or it is in the jussive according to the view of one who says that the lam of "li-yudillu" is the lam of supplication. The sight of the punishment appears as a limit and an end, because faith at that time neither benefits nor removes one from disbelief; and the painful punishment was their drowning. Ibn Abbas said: Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: Moses used to supplicate and Harun used to say "Amin," so the supplication was attributed to both of them. It is possible that both of them supplicated. The view of one who said that he referred to the singular with the dual form is unlikely, because the verse includes the addressing of both of them in what is not a matter of [their] address. It is narrated from Ibn Jurayj, Muhammad ibn Ali and al-Dahhak that the answer to the supplication did not become apparent until after forty years, and they both knew that their supplication had met what was decreed, and this is the meaning of the answering of supplication. It was said to them both: ﴿and do not follow the way of those who do not know﴾, that is, in seeking to hasten My decree, for My promise has no breaking. al-Sulami and al-Dahhak read "da'watukuma" in the plural.

Ibn al-Sumayqa read: "qad ujibtu da'watakuma" as a report from Allah the Exalted, with "da'wah" in the accusative. al-Rabi' read "da'wataykuma" in the dual, and this supports the view of one who said that Harun supplicated along with Moses.

The reading "da'wataykuma" indicates that he read "qad ujibtu" as a verb and subject; then both were commanded to steadfastness, and the meaning is: persistence upon it and upon what you were commanded of the call to Allah the Exalted and establishing the proof of Allah.

The majority read "tattabi'anni" with the taa' and nun both doubled. Ibn Abbas and Ibn Dhakwan read it with the taa' lightened and the nun doubled. Ibn Dhakwan also read it with the taa' doubled and the nun lightened. A group read it with the taa' lightened and the nun quiescent; al-Akhfash al-Dimashqi transmitted this from his companions from Ibn Amir. As for doubling the nun, it is the heavy emphatic nun attached to the prohibitive verb, with the dual pronoun connected to it. As for lightening it while kasra, it is said that it is the light emphatic nun, and it was kasra as the heavy one was kasra. The grammarians have reported the kasra of the light nun in such a construction from the Arabs. The view of Sibawayh and al-Kisa'i is that the light nun does not enter here, while Yunus and al-Farra' hold that it does. It was said: the kasra light nun is the sign of the nominative, and the verb is negated while meaning a prohibition; or it is a predicate in the position of a circumstantial clause, meaning: not following, said by al-Farisi. "Those who do not know" refers to Pharaoh and his people, said by Ibn Abbas; or those who hasten the decree before its coming, mentioned by Abu Sulayman.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (*al-Bahr al-Muhit*) on Surah 10, verses 90–92:**

﴿And We took the Children of Israel across the sea, and Pharaoh and his soldiers pursued them in rebellion and enmity, until, when drowning overtook him, he said: "I believe that there is no god except the One in whom the Children of Israel believe, and I am of those who submit."﴾ ﴿"Now? And you had rebelled before and were among the corrupters."﴾ ﴿"So today We will save your body, that you may be a sign to those who come after you. And indeed, many among the people are heedless of Our signs."﴾

Al-Hasan recited *wa-jawwaznā* (وجَوَّزْنا) with a doubled *wāw* (tashdid). The discussion of the *bā'* (الباء) in *bi-Banī Isrā'īl* has already been given, and the number of those who crossed with Musa (peace be upon him) was mentioned in Surah al-A'raf.

Al-Hasan and Qatadah recited *fa-ittaba'ahum* (فاتَّبَعَهم) with a doubled *tā'* (tashdid). The majority (al-Jumhur) recited *wa-jāwaznā bi-Banī* (وجاوَزْنا بِبَنِي) in the quadriliteral form (*ruba'i*, a verb of four radicals). Al-Zamakhshari said: "The one who used *jawwaza* (جَوَّزَ) in the verse of al-A'sha is not the same: it is in the line:

*"And when you cross with it the ropes of a tribe"*

because if it were from that root, its correct form would have been *wa-jawwaznā bi-Banī Isrā'īl fi al-baḥr* (وجَوَّزْنا بِـ بَنِي إسْرائِيلَ في البَحْرِ), as he said:

*"As al-Subki crossed in the chapter *faynaq*"*

End of quotation.

Al-Hawfi said: *taba'a* (تَبِعَ) and *ittaba'a* (اتَّبَعَ) have one meaning. Al-Zamakhshari said: *fa-atba'ahum* (فَأتْبَعَهم) means "he caught up with them"; it is said: "He followed him until he overtook him." In *al-Lawami'* it is said: *taba'ahu* means that he walked behind him, and *ittaba'ahu* is the same, except that *ittaba'ahu* means he drew level with him in walking and reached him. From this is the common recitation: *fa-atba'ahum* and the soldiers of Pharaoh. It is said they numbered a thousand thousand and six hundred thousand. It is also said to be other than that.

Al-Hasan recited *wa-'udūwan* (وعُدُوًّا) on the pattern of *'ulūwwin* (عُلُوٍّ), which was mentioned in al-An'am. *Adwan* (عَدْوًا) and *'udwān* (عُدُوًّا) are from *al-'udwān* (العُدْوان), meaning transgression. The following of Pharaoh was in crossing the sea. It is narrated that when Pharaoh reached the sea and found that it had split, and the Children of Israel had passed through it, he said to his people: "It only split by my command." He was on a male horse, so God sent Jibril (peace be upon him) on a female horse. They approached, and Jibril entered the sea with it. The horse of Pharaoh rushed after it, and the armies followed behind him. When he saw that the parting had become firm for him, he continued on. God sent Mika'il (peace be upon him) driving the people, until all of them were in the sea, and it closed over them.

The majority recited *annahu* (أنَّهُ) with a fatha on the hamza, with the *bā'* elided (*ḥadhf al-bā'*). Al-Kisa'i and Hamzah recited it with a kasra, as a resumption of speech (*isti'nāf*, beginning a new sentence), or as an apposition (*badal*) to *āmanat* (آمَنَتْ), or by supposing an omitted verb of saying, meaning: "saying that he..."

When the bewilderment that overtook him overtook him, he repeated the meaning in three expressions. This was either out of confusion, since it is a situation in which hearts are bewildered, or out of eagerness for acceptance; but God did not accept it from him, because the time of acceptance had passed him. That time is the state of choice and the continuance of obligation, and repentance after seeing (the punishment) does not benefit. Do you not see the words of the Exalted: ﴿So their faith did not benefit them when they saw Our punishment. This is the way of God which has passed among His servants﴾ [Ghafir: 85]. The disagreement over the recitation of *'ālān* (آلْآنَ) was mentioned in His words: ﴿Now? And you had been disbelieving before﴾ [Yunus: 51]. The meaning is: "Do you believe now, in a state of compulsion, when drowning has overtaken you and you have despaired of yourself?" It is said he said this when drowning choked him. It is also said he said it after he had drowned within himself.

Al-Zamakhshari said: what is related is that when he said "I believe," Jibril took a clump of mud from the sea and stuffed it into his mouth. This is out of anger for God, the Exalted, toward the state of the disbeliever at a time when it is known that his faith will not benefit him. As for what is added to it, that they said: "I feared that the mercy of God, the Exalted, would reach him," it is one of the additions of those who slander God, the Exalted, and His angels. In it are two errors. The first: that faith is valid in the heart, like the faith of the mute, so the mud of the sea does not prevent it. The second: that whoever dislikes faith for a disbeliever and loves that he remain in disbelief is himself a disbeliever, because satisfaction with disbelief is disbelief.

The apparent meaning is that His words *"Now?"* to the end are from God's speech to him, through the tongue of an angel. It is said that it is Jibril, and it is said Mika'il, and it is said other than these two, since the address is to him: ﴿So today We will save you﴾.

It is also said that it is from the words of Pharaoh to himself, and about his corruption, his misguidance of the people, and his claim to lordship.

﴿Those who disbelieved and barred from the way of God, We will add to them punishment upon punishment because of what they used to corrupt﴾ [al-Nahl: 88].

*Fa-al-yawma nunajjīka* (فاليَوْمَ نُنَجِّيكَ): The apparent meaning is that it is a declarative statement (*khabar*). It is also said that it is an interrogative with a threatening sense, meaning: "Then today will We save you? Why was faith not before the approach of destruction?" This is far-fetched, because the interrogative hamza is elided, and because of His words *"that you may be a sign,"* since the reason does not suit this interrogation.

Ibn 'Abbas said: *nunajjīka* (نُنَجِّيكَ) means "We will place you on a high place (*najwah*) of the earth," and it means the elevated place. *Bi-badanika* (بِبَدَنِكَ) means "with your armour" (*bi-dir'ika*). It was of pearls strung together, without any like it. It is also said it was of gold, and it is said of iron, and in it were chains of gold. *Al-badan* (البَدَنُ) is the human body, and *al-badan* also means a short coat of mail. He said:

*"You see the coats of mail upon them, fully covering the heroes and the strong dog"*

meaning: coats of mail (*duru*'). 'Amr ibn Ma'd Yakrib said:

*"O blamer, my coat of mail, my sword, and every swift one, smooth in its reins"*

He had a golden coat of mail by which he was recognised.

It is also said: "We will throw you with your body naked, with no garment or weapon on you," and this is more forceful in humiliating him.

It is also said: "We will bring you out healthy, with nothing of the beasts having devoured you." It is also said: "*badnan* without a soul," said by Mujahid. It is also said: "We will bring you out from your kingdom alone and solitary." It is also said: "We will throw you into the sea from *al-najā'*," and that is what you strip from the sheep or what you cast from yourself of garments or weapons. It is also said: "We will leave you until you drown," and *al-najā'* means leaving. It is also said: "We will make you a sign," and *al-najā'* means a sign. It is also said: "We will drown you," from their saying: "The sea saved (*najjā*) peoples" when it drowned them. Al-Kirmani said: it is possible that it is from *al-najāh*, which means haste, i.e., "We will hasten your destruction."

It is also said: the meaning of *bi-badanika* is "with your form by which you are recognised." He was short, reddish, blue-eyed, with a beard near to the stature. There was no one among the Children of Israel resembling him by whom they could know him by his form. And *bi-badanika*, if what is meant is the corpse, is an emphasis, as you say: "So-and-so spoke with his tongue," and "came himself."

Ya'qub recited *nunjīka* (نُنْجِيكَ) with a light form, the present tense of *anjā*. Ubayy, Ibn al-Sumaiqa, and Yazid al-Barbari recited *nunaḥḥīka* (نُنَحِّيكَ) with the unpointed *ḥā'* from *al-tanḥiyah* (التَّنْحِيَةِ, removal), and it is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, meaning: "We will place you on a side of the shore that faces the sea." Ka'b said: "The sea threw him to the shore as if he were a light." Abu Hanifa recited *bi-abdānika* (بِأبْدانِكَ), meaning with your coats of mail; or every part of the body is called a body, as they say: "His temples have grayed" (*shābat mafāriquhu*).

Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn al-Sumaiqa recited *bi-nidā'ika* (بِنِدائِكَ) in place of *bi-badanika*, meaning: "with your call," i.e., with your words "I believe," and so on, to the end. The sense is: "so that We make you a sign together with your call, which does not benefit," or "with what you called out among your people." Pharaoh called out to his people: ﴿Then he gathered and called out﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 23]. ﴿He said: I am your lord, the Most High﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 24], and ﴿O chiefs, I do not know of any god for you other than me﴾ [al-Qasas: 38].

When the Children of Israel denied the drowning of Pharaoh, the sea cast him onto its shore until they saw him: short and red, as if he were a bull.

*Li-man khalfaka* (لِمَن خَلْفَكَ): "for those behind you," as a sign, and they are the Children of Israel. It was in their minds that Pharaoh was too great in status to drown, and his body was cast on the route of the Children of Israel, so that it was said: ﴿as a sign for those behind you﴾. **Commentary of Abu Hayyan (*al-Bahr al-Muhit*) on Surah 10, verses 90–92:**

﴿And We took the Children of Israel across the sea, and Pharaoh and his soldiers pursued them in rebellion and enmity, until, when drowning overtook him, he said: "I believe that there is no god except the One in whom the Children of Israel believe, and I am of those who submit."﴾ ﴿"Now? And you had rebelled before and were among the corrupters."﴾ ﴿"So today We will save your body, that you may be a sign to those who come after you. And indeed, many among the people are heedless of Our signs."﴾

Al-Hasan recited *wa-jawwaznā* (وجَوَّزْنا) with a doubled *wāw* (tashdid). The discussion of the *bā'* (الباء) in *bi-Banī Isrā'īl* has already been given, and the number of those who crossed with Musa (peace be upon him) was mentioned in Surah al-A'raf.

Al-Hasan and Qatadah recited *fa-ittaba'ahum* (فاتَّبَعَهم) with a doubled *tā'* (tashdid). The majority (al-Jumhur) recited *wa-jāwaznā bi-Banī* (وجاوَزْنا بِبَنِي) in the quadriliteral form (*ruba'i*, a verb of four radicals). Al-Zamakhshari said: "The one who used *jawwaza* (جَوَّزَ) in the verse of al-A'sha is not the same: it is in the line:

*"And when you cross with it the ropes of a tribe"*

because if it were from that root, its correct form would have been *wa-jawwaznā bi-Banī Isrā'īl fi al-baḥr* (وجَوَّزْنا بِـ بَنِي إسْرائِيلَ في البَحْرِ), as he said:

*"As al-Subki crossed in the chapter *faynaq*"*

End of quotation.

Al-Hawfi said: *taba'a* (تَبِعَ) and *ittaba'a* (اتَّبَعَ) have one meaning. Al-Zamakhshari said: *fa-atba'ahum* (فَأتْبَعَهم) means "he caught up with them"; it is said: "He followed him until he overtook him." In *al-Lawami'* it is said: *taba'ahu* means that he walked behind him, and *ittaba'ahu* is the same, except that *ittaba'ahu* means he drew level with him in walking and reached him. From this is the common recitation: *fa-atba'ahum* and the soldiers of Pharaoh. It is said they numbered a thousand thousand and six hundred thousand. It is also said to be other than that.

Al-Hasan recited *wa-'udūwan* (وعُدُوًّا) on the pattern of *'ulūwwin* (عُلُوٍّ), which was mentioned in al-An'am. *Adwan* (عَدْوًا) and *'udwān* (عُدُوًّا) are from *al-'udwān* (العُدْوان), meaning transgression. The following of Pharaoh was in crossing the sea. It is narrated that when Pharaoh reached the sea and found that it had split, and the Children of Israel had passed through it, he said to his people: "It only split by my command." He was on a male horse, so God sent Jibril (peace be upon him) on a female horse. They approached, and Jibril entered the sea with it. The horse of Pharaoh rushed after it, and the armies followed behind him. When he saw that the parting had become firm for him, he continued on. God sent Mika'il (peace be upon him) driving the people, until all of them were in the sea, and it closed over them.

The majority recited *annahu* (أنَّهُ) with a fatha on the hamza, with the *bā'* elided (*ḥadhf al-bā'*). Al-Kisa'i and Hamzah recited it with a kasra, as a resumption of speech (*isti'nāf*, beginning a new sentence), or as an apposition (*badal*) to *āmanat* (آمَنَتْ), or by supposing an omitted verb of saying, meaning: "saying that he..."

When the bewilderment that overtook him overtook him, he repeated the meaning in three expressions. This was either out of confusion, since it is a situation in which hearts are bewildered, or out of eagerness for acceptance; but God did not accept it from him, because the time of acceptance had passed him. That time is the state of choice and the continuance of obligation, and repentance after seeing (the punishment) does not benefit. Do you not see the words of the Exalted: ﴿So their faith did not benefit them when they saw Our punishment. This is the way of God which has passed among His servants﴾ [Ghafir: 85]. The disagreement over the recitation of *'ālān* (آلْآنَ) was mentioned in His words: ﴿Now? And you had been disbelieving before﴾ [Yunus: 51]. The meaning is: "Do you believe now, in a state of compulsion, when drowning has overtaken you and you have despaired of yourself?" It is said he said this when drowning choked him. It is also said he said it after he had drowned within himself.

Al-Zamakhshari said: what is related is that when he said "I believe," Jibril took a clump of mud from the sea and stuffed it into his mouth. This is out of anger for God, the Exalted, toward the state of the disbeliever at a time when it is known that his faith will not benefit him. As for what is added to it, that they said: "I feared that the mercy of God, the Exalted, would reach him," it is one of the additions of those who slander God, the Exalted, and His angels. In it are two errors. The first: that faith is valid in the heart, like the faith of the mute, so the mud of the sea does not prevent it. The second: that whoever dislikes faith for a disbeliever and loves that he remain in disbelief is himself a disbeliever, because satisfaction with disbelief is disbelief.

The apparent meaning is that His words *"Now?"* to the end are from God's speech to him, through the tongue of an angel. It is said that it is Jibril, and it is said Mika'il, and it is said other than these two, since the address is to him: ﴿So today We will save you﴾.

It is also said that it is from the words of Pharaoh to himself, and about his corruption, his misguidance of the people, and his claim to lordship.

﴿Those who disbelieved and barred from the way of God, We will add to them punishment upon punishment because of what they used to corrupt﴾ [al-Nahl: 88].

*Fa-al-yawma nunajjīka* (فاليَوْمَ نُنَجِّيكَ): The apparent meaning is that it is a declarative statement (*khabar*). It is also said that it is an interrogative with a threatening sense, meaning: "Then today will We save you? Why was faith not before the approach of destruction?" This is far-fetched, because the interrogative hamza is elided, and because of His words *"that you may be a sign,"* since the reason does not suit this interrogation.

Ibn 'Abbas said: *nunajjīka* (نُنَجِّيكَ) means "We will place you on a high place (*najwah*) of the earth," and it means the elevated place. *Bi-badanika* (بِبَدَنِكَ) means "with your armour" (*bi-dir'ika*). It was of pearls strung together, without any like it. It is also said it was of gold, and it is said of iron, and in it were chains of gold. *Al-badan* (البَدَنُ) is the human body, and *al-badan* also means a short coat of mail. He said:

*"You see the coats of mail upon them, fully covering the heroes and the strong dog"*

meaning: coats of mail (*duru*'). 'Amr ibn Ma'd Yakrib said:

*"O blamer, my coat of mail, my sword, and every swift one, smooth in its reins"*

He had a golden coat of mail by which he was recognised.

It is also said: "We will throw you with your body naked, with no garment or weapon on you," and this is more forceful in humiliating him.

It is also said: "We will bring you out healthy, with nothing of the beasts having devoured you." It is also said: "*badnan* without a soul," said by Mujahid. It is also said: "We will bring you out from your kingdom alone and solitary." It is also said: "We will throw you into the sea from *al-najā'*," and that is what you strip from the sheep or what you cast from yourself of garments or weapons. It is also said: "We will leave you until you drown," and *al-najā'* means leaving. It is also said: "We will make you a sign," and *al-najā'* means a sign. It is also said: "We will drown you," from their saying: "The sea saved (*najjā*) peoples" when it drowned them. Al-Kirmani said: it is possible that it is from *al-najāh*, which means haste, i.e., "We will hasten your destruction."

It is also said: the meaning of *bi-badanika* is "with your form by which you are recognised." He was short, reddish, blue-eyed, with a beard near to the stature. There was no one among the Children of Israel resembling him by whom they could know him by his form. And *bi-badanika*, if what is meant is the corpse, is an emphasis, as you say: "So-and-so spoke with his tongue," and "came himself."

Ubayy, Ibn al-Sumaiqa, and Yazid al-Barbari recited *nunaḥḥīka* (نُنَحِّيكَ) with the unpointed *ḥā'* from *al-tanḥiyah* (التَّنْحِيَةِ, removal), and it is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, meaning: "We will place you on a side of the shore that faces the sea." Ka'b said: "The sea threw him to the shore as if he were a light." Abu Hanifa recited *bi-abdānika* (بِأبْدانِكَ), meaning with your coats of mail; or every part of the body is called a body, as they say: "His temples have grayed" (*shābat mafāriquhu*).

Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn al-Sumaiqa recited *bi-nidā'ika* (بِنِدائِكَ) in place of *bi-badanika*, meaning: "with your call," i.e., with your words "I believe," and so on, to the end. The sense is: "so that We make you a sign together with your call, which does not benefit," or "with what you called out among your people." Pharaoh called out to his people: ﴿Then he gathered and called out﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 23]. ﴿He said: I am your lord, the Most High﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 24], and ﴿O chiefs, I do not know of any god for you other than me﴾ [al-Qasas: 38].

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 10, verse 93:

﴿And We certainly settled the Children of Israel in a good dwelling-place, and provided for them of the good things. And they did not differ until knowledge came to them. Indeed your Lord will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that wherein they used to differ.﴾: When the Exalted mentioned what befell Pharaoh and his followers of destruction, He mentioned the good He bestowed upon the Children of Israel and the favour He conferred upon them, since the Children of Israel had been expelled from their homes, fearing Pharaoh. So the Exalted mentioned that He chose for them the best of places.

The apparent meaning is that the Children of Israel are those who had believed in Musa and were saved from drowning, and the context of the verses supports this. It has also been said: they are the Children of Israel who were present in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ), namely Qurayza, al-Nadir and Banu Qaynuqa. The phrase ﴿mubawwa' sidq﴾ is in the accusative as a second object of "bawwa'na" (We settled), like His saying: ﴿We will surely settle them in lofty chambers in Paradise﴾ [al-Ankabut: 58]. It has also been said that it may be a verbal noun (masdar).

The meaning of "sidq" is: virtue, honour and grace, as in ﴿in a seat of truth﴾ [al-Qamar: 55]. It has been said: a place of the truth of promise, for He had promised them and He made true His promise to them. It has been said: "sidq" means that He gave it to them as charity (tasaddaqa), since charity and righteousness are from truthfulness. It has been said: the expectation of its intender and its inhabitant was truthful. It has been said: a fine, pleasing dwelling. And from Ibn 'Abbas: it is al-Urdunn and Filastin. Al-Dahhak, Ibn Zayd and Qatada said: al-Sham and Bayt al-Maqdis. Muqatil said: Bayt al-Maqdis. And from al-Dahhak also: Egypt, and from him also: Egypt and al-Sham. Ibn 'Atiyya said: the most correct is that it is al-Sham and Bayt al-Maqdis, according to what has been preserved that they did not return to Egypt, and on the basis that the Qur'an says so.

﴿And We caused the Children of Israel to inherit it﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 59], meaning what the Copts left of gardens, springs and other things. It may be that "awrathna-ha" (We caused them to inherit it) means: the state of blessing, even if it was not in a single region, end.

It has been said: what lies between Madina and al-Sham of the land of Yathrib, mentioned by 'Ali ibn Ahmad al-Naysaburi, and this is according to the view of those who said that the Children of Israel are those present in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ). When He mentioned that He settled them in a dwelling of truth, He mentioned His favour upon them in providing them of the good things, which are: the foods that are delicious, or the lawful. "Fa-ma ikhtalafu" (so they did not differ): that is, they were upon one religion and one way with Musa (peace be upon him) at the beginning of his state, "until knowledge came to them", that is, the knowledge of the Torah, and then they differed. This is a censure of them.

That is, the cause of stopping was knowledge, so it became for them the cause of difference, and they split into factions after they had read the Torah. It has been said: "knowledge" means the known, which is Muhammad, because his mission was known to them, written in the Torah, and they used to seek victory through him (yastaftihuna bihi), that is, they sought help through him. Before his coming to Madina they were unanimous regarding his prophethood, seeking victory through him in wars, saying: "O Allah, by the sanctity of the Prophet sent at the end of time, help us," and they were helped. When he came, they said: "The Prophet promised is from the descendants of Ya'qub, and this one is from the descendants of Isma'il, so he is not that one." So some of them believed in him, such as 'Abd Allah ibn Salam and his companions.

It has been said: "knowledge" is the Qur'an, and their difference is the saying of some of them: "It is from the speech of Muhammad," and the saying of some: "It is from the speech of Allah, and it is not for us; it is only for the Arabs." A group confirmed it and believed. This difference cannot be eliminated in this world, and He, the Exalted, will judge concerning it in the Hereafter, distinguishing the one who is in the right from the one who is in falsehood.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 10, verses 94–95:

﴿So if you are in doubt about what We have sent down to you, then ask those who have been reading the Book before you. Certainly the truth has come to you from your Lord, so do not be among the doubters.﴾ ﴿And do not be among those who denied the signs of Allah, lest you be among the losers.﴾ (p-191) The apparent reading is that (in) is conditional (shartiyyah). It is narrated from al-Hasan and al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl that (in) is negating (nafiyah). Al-Zamakhshari said: That is, "Of what you were in doubt, ask," meaning: We do not command you to ask because you are in doubt, but so that you may increase in certainty, just as Ibrahim, peace be upon him, increased in certainty by witnessing the giving of life to the dead, end of quote.

When (in) is conditional, they mention that it is used with something whose occurrence is possible, or with something whose occurrence is certain but whose time of happening is unspecified, as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿Then if you die, will they be the ones who abide forever?﴾ [al-Anbiya': 34]. What I say is that the conditional in (in) requires the linking of one thing to another, and does not necessitate that the condition occurs or that it is possible. Indeed, this may occur with something rationally impossible, as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿Say: If the Most Merciful had a son, then I would be the first of the worshippers﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 81]. It is impossible that He should have a son, so likewise this is impossible: that you should be in doubt. It also occurs with something customarily impossible, as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿And if you are able to seek a tunnel in the earth or a ladder in the sky to bring them a sign﴾ [al-An'am: 35], meaning: then do it. However, the use of (in) for conditioning on the impossible is rare, and this verse is of that kind. Since this aspect was hidden from most people, they differed in interpreting this verse. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: The correct view is that it is addressed to the Prophet, but what is meant is other than him, from every person who might doubt or oppose, end of quote.

For this reason, the verse came: ﴿Say: O people, if you are in doubt about my religion﴾ [Yunus: 104]. Some people said: the speech is like your saying, "If you are my son, then be dutiful to me," though this example is not a good one. The closest example to this is the saying of the Exalted to 'Isa, peace be upon him: ﴿Did you say to the people...﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116], end of quote.

This view is narrated from al-Farra'. Al-Kirmani said: A group chose it, but it is weak, because the meaning of the verse would become: "Are you in doubt?" since there is nothing in the verse indicating the negation of doubt. It was said: Here doubt is a metaphor for distress, meaning: if you are in distress over their disagreement concerning what was sent down to you and their obstinacy against you. It was said: doubt is a metaphor for wonder, meaning: if you are amazed at the stubbornness of Pharaoh.

The relation of the figurative use is that wonder involves hesitation, just as doubt is hesitation between two matters. Al-Kisa'i said: its meaning is: if you are in doubt that this is their custom with the prophets, then ask them how the patience of Musa, peace be upon him, was when they disagreed with him. Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you are in doubt" is in the sense of presentation and supposition, as if it were said: if a doubt befalls you, for example, and Satan imagines to you a fancy of it by way of assumption, then ask those who read the Book. The meaning is: Allah the Exalted mentioned the Children of Israel first, and they are the readers of the Book, and He described them as having been given knowledge, because the matter of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is written with them in the Torah and the Gospel, and they recognise him as they recognise their own sons. So He wished to emphasise to them the soundness of the Qur'an and the soundness of the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ, and to exaggerate in that, so He said: if a doubt befalls you hypothetically and by assumption. The way of one whom a doubt in religion troubles is to hasten to resolve it and remove it, either by returning to the principles and proofs of the religion, or by discussing with the scholars who point to the truth, end of quote.

Other views besides these have been stated. Yahya and Ibrahim read: ﴿يَقْرَءُونَ الكُتُبَ﴾ in the plural. The truth here is: Islam, or the Qur'an, or prophethood, or the clear signs and proofs; these are views. So remain firm and persist in what you are upon of the absence of doubt and denial.

The address is to the hearer other than the Messenger. Often the address appears in its outward form to a person while the intended meaning is someone else. It is narrated that he, peace be upon him, said: "I do not doubt, nor do I ask, rather I testify that it is the truth." And from Ibn 'Abbas: By Allah, he did not doubt for the blink of an eye, nor did he ask any of them.

Al-imtira' is hesitation regarding a matter and doubt about it. Its matter is easier than the matter of the denier, so it was begun with first, and he was forbidden from it; then it was followed by mention of the denier, and he was forbidden to be among them.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 10, verses 96–97:

﴿Indeed, those upon whom the word of your Lord has come into effect will not believe﴾ ﴿Even if every sign should come to them, until they see the painful punishment﴾: He, the Exalted, mentioned servants for whom He has decreed wretchedness, so it does not change. The word that has come into effect upon them, Qatadah said: it is the curse and the wrath. It was also said: its threat is that they will come to the punishment. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is the saying of Allah the Exalted which He wrote on the Preserved Tablet, and informed the angels that they will die as disbelievers, so it cannot be other than that. That is the writing of knowledge, not the writing of a decree (p-192), and Allah the Exalted is exalted above that, ended.

His words at the end are in the manner of the Mu'tazilah. Abu 'Abdullah al-Razi said: what is meant by this word is the decree of Allah with that and His information about it, and His creating in the servant the totality of power and motive, and this necessitates the occurrence of that matter. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the meaning is that Allah made His wrath obligatory for them from eternity and created them for His punishment, so they do not believe, even if every proof and every clarity should come to them, except at the time when faith will not benefit them, as Pharaoh and his like did, and that is the time of direct witnessing.

Within the wording there is a warning against this state, and an urging of each person to hasten to faith and to flee from the wrath of Allah. It is permissible that the painful punishment refers to the moment when their means are cut off on the Day of Resurrection. The disagreement regarding the reading of (kalimah) as singular and as plural has already been mentioned.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 10, verse 98:

﴿Why was there not a town that believed, so that its faith would benefit it, except the people of Yunus? When they believed, We removed from them the punishment of disgrace in the life of this world, and We let them enjoy for a time.﴾

Here, "law" (lawla) is the interrogative of urging (al-tahdid, "urging, exhortation") accompanied by reproach (al-tawbikh, "rebuke"), and it frequently occurs in the Qur'an in the sense of urging. It therefore means: "halla" (why not, "would that").

Ubayy and Abdullah read: fa-halla (فَهَلّا), and so it is in their codices. Al-tahdid (urging) is when a person wishes to do the thing toward which he urges. When it is for reproach, the speaker does not intend to urge toward that thing, as in the saying of the poet:

"You count the slaughter of the she-camel the best of your glory, O sons of Dawtara, were it not for the armoured warrior (al-kami al-muqanna')."

He did not intend to urge them to slaughter the armoured warrior; rather, he rebuked them for leaving off faith that benefits. The meaning is: "Why did the people of the town not believe while they had respite, the punishment not yet having befallen them, so that faith would benefit them in that state?"

"Qawma" (قَوْمَ) is in the accusative as an exceptive of disconnection (istithna' munqati'), which is the view of Sibawayh, al-Kisa'i, al-Farra' and al-Akhfash, since they are not included under the word "town" (qarya). Al-Zamakhshari said: "It may also be connected (muttasil), the sentence having the sense of negation, as if it were said: No town of the destroyed towns believed except the people of Yunus." Ibn Atiyya said: "Verbally it is an exceptive of disconnection, as the grammarians have written it, but in meaning it is connected, since its sense is: No people of a town believed except the people of Yunus." The accusative is the preferred form, and for this reason Sibawayh placed it in the category of cases where only the accusative is used, and this is with disconnected exception. A group said: the nominative is also permissible here, and this is with connected exception.

Al-Mahdawi said: "The nominative is in apposition (badal) to (qarya)." Al-Zamakhshari said: "It was also read in the nominative as an apposition, from the Meccan and Medinan reciters and al-Kisa'i." The disagreement concerning the reading of "Yunus" with a damma or a kasra on the nun has already been mentioned, and it was noted that a fatha is also permissible.

The people of Yunus are the people of Nineveh (Ninawa) from the lands of Mosul. They worshipped idols, so God sent Yunus (Jonah) to them, and they persisted in denying him for seven years, and he threatened them with punishment after three days. It was said: after forty days.

The exegetes have mentioned the story of the people of Yunus and its details, and how they were punished. God knows best the soundness of that, and it may be checked in their books. Al-Tabari said, relating from a group, that the people of Yunus were singled out among the nations in that repentance was accepted from them after they had witnessed the punishment. Al-Zajjaj said: "The punishment drew near to them but did not overtake them as it overtook Pharaoh, so they were like the sick person who fears death and hopes for recovery. As for one whom the punishment overtakes, there is no repentance for him."

Ibn al-Anbari said: "He knew from them the sincerity of their intentions, unlike those who preceded them among the destroyed." Al-Suddi said: "(ila hin): until the time of the end of their lifespans." It was also said: "until the Day of Resurrection," and it is narrated from Ibn Abbas, though it is perhaps not authentic; according to this view they remain alive, and God concealed them from the people.

(p-193) ﴿And had your Lord willed, all those on earth would have believed, all of them together. Would you then compel people until they become believers?﴾ ﴿No soul could believe except by Allah's permission, and He places defilement upon those who do not reason.﴾ It is said: it was revealed concerning Abu Talib, because the Prophet (ﷺ) grieved over his death upon the creed of ʿAbd al-Muttalib, and he was eager for his faith.

Since he (ﷺ) was the most eager of people for their guidance, the most anxious for good to reach them and for them to attain faith, and the most diligent in saving the worlds from punishment, Allah the Exalted informed him that He had created some fit for happiness and some fit for wretchedness, and that had He willed the faith of them all, He would have done so, and that no one has power to dispose of anyone.

The purpose is to show that overpowering capability and effective will belong to Allah the Exalted alone. The placing of the noun before the verb in the interrogative indicates the possibility of the act occurring, but from someone other than that noun: Allah the Exalted may compel people to faith if He wills, and this belongs to no one else.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿And had your Lord willed﴾ — the will of compulsion and coercion — ﴿all those on earth would have believed﴾ in an encompassing and comprehensive manner; ﴿all of them together﴾: gathered upon faith, unanimously upon it, not differing regarding it.

Do you not see His saying, ﴿Would you then compel people﴾? It means: who is it that can compel them and force them into faith? Are you (able to do so)? The prefixing of the interrogative particle to the noun informs that compulsion is possible and within capability, but the matter concerns who the one compelling is. And none but He alone is that one, and none shares in it, because He, the Exalted, is the One able to do in their hearts what makes them compelled toward faith, and that is beyond human capacity. End of quote.

His statement "the will of compulsion and coercion" is the doctrine of the Mu'tazila. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: the meaning is that all of what was mentioned earlier occurred by Allah's decree upon them and His will regarding them; had Allah willed, all of them would have been believers. So do not grieve, O Muhammad, over the disbelief of those who do not believe in you; call them, and do not be concerned about them, for the matter is decreed. Do you want to compel people by placing faith in their hearts and force them to it, while Allah the Mighty and Majestic has willed otherwise? This interpretation makes the verse decisive (muhkama), i.e., call and fight those who oppose you.

The faith of whoever believes is subject to the will (of Allah). Another group said: the meaning is, "Would you compel people by fighting until they enter into faith?" and they claimed this verse was early in Islam and abrogated (mansukha) by the verse of the sword. The verse, under both interpretations, refutes the Mu'tazila. End of quote.

For this reason al-Zamakhshari went to interpreting the will as the will of compulsion and coercion, which is the interpretation of al-Jubba'i and al-Qadi. The meaning of ﴿except by Allah's permission﴾ is: by His will, His decree for that, and enabling of it. Al-Zamakhshari said: by His facilitating it, which is the granting of grace (lutf).

﴿And He places defilement﴾ — which is abandonment (khidhlan) — ﴿upon those who do not reason﴾, namely those who persist in disbelief. Abandonment was called defilement (rijs), which is punishment, because it is its cause. End of quote.

This is in the way of the Mu'tazila. Ibn ʿAbbas said: al-rijs is wrath; and from him: sin and transgression. Mujahid said: whatever has no good in it. Al-Hasan, Abu ʿUbayda and al-Zajjaj said: punishment. Al-Farra' said: punishment and anger. Al-Hasan also said: disbelief. Qatada said: Satan, and its explanation has already been given, but we have cited here what the scholars said. Abu Bakr and Zayd ibn ʿAli read ﴿wanajʿalu﴾ with the nun; al-Aʿmash read ﴿wayajʿalu Allahu al-rijza﴾ with a zayn.

(p-194) ﴿Say: "Look at what is in the heavens and the earth. But signs and warnings do not avail a people who do not believe."﴾ ﴿Do they then await anything but the like of the days of those who passed away before them? Say: "Then wait; I am with you among those who wait."﴾

God, exalted is He, commanded reflection (tafakkur) upon what He has placed in the heavens and the earth, since the path to knowing Him, exalted is He, is through contemplating His creatures. In the upper world (al-'alam al-'ulwi) there are the movements of the spheres (al-aflak), their measures, their positions, and the stars, along with the benefits and advantages pertaining to them. In the lower world (al-'alam al-sufli) there are the states of the elements, the minerals, the plants, and the animals, and especially the state of man. God, exalted is He, often mentioned in His Book the urging to reflect upon His creation, and He said: ﴿What is in the heavens and the earth?﴾, as an alert to the universal principle, and the intelligent person will be alert to its details and divisions. Then, when He commanded looking, He informed that whoever does not believe, the signs do not avail him.

*Al-nudhur* is the plural of *nadhir*. It may be a verbal noun (masdar), in which case its meaning is "the warnings," or it may mean *mundhir*, in which case its meaning is "those who warn," that is, the messengers. As for *ma*, the apparent view is that it is negative, but it may also be interrogative, meaning: "And what avail the signs, which are the proofs?" This is an interrogation in the form of affirmation (istifham 'ala jihat al-taqrir, an interrogative that establishes a fact). In the verse there is a rebuke to the polytheists present with the Messenger of God ﷺ.

Al-Haramayn (the two sanctuaries, i.e., the readers of Makka and Madina) and al-'Arabiyyan (the two Arab readers) and al-Kisa'i read ﴿qul onzuru﴾ with a *damma* on the *lam*. It is also read ﴿wa ma tughni﴾ with the *ta'* (the reading of the majority), and with the *ya'*. As for *madha*, it may be an interrogative in the nominative position as a mubtada' (subject), with the predicate being ﴿fi al-samawat﴾. It may also be that the predicate is *dha* in the sense of *alladhi* (the relative pronoun), with its relative clause being ﴿fi al-samawat﴾. The verb *unzuru* is suspended (mu'allaqa), so the initial clause is in the accusative position. It is unlikely that the whole *madha* is a relative pronoun in the sense of *alladhi* functioning as the object of the verb *unzuru*, because if the verb is visual (basariyya), it takes *ila*, and if it is mental (qalbiyya), it takes *fi*.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is possible that *ma* in His saying *wa ma tughni* is an object of His saying *unzuru*, coordinated with His saying *madha*, meaning: "Consider the warnings of the sufficiency of the signs and the warnings regarding the unbelievers, if they accept that, like the action of the people of Yunus, for he removed the punishment in this world and the Hereafter and saved them from destructions."

According to this, the verse is an encouragement to faith, and the figurative usage of the expression on this interpretation lies only in His saying *la yu'minun*, end of quote. But this is a possibility with weakness. As for his saying "an object coordinated with 'madha'," it involves figurative usage, meaning that the interrogative clause "madha fi al-samawat wa al-ard" stands in the position of the object, since *madha* is in the accusative alone by *unzuru*, so *madha* would be a relative pronoun, and *unzuru* is visual for what has preceded.

*Al-ayyam* here means the events of God concerning them, as it is said "ayyam al-'Arab" (the days of the Arabs) for their battles.

In the interrogation there is confirmation, threat, and urging to faith. The meaning is: if they persist in disbelief, punishment befalls them, and if they believe, they are saved. This is the custom of God regarding the earlier nations.

﴿Say: "Then wait"﴾: a command of threat, meaning: "Wait for what will befall you, just as it befell those before you among the deniers of the messengers."

(p-194) ﴿Say: "Look at what is in the heavens and the earth. But signs and warnings do not avail a people who do not believe."﴾ ﴿Do they then await anything but the like of the days of those who passed away before them? Say: "Then wait; I am with you among those who wait."﴾

God, exalted is He, commanded reflection (tafakkur) upon what He has placed in the heavens and the earth, since the path to knowing Him, exalted is He, is through contemplating His creatures. In the upper world (al-'alam al-'ulwi) there are the movements of the spheres (al-aflak), their measures, their positions, and the stars, along with the benefits and advantages pertaining to them. In the lower world (al-'alam al-sufli) there are the states of the elements, the minerals, the plants, and the animals, and especially the state of man.
